Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang
events.summary: US president calls tech giant to give former CEO ‘a second chance’ and urges him to ‘make a big apology’. US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs. “You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.” list 1 of 3 Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO list 2 of 3 US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months list 3 of 3 Asia’s stock markets dive as Anthropic debut fails to allay AI bubble fears Trump also described Jensen Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions”. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back, because he created something with Blackwell,” Trump said, referring to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Huang resigned on November 12, following media reports of an intimate relationship with an alleged spy for Beijing who may have helped route restricted chips to China. US intelligence officials are said to have previously known about the possible espionage link. Two more affairs have since been reported. The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China’s defence industry through her family and associates. Trump also appeared to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had said earlier on Friday that Jensen Huang did not come up in talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week. “I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man,'” said Trump of his meeting with the Chinese president. In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang offered to return to the company. However, Nvidia’s board has ruled out his comeback. Board chairperson Harvey Jones said on an earnings call later that day that the directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and do not plan to reinstate him. The scandal has also drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas told The Wall Street Journal that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke, though he stopped short of calling for the commerce secretary’s resignation. Trump said he still supported Lutnick. “I have not lost confidence,” Trump said, calling Lutnick “a different kind of a guy, very good businessman”. Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, are investigating whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm run by his sons, avoid losses tied to scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to a Chinese company.

events.title: Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
events.summary: The new African agency aims to bring greater transparency to credit ratings. Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative first endorsed by African leaders in 2017. The agency, based in Port Louis, Mauritius, is designed to provide independent assessments of African governments and corporate borrowers, drawing on local data and expertise to complement ratings issued by international agencies. Its first sovereign ratings are expected by the end of March. Its interim chief executive, Sifiso Falala, says AfCRA is already in discussions with 15 African governments with research planned in countries that include Mauritius, Kenya, Togo, the Seychelles and Burundi. The case for AfCRA rests partly on the cost of how African economies are perceived by financial markets. A 2023 study by the United Nations Development Programme estimated that subjectivities in sovereign credit ratings cost African countries $74.5bn through excessive interest payments and foregone lending. African governments have long argued that international rating methodologies do not adequately account for the continent’s economic structures and circumstances. The major international agencies – Moody’s, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings – have disputed suggestions that their assessments systematically disadvantage African borrowers. At a Chatham House discussion in June, Moody’s Marie Diron argued that the agency’s analysis of four decades of global sovereign default data showed that African countries with a particular rating had broadly the same probability of default as equally rated borrowers elsewhere. For example, she said, a sovereign with a B rating had an estimated one-year default probability of about 5 percent regardless of whether it was African or from another region. That is an important counterargument. AfCRA’s challenge will not simply be to produce different ratings but to demonstrate that its assessments are more comprehensive, transparent and predictive of actual credit risk. Its credibility will ultimately depend on the evidence behind its conclusions, including when those conclusions are unfavourable to African borrowers. For Falala, the agency’s priority is to ensure that assessments better reflect the economic realities of African countries. Speaking to Al Jazeera, he said: “A significant number of African countries carry speculative-grade ratings despite having no history of sovereign default. “This raises legitimate questions about whether prevailing models adequately capture African economic realities. We believe our analytical framework can contribute to a constructive reassessment of these assumptions, encouraging the entire industry to examine whether the indicators used to determine creditworthiness remain relevant, proportionate and sufficiently predictive of actual default risk.” Falala said the agency was not seeking more favourable ratings for African borrowers but greater accuracy through engagement with established rating agencies. “Our objective is not to manufacture better ratings for Africa, but to produce more accurate ratings of Africa in collaboration with established rating agencies. Importantly, we believe that a stronger AfCRA will contribute to a stronger credit rating industry overall,” he said. That distinction will be central to the agency’s credibility. An institution established partly in response to dissatisfaction with existing ratings must demonstrate that its own assessments are independent of political pressure and the interests of the governments and companies it evaluates. Falala acknowledged the scepticism surrounding the industry, saying AfCRA has an opportunity to rebuild confidence through transparency and analytical independence. He said the agency was not seeking confrontation with established rating providers but saw considerable scope for collaboration and mutual learning. Beyond sovereign ratings, AfCRA intends to assess companies, municipalities, banks and local-currency debt. This broader coverage could address gaps in information about borrowers that receive limited attention from international agencies while providing domestic investors with additional assessments of credit risk. The potential benefits extend beyond the ratings themselves. African pension funds, banks and other institutional investors need reliable information to assess domestic borrowers and allocate capital. More comprehensive coverage, supported by stronger local data, could help reduce information gaps and support the development of domestic capital markets. However, additional ratings will not automatically translate into cheaper borrowing. Their influence will depend on whether investors consider the assessments credible and useful in making investment decisions.

events.title: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
events.summary: Copenhagen accuses Moscow of planning assassination with banned local gang; Russia says no evidence for allegation. Denmark has said it is expelling Russia’s defence attaché after accusing Moscow intelligence of plotting to kill a Ukrainian rapper at a concert near Copenhagen. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attaché from Denmark” within seven days, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference on Friday. list 1 of 3 Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges list 2 of 3 Russia complains of ‘new Iron Curtain’ as Estonia shuts its borders list 3 of 3 Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations Denmark is also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians, he added. The expulsion ultimatum comes hours after Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said it suspected Russia of planning the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb with help of a Danish gang. Danish public broadcaster DR named the rapper as Kyivstoner, who has both Ukrainian and US citizenship. “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia,” PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told journalists on Friday. “The case shows, in our assessment, that the Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out an execution in Denmark,” he said. According to PET, three people were stopped in a car near the music venue where the rapper was scheduled to perform on September 25. Police found firearms and knives in the vehicle. Two people were placed under formal investigation on Friday for attempted murder and for helping a foreign intelligence service operate in Denmark. Police and PET suspect Loyal to Familia, a street gang and criminal network banned since 2021, helped plan the attack. Police and intelligence services made their announcements as two Danish men appeared ⁠in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder, court documents showed. According to the court documents, the suspects were arrested five minutes before the concert was set to begin and one of them had bought a ticket to the performance. The ‌concert was cancelled. In response to Friday’s announcement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said, “We are facing a cornered Russia, acting more aggressively and with a greater propensity to take risks.” The strongest response would be to “not waver” and to keep supporting Ukraine, she added. European Council President Antonio Costa said the alleged assassination attempt was “unacceptable” and “will not go unanswered”. He promised Denmark the European Union’s full backing against what he called Russian hybrid attacks. Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would give “an appropriate response”, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen called the expulsion “vengeful” and said Denmark had not presented “any evidence of Russia’s involvement in this mysterious crime”. Copenhagen has accused Moscow of other hybrid attacks, which are acts short of open war, such as sabotage and disruption. In September 2025, drones shut down Copenhagen airport for hours, in what Denmark called a hybrid attack. PET said in September that Russia was recruiting Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against Danish defence firms with ties to Ukraine. Russia has denied involvement in such operations.

events.title: Can Mauricio Pochettino save Man United from Premier League relegation?
events.summary: Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time on Sunday, in a trip to rivals Liverpool. Manchester United will be led by a third manager in three years when Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of his first match since replacing Michael Carrick . The fact that the Premier League clash is against their fierce rivals Liverpool – the team that, with United, are joint record English top-flight champions – is an added twist to a sordid recent tale for the Manchester club. list 1 of 4 Leaders Arsenal travel to beleaguered Newcastle as Premier League returns list 2 of 4 ‘Total error of judgement’: Drone operator removes United training footage list 3 of 4 In Qatar, Nepali fans hope to see their cricket team reach Everest heights list 4 of 4 From Kansas to the Casbah: How the World Cup built an unexpected friendship When Sir Alex Ferguson retired after lifting a then-record 20th league title in 2013, the Red Devils had climbed to the biggest and richest club in the world. Now, apart from not being able to claim a Premier League crown since 2013, they are laden with debt – and worse still, they sit inside the relegation zone. Can Pochettino save Man United from relegation? The last time United were relegated from the top flight was in the 1973–1974 season. That came only six years after one of the club’s greatest nights – the lifting of the European Cup (now the Champions League), making them the first English club to do so. Their fall this time around has not come quite as quickly, with their last crowning as European champions in 2008, and they have not been relegated – yet. Few expect them to be. It would be unthinkable given the changed landscape of the entire footballing world, which has become awash with finances that clearly separate the elite and their resources from the rest. When Pochettino was introduced to the media for the first time on Friday, the gathered press did not mention the word “relegation” even once. So the simple answer is: yes, he can save the club from relegation. The longer equation is that the alternative would surely be the greatest shock in the history of a game famed for upsets and underdogs. What problem does Pochettino need to solve first at United? Words like identity, fitness, formation, and one that Pochettino awkwardly dropped on Friday, “philosophy”, have dogged every manager at Old Trafford since Ferguson’s departure. “We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, with our own philosophy and how we like to work,” Pochettino told the gathered reporters. “We need to improve our players, find a way to perform, but the future and identity of the club is very clear. “It is an historic club with an amazing years competing and being one of the best in the world. “It is difficult to find another club that is the size of United. We need to be open-minded to do our best, and the players need to buy the idea that we need to improve. “The job is to get the rest of the historic club, Manchester United, into a different place to where we are now.” All of that can wait, because Liverpool are the next opponents, and for United, they do not come any bigger. The Manchester derby has taken on a new level in recent years – although the tide there may also soon turn, depending on City’s appeal against their charges – but the rivalries against the Reds and Leeds United have the deepest roots for United fans. A recent defeat to the revived latter still weighs heavily. Pochettino needs to find a way for the team to start winning, and it needs to come soon. The club’s opening to the season is their worst since 1986, and one win – the worst return in the league – has left United just one point off bottom place. By the time Pochettino and his United players walk out to the hostility of the Anfield crowd, they could be at the very foot of the table. Will Pochettino change United’s formation? The easiest part of the equation for Pochettino is the formation. With the United States national team, which he left to join United, the Argentinian deployed the 4-2-3-1 tactic that even Ferguson had evolved to in his final years. Pochettino’s Tottenham, the club he made his managerial name with, were always set out in the same way with Harry Kane leading the line. The United squad – which were moved to an uncomfortable 3-4-3 by Carrick’s predecessor, Ruben Amorim – are built for Pochettino’s style, but the task of melding them together had eluded Carrick and will be the key to their imminent return. What long-term problems does Pochettino face at United? The off-field troubles at United are well documented . The club are weighed down by the debts accrued with the Glazer family’s 2005 purchase. Jim Ratcliffe’s investment three years ago has seen the Englishman and his INEOS group take control of footballing matters, but the annual interest the club pays remains a heavy burden.

events.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
events.summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge. The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days. A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge. “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.” Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further. The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge. In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit. “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.” The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf. “I

events.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
events.summary: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year NEW YORK -- A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S & P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark S & P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S & P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.2%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 14% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang , its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 30%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 8.5% to $88.91, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, several companies managed to gain ground despite strong downward pressure on the market. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S & P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

events.title: Wall Street just put an astonishing price on Nvidia's Jensen Huang: $1 trillion
events.summary: Jensen Huang, cofounder and recently ousted CEO of Nvidia. Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Nvidia has now lost $1 trillion in market value since CEO Jensen Huang was ousted. This raises a question whether Nvidia's board is doing what's best for shareholders. The Nvidia stock plunge highlights how the AI chip leader relied heavily on its visionary founder. It's rare that investors get a chance to put a clear dollar value on a CEO . With Jensen Huang , we just got one. And it's an astonishing number: $1 trillion. That's how much Nvidia has lost in market value since Huang was forced out of the AI chip giant last week. It's potentially a terrible look for Nvidia's board of directors . After all, the fundamental job of a public company's board is to look after the interests of shareholders. That doesn't mean maximizing the stock price every day, or keeping a CEO at all costs. Directors have broader legal duties and sometimes must make difficult decisions that hurt investors in the short term. But when a board oversees the departure of a CEO and shareholders subsequently lose $1 trillion, it's reasonable to ask whether the directors have fulfilled their most important responsibility. On November 11, the day before Nvidia announced Huang's departure, the company's shares closed at $173.73, giving it a market value of about $4.2 trillion. By Friday afternoon, the stock had fallen to roughly $128, wiping out more than a quarter of Nvidia's market value. According to Bloomberg data, the company's market capitalization has shrunk to about $3.14 trillion since Huang was ousted. That's a staggering $1.04 trillion decline in just over a week. Of course, stock prices move for all sorts of reasons. And it's impossible to attribute every dollar of that decline to Huang's departure. But here's what makes this particularly interesting. Much of the bad news surrounding Nvidia was already out in the open before Huang left. The original New York Times story about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and his relationship with Alice Huang was published in October 2025 — more than a year ago . And the unconfirmed allegation that she might be a Chinese spy was reported on Oct. 29, a full two weeks before Huang's ouster. Those worries had already pushed Nvidia shares down substantially. Then Huang was gone early on Nov. 12. From that point on, Nvidia's share price became mostly a referendum on the man himself. Suddenly investors were looking at something very different: Nvidia without the visionary founder who built it into the world's dominant AI chip company. That's a particularly unsettling prospect in technology, where the person at the top can have an extraordinary influence on which products get built, which bets get made, and where an entire industry goes next. Does Nvidia's board believe it acted in shareholders' best interests? How does it assess the enormous decline in market value since Huang left? I asked Nvidia's press office these questions on Friday and haven't got an answer yet. There are plenty of ways to value a company. Revenue. Profits. Growth prospects. But sometimes the market gives us a rare glimpse of something harder to measure: The value of one person. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Petition against AI cameras at junior basketball attracts 13,000 signatures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Concerns raised over Basketball Australia's use of AI cameras at junior games Pixellot smart cameras will soon be used to film basketball games around Australia. ( Source: Pixellot ) New AI-powered filming technology that will allow basketball players to watch games and view stats online is being rolled out by three basketball associations. A cyber-safety expert and activist groups have raised privacy and monetisation concerns. Basketball Australia plans to roll out the technology in more stadiums in coming months. Basketball Australia has defended the use of new AI-powered recording software set to be introduced at stadiums around Australia, after criticism from activist groups and a prominent cybersecurity expert. The software, called Hoops TV, was developed from a partnership between Basketball Australia and Israel-based sports footage company Pixellot. It uses "smart cameras" installed in stadiums to record games, including amateur and junior matches. The footage and game statistics, which are gathered using AI, are then made available for players and their guardians to access online through their Basketball Australia log-ons. Basketball Australia says the technology is an "exciting opportunity for Australian community basketball". ( ABC News: Mackenzie Heard ) The cameras have been trialled with three basketball associations this week — in Darwin, the Illawarra region in NSW, and Brisbane's northern suburbs — and are set to be rolled out more widely in coming months. Basketball Australia spokesman Tim Brenton said Hoops TV presented an "exciting opportunity for Australian community basketball". "Video recording and capturing kids on video isn't new in Australian basketball. It's quite uncontrolled and you can go into any stadium around Australia at any night of the week and find people videotaping," he said. Tim Brenton says any revenue generated via Basketball Australia-led programs and products is reinvested back into basketball. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) However, cyber-safety expert and former member of the federal government's Online Safety Working Group, Susan McLean, said the software's privacy implications were "particularly concerning". "I'm not sure why Basketball Australia and all the states and territories are hell-bent on putting filming before child safeguarding concerns," she said. "We have seen almost on a weekly basis [that] things are getting hacked. Coles has been hacked, Medicare has been hacked, Optus has been hacked. Activist groups GetUp! and Not All Clubs launched a petition last month urging Basketball Australia to "stop filming kids with Israeli AI Cameras", which has so far collected more than 13,000 signatures. The petition cites concerns Pixellot's co-founders previously worked for an Israeli weapons company and an "IDF [Israel Defence Forces] intelligence unit". It also alleges a woman protected by a family violence intervention was "contacted by the man in it" after her game was live-streamed during an earlier trial in Victoria. A petition opposing the rollout has so far collected more than 13,000 signatures. ( ABC News: Sam Bradbrook ) "The association had been warned a week before, and said only Pixellot could block the stream," the petition reads. Pixellot did not respond to a request for comment. GetUp! media and campaigns lead David Sharaz said the group was concerned children's sport may be being monetised by Basketball Australia. "These aren't professional athletes who are being critiqued at half-time on ESPN, these are kids. And the overall question is why are we filming kids?" he said. "Are we going to be watching kids' sport and seeing an advert for Woolworths? Are your children being monetised?" David Sharaz says GetUp! is concerned about the potential monetisation of children's sport. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) Asked about concerns around monetisation, Mr Brenton did not answer a question from the ABC during an interview, but he later responded in a statement. "As a non-profit governing body, any revenue generated via BA-led programs and products are reinvested back into basketball nationally," he said in the statement. "Our aim is to create a model that benefits participants and contributes to the long-term growth of the sport." The Hoops TV trial is operating on a opt-out model, which means games will be recorded using the technology unless parents or players object. Ms McLean said an opt-out model was "not a legally sound process for filming permissions".

events.title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
events.summary: German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade. Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”. He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more. The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid. Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job. The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US. “The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement. Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto , which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018. The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, ‌but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims. Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades ​of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer. The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Get the most important news as it breaks In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under ⁠state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits. Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for ​many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell ​decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims ​to pursue claims in court. “We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all ​Roundup victims as quickly ‌as possible,” he ​said in a statement. Lawyers for ​some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

events.summary: Police say two children among dead as search continues for more victims. A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of people to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least four people, according to police. The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, police spokesperson Musa Mohammed told the Reuters news agency. list 1 of 3 Nigeria launches hunt for hundreds of kidnapped mosque worshippers list 2 of 3 Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next? list 3 of 3 More than 80 reported abducted in Nigeria as police find human remains He said the dead were two adults and two children. Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance or failure to comply with safety regulations. events.title: The race to prove the Riemann Hypothesis just became a human-versus-AI showdown
events.summary: The drama in the math community is reaching a fever pitch. tiero/Getty Images An Anthropic mathematician said he solved the most famous open problem in mathematics on Friday. Then, another mathematician said he also solved it — without using AI. The double whammy has roiled a math community already shaken by AI's effect on the field. The drama over AI in the math community is getting real. Hours after Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said he solved the most famous open problem in the field using AI on Friday, another mathematician came out of the woodwork to announce he'd also solved the problem. Only this mathematician said he did it without using AI. Alessandro Masullo, a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford, said he's been working on the problem for 12 years and was about a year away from releasing his results when he was blindsided by Alpöge's report. "In light of the current climate I am being advised to release the current version as it is," he said in a paper posted online, adding that there may be errors in it because it was rushed. And in a thinly veiled slight against Alpöge, who described working with Claude for weeks to reach his solution, Masullo said that human mathematicians still have a place in the age of AI. "If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here," he said. "We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere." Masullo's solution, which is far shorter than Alpöge's, immediately sparked a further firestorm in a math community already reeling from the unprecedented Anthropic paper and months of AI companies announcing high-profile solutions to long-standing math problems. "The plot thickens!" Steven Strogatz, a math professor at Cornell, said on X on Friday. "Now it's getting more complicated," Sergei Gukov, a math professor at Caltech , told Business Insider. Mathematicians are now racing to scrutinize both solutions with their own brains and with AI. Neither had, by Friday afternoon, been formally proven. At stake is nothing less than the credibility of human mathematicians in the age of AI, and who's solution is right will have grave implications for the future of mathematics. Masullo, his partner at Stanford, Brian Conrad, and Alpöge did not respond to requests for comment on Friday. The problem in question is the Riemann Hypothesis, which Strogatz described to Business Insider as the "White Whale" of mathematics. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers. The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician $1 million. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category. Gukov, the math professor at Caltech, called the claim that it was solved a "HUGE deal." "RH was the biggest problem in math," he said, using the past tense. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
events.summary: Anthropic’s stock closed at US$88.91, 8.5% below the Nov 19 close and not far from its US$83 IPO price. Anthropic’s Wall Street debut disappointed, with shares closing at US$88.91, 8.5% lower, showing the AI trade is still under pressure. Investors worry AI spending may top US$1 trillion in 2026 without quick returns, while Nvidia, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell. Analysts expect more volatility, with OpenAI’s planned listing, index buying and Morgan Stanley’s ended support all likely to test demand for AI stocks. Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Nov 20 as a dramatic unravelling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. As the first large machine-learning model maker to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, and its listing had been viewed as a potential boost for a sector struggling to regain its footing. But the stock closed at US$88.91, 8.5% below the Nov 19 close and not far from its US$83 IPO price, while declines in other technology heavyweights suggested the listing had done little to stem the broader selloff. “Anthropic faded relatively quickly. I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company, management or business. I think they’re just skeptical of this market,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. The AI boom has come under pressure over the past month as concerns mount that spending on the technology, expected by some estimates to top US$1 trillion in 2026, is not generating returns quickly enough. Fears of political hurdles to data centre construction and the leadership turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia have also added to those worries. “Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds. Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia fell about 14% and Meta Platforms dropped nearly 6%, Amazon lost about 4% and Microsoft ended3% lower. Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Marvell Technology down about 13% and 12%, respectively, and Intel losing roughly 8%. The focus now shifts to a potential listing by another AI leader, OpenAI, which could provide another test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year. Despite a strong IPO pipeline of high-profile AI and infrastructure companies, many have pushed their IPO plans to 2027. Anthropic’s stock could find support in the coming weeks. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30% of Anthropic’s shares by year-end. Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained. But Morgan Stanley, the underwriter tasked with stabilizing Anthropic’s shares after its market debut, closed a position meant to do that, the company said, removing a potential pillar of support for shares. Anthropic had a fully diluted valuation of about $1.6 trillion at the latest price, and a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding. “We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results,” said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Nov 20. Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , whose June listing was the second-biggest on record. Anthropic raised US$93.5 billion in its IPO after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, surpassing SpaceX’s US$85.7 billion haul to become the biggest listing on record. While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing. “There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co. Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012. The stock’s sharp swings have left investors weighing the prospects of a rebound against further losses. Options trading, set to begin next week, could add to the volatility. “It’s not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment,” said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg. REUTERS

events.title: Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
events.summary: EU warns COP31 risks turning into a ‘fossil summit’ as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal. The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that no longer mentions fossil fuels. The two-week talks in Antalya, Turkiye, were due to end on Friday, when a late closing session approved some technical matters, but not the wider political deal. list 1 of 3 Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future list 2 of 3 COP31 opens amid energy crisis as activists demand climate action list 3 of 3 Tensions rise over draft climate deal at COP31 “We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet,” COP31 President and Turkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates. Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference said the meeting lacked ambition to address the ‌worsening climate crisis and was on track to be the “worst COP ever”. A third draft is expected on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported. An opening draft from cohost and lead negotiator Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected. Oil producers have also resisted similar language at past talks, including at COP28 in 2023. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for money to help poorer countries adapt to climate change. The European Union said the draft “risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit”. Panama, which signed a letter with a dozen other countries demanding “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”, threatened to walk away from the talks. “It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told a news conference. The draft proposes raising the share of the world’s final energy consumption that comes from electricity to 35 percent by 2035. It does not say the power must come from renewables, and some countries want the target to say “clean”. Some countries also reject a push to expand carbon capture, a technology that traps emissions from power plants and factories. They say it is costly and unproven, and could let polluters keep burning oil and gas. “We want to see the references to false solutions removed,” said Vanuatu’s climate minister, Ralph Regenvanu. Developing countries are angry that rich nations are falling short on climate finance. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings. A UN report last month found the world is set to pass the 1.5-degree-Celsius (2.7F) warming limit set under the 2015 Paris Agreement. The United States, the largest historical emitter, is absent for a second year after President Donald Trump ended climate cooperation. The US-Israel war on Iran and higher living costs have also drawn attention away from the talks. Environmental groups say the summit lacks ambition. “This has been the worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa.

events.title: Nvidia stock plunges 14%, wraps up longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
events.summary: Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday and headed for their seventh straight weekly drop. The stock is down 46% over the period, shedding about $2.6 trillion in market cap. Once the most valuable company, Nvidia is now fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet. The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis. Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008. On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further. Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple , Microsoft and Alphabet . Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD. Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere. On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December. For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT. Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression. WATCH: Walter Isaacson on Nvidia export control scrutiny

events.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
events.summary: GTA 6 central characters Lucia and Jason Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in its first full-day of release , hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history. Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game. To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made $2.5bn (£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas . Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access . In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast. In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany. The record smashes that of its predecessor - from 13 years prior - Grand Theft Auto V. The game previously held the best opening week sales in video-game history, earning $1.15bn (£1.2bn) in just five days. The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history . At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state. The latest release follows new characters, a pair of small-time criminals Lucia and her partner Jason. GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop , which would make it the most expensive video game in history. BBC News Mundo’s Rafael Rojas visits the real-life Miami locations that inspired GTA 6's Vice City. Research firm Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%. The firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available. Around three quarters of the game's sales have been on PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said. Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year. That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind , which has made an estimated $4.5bn (£3.44bn), adjusted for inflation. Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years. The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet. If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks. GTA 6 launched around the world on 19 November Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait. GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece. The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play. The launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles. The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China. Police departments have also reminded Americans that street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement reached a fever pitch in the US. events.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
events.summary: Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold? Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago. The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when. Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development. Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday. The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17. Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers. Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading. Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market. While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth. "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said. "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability." Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices. Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record. But tech stocks more broadly also fell. Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls. Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit. Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower. Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses. Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990. Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting? events.title: The Covey is important in 'Sunrise on the Reaping.' Here's a guide to the family and their relationship to Katniss.
events.summary: Katniss Everdeen is related to the Covey family in "The Hunger Games" universe. Murray Close/Lionsgate In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Suzanne Collins revealed that the Covey has ties to Katniss Everdeen. Collins introduced readers to the Covey family in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." A spark of rebellion runs in the Covey family throughout the "Hunger Games" series. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is poised to be a hit for Lionsgate. "Sunrise on the Reaping" is the second prequel Suzanne Collins wrote in her "Hunger Games" series, following Haymitch Abernathy's experience in the 50th Hunger Games. It was an instant bestseller when it was published in March 2025, selling over 1.5 million copies in its first week alone. The film adaptation is following a similar trajectory, already raking in $21 million from preview screenings alone, Variety reported . It's not a surprise, given how much there is to love about "Sunrise on the Reaping." The novel dives deep into Haymitch's time in the arena, but it's also full of revelations about the "Hunger Games" universe. Many of those revelations center on the Covey family, who were introduced in Collins' first "Hunger Games" prequel . Most importantly, it reveals that Katniss Everdeen has Covey ancestry, tying her to other girls who defied the Capitol before she was even born. Spoilers ahead for the "Hunger Games" series. The Covey first appears in 'The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes' Collins released her first "Hunger Games" prequel, " The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes ," in May 2020. Set 64 years before "The Hunger Games," the book follows a young Coriolanus Snow long before he is president. As a student, he mentors the Victor of the 10th Hunger Games: the female tribute from District 12, Lucy Gray Baird. After she is reaped for the Games and taken to the Capitol, Lucy Gray tells a reporter that she is a member of the Covey family who isn't originally from District 12. Tom Blyth as Coriolanus Snow and Rachel Zegler as Lucy Gray Baird in "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." Murray Close/Lionsgate "My people are Covey. Musicians by trade. We just took a wrong turn one day and were obliged to stay," Lucy Gray said. She explained they were from "no district in particular" and used to "move from place to place" playing music before Peacekeepers forced them to stay in District 12 after the first rebellion. When the book opens, there are six living members of the Covey family living in District 12: Billy Taupe Clade, Clerk Carmine Clade, Tam Amber, Maude Ivory Baird, Barb Azure Baird, and Lucy Gray Baird. Billy Taupe and Clerk Carmine are brothers, and Maude Ivory, Barb Azure, and Lucy Gray are cousins. Tam Amber is not related to the rest of the Covey by blood, but the group treats each other as a found family. By the end of the book , only four Covey members are left in District 12. A local kills Billy Taupe after Coriolanus shoots his friend, while Lucy Gray's status is more of a mystery. Coriolanus may have killed her, or she could have fled from him and disappeared into the woods, never to be heard from again in Panem. The Covey has blended into District 12 in 'Sunrise on the Reaping' When Collins brings readers back to District 12 in "Sunrise on the Reaping," the Covey has assimilated into the district in the years since the events of "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." Tam Amber and Clerk Carmine are still living in the district and are raising their niece, Lenore Dove Baird, together. Lenore Dove is Haymitch's girlfriend, and Haymitch says in the text that her mother died giving birth to her. Any of the three Covey girls could be Lenore Dove's mother, but based on the text, it's most likely Maude Ivory. At the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch finds graves for both Lucy Gray and Maude Ivory near Lenore Dove's resting place. Lucy Gray's is described as a "mossy slab of stone," while Maude Ivory's is "a creamy white stone," making Maude Ivory's seem slightly newer. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate The timeline also makes Maude Ivory the stronger candidate. Lenore Dove is around 16 in "Sunrise on the Reaping," meaning she was born about 24 years after Lucy Gray's Hunger Games. Lucy Gray would have been around 40 when Lenore Dove was born, while Maude Ivory would have been in her early 30s. Neither age rules out either woman, but Maude Ivory seems the more likely choice. Katniss is a Covey descendant In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch says he met Lenore Dove through his friend Burdock Everdeen, Katniss' father. "She wasn't one of Burdock's Everdeen cousins, but I knew he had some distant ones on his ma's side," Haymitch says of Burdock's ancestry. Given Maude Ivory's and Lucy Gray's fates, it seems likely Burdock and Katniss were descendants of Barb Azure Baird and distant relatives of the other Covey girls. Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate Collins laid the groundwork for the similarity between Katniss and the Covey girls throughout "The Hunger Games." She has a rebellious spirit like her ancestors, and both Katniss and her father are described as having beautiful singing voices throughout the series. Haymitch reinforces singing as a trait Burdock inherited from the Covey in "Sunrise on the Reaping." He says Burdock has a "remarkable voice." A few pages later, he says Lenore Dove loves music: "Like all the Covey, music in her blood." Later, at Haymitch's mother and brother's funeral, Burdock sings "The Old Therebefore," a song Lucy Gray sings when she thinks she is about to die in the Games. Music, specifically Covey music, is in Burdock's blood, too. The Covey also inadvertently gives Katniss her mockingjay pin The mockingjay token Katniss wears in her first Hunger Games becomes an important symbol throughout Collins' series. The bird represents that the Capitol cannot control everything, as it results from the mating of Capitol jabberjays and naturally born mockingbirds. Katniss embodies that spirit when she leads the rebellion against President Coriolanus Snow and his government, using the mockingjay symbol to help inspire others to act. A Mockingjay pin from "The Hunger Games." MediaNews Group/Bay Area News via Getty Images Katniss' friend, Madge Undersee, gave her the pin to wear after she volunteered as a tribute for District 12. In "Catching Fire," Madge tells Katniss the pin originally belonged to her aunt, Maysilee Donner, who competed alongside Haymitch for District 12 in the 50th Hunger Games. In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch reveals that Tam Amber originally forged the pin. Maysilee never wore it, saying that mockingjays were "ugly old things," to Lenore Dove's anger. events.title: Trump threatens a 'tremendous tax' on tech companies building data centers outside the US
events.summary: Trump threatened a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers outside the US. Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images Trump threatened a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers outside the US. The warning comes as tech giants invest billions in overseas data center projects. Trump said local officials should "take advantage of the data centers" and ask for payment. Donald Trump gave a stark warning to companies looking to build data centers overseas. Trump said at Friday's White House press briefing that his administration would impose a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers outside the US, adding that "China will take all of them." "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said. "We're not going to allow that to happen." Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI have backed data-center projects outside the United States. Companies often build abroad to serve regional users, meet local data requirements, improve reliability, or secure available power and land while avoiding battles at home . "We want them to build it here. If they won't go in Texas or they won't go in California, they're going to go in West Virginia," Trump added. "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places." Across the country, Americans have raised concerns at town halls and in local fights over data-center projects that the facilities could drive up electricity bills , create pollution, and strain power grids. Trump also urged local governments to work with data center builders. "You have to take advantage of the data centers," Trump said, addressing local representatives. "Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage; don't shut them off." Trump returned to Washington on Thursday after a trip to China, where he met with Xi Jinping, China's leader, in Shenzhen, a major technology hub . Trump said they discussed AI development and agreed to work together on AI guardrails. Read the original article on Business Insider
