events.title: Do not threaten to pee on your employees, no matter how effective the results may be
events.summary: Jensen Huang giving a toast. If the liquid brings to mind something else, that's on you! Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images The NYT reports Jensen Huang once threatened to cut off the top of an employee's head and pee on their brain. Hmm. This was part of an alleged pattern of verbal outbursts that humiliated workers as part of his management style. Bosses: I truly recommend that you never, ever do this. Let me be clear: you should not threaten your employees with physical harm or death. You should not do that to anyone you work with. Seriously. No matter how tempting it may be. Why, you might ask, am I stating what should be obvious to every CEO and manager? Because Friday's talker from  The New York Times  about Huang's notorious, uh, management style reportedly included two settled lawsuits from former employees who complained about the verbal tirades. This was not simply a rude boss — according to the Times' reporting: He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and "pee on your brain." I know what you're thinking: maybe that employee did deserve to have their brain peed on. I know that some days my brain functions at such a low level that a splash of urine could only be an improvement. But do not , I implore you, do not threaten to rip your employees' arms off or the tip of their heads off. No threats to rip any parts off, in fact. And especially, crucially, do not threaten to pee on their brains or any other organs —internal or external— under almost all circumstances (I'm still working through possibilities where this might be acceptable but haven't come up with one yet. Let me know if you do). A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment when contacted by Business Insider. The Times reports that a Huang spokesperson said that specific claims from a former employee's lawsuit were "false" and didn't answer other questions about the Nvidia founder's behavior. Until the events of the last few weeks , Huang was considered a rock star in the tech world, a visionary in business who smartly positioned his company for the AI boom years before it happened. To many people, especially those who would like to see him brought back as CEO , he still is. Yes, it may be tempting to look at the results — Nvidia's rise to become one of the most valuable companies in the world — and think that his communication style is something to emulate if you want to motivate employees. Huang's management style has its supporters, including Chamath Palihapitiya, who said , "This makes me want to work for him MORE." "Are there other ways of doing it? Yes. But this way is proven…and peeing on someone's brain is just funny," said the "All-In" podcast host. This makes me want to work for him MORE. I’d rather work for someone like this. Someone with ridiculous expectations, impatience and vision and take the lumps that come with that. Guys like this will filter out all the mediocre people that can’t take the heat and won’t take you to greatness. What’s left are a team of killers capable of building the largest, most valuable company in the world. Are there other ways of doing it? Yes. But this way is proven…and peeing on someone’s brain is just funny. — Chamath Palihapitiya (@chamath) November 20, 2026 Again — Chamath, Jensen fans, future business leaders, anyone reading this — I truly must warn you that you really, really should not threaten to pee on your employees. No matter how effective that sounds as a management technique. Trust me, I think there are better ways to deliver tough feedback to deliver to your direct reports (if urine-based threats are all that come to mind, perhaps ask ChatGPT to help you draft it). Absolutely do not tell them their mother should've aborted them; if nothing else, you typically don't want to discuss hot-button political topics like abortion with employees, even in highly theoretical contexts. Am I an expert on executive management techniques? No, I am not. I am but a humble reporter, living my life on the IC track with no direct reports. However, having attended several mandatory workplace harassment webinars, I can promise you that bosses should absolutely avoid doing this: In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead. As a human resources person using ChatGPT might say: you're not just issuing death threats — you're doing age discrimination. A bigger question you might be asking is: are these incredibly funny? Well, yes, generally speaking, it is. However, you might feel quite differently if you were experiencing such a bizarre barrage in person, in front of your peers. I would also be remiss not to mention that these insults, even the "pee on your brain" one, are not totally original. I get it; in the heat of the moment, sometimes you reach for a cliché. I have personally used the threat of tearing someone's arms off and beating them with said arms on loved ones in my personal life (they know what they did, but we're good now). Bosses who deliver mortal blows with insults are a rich vein in pop culture. Selina Meyer from "Veep" or Ari Gold from "Entourage" had deliciously creative one-liner insults to their underlings. Miranda Priestly and Don Draper had withering cruelty (is there anything harsher than the " I don't think about you at all " line in "Mad Men"?). We, as a society, love a fictional Mean Boss! And it's partly wish fulfillment: wouldn't it be freeing to be able to just yell at whoever you want at work? To have the power to get away with saying outlandish things to the people who are pissing you off (metaphorically) at that moment, and not face consequences for it? Let me suggest something: there is a lot of power in not telling someone you'll rip their arms off. There is powerful restraint in being able to control your unpleasant feelings and handle difficult interpersonal conversations without yelling or insulting. Try that! But do not — please, I beg you — do not threaten to pee on anyone at work. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Wall St ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
events.summary: Specialist traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City, on Nov 20. US stocks fell sharply as AI shares sold off, pushing the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory after Anthropic’s weak debut failed to calm fears. The S&P 500 had its seventh straight fall, while the Nasdaq had its worst weekly drop since March 2020. Nvidia, Amazon, Meta and other AI-linked names all slid. Investors now focus on inflation and the Fed, with markets pricing a near-certain December rate hike and next week’s PCE data set to guide policy hopes. NEW YORK - US stocks extended their rout on Nov 20, and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally. All three major US equity indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10% below their record closing highs,confirming both indexes have entered a correction. The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020. The S&P 500 and the Dowlogged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “liberation day” tariff package. The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index has dipped into negative territory for the year. “This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, appears to be accelerating to a certain degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana. “But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.” “Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things. Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) in market cap, failed to catch fire on Nov 19, closing 17.1% above its US$83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session. In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1%. Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8%. The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology. “Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. “A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.” The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6% in mid-June. That lustre has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7%. Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9%, while Meta dropped 5.9%. Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1% and its peer Nebius slid 16.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73. The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025. Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said the central bank’s policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels. Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Next week’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed’s monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week. Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 12.8% after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about US$3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much. UnitedHealth rose 2.8% after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a “buy” from a “hold” rating. The AI selloff also sent Caterpillar 5% lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment. Cryptocurrency firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3% and 9.6% after bitcoin dropped below the $60,000 level. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 38 new highs and 1,199 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 928 stocks rose and 3,964 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio.

events.title: One hand on the controller, one on the pizza roll: How America fed itself through GTA VI’s $3.79 billion launch night
events.summary: The biggest video game launch in years left millions of players with a practical problem: how to eat without putting down the controller. Rockstar Games, a unit of Take-Two Interactive, said the game brought in an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales worldwide on its first day, which it called the biggest entertainment launch in history. With that demand, there are surely some tired people holding onto those controllers but hungry for a snack. It seems like the delivery apps already planned for it. Uber Eats picked several of its Grand Theft Auto VI launch-day deals for food that could be eaten with one hand. In the U.S., the list included buy-one-get-one McNuggets at McDonald’s, boneless wings at Wingstop, pizza at Papa John’s and Whopper Jr. burgers at Burger King. “We even picked some of our food deals with one-handed eating in mind, so fans can keep their focus on the game,” Uber President and COO Andrew Macdonald said in a statement to Fortune . Gamers ordered accordingly. Between midnight and 5 a.m. on launch night, Uber Eats orders in Miami, the real city behind the game’s Vice City, rose more than 30% from the prior two Thursdays, Macdonald said on X . Nationwide, orders of Red Bull Watermelon rose 95%, Totino’s Pizza Rolls 54% and Ghost Sour Strips 46%. Uber told Fortune it had no separate data on one-handed food orders. DoorDash reported a similar pattern. Between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m. ET, orders for chips, burgers, fries and pizza each rose more than 10% compared with the average of the six prior Wednesdays, the company told Fortune . Energy drinks rose more than 20%. Miami led all major markets, with late-night orders up nearly 25%, and Philadelphia, Detroit and Atlanta also saw double-digit increases, according to DoorDash’s data dashboard . DoorDash said it could not compare the food increases with its overall order growth. “A cultural moment” Some of the biggest jumps were for gear, not food. Orders for controllers and gaming accessories rose 450% on DoorDash, HDMI cables 440% and headsets 70%. Searches for GTA VI on the app rose more than 940% in the week before launch. “GTA 6 is more than a game launch. It’s a cultural moment that fans have been waiting years for,” Gina Igwe, DoorDash’s vice president of brand, creative and consumer marketing, said in a statement to Fortune . Players who weren’t playing were watching. In its first two days, GTA VI drew more livestream watch time than any game has in its entire launch week, more than Elden Ring , Hogwarts Legacy and Cyberpunk 2077 drew in their first weeks combined, according to Streams Charts . Total Twitch watch time rose 61% compared with the two days before launch, the firm said, while World of Warcraft and Counter-Strike lost about 31% of their Twitch watch time and Fortnite fell 60% on YouTube. Kick’s “Just Sleeping” category rose 176% as streamers ran round-the-clock GTA VI marathons. Restaurant chains also moved to get a share. Popeyes is selling a Spice City sandwich , named after the game’s setting, through Nov. 22 and told players to order it through its app “between missions.” McDonald’s began taking delivery orders on Discord, the chat app many gamers use while they play. DoorDash ran offers with Wendy’s and the Cheesecake Factory , and Grubhub offered $10 off to its first 1,000 customers. Analytics firm Sensor Tower expects the game to drive more than 50 million additional visits to U.S. food delivery and restaurant apps in its first 30 days, Reuters reported . Neither company put a dollar figure on launch night. A rough Fortune estimate suggests the extra takeout spending was small next to the game itself. Uber and DoorDash together handled about $680 million in delivery orders a day worldwide in the third quarter, based on their earnings reports . If late-night hours make up roughly a tenth of that, and launch night lifted those orders 10% to 25%, the extra spending comes to roughly $7 million to $17 million. That’s about 1% to 2.5% of a normal day’s delivery business for the two companies, and less than half a percent of the $3.79 billion Rockstar says the game brought in on day one. That shift fits what economists say about events like this one . Much of the money moves from one kind of spending to another rather than appearing from nowhere. “People just rearrange how they’re spending their free time,” Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, told Fortune before the launch. Restaurants also had fewer hands. Missed restaurant shifts rose 92% week over week on Nov. 19, according to data from scheduling platform Harri shared with Fortune , covering 280,000 shifts. One in 14 shifts went unworked, compared with one in 27 the Thursday before, while sales at those restaurants fell less than 2%. Grand Theft Auto VI came out Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, more than 13 years after its predecessor. Before the launch, a widely shared estimate claimed workers skipping their jobs to play would cost the U.S. economy $1 billion, a figure Matheson told Fortune he doesn’t believe. Office attendance barely moved. Wi-Fi logins at the more than 250 U.S. locations of Industrious, a coworking company owned by CBRE , fell about 5% on launch day compared with the previous three Thursdays, the company told Fortune . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: US lawmakers push for tougher AI chip rules amid China export crackdown
events.summary: Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Key takeaways Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Washington has new rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips, but lawmakers want more. United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they support the recently imposed chip export controls. This week, the US Department of Commerce announced a new rule to restrict how advanced US AI chips can be accessed remotely in the wake of the previous Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected spy for Beijing. The move would close what officials described as a loophole that allows Chinese companies to tap into computing power through data centres in third countries, bypassing US restrictions. list 1 of 4 Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate? list 2 of 4 Nvidia dismisses calls to reinstate Jensen Huang amid blockbuster earnings list 3 of 4 US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal list 4 of 4 US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which sits under the Commerce Department, said the rule would require data centre customers in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brazil to apply for a special licence to buy advanced chips from US companies, including Nvidia, because they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion”. “The export controls should have been in place, certainly,” Democratic Representative Pramila Jayapal told Al Jazeera. “I also think it’s a bigger conversation about who dominates the AI market. We should not have this consolidation of all the AI knowledge in a couple of companies because that poses an enormous threat on multiple levels, including national security.” In October, Jayapal introduced a policy framework that would require every AI company operating in the US to obtain a federal charter in an effort to protect the public interest. The AI charter, the framework says, is modelled after existing regulatory frameworks, combining the round-the-clock federal oversight, strict safety mandates, and structural separation built into national bank charters with the rigorous pre-release federal testing required for nuclear materials and dangerous weapons. The framework also bans AI companies from building empires, releasing risky models, stealing through surveillance, exploiting workers, or causing harm. Jayapal is a member of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, whose ranking members announced a probe to determine whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China. Lutnick is facing criticism, including from members of US President Donald Trump’s cabinet, for allegedly refusing to impose restrictions on companies accused of diverting advanced chips to China, including Megaspeed, which is at the centre of the Nvidia probe. The House Foreign Affairs Committee also announced that the Trump administration had approved exports of 879,000 chips manufactured by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026. Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress in January, expressed a desire to better limit chip exports amid growing scrutiny over the extent to which US computing power may have reached China. “I’m excited to get these gavels and go through the investigatory work that’s necessary, but also to rein in and regulate artificial intelligence. The very industry is asking to be regulated by Congress,” Democratic Representative Everton Blair told Al Jazeera. The US accounts for nearly 75 percent of the world’s AI spending and computing power, followed by China. US tech giants, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, operate nearly 90 major AI computing hubs globally, according to an Oxford University study. The same research found that US companies were building 63 AI computing hubs outside the country as of 2025. Stephen Ezell, vice president for global innovation policy at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), said Washington would find it difficult to enforce the BIS rule. China has rejected the restriction, calling it “economic coercion” by the US. On Friday, after his return to the White House from his historic trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian presidents in Shenzhen, China, Trump promised to prohibit US companies from developing data centres in other countries. “We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” Trump said. It was unclear what Trump had envisioned, or how he would enforce it. At the same time, he urged Americans to embrace data centres in their neighbourhoods, despite communities’ increasing concern about the centres’ impact on quality of life, environment and energy demands. Analysts say the recent export regulation has likely not had much effect on China’s efforts to become the global leader in AI semiconductor chips.

events.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
events.summary: President Donald Trump said Chinese leader Xi Jinping called Jensen Huang a "brilliant man" when they discussed the former Nvidia CEO. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that Huang was not mentioned in the talks he had while in China. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged. President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference. Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating. A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations. Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO. "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies." Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week. The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries. Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week. "We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said. "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China. The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors. Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO. Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race. Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI. They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI. In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed. Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.

events.title: Farmers warned to pay up or potentially lose drivers licences
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Farmers could be put off road for not paying transmission protest fines Colin Fenton (right) says he will not cave to pressure to pay his fine. ( Supplied: Colin Fenton ) Victorian drivers can lose their licence if they do not pay a fine, even if the offence is not driving-related. Many farmers in the path of VNI West have been fined for refusing access to their land. The Coalition says it will scrap VNI West and waive associated fines if it wins the state election. Farmers fined for fighting the controversial VNI West transmission line are being warned they face penalties including no longer being able to drive. If you do not pay a fine in Victoria, the state government can take away your drivers licence, deregister your vehicle, take money from your bank account or sell your land or other assets. These penalties are now confronting farmers in Victoria's north-west who have been fined for denying VNI West developers access to their land and are refusing to pay up. The threat of being put off the road was met with incredulity and outrage among farmers, given the fines they received had no connection to driving offences. Many farmers have locked the gate to VNI West transmission line builders, despite threats of fines and further penalties. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Colin Fenton, who is in his 80s, farms near Kerang. In 2024, he learned the VNI West transmission line would cut through his farm. Since then, he has fought against the project, which he says would disrupt his farming operations and devalue his property. He has refused to grant project planners access to his land, and in August this year was one of 12 farmers fined $814 each for doing so. He said he would not pay the fine, which is now overdue. He now faces losing his drivers licence and having his vehicles deregistered. Farmers have received this information on their infringement notices, describing the penalties they face if they do not pay up. ( Supplied: Trent Carter ) Mr Fenton said that was an inexplicable and unjust penalty. "I was appalled due to the fact they've connected the fine to road traffic offences," he said. Mr Fenton said despite the threat of losing his licence, he would not be paying the fine, and would risk driving while unlicensed. "We live out of town and there is no public transport and we need our drivers licences to run our farms, to get provisions, and in my case I've got a very sick wife and we take regular trips to Bendigo, an hour and a half away," he said. "I find it pretty intolerable — are we living in a communistic country, or where are we living?" Farmers have held numerous rallies against VNI West, which they do not want built across their land. ( ABC News: Tamara Clark ) Mark Woods is a specialist in criminal law and past president of the Law Institute of Victoria. He said driving-related penalties for unpaid fines disproportionately punished rural and regional Victorians. "It's particularly concerning, because whether you have your licence suspended has nothing to do with where you live," he said. "So if you're in a regional area with no access to public transport … you can lose your ability to travel about, notwithstanding that you might be the safest driver in the state. 'It's interesting that it's state election time, and therefore if people are concerned about the law, they ought to find out what candidates are going to do it about it, particularly for people in regional Victoria." Mark Woods says driving-related penalties affect regional Victorians more than their urban counterparts. ( Supplied: Mark Woods ) Mr Woods said the current penalty structure had been in place since 2014. "In 2014 there was a law passed called the Fines Reform Act, and that created an agency called Fines Victoria, and there's a director of Fines Victoria who has a whole lot of powers to do things to you if you don't pay your fines," he said. "Fines Victoria can direct VicRoads to suspend your licence or suspend the registration of the car, direct the sheriff to go out and find property that you own that can be sold to pay the fine, or seize control of your land and have that sold for the purposes of paying the fine." Mr Woods said a term of imprisonment was also possible under the legislation, although there had been a moratorium on that since 2024. Mr Fenton is hinging his hopes on a change of government on November 28. "That'd be an understatement, wouldn't it," he said. While Labor is firmly committed to VNI West, the Coalition and One Nation have vowed to scrap it and waive the fines of those who have resisted it.

events.title: Intuit asks Mailchimp employees to 'care for one another' after Bending Spoons acquisition news
events.summary: Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Intuit agreed to sell email marketing platform Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion. Bending Spoons is known for buying struggling software businesses and has previously conducted cuts. An Intuit memo asked employees to "care for one another" and said some are "feeling unsettled." Some Mailchimp employees are feeling "unsettled" after news that it's getting sold, an internal memo said. Intuit announced Thursday that it was selling the email marketing platform to Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion — a sharp markdown from the $12 billion it paid back in 2021. The note, which was obtained by Business Insider and sent on Thursday from Intuit's Atlanta office where many of Mailchimp's employees are based, asks employees to take care of each other between now and the deal's closing. "Between now and then, I'm asking all of us to care for one another," it reads. "Some of our colleagues are feeling unsettled, and some may be quiet about it, so please lead with kindness, check in on the people around you, and be mindful in shared spaces where conversations carry," it adds. Mailchimp employs about 575 people at Intuit , and they are expected to transition to Bending Spoons in early 2027, according to further correspondence viewed by Business Insider. An Intuit spokesperson said that it's committed to making the transition smooth. "We want to see continued success for everyone, and are committed to making this transition as seamless as possible for customers and employees," it said in a statement. Bending Spoons didn't respond to a request for comment. The email obtained by Business Insider says that "nothing changes" for Mailchimp employees until the deal closes, and that Intuit may sublease some of its Atlanta office space to Bending Spoons so that Mailchimp employees can remain in the same location. Bending Spoons has become known for buying struggling software businesses and turning them around through layoffs. Over the years, it has snapped up companies like Evernote, AOL, and Vimeo. In September, Bending Spoons bought the database software startup Airtable for $1.28 billion and, shortly thereafter, laid off a "large part" of the company's workforce. In an X post, Federico Simionato, Bending Spoons' product leader, said the cuts were not a reflection of employees' work and rather of the company's "deep belief that small teams ship more and better." The Intuit spokesperson told Business Insider that selling Mailchimp will allow it to concentrate on its core areas. "Selling Mailchimp lets us focus on fewer, bigger priorities, while positioning Mailchimp and the team for continued success with Bending Spoons," Intuit said. Read the note Intuit sent to Mailchimp employees below: Team, By now you're likely aware that Intuit has entered an agreement to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons. I am reaching out because many of you work alongside Mailchimp colleagues here in Atlanta, joined Intuit through the Mailchimp acquisition, or, like me, previously worked on Mailchimp. I know decisions like this come with a range of emotions, and questions, including what it means for the Atlanta site. First, Intuit remains committed to the Atlanta site and this community. This office is a key hub for Intuit, and will be home to about 650 employees who will remain at Intuit after the deal closes. It will also continue to be an important place for us to attract and retain top talent. As for space, once the deal closes, Bending Spoons may sublease some of our existing space so Atlanta-based teammates who transition to Bending Spoons can stay in the same location-just work on different floors. Until we close in early calendar year 2027, nothing changes. Everyone remains part of Intuit and we are all still teammates. Between now and then, I'm asking all of us to care for one another. Some of our colleagues are feeling unsettled, and some may be quiet about it, so please lead with kindness, check in on the people around you, and be mindful in shared spaces where conversations carry. events.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
events.summary: President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan. In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war. Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders. At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil. “We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said. He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms. “You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said. With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built. The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months. China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China. In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.” He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.” Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”. “I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran. “I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.” He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election. “I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said. Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.” And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

events.title: BNP Paribas sees ‘panic selling’ as the AI selloff drags the S&P 500 into a correction and wipes out the Nasdaq’s 2026 gains
events.summary: The S&P 500 fell into a correction Friday, and the Nasdaq Composite gave back everything it had gained in 2026. The S&P 500 closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record close, and the Dow also ended in correction territory. The S&P fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing streak since February 2020. Investors were “panic selling” as they tried to judge whether enthusiasm for AI had peaked, Benedicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas , told CNBC . Anthropic led the AI slide, as Fortune reported Friday morning . The Claude maker raised $81.34 billion in an IPO that valued it at $1.414 trillion, and its shares fell about 9% Friday, their second day of trading, giving back much of Thursday’s 17% pop. Reuters cited worries about slower data-center expansion, higher borrowing costs and Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The people with the most money in stocks already felt it. Those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances in the University of Michigan’s November survey, which ran through Nov. 16, “consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets,” survey director Joanne Hsu said . What the panic looked like Chipmakers took the worst of it. Micron , hotlink]Broadcom[/hotlink], Nvidia, and AMD were down between roughly 12% and 14%. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, topped 30 for the first time since March, CNBC reported. The selling wasn’t only in the U.S. Taiwan’s stock index fell 5.65% Friday, capping its steepest weekly drop since October 1997, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC . Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell about 5%. Washington added to it. President Donald Trump threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. companies that build data centers abroad, CNBC reported . At midday, some analysts still saw a rotation. “Money is leaving tech, not the market,” independent tech analyst Luke Lango, editor of the Innovation Investor newsletter, wrote in a note at 12:59 p.m. He said the Dow and the equal-weight S&P were higher at the time. His advice: Avoid AI stocks “while they’re being combative teenagers.” He also pointed to credit: SpaceX had to raise the yield on its $32 billion debt sale to 8.3%, which he read as the “capital spigot” closing for weaker AI borrowers such as CoreWeave and Nebius. The calm-down chorus Most of the Street said the drop would pass. “Given the solid economic and fundamental backdrop, the move appears to be highly sentiment driven,” Chris Larkin, head of trading at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley , said in commentary sent to Fortune . He added that “only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983” turned into bear markets. Deutsche Bank’s Binky Chadha called the market “very oversold” and said growth and earnings remained strong, according to CNBC . JPMorgan Asset Management chief global strategist David Kelly told Seeking Alpha markets were overdue for a tech correction. Chuck Carlson, CEO of Horizon Investment Services, told Reuters the market may be in a correction within a bull market. E*Trade’s own research is less soothing. A March 2025 E*TRADE study of the 14 times since 1983 that the S&P 500 first closed 10% or more below a record found five became bear markets. But the index fell another 10% or more after closing in correction six of those 14 times, and in 1990 and 1998 it came within a point of bear territory. The median total drop from the record was 19.9%. The backdrop Larkin calls solid includes a rate hike on the way. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday the central bank will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high, Reuters reported. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, per CME FedWatch, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%. The Fed meets Dec. 9. Investors will find out then whether Friday was panic or just early. Generative AI was used for research assistance and/or transcription of this article. events.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
events.summary: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began. US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap. Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.” Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies. In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI. European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO . Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said. Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending. “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.” Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China. Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war. Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March. Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

events.title: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
events.summary: CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, according to a report from Bloomberg. Zscaler shares popped in extended trading after the report. CrowdStrike is currently valued at $235 billion, and Zscaler has a market cap of $32 billion. Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion. Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap. Should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion . CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode. events.title: Second judge to block Trump's contested D.C. arch
events.summary: A second federal judge will block construction on President Trump 's embattled arch set to be erected near Arlington National Cemetery , multiple outlets reported Friday. Why it matters: It represents yet another barrier to the multi-year project to build a 250-foot arch that challengers said would obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said she will issue preliminary injunction that will indefinitely block the project, which she reportedly called a "rushed job" from the bench Friday. Zoom out: Brinkema's rebuke comes after D.C.-based District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday extended her separate order blocking construction on the arch for two weeks. Chutkan, who is overseeing consolidated challenges from military veterans and from the District of Columbia and Virginia, issued her initial temporary restraining order earlier this month. That order prohibited construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch, Axios D.C.'s Mimi Montgomery reported. What they're saying: "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The National Park Service did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. State of play: The legal hurdles came after the National Capital Planning Commission , which is stacked with Trump loyalists, gave its final approval for the project. Challengers, however, have argued the project requires congressional approval — and as Chutkan noted , "Congress has not enacted any statute authorizing construction of the Arch." Between the lines: The arch is one prime example of the president's quest to remake the nation's capital as he sees fit, from a sprawling White House ballroom to a community golf course . The NPS has backed Trump's arch, despite noting it "would alter several historic views." The FAA deemed the arch, which would sit near Ronald Reagan National Airport, safe for air travel, but said it should have "a non-standard eternal flame on top" and "floodlight projectors pointed" toward it. What we're watching: A Justice Department spokesperson said they would appeal the decision "immediately." Go deeper: The next two months are pivotal for Trump's D.C. projects

events.title: 'Sunrise on the Reaping' answers lingering questions about 'The Hunger Games.' Here's what you might've missed.
events.summary: Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Courtesy of Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is finally out in theaters. It's based on the novel by Suzanne Collins about Haymitch Abernathy. "Sunrise on the Reaping" sheds new light on the entire "Hunger Games" series. It's a good time to be a "Hunger Games" fan . On Friday, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" premiered worldwide, bringing Haymitch Abernathy's Hunger Games to the big screen. The film is an adaptation of Suzanne Collins' novel " Sunrise on the Reaping ," released in March 2025. Joseph Zada stars as a young Haymitch in the adaptation, and he's joined on screen by a slew of A-list actors , including Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson in a much-anticipated return to their roles as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark. Fans have been curious about Haymitch's Hunger Games since Katniss and Peeta got a peek at them in "Catching Fire," where they learned Haymitch outsmarted the gamemakers to survive the arena. "Sunrise on the Reaping" breaks down how Haymitch took aim at the arena itself and offers new details about the entire "Hunger Games" series , from lore about Katniss' family to backstory on how the revolution came to be. Here are some of the details from the novel (and some snippets left out of the movie) you might have missed. Warning: Heavy spoilers for the entire "Hunger Games" series ahead. The book is full of information about Katniss Everdeen's family Katniss is the protagonist of the original "Hunger Games" trilogy , but the books don't include much information about her family beyond her and her sister Primrose. Her parents' names aren't even mentioned in books one through three. Her parents do appear by name in "Sunrise on the Reaping," though. Collins reveals that Katniss' father, Burdock, was one of Haymitch's best friends and that he was already courting Asterid, Katniss' mother, when Haymitch was sent to the Hunger Games. Haymitch's interactions with Burdock highlight the similarities between Katniss and her father, as they are full of nods to Katniss . For instance, in the book, Burdock takes Haymitch into the woods, where he sings and shows Haymitch how to get apples and set hunting snares. Katniss uses those same hunting skills she learned in the woods to survive her first Hunger Games, and her beautiful singing voice comes up multiple times in the original series. Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate Katniss' parents' long-awaited names also reflect those they gave their children; both Asterid and Burdock are plants, as are Primrose and Katniss. Haymitch also mentions that Burdock is a distant cousin of his girlfriend, Lenore Dove Baird, a member of the Covey family. The Covey first appears in Collins' "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." They are the musically inclined family of Lucy Gray Baird, who wins the Hunger Games and has a doomed relationship with Coriolanus Snow . Haymitch sees the graves of Lucy Gray  and her cousin, Maude Ivory Baird, while visiting Lenore Dove's resting place, and he notes that Lenore Dove's mother died in childbirth with her in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Based on Haymitch's comment, Katniss seems to be a descendant of Lucy Gray's other cousin, Barb Azure Baird, on her dad's side. Katniss' and Peeta's fathers share an important interaction During the reaping for the Hunger Games, one of the boys reaped from District 12, Woodbine Chance, flees, and Peacekeepers immediately shoot him. They order everyone to the ground, and most people in the area obey, though Otho Mellark, Peeta's father, freezes. Burdock gets Otho to lie down on the ground by punching him in the knee, saving him from becoming the Peacekeepers' next target. If Otho had died in the shooting, Peeta would never have been born, so he wouldn't have been there to fight alongside Katniss. In fact, Katniss likely wouldn't have made it to the Hunger Games without Peeta, as he saved her from starvation by giving her bread after her father died. The small interaction between their fathers — at a pivotal moment in Haymitch's life — eventually leads to Peeta, Katniss, and Haymitch uniting decades later. Haymitch's nickname for Katniss holds special meaning In the original "Hunger Games" trilogy, Haymitch often refers to Katniss as "sweetheart." She initially takes the nickname as condescending but later comes to see it as a term of endearment. "Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the pet name was always a term of affection for Haymitch. Woody Harrelson as Haymitch Abernathy and Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate One of the three people Haymitch competes in the Hunger Games with from District 12 is Louella McCoy. Louella is three years younger than Haymitch, and he shares in "Sunrise on the Reaping" that he has long called her "sweetheart" as an inside joke, referencing a crush she had on him when she was 5. The pair were close and planned to be allies in the Hunger Games, but Louella died before even reaching the arena. As Haymitch mourns her, he calls her "my one and only sweetheart." In the book's epilogue, Haymitch says that Katniss reminded him of Louella when he saw her at the Hob after her father died, as she wore her hair in braids like his old friend. He said the resemblance was so strong in his mind that "the nickname couldn't help but slip out" when he became Katniss' mentor for the Hunger Games . Haymitch also sits in some katniss during his games, foreshadowing her eventual presence in the arena. Haymitch's Hunger Games offer more insight into the plot of 'Catching Fire' "Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals that Haymitch has a long history with several characters from "Catching Fire," including Plutarch Heavensbee, Beetee Latier, Mags Flanagan, and Wiress, as he tried to break the arena with their help during his time in the games. When Mags and Wiress compete alongside Katniss in "Catching Fire," Mags is said to be weakened from a stroke, while Wiress' mind seems damaged. Katniss assumes they are both in poor health because they fought in the Hunger Games. But in "Sunrise on the Reaping," Mags and Wiress are mentors to Haymitch and the other District 12 tributes, and both are physically and mentally sound when he meets them. Lili Taylor as Mags Flanagan and Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate/Murray Close/Lionsgate After he wins his games, Haymitch discovers that they were both tortured because they attempted to help him break the arena. He spots Mags in a wheelchair and sees Wiress mumbling to herself. It was Capitol torture that caused lasting damage to them, not the games themselves. events.title: Abu Dhabi's MGX emerges as major winner in Anthropic IPO
events.summary: Investment firm MGX 's windfall from Anthropic 's historic public debut made it a major winner in the Claude maker's IPO, as Abu Dhabi seeks more opportunities to deepen its ties with US companies. Anthropic closed at $97.17 per share in its Thursday debut, giving MGX's stake an unrealised market-to-market gain of roughly $20 billion and establishing it as one of the Silicon Valley-based company's largest institutional investors, a spokesperson told The National . MGX co-led Anthropic's $30 billion funding round in February, participated in its $65 billion Series H in May and added to its position during the company's public debut. The Abu Dhabi Investment Council was also among the Claude maker's major backers, as was the Qatar Investment Authority. Anthropic fell roughly 8.5 per cent during Friday's session to about $88.9 per share, slightly higher the the $83 per share at which it priced its IPO. The MGX spokesperson said Anthropic's IPO represents a significant validation of the Emirati firm's investment strategy and confidence of its global investor base. The company's portfolio spans the AI stack from frontier AI labs to infrastructure. It raised $49 billion in July from global investors for its AI Fund. Anthropic's public listing on Thursday coincided with the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in New York, as the emirate sought to deepen ties with US companies looking to establish a presence in the Gulf. Tom Hudson, advisor to the director general of the Abu Dhabi Investment Office (Adio), said between 80 and 100 people were expected to have made the trip. "It's basically matchmaking, and the idea is that we're bigger than the sum of our parts," he said of the investment forum. While the forum and the Anthropic IPO were unrelated, it signalled the growing role of the US-UAE AI nexus . Health care and artificial intelligence were expected to be among two high-priority sector for investment. "AI has genuinely been a part of the discourse in the UAE for 10 years, if not more," Mr Hudson said. "With Adio, we are looking also at how we support AI companies on their regional expansion," Mr Hudson said, pointing to AI for drug discovery and AI with autonomous vehicles. "AI cuts across a lot of the clusters that we are working with and bringing them to Abu Dhabi," he said. Milind Singh, head of technology at Adio, pointed to Anthropic's historic IPO during a panel session at the forum. "We're privileged to have been associated with this story for a long time," he said. MGX plans to invest up to 80 per cent of its total portfolio in US projects. The company also co-led OpenAI's $122 billion raise in March, and participated in xAI's $20 billion funding round in January before it merged with SpaceX. US tech companies Oracle, IBM and Cisco also operate in the UAE's AI infrastructure. Last November, Microsoft announced a $15.2 billion investment in the UAE support its cloud and AI infrastructure, as well as talent. Abu Dhabi is committing $3.5 billion to become the world's first AI-native government by the end of next year. Nvidia, OpenAI, Cisco, Oracle and Japan's SoftBank are working with UAE AI company G42 one a one-gigawatt Stargate cluster in Abu Dhabi. A similar project is being undertaken in Texas.

events.title: Congress gets a historic overhaul from every direction
events.summary: Senate data includes members who served nonconsecutive terms; House data does not. Data: House historian, U.S. Senate ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Americans want change , and they're about to get it: A perfect storm of congressional retirements, primary upsets, gerrymandering, flipped seats and lawmakers who died in office has created the biggest freshman class in decades. Why it matters : Congress had a 14% approval rating (not a typo) when Gallup polled registered voters in October. That's its lowest pre-midterm number since 1974. The big picture: The Senate is on track for its biggest freshman class since 1946. In the House, it's shaping up to be the biggest since 1992. Zoom in: The turnover featured data points that would be stunning on their own, let alone together. 28 House lawmakers chose to run for their next elected office outside the House, Pew noted in September. Six lawmakers died in office this Congress, the most in nearly 20 years. Thirteen House and Senate incumbents lost primary races. The bottom line: Congress is saying goodbye to former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). They've been in Congress since 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987, respectively.

events.title: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
events.summary: The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations. events.title: Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more
events.summary: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh wants central bankers to talk less about where they expect interest rates to go. Instead, they're talking more. Bank of America says there has been more so-called Fedspeak over the past two weeks than in any similar period going back to the beginning of 2025. The conflicting communications strategies come at a critical time for monetary policy and the economy. In his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void. Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake. Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem , entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time. Largely on the sidelines in the debate is Warsh, who has expressed disdain for that sort of forward guidance and argued that it handcuffs policymakers long before they actually have to make a decision. But that hasn't stopped most of the other 18 officials who sit in on Federal Open Market Committee meetings. In fact, according to a Bank of America analysis, there has been more so-called Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any similar period since the start of 2025. "Warsh's refusal to guide markets might be encouraging the rest of the FOMC to speak more, not less," Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave said in a note Thursday. "There is always a range of views across the 19 FOMC participants. Typically, the Chair would weigh in, indicating to markets whether the hawks or doves are in ascendence," he added. "Absent this leadership, however, both sides might feel incentivized to speak more often and more forcefully." The increasingly vocal debate comes at a critical time for the Fed and has myriad policy implications. Bhave noted "a deepening divide" on the FOMC. The Fed's decision not to increase its benchmark rate at its October meeting "increasingly looks like a mistake," and as a result "the hawks have been very vocal of late," he wrote. Leading the charge is Waller, who has raised the possibility of hiking by half a percentage point when the committee next meets in December. Minutes from the October meeting hint at the tension, particularly when it comes to Warsh's refusal to provide guidance. The summary related that some officials who were looking for a hike in October "could have supported no change in the federal funds rate provided that it was clearly understood by market participants that further tightening was likely" — a statement that points toward the forward guidance that Warsh has insisted the Fed avoid. The minutes "revealed that some officials favoring a hike would have accepted a hold if the Fed had clearly communicated further tightening," market veteran Ed Yardeni wrote Thursday. "Warsh's communication philosophy may thus be limiting the Fed's flexibility precisely when it needs it most." Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted against the October pause in favor of a quarter-point hike, tiptoed around the forward guidance issue during a recent public appearance. Prefacing some observations she made about where she sees policy headed, Hammack noted that, "Those are not promises. Those are not commitments. They're not forward guidance, which is a hot-button topic. But what they are are a conditional set of expectations of where I think the economy can go, based on what I'm seeing." Hammack's comments illustrate a needle that Fed officials have been trying to thread: continuing to be transparent about their thinking without appearing locked into a future policy that changing economic conditions could render obsolete. Speaking Thursday, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee framed the argument around credibility. "I am sympathetic to the view that [Warsh] has expressed that let's not be so, in in our language, forward guidance-oriented, saying here is what I think rates are going to be at the next meeting," Goolsbee said, calling such pronouncements "falsely precise." However, he quickly separated forward guidance from transparency. "I think central banks should be careful about doing anything that undermines credibility," Goolsbee said. "That said, I also think that it's pretty important [that] each person who sits around that table explain how they see the world. What do you see in business conditions? You don't want to surprise everybody.

events.title: Fed governor admits people now think higher inflation is the new normal: ‘That’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking’
events.summary: Fed Governor Chris Waller says Americans are starting to treat 3% inflation as normal, and he thinks the central bank may need to “shock people” out of it. The latest consumer price index also showed inflation is heating up more than expected, drifting further away from the Fed’s 2% target. And given that it’s been above that threshold for more than five years, it’s getting harder for consumers and businesses to see higher prices as a temporary blip. In a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Waller warned that inflation is spreading beyond the areas most affected by higher energy prices or tariffs, including into so-called core services. He recalled talking to someone last week who said his business passed on a 3% price hike to consumers because that’s what he thinks his customers can swallow. “And that’s when you start having problems of trying to get inflation down,” Waller explained. “So you might need to, like, shock people to say, ‘Wait a minute, 3% is not the number you should be thinking about going forward.’” Once households and businesses expect prices to keep rising 3% a year, they set wages and prices to match, the kind of spiral the Fed worries about after more than five years above its 2% target. Maintaining consumers’ inflation expectations is a top priority for the Fed. It previously held off on a more hawkish stance, saying expectations were still well anchored. But in Waller’s view, that’s no longer the case. “People are starting to think 3% may be the norm. And if you’re a firm, and the consumer’s resilient and seems to be spending, why not pass through three,” Waller warned. “And that’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking, is that it’s not going to be three, and we have to do something to try to bring it back down. We can’t wait. We can’t do this in, like, the next two years.” Because people are starting to become more accepting of higher prices, he thinks the central bank needs to be “a little more aggressive” with rate hikes, including a potential jumbo-size half-point increase at the Fed’s Dec. 8–9 meetings. A half-point move would lift the Fed’s benchmark rate to a range of 4.25% to 4.5%, from 3.75% to 4% now. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years, then held steady in October. Wall Street isn’t there yet. Futures are fully pricing in a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Waller said a quarter-point could do the job if the Fed clearly signaled another hike in January. But Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on the grounds that it ties policymakers’ hands. The problem has been complicated by the fact that the effects of President Donald Trump’s tariffs have been dragged out instead of hitting all at once, as negotiations and legal challenges kept the levies on again and off again. Meanwhile, businesses didn’t pass on the full cost of tariffs at once but spread it out. At the same time, the Iran war doesn’t seem to be winding down anytime soon as Trump has shot down further talks. Although oil prices have come down from highs, they are still volatile and spike whenever fighting in the Persian Gulf heats up again. The cumulative effect is weighing on attitudes. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting , released the same day as Waller’s interview, back up his worry: Fed staff flagged the risk that longer-run inflation expectations could have become unanchored after five years of elevated inflation. On Friday, Fed Governor Lisa Cook echoed Waller’s concerns about consumer psychology as she explained her dissenting vote to hike rates at the last meeting. “My vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation,” which “has been above target for more than ‌five and ⁠a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward,” she said, according to the text of a speech to be presented at a conference in Chile. Still, other policymakers signaled more caution. New York Fed President John Williams said on Tuesday that there’s no need for “dramatic action,” arguing that the more gradual approach in recent months is working well. He added that the economy remains resilient and the labor market is solid, even as he acknowledged that inflation isn’t moving in the right direction. But that resilience is also what’s allowing businesses to pass on bigger price hikes. As a result, one big hike may not be the end of it. Waller said the Fed needs to reverse the three rate cuts it made in 2025, and may have to go further. “If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn’t bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn’t going to bring it down,” he told CNBC . “So we may have to go above … three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
