events.title: Trump defends Putin relationship, warns AI data centres must stay in US
events.summary: Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Key takeaways Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference. United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US. On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US. list 1 of 3 Xi’s greatest power is what he chooses not to do list 2 of 3 Trump, Putin, Xi pledge to increase global petrol supplies – but how? list 3 of 3 Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records “I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign. “I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities. “I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said. Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”. He said there was “great electricity” between the leaders of the world’s main nuclear powers. “We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that,” he also said. No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation. The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed. Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war , which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary. “They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.” Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.” During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present. Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.” “I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.” Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing. “I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.” Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”. “We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.” Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan. Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.

events.title: Gap names new Athleta CEO, says Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress
events.summary: Gap on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the new CEO of Athleta effective next month. Athleta's previous CEO, Maggie Gauger, left the company for Lululemon last month. Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC that he's "disappointed" with Athleta's performance but confident in its turnaround strategy and potential. The retailer also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings, with overall comparable sales coming in flat. Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14. The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday. Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that. "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement. The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month. "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode." Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success. While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential. Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount. Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%. Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year. The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share. Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season. "We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 82 cents adjusted vs. 78 cents expected Revenue: $4.01 billion vs. $4.02 billion expected For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior. At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. ` The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales. "Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said. The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2. Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount. Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country. "We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said.

events.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
events.summary: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. events.title: Two Salvadoran soldiers killed in Haiti while handling explosives
events.summary: Two others were injured in the explosion, marking the first deaths among troops deployed to Haiti since late October. Two Salvadoran soldiers have been killed in Haiti while handling explosive material, El Salvador’s army said, marking the first deaths among the roughly 2,500 troops who have been deployed to the country since late October. Two others were injured in the explosion at one of the camps and are receiving medical care, the army said in a post on X on Friday. It did not reveal the identities of the soldiers. The deaths come just over a month after El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele sent troops into Haiti, announcing a rescue mission to find four aviation technicians who went missing on October 18 after an attack on their vehicle near the capital, Port-au-Prince. They were working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) at the time. The rescue mission has since broadened into an offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers working alongside Haitian and international forces. Salvadoran officials have said they plan to leave once the four missing technicians are found. Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told The Associated Press news agency earlier this month that the men were dead, although he provided no evidence. El Salvador’s government maintains they are alive. The Haitian government has suggested it wants the deployment to be extended, and some Haitians took to the streets in Haiti and elsewhere earlier this week in large rallies to express support for the troops and Bukele. The terms of the bilateral agreement between Haiti and El Salvador have not been revealed publicly, but according to the UN, most Salvadoran soldiers are operating outside the GSF and do not fall under the UN’s reporting mechanism for that mission. Bukele has been promoting the intervention on social media, posting videos of strikes on homes belonging to gang leaders, and Haitian officials announced earlier this week that they retook control of the national football stadium. Analysts, however, have questioned how much the Salvadoran deployment has contributed to recent gains and whether those gains would last. They have also raised concerns about the risk to civilians, citing a lack of transparency around the rules of engagement and how Salvadoran troops are monitored. On Thursday, Bukele officially launched his bid for a third presidential term . The elections are scheduled for February.

events.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
events.summary: Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk. “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch. That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers. But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.” Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China. After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap. And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said. Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.” What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others. “Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch. Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail. Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls. “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.” The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said. “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.” Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information. Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?” It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company. Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said. “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
events.summary: Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so. "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time. Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction. Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear. "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said. Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI. It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them. Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China. The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas. Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Published 1 day ago Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT. As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre. Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November. "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said. "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets." Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far. Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia. The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks. In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres. Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen". Google has been contacted for comment. events.summary: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here," Trump said. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures. CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one. If Trump follows through on his threat to clamp down on overseas data center construction, he will have to contend with the fact that numerous U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta and Oracle — have already built them in other countries. International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said. Representatives at cloud providers Amazon , Google , Microsoft and Oracle did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Trump's remarks came a day after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit that appeared to produce few concrete deliverables on an array of pressing global issues. Xi "congratulated me on how well we're doing" in artificial intelligence, Trump said, using his preferred term "super intelligence," which he said the Chinese president also likes better. — CNBC's Jordan Novet and Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

events.title: Sudan’s war leaves disabled children missing out on education
events.summary: War forces schools, rehabilitation centres to close, forcing children with disabilities to lose access to education. Khartoum, Sudan – Four-year-old Muzan Abdelrahman should be preparing to start her educational journey. But she has a hearing impairment, and in Sudan, a country devastated by war, the specialised support she needs to attend school is not available. When conflict broke out in April 2023, Muzan was only a few months old. Many hoped that the war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces would be over by now, and Muzan could grow up in an environment where she could get the assistance she needs. list 1 of 3 Islam set to be the largest religion by 2035: Where will most Muslims live? list 2 of 3 Trump makes third Supreme Court bid to end Venezuelan migrant protections list 3 of 3 Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction Instead, the war has dragged on, with no end in sight and a humanitarian crisis consuming the country. For Muzan, that means the specialised education and rehabilitation centres she relies on have closed. “My daughter needs training and continuous follow-up at this age. I try to help her at home, but I am not a specialist and cannot provide the rehabilitation sessions or educational tools she needs,” Muzan’s mother, Abeer Osman, told Al Jazeera. “What frightens me most is that these important years will pass without her getting the opportunity to learn how to communicate and express herself.” The family’s experience is not isolated. Across Sudan, children with disabilities face obstacles to education and support as institutions are destroyed and families are displaced. For 14-year-old Mohammed Ahmed, who has a physical disability, getting to school is a challenge, but so is moving around once he arrives. Inaccessible entrances and staircases leave him dependent on others. “I want to continue my education like the rest of my classmates, but I struggle to reach classrooms and move between them,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera. “What frustrates me most is that I want to learn, but the school environment does not always make that possible.” “I do not want my disability to deprive me of education or limit my future opportunities,” he added. “I want a school where I can access classrooms and facilities independently and with dignity.” The war is restricting access to schooling for children across Sudan. According to UNICEF, at least 8 million school-age children lack access to formal education. As of August, about 30 percent of the country’s schools were not operational, with around 1 percent being used as shelters for displaced people. But the issue is particularly acute for children with disabilities . Before the war, Sudan had more than 230 schools for disabled children, according to figures from the UN children’s agency. Many have since closed, although the exact number is uncertain, with no up-to-date information available. Al Jazeera reached out to the Sudanese government for comment, but had not received a response at the time of publishing. Aisha Abbo remembers the services her son, eight-year-old Ali Hassan, had access to before the war. Ali, who has Down’s syndrome, used to attend a school for children with disabilities before the war, and received support to develop academic, communication, and social skills. Those services were provided by the government, but now the same facilities are shut, and private centres are simply too expensive. “When the war broke out in Khartoum, we could no longer afford to continue his education,” Aisha told Al Jazeera. “We are calling on the government to pay attention to children with disabilities, reopen specialised centres and provide the teachers, specialists, and programmes they need. These children cannot wait until the war ends and life returns to normal. Every day without education or training affects their development and abilities.” In Khartoum, the impact is clear at the Usratuna Sudanese Association for Children with Disabilities, whose facilities were partly hit by shelling at the start of the war more than three-and-a-half years ago. A projectile struck its classrooms, while damage to buildings and the loss of equipment have made it harder to resume activities. Badr al-Din Tawfiq, the association’s project manager and representative of its director, said most rehabilitation and support services had stopped because of the war, funding shortages and damage to its facilities. “At present, we are unable to provide most of our services. We receive children’s registrations and collect their information, but we cannot respond to families’ requests because funding is unavailable. The premises need rehabilitation, the classrooms are unsafe, and we do not have the equipment needed to run rehabilitation programmes,” he told Al Jazeera. Tawfiq said the association had registered more than 100 children for physiotherapy, speech therapy, behavioural support and vocational rehabilitation.

events.title: Here’s who’s getting the richest from Anthropic’s $81 billion IPO
events.summary: Anthropic’s seven cofounders are each worth about $20 billion on paper after the company’s record-breaking IPO on Thursday, which also made thousands of its employees and some Silicon Valley investors extremely rich. Dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes. These commitments, though, are voluntary and not legally binding, according to Anthropic’s IPO filing. The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer. On Friday, Anthropic announced that underwriters had purchased millions more shares, bringing the offering’s total to about $93.5 billion. After pricing its shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, the company opened trading significantly higher and closed out the day at around $97. Despite shares falling to $85 on Friday afternoon amid a broader tech-fueled stock retreat , the company is still worth around $1.1 trillion—surpassing the market cap of Walmart . The record IPO is great news for the cofounders and insiders who have been supporting Anthropic since it was founded in 2021. The biggest gains, though, belong to Amazon and Google, whose stakes are worth about $316 billion combined—more than twice the roughly $142 billion held by the seven cofounders. Here are some of the people and companies who stand to benefit the most. Billionaire founders Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic’s president and chair of the board, Daniela Amodei, are among the figures most commonly associated with the company. But there are another five cofounders who are cashing in as well. Each of its seven cofounders owns between 237 million and 241 million shares after the offering. At the stock’s price of about $85 on Friday, that means each founder has holdings worth approximately $20 billion, putting them (at least on paper) in the same league as Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who has a net worth of $21 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Each founder also sold approximately 3.38 million shares in the IPO, worth about $280 million at the offering price. Despite owning a minority of the company’s equity, Anthropic’s cofounders control 50.1% of its shareholder voting power. The nearly equal distribution of shares among the seven founders is unusual for a Silicon Valley startup, Fortune reported . Venture capital winners Besides its cofounders, some Silicon Valley investors are also set to win big. Lightspeed Venture Partners, an early backer of Snapchat, led a $3.5 billion funding round in Anthropic in March 2025 when the company was valued at $61.5 billion. The VC firm owns less than 2% of the company, according to Bloomberg , yet its stake is still reportedly worth tens of billions of dollars. Other VCs like Menlo Ventures also own a stake representing less than 2% of the company, Bloomberg reported. Iconiq has invested more than $6 billion in Anthropic since 2025, and its stake is worth more than $26 billion, the outlet reported. Anthropic in total has more than 400 venture investors, according to PitchBook, yet no VC firm owns more than 5%, Fortune reported . The company’s historic IPO means even some smaller stakes are now worth billions. Sound Ventures, the venture firm cofounded by Ashton Kutcher, invested about $435 million in Anthropic and owns about 0.5% of the company , Bloomberg reported. It’s unclear, though, how much Kutcher himself benefited from the trade as the actor best known for his role on That ’70s Show stepped down as general partner at the firm earlier this year. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt also owns about 1% of Anthropic , according to Bloomberg , putting his stake’s value at about $11 billion at Friday’s share price. One early investor who won’t be reaping the rewards is FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is serving a sentence of 25 years in prison after being convicted on fraud and conspiracy charges. Bankman-Fried has appealed his sentence to the Supreme Court. The trading firm he founded, Alameda Research, invested $500 million in Anthropic, but FTX’s bankruptcy estate sold most of its stake in 2024 to repay creditors. Among the buyers was Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street, which stands to reap a multibillion-dollar windfall . Employee millionaires Many of the company’s roughly 5,300 employees are also getting rich thanks to generous stock-based compensation. Private-markets research firm Sacra estimated that 2,800 current and former employees could hold at least $1 million in pretax vested equity in the company at a $1.35 trillion valuation, Reuters reported . Some of the earliest employees stand to benefit disproportionately. At least 400 early hires could hold equity worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC. To be sure, it’s hard to estimate which employees hold how much stock because Anthropic’s IPO filing discloses aggregate equity awards but not their distribution among individual employees. Now that Anthropic is public, non-founder employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of certain holdings, and up to another 35% following the release of Anthropic’s 2026 financial results. Big Tech gains Some of the biggest gains from the company’s IPO will go to two Big Tech giants, Amazon and Google. Anthropic’s IPO filing estimated that Amazon would own 14.6% of the company’s outstanding shares and Google would own 13.4%. Amazon’s stake stems from billions of dollars in investments the company has made in Anthropic dating back to 2023, around the time it had just 160 employees. At the time, Amazon committed an initial $1.25 billion as part of a deal to ultimately invest $4 billion in Anthropic. In exchange Anthropic agreed to make Amazon Web Services its primary cloud provider for critical workloads and make Claude available to AWS customers.  In total, Amazon invested $8 billion in convertible notes between 2023 and 2025 and put in another $10 billion in preferred stock in 2026. Google has also poured billions into Anthropic, including $10 billion it invested in a financing round earlier this year and another $10 billion in a private placement alongside the IPO. At the company’s roughly $85 per share stock price Friday, Amazon’s 1.94 billion shares would be worth about $165 billion, while Google’s 1.77 billion shares would be worth around $151 billion. events.title: Senators fret over fate of college sports bill
events.summary: The House-Senate tension over bipartisan college sports legislation is reaching a fever pitch. Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., said in an interview on Friday that he has told House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., it would be a “mistake” for the House to change the Senate-passed version. He also talked to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and said he’s pushing House leaders to give the bill an “up-or-down vote.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune suggested in an interview that the House could try to pass the bill on its suspension calendar, requiring a two-thirds majority vote, if there’s too much internal GOP opposition. Scalise says the issue is “an important priority” but said the House is going to make “very narrow changes” to the bill and be “ready to go” in December. It’s a delicate dance: No senator wants to appear to pressure the House too much, but there’s no guarantee that next year’s Democratic Congress prioritizes the issue; several backers see this year as the best chance for the bill. “There’s still a possibility to get something done, but I know that time is of the essence. We’re listening to what [House members] have to say,” said Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash. Thune also said he met with Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti ahead of Petitti’s meeting with Scalise. An avid sports fan, Thune said that the decision by the LSU’s men’s basketball team to play RJ Luis after he signed a two-way NBA contract exposed the absurdity of today’s college sports landscape. The bill bars pro athletes from playing college sports, in addition to establishing transfer portal restrictions. President Donald Trump is a vocal supporter. Texas Tech Board of Regents Chair Cody Campbell, who also runs the Saving College Sports group, and Randy Levine, one of the president’s point men on the issue and the president of the New York Yankees, also met with House lawmakers in both parties this week, according to a person familiar with the matter. “Unless you codify it, you’re going to spend your next decade in court,” Thune said. “This is our one real opportunity to get this done.”

events.title: Blackout prompts questions over ElectraNet's recent $300m network upgrade
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA government questions ElectraNet over 'failure' of $300m Eyre Peninsula network upgrade Topic: Electricity Production and Distribution Three ElectraNet transmission towers were toppled on Thursday, causing a blackout across the Eyre Peninsula. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) Electricity transmission service provider ElectraNet is facing uncomfortable questions over Thursday's blackout on the Eyre Peninsula. The company spent $300 million on a network upgrade which it said would provide more reliable power. ElectraNet says the transmission towers will be standing again "in a few months' time". The owner of South Australia's high-voltage transmission network is facing uncomfortable questions over Thursday's blackout on the Eyre Peninsula, after pledging a $300 million network upgrade would provide more reliable power. ElectraNet, the state's monopoly provider of electricity transmission services, has attributed the blackout to a "very unique, very rare" weather event that, at around 2.30pm on Thursday, damaged three transmission towers on the Eyre Peninsula. The downed towers were located at Wharminda, a small rural locality that sits along a 270-kilometre transmission line between Port Lincoln and Cultana. The transmission towers were on a 270-kilometre high-voltage line that opened in 2023. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) ElectraNet spent $300 million on the high-voltage line, constructing 500 new transmission towers and upgrading five substations. The project, named Eyre Peninsula Link, was completed in March 2023 . In a media release heralding its opening, ElectraNet CEO Simon Emms said it would give "residential and business electricity users a more secure and reliable power supply". $300 million Electranet project completed Electranet's completion of a 270-kilometre line will help unlock the Eyre Peninsula's potential as a green energy zone, the company says. But the blackout that unfolded over Thursday afternoon and into Friday left ElectraNet fielding uncomfortable questions from residents, cabinet ministers and the media about how an outage of this scale could still happen. ElectraNet executive Alex Trento was peppered with questions at a state government press conference on Friday morning. But when asked whether he would be having a conversation with the premier about more funding, Premier Peter Malinauskas stepped in. "This is not a question for us. That's a question for them." ElectraNet executive Alex Trento (left) watches on as Peter Malinauskas addresses the media. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Earlier in the day, Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis struck a similar tone. "There'll be a lot of questions after this is all over about how these over $300 million worth of upgrades on the Eyre Peninsula just three years ago — that we've all paid for in our power bills — have failed, and what was the weather event that caused them," he told 891 ABC Adelaide. ElectraNet confident in transmission tower strength ElectraNet is of the "strong belief" that the wind that hit the transmission towers was more than 172km/h. That would be above the winds they were built to withstand under Australian engineering specifications. Those specifications, Mr Trento said, were strengthened in 2016 following South Australia's statewide blackout . Farmers count their losses after wild storm Shed doors were blown off and crops wiped out during a "rare" storm supercell that damaged major electricity transmission towers on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula. While a structural fault could not be ruled out, Mr Trento said: "At this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively". As to whether the engineering standards would need to be strengthened again, he said he had to wait for all the facts to be available. "We could have been looking at a 215km/h hour wind event, we just don't know," Mr Trento said. "So, until we have all that information, I really can't answer that question on whether the standards need to be updated." The transmission towers will be standing again "in a few months' time", Mr Trento added. The blackout has also put renewed attention on the relationship between ElectraNet and the Australian Energy Regulator (AER). The regulator has the final say on what transmission companies can spend on big infrastructure upgrades, balancing this with what they will need to raise from higher energy bills. In September 2020, it gave ElectraNet approval to spend $280 million on Eyre Peninsula Link.

events.title: Anthropic value drops after record-breaking IPO
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Anthropic's record-breaking IPO fails to calm AI jitters as tech stocks fall further The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. ( Reuters: Shannon Stapleton ) Technology shares have fallen across the world after Anthropic's market debut. Following its initial public offering, shares rocketed to more than $US110 ($166) before falling below $US90. Nvidia also shed value, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 fell in value by the end of the week. Technology shares have nosedived and dragged stocks into the red across the world, after AI firm Anthropic's bumper market debut failed to dispel growing worries about the sector's massive investments and sky-high valuations. Anthropic shares briefly rocketed from an initial offering price of $US83 ($125) to more than $US110 on Thursday, despite a broader sell-off on Wall Street, but fell back sharply with the price plunging back below $US90 after Friday morning trades. "The performance of the shares over the coming days and weeks could provide one of the clearest tests yet of whether investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI will ultimately generate attractive returns," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell. While Anthropic surged on its Nasdaq debut, the tech-dominated index struggled for the rest of the day and was 3.2 per cent further down after Friday morning trading. Anthropic's stock fell 10.8 per cent to $US86.72 ($125). It is still above its IPO price of $US83 per share. ( Reuters: Brendan McDermid ) New York's broader S&P 500, which also trades the shares of the world's biggest tech companies, shed 2 per cent on Thursday and continued to fall on Friday, extending a major run of losses. The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10 per cent from its October 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the market's big slide. "We think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run," wrote James Reilly, from Capital Economics, who said the prospect of an "AI bust in 2027" was his central forecast and a growing worry for investors. AI stocks have been losing ground partly due to worries their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at federal and state levels. Despite massive earnings, shares at Nvidia slumped by 6.9 per cent on Friday. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) "The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. Dr Sue Keay of the University of NSW AI Institute told ABC News it was a bit early to suggest the AI bubble had burst. "I think it is showing that investors are actually starting to examine the long-term viability of these companies and whether they really can be valued at over $1 trillion," Dr Keay said. "One of the challenges with the Anthropic IPO has been that in raising $81bn, that's essentially taking $81bn out of the capital markets that could have been invested elsewhere. "I think on the one hand, it shows that people still do have confidence in AI as a business, but the fact that most of the investment is only happening in a handful of companies means that the benefits really aren't being distributed and so we do have quite a high concentration risk because we're not funding a range of different AI businesses." Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector.

events.title: Melania Trump says public displays of affection with Donald Trump are 'not my style'
events.summary: First lady Melania Trump spoke about her relationship with President Donald Trump in her new Amazon docuseries. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images "Melania: The Series," a companion to her documentary, premiered on Amazon Prime Video on Friday. Melania Trump spoke about her relationship with President Donald Trump. She said public displays of affection are "not my style," and she's not always a fan of his dancing. Toward the end of the second episode of "Melania: The Series," director Brett Ratner told first lady Melania Trump that one of his takeaways from filming her is the "beautiful relationship" that she shares with President Donald Trump. "Well, people, they don't see that because we are not so public outside," Melania Trump said in the two-part docuseries, which premiered on Amazon Prime Video on Friday. "We are not that way. It's not my style. You know, that's private." In "Melania: The Series" — for which Amazon paid $40 million for the licensing rights, alongside the " Melania" documentary released in January — the notoriously private first lady opens up about her nearly 22-year marriage to Donald Trump, including their public disagreements. Donald Trump and Melania Trump married in January 2005 at Bethesda-by-the-Sea Episcopal Church in Palm Beach, Florida. Their reception was held at Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate. Marc Beckman, senior advisor to Melania Trump and an executive producer of both the film and docuseries, told Business Insider that the series "goes deeper into her relationships with her husband, her son, and her father, so at a certain level, it's more personal." The Office of the First Lady declined to comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. PDA and public scrutiny The president and first lady's public displays of affection — or apparent lack thereof — have made headlines in the past. In her 2024 memoir, also titled "Melania," the first lady recalled a widely reported incident where she appeared to swat her husband's hand away on a 2017 trip to Israel, characterizing it as "a mere misunderstanding" caused by protocol when greeting foreign leaders. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport in 2017. JACK GUEZ/AFP via Getty Images In the docuseries, the first lady said that she doesn't dwell on the public scrutiny. "I don't need to answer to anybody," she said. "I don't need to explain anything to anybody. Whatever anybody thinks about me, let them think. I know who I am and that's all that matters." 'I let him be who he is' When asked about being married to Donald Trump for over 20 years, Melania Trump cited their support for each other despite their differences of opinion. "I think you need to let them be who they are, and you cannot change the person," she said in the docuseries aboard a presidential jet . "Sometimes, of course, you disagree with them, and that's normal. That's healthy for the relationship. That's nothing wrong. I let him be who he is, and he supports me and lets me be who I am." First lady Melania Trump is not always a fan of President Donald Trump's dance moves. Alex Brandon - Pool/Getty Images Melania Trump has occasionally publicly broken with her husband and the Republican Party on political issues. In her 2024 "Melania" memoir, she expressed support for abortion rights, writing that "a woman's fundamental right of individual liberty, to her own life, grants her the authority to terminate her pregnancy if she wishes" — a different stance than that of the GOP, which generally favors abortion restrictions. In the docuseries, Donald Trump said that he and his wife "don't have very many arguments," but that when she spoke about her stance on abortion, "people respected her views." Another issue the couple will continue to disagree on: Donald Trump's dance moves . "She feels very strongly that everything should be very presidential," Donald Trump said. "And when we were doing rallies, if, on occasion, I'd break into a dance, I'm not sure she loved it so much. But the people loved it." "Well, sometimes the situations were like, 'I don't think it's a good day to dance,'" Melania Trump said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Buzzing of drones causes ‘fear and panic’ among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite ‘ceasefire’. Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement. Four Palestinians were killed on Friday when an Israeli drone struck the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera. list 1 of 3 Palestinians in Gaza face new displacement after Israeli army operation list 2 of 3 Families flee Gaza’s Bureij camp as Israel launches new offensive list 3 of 3 Save the Children: Gaza’s children face ‘unmatched dangers’ Witnesses said the drone targeted a group of civilians within the camp. Separately, a medical source at al-Awda Hospital reported the arrival of the body of a Palestinian killed by an Israeli drone strike in the Nuseirat refugee camp. Two Palestinians were also killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah. Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the injured were brought to hospitals in central Gaza that operate at reduced capacity due to a lack of medical supplies and staff. Mahmoud added that drones were “causing fear and panic” among Palestinians in Gaza. “People cannot run simple errands because of the ongoing fear of being attacked and killed on the road,” he said. The buzzing of drones adds to the sound of explosions from home demolitions and to that of fighter jets, our correspondent added. The Israeli army on Friday carried out demolition operations near areas under its control in the al-Shuja’iya neighbourhood in the eastern part of Gaza City using explosive-laden drones. It also carried out three large-scale demolitions near the “Yellow Line”, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza. By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT). Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and homes in the Gaza Strip amid ongoing military operations and disputes over the “ceasefire” line. Israel has repeatedly violated the so-called “ceasefire” agreement that entered into force on October 10, 2025. Since then, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza. Since the genocidal war began in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured 176,000 others. Separately on Friday, which marks World Children’s Day, Palestinian prisoner groups said that around 350 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons, where they face torture, starvation and deprivation of medical care, education, and family visits. The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society said dozens of children from Gaza were detained during the war, but enforced disappearance and restrictions on visits have made it impossible to determine their numbers.

events.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ reaches $3.79 billion in sales in one day
events.summary: People walk past a large banner promoting "Grand Theft Auto VI." LaMaxitie/Nexpher Images via Getty Images Take-Two said "Grand Theft Auto 6" generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales. It took "Grand Theft Auto 5" three days to reach $1 billion in sales when it came out in 2013. Hype around the new game's debut was exceptional, and many workers said they were taking PTO to play it. For "Grand Theft Auto 6" to become the fastest-selling entertainment property — video game or movie — of all time, publisher Take-Two Interactive Software only had to beat itself. Mission accomplished, and by a landslide. Take-Two said on Friday that the latest installment in the crime-drama series generated $3.79 billion in worldwide sales in its first day. The last game in the series, "GTA 5," rang up $1 billion in worldwide sales within three days of its 2013 release, making it the fastest-selling entertainment property at the time, per Guinness World Records. It beat Activision Blizzard's "Call of Duty: Black Ops II," which reached the milestone in 15 days in 2012, and Hollywood's then-fastest-grossing film, "The Avengers," which did so at the worldwide box office in 10 days. Now, "GTA 6," made by Take-Two's Rockstar Games studio, owns the top spot. Its predecessor had held onto the video game record all this time, while the previous movie benchmark, the 2019 Marvel release "Avengers: Endgame," reached $1 billion at the worldwide box office in five days, according to Guinness World Records. "It's a cultural event," said former longtime game-industry analyst Michael Pachter of the launch of "GTA 6" on November 19. "People are going to remember this day." The higher price tag for "GTA 6" versus its predecessor likely helped. The new standard edition costs $80, while a $100 Ultimate Edition includes premium vehicles, weapons, apparel, and other in-game content tied to the story. When "GTA 5" debuted, the standard edition retailed for $60, and a special version for $80. 'GTA 6' frenzy Early forecasts had pointed to a blockbuster launch for the new game, so the milestone isn't all that surprising. Analytics firm Newzoo estimated in July that "GTA 6" was on pace for $3.3 billion to $5.2 billion in worldwide sales by the end of its launch week, while Benchmark analyst Mike Hickey noted in August that Take-Two's fiscal 2027 guidance embedded roughly 30 million unit sales. Take-Two's fiscal year ends March 31, 2027. Hype surrounding the game's debut was exceptional. Workforce management tech company UKG said time-off requests for the day "GTA 6" debuted were about 20% higher than it has seen in comparable pre-Thanksgiving weeks. Some employers leaned into the frenzy. The CEO of UK-based Raptor PR gave the agency's nine employees an extra day of annual leave for the release and bought each a copy of the game. Logitech, meanwhile, offered its more than 7,000 employees an extra paid day off to play any game they choose through a new "Logi Game Day" benefit. In addition to "GTA 6," two other nostalgia-filled games debuted this month: Activision Blizzard's "World of Warcraft: Forever" and Nintendo's "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" remake. Beyond the initial rush, "GTA 6" has more sales drivers ahead. A PC version expected next year could bring another wave of buyers, while price cuts and downloadable add-on content could also keep money flowing to Take-Two. "I think people are still pricing the stock like it's a one-hit wonder," said Pachter, now managing director of strategic planning at financial-services firm Wedbush Securities. "It's not." events.title: Feral fur is having a moment, but does it help pest control?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Feral fur is having a moment but might not help Australia's pest animal problem Topic: Pests, Diseases and Control Methods Amity Scarth loves her rabbit vest and fox scarf but mostly loves that they are ethically sourced. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) Amity Scarth loves fur and isn't afraid to wear it, but she won't just wear any dead animal. There are strict rules around where her furs come from and how they are made. The animal must be a pest in Australia, be killed ethically and its fur treated and made into clothing in Australia. "Fur is designed to last a really long time," she says. "So this fur, even if I didn't want it, it could go through multiple hands for a really long time and still hold up." Amity Scarth wears her rabbit vest everywhere: out to dinner, to parties and down to the shops to get groceries. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) Part of her clothing philosophy comes from her rejection of the fast-fashion industry. "If [the fur] did end up in landfill, then it would biodegrade, which can't be said for a number of mass-produced fast-fashion clothes." Like the gate-to-plate food movement, Amity knows where her fur started life. "Fur that's not coming from sustainable sources is coming from fur farms, which are obviously extremely cruel." The 22-year-old believes her fashion perspective is shifting attitudes, and she often gets complimented on her rabbit vest. There is evidence that the fur-curious scene in Australia is growing. Michelle Cozzaglio says people look for the weird and wonderful at the Oddities and Curiosities Expo. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) This week saw the start of a national tour of the Oddities and Curiosities Expo, a subculture arts and handicrafts festival that celebrates the strange and bizarre. Michelle Cozzaglio from the United States is one of its founders. She said North American expos attracted about 4,000 applications, and this year Australia's event had hit a new high of 2,000 applicants. The expo focuses on sustainable leather, handcrafted goods and general taxidermy. "We're really focused on the sustainable side of leather, handcrafted goods and just general taxidermy, sometimes it's art, sometimes it's, you know, skulls, bones, things like that," she says. "People are looking for something different and just generally the word oddities has such a wide range of meaning for people." Among the weird and wonderful creations is a preserved rat in a dress. "People really like the cute, funny taxidermy that has been something that's really kind of blown up within our community too," she says. Taxidermy was all the rage in the Victorian era and is again having a moment. Taxidermy is experiencing a global resurgence and feral animals provide an ethical source. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) "I think taxidermy itself is just really popular right now," she says. "We also even offer taxidermy classes, so people get to learn how to do taxidermy on their own." Heidi Beynon is a self-taught taxidermist and also the creator of the clothes Amity Scarth wears. The former art and woodwork teacher turned tanner and goat farmer loves creating products from every part of an animal but fell into the fur industry accidentally. Heidi Beynon uses every part of the animal in her fur creations. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) "I absolutely love goats and I sell goats mainly alive," she said. "But then we harvested some for meat and so I tanned the hides." From there she connected with hunters, particularly feral deer and fox hunters. Her tanning and fur creations have turned into a full-time job, and she has even employed someone part time to keep up with demand. Heidi Beynon at her stall at this year's Oddities and Curiosities Expo in Brisbane. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) Heidi says fake fur is on the decline as people make more environmentally sustainable choices. "People appreciate what I'm doing, and they see it as a valuable, beautiful, authentic product," she says. "I'm using something that would otherwise be wasted because they're going to be culled anyway. "I feel like everyone in Australia should have a fox fur jacket. Heidi Beynon now works full time as a tanner and fur creator, working with ethically sourced animals and using as much of the animal as she can. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) "If we don't do this, we will have mass extinction of native animals, that's my priority, to help protect native animals." Jack Gough from the Invasive Species Council says feral animal populations grow rapidly.

events.title: Nepali cricket fans in Qatar want to see their team competing with the best
events.summary: As thousands from Qatar’s Nepali community watch their team play, they hope for the team to rise in global rankings. Nepal cricket fans celebrate their team’s global rise Doha, Qatar – On a warm Friday afternoon in Qatar, the country’s only international cricket stadium was a sea of Nepal’s uniquely triangular crimson and deep blue flags. Nepal’s supporters arrived with flags draped across their shoulders, held them aloft to flutter in the breeze, cheering every delivery and waving them wildly in celebration of every wicket. The events on the field seemed nearly inconsequential against the loud cheers of the thousands of fans who had filled the West End International Cricket Stadium on the outskirts of the Qatari capital, as the nation with the world’s highest mountain faced the most powerful force in cricket. Nepal were bowling first against India A – India’s second XI – in their first group match of the Asian Cricket Council’s (ACC) Rising Star Asia Cup 2026 in Qatar. Indian captain Tilak Varma and his batting partner Kumar Kushagra kept finding boundaries. Nepal’s bowlers faced the wrath and their fielders could barely keep up. But the noise in the stands barely subsided. The supporters followed every ball closely, their attention firmly focused on the team they rarely get to watch up close, especially living thousands of kilometres from home. Qatar is home to at least 367,000 Nepalis, according to the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Qatar, making them the Gulf country’s third-biggest diaspora community. Pradeep Kumar Yadav was one of the few thousand Nepali fans who were on a mission to provide vociferous support to their cricket team this weekend. Yadav arrived at the stadium with seven Nepali friends, who had been planning to come as soon as the tournament’s fixtures were announced. “This is our first time watching Nepal play outside our country,” Yadav told Al Jazeera. For Nepal’s sizeable diaspora in Qatar, the cricket team provides a reason to gather around a national passion and often draws large crowds. The supporters are happy to travel to stadiums to back a team that has risen through the international ranks over the past decade. Nepal’s modern cricketing journey can be traced back to 1996, when the country became a member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) and the men’s team first competed in an international tournament. The turning point came when the South Asian nation qualified for its first ICC event at the T20 World Cup 2014. Soon, Nepal’s players were being noticed on the international stage and leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane’s selection in major T20 leagues around the world raised the country’s cricketing profile. Back home, cricket has spread far beyond the capital Kathmandu into towns and villages, backed by efforts to build the sport’s structure at grassroots level. For Qatar-based fan Himmat Joshi, the Nepali cricket team’s success has resulted in a sharp rise in the popularity of the sport. “I feel a lot of happiness,” Joshi said while watching the team play against India. “In the past, fewer people followed it but it has grown over the years,” he said. Mohammad Zahoor, who was among the thousands in the stands, sees the national team’s progress as a source of pride. He describes the Nepalis as a hardworking nation and says the country is building a domestic cricket system capable of competing with higher-ranked international teams. “There is a lot of pride in seeing Nepali cricketers represent the country. We are a passionate people,” Zahoor said. The ambitions extend beyond the T20 format. Nepal’s supporters want to see the country compete against established cricketing nations and eventually earn a place among the teams playing Test cricket. For Zahoor, defeating a Test-playing country would be an important step towards that ambition. He also hopes cricket will become part of Nepal’s international identity, alongside its reputation for mountaineering, the Himalayas and being home to Mount Everest. “Nepalis play the game like a festival,” Zahoor explained. “Our expectations and hopes are that one day Nepali people are known for their cricket as they are known for their culture of mountaineering and Mount Everest.” At the stadium in Qatar, the flags, chants and sheer number of supporters reflected that ambition. In the end, India broke their hearts with a crushing 306-run win. But it mattered little to the thousands cheering on their team, despite the loss. For some, including Yadav and his friends, it offered a unique opportunity to watch Nepal play abroad. Others were simply happy to get a chance to follow a team that has given the country, and its passionate supporters, a growing presence in international cricket.

events.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
events.summary: A 'Saturday Night Live' parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem. Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people . The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. A growing trend One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion . The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving. Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 . But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members. NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores. Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

events.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
events.summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion. Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California. Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations. Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy. Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption. Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI. “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
