events.title: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
events.summary: Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs , including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors , according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members. While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy. But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf. According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED. After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.” “It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said. In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified. Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia. For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis. Already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls. Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board. In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18 , board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.” Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk , have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “ honored ” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.” The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return. Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him.

events.title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
events.summary: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan , which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger. Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters. Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”. JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported. events.title: Anthropic mathematician says he used AI to solve the Riemann hypothesis
events.summary: Math's "white whale" may have just been cracked with the help of Anthropic's Claude. J Studios/Getty Images A mathematician said on Friday that he cracked one of the biggest problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said he used Claude to solve it. Mathematicians told Business Insider the result hasn't been fully verified yet. One of the biggest open problems in all of mathematics may have just been cracked by a mathematician using AI. Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said on Friday that he solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which involves prime numbers, using Claude. "I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe," Alpöge said in a post on his website. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Though Alpöge's solution has yet to be formally verified, leading scholars in the field told Business Insider on Friday that should it stand, this would be the biggest breakthrough in math yet. "If it holds up, it's an extremely big deal," said Steven Strogatz , a math professor at Cornell. "This is the Moby Dick of Mathematics, the great white whale." Sergei Gukov , a math professor at Caltech, called the claim a "HUGE deal." "This is not a small potato," he said. "RH was the biggest problem in math." Strogatz said Alpöge's solution has been verified by a computer-based system, but added that it sometimes makes mistakes . "So it's fair to say that the claimed proof has not yet been independently verified," he said. The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed 167 years ago by a German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers. The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician a $1 million prize. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category. Alpöge's solution is, by his own admission, incredibly long and complicated. The solution's written proof comprises more than 250,000 pages, Alpöge said. Terence Tao, a leading scholar based at UCLA, said in a post on his website Friday that "digesting" the proposed solution "will take some time." Alpöge, who joined Anthropic in 2024, said he actually solved the problem on Sunday, but decided to hold off on announcing it after speaking with CEO Dario Amodei and consulting with other mathematicians. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, went public on the stock market on Thursday. As of Friday afternoon, the price of Anthropic shares has steadily declined. Alpöge said he didn't want to release "slop" to the public, adding that he still doesn't fully understand the math involved. Still, he said that as other mathematicians attempt to grapple with the results, Alpöge said he plans to be there every step of the way to help them. "I intend to do my best to understand and impart understanding of this argument," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A massive bearish trade just happened in the chip stocks
events.summary: The biggest options trade of the day was a bearish bet on the SMH. Traders are targeting an additional 8% decline. So much for buying the dip. As the S&P 500 entered correction territory and the Nasdaq-100 flirted with bear-market territory, down 19% from highs as of midday Friday, the single biggest options trade of the day was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) has a long way more to fall. Around 12:30 E.T., someone spent $93 million buying 20,000 380-strike puts expiring Sep. 17, 2027, according to trading data reviewed by SpotGamma and Volland, options-analytics platforms that both show the trade as a likely opening position, with volume exceeding existing open interest in the contract. The trade bets that the index will fall below $380, a nearly 8% decline from its current level. The SMH is off 40% from its recent all-time highs. "That trade stands out big-time," wrote Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner of Volland. "It is either a hedge or speculative, but either way it isn't a vote of confidence." The puts were bought for $46.50 a piece, an arguably expensive choice for a downside bet with volatility in the ETF trading at 70. "You're paying a metric ton of Vega for that thing," added SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, referring to the contract's sensitivity to changes in volatility of the underlying chip ETF. "Maybe they were a forced buyer, or maybe they're actually selling this, which can still be the case even though the price shows it happening closer to the ask." The semiconductor index headed for a 9% drop this week alone.

events.title: Trump floats major tax on U.S. companies constructing data centers overseas
events.summary: President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do. Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint , as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose. What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials. "They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he said of the data centers being built across the country. Trump also claimed data center expansion would help lower Americans' costs and taxes. He also encouraged Americans to negotiate deals with companies proposing data centers in their communities. "They have plenty of money," he said. "Take it." Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes. Trump did not specify whether he would seek congressional approval or use existing executive powers to penalize companies that attempt to build data centers globally. Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried : Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country. Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S. "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said Friday. Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence." events.title: The ending of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' didn't quite match the book's epilogue. Here's what changed.
events.summary: Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is finally in theaters. The final scenes include appearances by Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence, and Josh Hutcherson. The scene is adapted from the novel's epilogue, but it left out some important details. There were many reasons to be excited for the premiere of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," and the star-studded cast was one of the biggest. The film, released on Friday, is an adaptation of Suzanne Collins' prequel to "The Hunger Games" trilogy about Haymitch Abernathy's experience in the 50th Hunger Games. It featured newcomers to the "The Hunger Games" universe, such as Joseph Zada as a younger Haymitch and Elle Fanning as young Effie Trinket. It also brought back three of the franchise's original stars for the end of the movie. Woody Harrelson reprised his performance as Haymitch in the film's final scene, alongside Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark. Fans were thrilled to see the trio reunite on screen, but their appearance differed slightly from the epilogue of the  "Sunrise on the Reaping" book . In particular, the scenes omitted some important details about Haymitch and Katniss' relationship . Spoilers ahead for "Sunrise on the Reaping." Haymitch and Katniss The brief epilogue in "Sunrise on the Reaping" ties together Haymitch's experience after the 50th Hunger Games and the life readers know he has in the postwar world of "Mockingjay," where he has returned to District 12 with Katniss and Peeta. "Haymitch drinks until the liquor runs out, and then raises geese until the next train arrives," Katniss says of her mentor in "Mockingjay." "Fortunately, the geese can take pretty good care of themselves." The "Sunrise on the Reaping" epilogue opens with Haymitch saying he still has visions of his love, Lenore Dove, over 25 years after her death. He then details how he came to know Katniss after pushing her father, Burdock Everdeen, away before she was born for his safety. (Burdock and Katniss are also revealed to be relatives of Lenore Dove and the Covey family earlier in the novel.) Woody Harrelson as Haymitch Abernathy and Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in "The Hunger Games." Lionsgate Haymitch says he saw Burdock carrying Katniss around when she was a baby, and he later noticed her at the Hob when she came to trade "the odd squirrel or rabbit" after her father died. "Tough and smart, her hair in two braids then, reminding me for all the world of Louella McCoy, my sweetheart of old," Haymitch says of Katniss in the book. Louella was reaped into the Hunger Games with Haymitch, and he jokingly called her sweetheart because she had a crush on him briefly when she was young. Louella dies before the Games begin and is replaced by a body double, Lou Lou. Her loss profoundly impacts Haymitch, kickstarting his acts of rebellion against President Snow and the Capitol. In the "Sunrise on the Reaping" epilogue, Haymitch reveals he began calling Katniss sweetheart after they met because of her resemblance to Louella. "And after she volunteered for the Games, that nickname couldn't help but slip out," Haymitch says of Katniss. Haymitch does see a young Katniss in the final scenes of the movie, but only as a baby. Zada as Haymitch spots Burdock and her mother Asterid walking with an infant Katniss in the woods, before cutting to Woody Harrelson as Haymitch after the war. Because Haymitch doesn't see Katniss with two braids on screen, the tether between her and Louella in Haymitch's mind isn't clear. Die-hard "Hunger Games" fans probably still caught the connection, but more casual viewers may have missed it. The geese The movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping" also left out an important interaction between Haymitch and Katniss involving geese. In the epilogue, Haymitch tells Katniss and Peeta the truth about his experience in the Quarter Quell and the loss of his loved ones as they work on a memorial book about the war. After he shares his past with them, Katniss brings Haymitch goose eggs for him to raise. The gift harkens back to Lenore Dove, as a gaggle followed her around when she was alive, particularly when she sang. Lenore Dove raised geese in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate Katniss' offering highlights her deep understanding of Haymitch, a theme Collins played up in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Plutarch Heavensbee tells Haymitch the revolution needs "someone exactly like" him, only "luckier, or with better timing," to bring the Capitol down. Katniss is that person, the flame finally lit from the spark of rebellion Haymitch stoked. The goose eggs underscore their connection in the book, while the movie relies on Haymitch and Plutarch's conversation to show that Katniss was the luckier, better-timed version of Haymitch. At the end of the film, Lawrence as Katniss and Hutcherson as Peeta embrace Haymitch, again played by Harrelson, on his birthday, which always fell on Reaping Day. He overlooks a memorial listing the number of children who died in the Hunger Games, which seems to be a stand-in for the memorial book that Peeta and Katniss worked on in the novel. Haymitch then decides to visit the geese in the meadow on his own, sitting on the same log he and Lenore Dove did years ago. Haymitch doesn't make it clear that the geese belong to him or indicate that Katniss gave them to him, but Katniss and Peeta do thank Haymitch before he heads off to sit with the geese. The interaction is sweet — if a bit cheesy — but it didn't include the full scope of Katniss' care for Haymitch after the war. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Here's what our readers are saying about Amazon's threat to raise NYC delivery costs
events.summary: A worker carries an Amazon package. Bloomberg/Getty Images Amazon said it would increase delivery fees if the New York City Council passes a delivery bill. The threat sparked debate, including in Business Insider's comment section. Here's what our readers make of the Delivery Protection Act — and Amazon's response. Amazon's in-app call to action in New York City is provoking debate — including in Business Insider's comment section. On Thursday, we wrote about Amazon adding a notice in its app and on its website pushing back against the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, the proposal, which is before the New York City Council and has the support of Mayor Zohran Mamdani , would require companies like Amazon to directly employ their delivery drivers rather than use contractors. The notice, marked with a bright red "Attention" tag, indicated that Amazon would increase its fees by up to $5 per order if the measure becomes law. The strategy drew reactions from Amazon customers to the speaker of the New York City Council. Our readers also had thoughts, as evidenced by roughly three dozen comments on the story. Screenshot of the message Amazon began showing to customers in New York City on Thursday. Andy Kiersz/BI Some came out in support of the Delivery Protection Act, saying the proposal could benefit the workers who deliver Amazon orders in the city as well as other businesses. "It is time these trillion dollar companies to pay their workers their fair share," one commenter wrote. Another commenter compared Amazon to "the robber barons of old trying to dictate laws that it may not like." "I'm hoping we restore mom and pop stores," the commenter said. Even if Amazon goes through with charging more for delivery, some commenters wrote, New Yorkers will either absorb the cost or find other places to shop. "You can just take the hit to your pockets like the rest of us normal people do every day," one commenter wrote. "Or just leave the city then. I'm sure another company will be happy to take your place." Other commenters said the proposal could hurt businesses like those that Amazon contracts with under its current delivery service provider model. One reader wrote that last-mile delivery is "inherently unpredictable and messy" and lends itself to using contractors instead of full-time employees. "Anyoneeee who thinks this is a good idea doesn't know what they are talking about," the commenter wrote of the Delivery Protection Act. "People will just lose their jobs." "People who don't work in the industry don't understand what a nightmare for logistics this legislation will be," another wrote. "The only losers will be the customers and the 100's of people who do the deliveries," still another commenter wrote. Do you have a story idea about Amazon ' s delivery efforts? events.title: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes
events.summary: Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all. The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal. Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers. An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential. The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more. Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep. Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo. Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists. XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches. Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures. Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool. The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO 2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO 2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused. In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive. Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates. As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO 2 -cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch. That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up. events.title: OpenAI tightens grip on model resellers
events.summary: OpenAI put a new rule in place that gives the company more control over how much of the world — including China — can access its AI models. Gateways and routers that provide third-party access to OpenAI’s tech now need the company’s review and approval . Such gateways, the most prominent of which is OpenRouter, have become increasingly popular with developers and companies seeking access to a wide range of AI models: Instead of individual contracts with each lab, one account with a router can let you access hundreds of models from the US, Europe, and China. Beyond the technical details, the move has implications in the global AI race. US security agencies and companies, including Anthropic, have accused Chinese AI labs of distilling, or copying, American frontier models by routing requests through intermediaries that resell access to their models, which obscures the identity of the end user. Those cases largely involved gray-market resellers, known in China as “transfer stations,” but OpenAI’s new rule extends its oversight to any service standing between it and the people using its models. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Johnson urges Republicans to show up to work
events.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is warning House Republicans that their jobs aren't over yet after so many skipped town this week that GOP leaders had to call it quits. Why it matters: Republicans still have a month-plus left in the majority, but Johnson is struggling to get enough members to show up to make last-minute headway on the GOP's legislative agenda. GOP leaders were forced to cut the week short after 14 Republicans missed votes, leaving Johnson without the headcount needed to advance party-line legislation. Eleven of those 14 won't be returning next Congress. Driving the news: "To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote in a Friday letter to his colleagues . "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," he added. Zoom in: The outgoing speaker pointed to government funding, the annual defense authorization bill and permitting reform as priorities for the final weeks of the Republican majority. He also said he wants to pass "every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes" and force Democrats to take politically difficult votes. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson wrote.

events.title: Silicon Valley should ditch the 'handover' talking point
events.summary: The tech industry has enough of a public image problem with its warnings about AI leading to human extinction, and it risks further alienating people outside of Silicon Valley if it starts popularizing “the handover.” The handover is the period in which AI becomes so intelligent that it no longer makes sense for humans to make any decisions. Sam Altman brought the idea up on stage with me this week at Silicon Valley & The World, and he believes AI companies should do everything possible to avoid it. In a “positive” scenario, the handover turns humans into pets of AI overlords (Altman referenced Labradors): Humans have everything they need, from food to entertainment, and don’t need to work much. The dystopian idea is mostly a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where those inside AI companies see advanced models in their raw forms, doing both scary things like breaking into the internet and amazing things like solving the world’s most difficult math theorems. There’s no evidence we’re on the verge of a handover or anything remotely like it, so tech leaders would be wise to find a more optimistic talking point.

events.title: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
events.summary: The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10 After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed? The two sides have struck three deals long expected from this summit: food and drink, emissions trading and a youth exchange programme. The food and drink deal will ease Brexit controls on the vast majority of animal and plant products being traded between Britain and the EU, a boon for producers of meat, dairy, wine and flowers among many other products. If all goes well – and there is still an if – the deal will apply from 1 March 2028. The energy deal relinks the British and EU emissions trading schemes, shielding industrial producers on both sides from levies on polluting products, such as steel and fertilisers, as well as electricity. This should enter into force in 2028. Under the youth experience scheme, up to 100,000 British people each year would be able to live, work, travel and study in the EU for up to three years. The same number of young Europeans would be able to come to the UK. Young people should be able to take advantage of the scheme by 2030 at the latest. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, who studied at the London School of Economics when she was young, said it was a “very emotional moment” to strike the youth mobility agreement, while Andy Burnham addressed young people – saying: “This deal really is about lifting your life chances.” The two sides agreed to kick the can down the road for six months. The EU wants to ensure that young Europeans pay the domestic rate of tuition to study at British universities, capped at £9,790 in the current academic year, rather than the international rate, which can be four or five times higher. Under pressure from cash-strapped universities, the government has resisted this claim. The EU agreed a statement on Friday – not part of the joint text – that said it would not sign off the three deals (food and drink, emissions trading youth mobility), without a deal on equal treatment on tuition fees. The prime minister rejected this link, saying the deal was done. EU leaders have also expressed confidence in resolving the issue within six months. As a condition of getting the food and drink and emissions trading deals, the UK will be required to align with EU law in these areas, including new rules that it never had a say in writing. The UK will be allowed to attend relevant EU meetings as an observer without voting rights. After lobbying from Britain’s EU allies in northern Europe, Britain got a small upgrade to be in the room to observe discussions on future laws when they relate to “emergencies of specific relevance” to the UK, such as animal disease outbreaks. But it still cannot vote. The details are outlined in a separate text not in the main agreement. The next major agreement is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. The two sides aimed to wrap up this deal in 2027. This is a priority for five EU member states : Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions. But there are no details on the size of the UK contribution. The UK agreed to work closely with the EU’s “Channel action plan”, which aims to crack down on smugglers who organise small boat crossings. The agreement will see law enforcement intelligence sharing between the UK and the EU, working closer with agencies such as Europol and the European border agency Frontex, and improved maritime surveillance from French authorities. The agreement promises “a new structured dialogue” on migration, with both sides pledging to disrupt smuggling networks, strengthening border management in the Channel to stop small boat crossings, and work more closely with countries along migration routes. Both sides will require “shared financial commitments” given the “shared nature” of the challenges, according to the agreement. Von der Leyen said Britain and the bloc would work together along the entire migration route and to prevent dangerous Channel crossings, which she argued would also save lives. Burnham also expressed interest in the plans of five EU member states to negotiate an offshore “returns hub” with Rwanda for people with no right to stay in the EU. In a significant win for the UK, the EU has agreed to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” on touring artists. This does not sound like much.

events.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
events.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. events.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains A ndy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits? Mr Burnham is on to something: polls consistently show that many voters think that Brexit has not worked out well and rejoining the bloc has gained popularity. The rise of the European radical right also probably changes the EU’s calculation about Britain. Building closer ties with a broadly pro-European British government could mean the terms of future agreements allow for Britain’s preferential access to the bloc. However, Brussels won’t offer something for nothing. As the Swiss ambassador to the UK told a Lords committee earlier this year: “If you want to have access to the common market, you will need to pay some cohesion money.” Horse-trading is a feature of geopolitical life for Brexit Britain. The EU is using public borrowing and procurement rules to encourage defence production within Europe, create economies of scale and strengthen European supply chains. Britain balked at the financial contrib ution Brussels wanted in order to join up. With British defence manufacturers in danger of losing access to an expanding European market, both sides have made noises about getting around the table – but so far a deal remains elusive. Brussels’ “ Made in Europe ” industrial strategy poses another challenge. Britain imports cheap Chinese electric vehicles while the EU seeks to protect its producers. British carmakers, however, depend on European demand. Under proposals advanced before this meeting they risked being shut out of the market. The summit recognised this danger, promising closer cooperation on electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require Britain to align its policies with Brussels – without having a vote over them. This week Labour’s Stella Creasy, and Bernd Lange, a senior German MEP, proposed a Swiss-style deal to restore Britain’s economic and diplomatic influence without rejoining the EU. But greater market access without membership means accepting rules that Britain cannot influence. Mr Burnham’s reset pursued selective agreements – allowing Brussels to press for concessions. Switzerland offers a warning: frustrated by more than 120 bilateral deals , the EU insisted on a new framework. Down the line, Britain could face the same dilemma. Mr Burnham must calculate how long the country can negotiate the benefits of membership without confronting the costs of staying outside. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Bitcoin's regulation bull case is played out. What could drive crypto gains moving forward
events.summary: The Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act on Sept. 15, leaving the industry without the broad market-structure law it had sought. Crypto executives interviewed by CNBC point to tokenization and Wall Street's use of blockchain infrastructure as a potential next catalyst. Investors are also watching inflation, geopolitical risk, cybersecurity and the maturation of the artificial intelligence trade. Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said.

events.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
events.summary: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged. An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable. News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries. Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran . The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August. Experts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious. “This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM). He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.” After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM. Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.” Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence. That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said. He added that Pen Test Partners had also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said. “The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.” A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it had “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”. RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved as it “included dismantling our hardware”. Evans saidd: “In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps.”

events.title: The case for an AI downturn
events.summary: Reed’s view Anthropic’s IPO went on as well as anyone could have reasonably hoped. It was up 17% over its initial price with a valuation of about $1.3 trillion, making it the biggest debut in history. But Anthropic shares are down 11% so far today, and the rest of the market is down, too, as skepticism of the AI trade builds. The funny thing is, there are a lot of people in the tech industry who say they would actually like to see things slow down. That’s because all of the resources are being funneled into a small group of companies building essentially the same product, leaving little room for other ideas. The “tokenmaxxing” craze earlier this year has accelerated revenue growth at the frontier labs and hyperscalers. But if every unit of computer memory and every accelerator is concentrated among only a handful of players, innovation — and AI adoption — starts to slow down. I’ve heard this from tech companies that work with industry players but it’s also backed up by a report by Wasabi and the Centre for Economics and Business Research. Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia is also bad news for the pro-innovation crowd. Huang was a major proponent of open-weight AI models and a healthy startup ecosystem. The open-weight models, many of them coming out of China, were helping seed wider AI adoption, and it’s likely that will slow down if Chinese entrepreneurs and tech companies can’t get their hands on enough Nvidia chips. Another thing that could slow AI development: the number of cybersecurity worries building up at businesses around the world (more on that below). AI is helping everyone become more productive, including threat actors and nefarious nation states. The next period could be one of massive growth for the biggest players in tech, but it’s increasingly looking like one in which the real-life impacts of AI take longer to materialize than we initially expected. Notable Despite CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to slow down model development , Anthropic is accelerating its AI advancement , AP reported.

events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today issued a proposal to address the inefficiencies in the current governance and funding model of the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT). The Commission is proposing to rescind Rule 613 of Regulation NMS, which obligates the national securities exchanges and national securities associations (SROs) to establish, implement, and maintain the CAT. In its place, the Commission proposes to require SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to the Commission or its designee substantially the same information currently required to be recorded and reported pursuant to current CAT requirements. This proposal would bring the CAT under the SEC’s direct control, while ensuring its continued operation with minimal disruption. The proposal came as a result of the comprehensive review of the CAT directed by SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins and follows exemptive relief and approved amendments that have, among other benefits, helped reduce the CAT’s projected annual operating costs by over $100 million and permanently eliminated the reporting of personally identifiable information to the CAT. In April, the Commission issued a concept release soliciting public comment on the CAT. In public comment, both investors and market participants voiced support for the Commission exercising more control over the management and funding of the CAT. “Today’s proposal addresses persistent concerns with cost overruns, funding, and governance of the Consolidated Audit Trail. The proposed rule would encompass the changes that we have already made towards rightsizing the CAT, including increasing its cost-effectiveness and eliminating the collection of personally identifiable information. The proposal is intended to put the CAT on a sustainable footing: accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs, to the benefit of our markets and those who participate in them,” said Chairman Atkins. The CAT supports regulatory efforts to administer and enforce the federal securities laws, but the decentralized governance structure established by the CAT NMS Plan has presented certain challenges to administering the CAT and warrants revisiting. The proposal would rescind Rule 613 of Regulation NMS and add new Rule 17a-26 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, requiring SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to the Commission or its designee substantially the same information that is currently required pursuant to current CAT requirements, such as Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, related SRO compliance rules, and related exemptive relief previously issued by the Commission. Proposed Rule 17a-26 would require that data to be reported to the Commission or its designee instead of to a CAT system independently administered by the participants under a national market system plan. The Commission intends to use funds appropriated by Congress to pay the Commission’s costs relating to use, operation, and maintenance of the CAT system. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. events.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
events.summary: Staffers at the Internet Archive , the nonprofit “ digital library ” that runs the Wayback Machine , are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996 . Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals. “Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED. Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company. “We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.” The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation , the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet. Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit. Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI . The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.) Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better. “We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.” Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. events.title: Questions over future for Australian workers as mass lay-offs hit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Slowing economy and rising AI create new generation of unemployed Tom Kearney lost his job in advertising and was forced to sell his home. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) More Australians are losing their jobs as the economy slows and the use of AI rises. One former advertising worker has been laid off four times since 2019 and now has to sell his house. Unemployment could hit 5 per cent amid questions about what will happen to older workers whose jobs no longer exist. For Tom Kearney, the past two years have meant agonising uncertainty. He lost his job in advertising in February last year and has not been able to get full-time work since. He has been through four redundancies since 2019. After falling months behind on mortgage repayments, he put his home up for sale at the end of September, and signed the sale contract this week. "I've really held on as long as I can." Mr Kearney said his bank had allowed him to pause mortgage repayments for about five months, but he had not been able to make repayments since about June. "It has been an absolute roller-coaster," he explained. "I've been through the seven stages of grief and I've hit acceptance. "But I have had rage. I have had sadness. I have had disbelief. I just can't believe what's happening." Mr Kearney had built up 17 years of experience in advertising, but like many other white-collar workers, he has been hit by a slowing economy and the rise of AI. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com Since the latest job loss in February, he said he had put in more than 100 job applications but had only had three interviews. Mr Kearney fears things are going to get far worse as AI takes away more jobs. 'Collateral damage' the RBA expected The number of Australians losing their jobs is rapidly accelerating. Unemployment rate surges to 4.9pc in October The number of people in employment fell by 43,500 last month and the number of officially unemployed increased by 17,800, in seasonally adjusted terms. The unemployment rate jumped to 4.9 per cent in October as the number of unemployed Australians grew by 17,800. Some also dropped out of the workforce, pushing the participation rate down. It is the highest unemployment rate in the post-COVID era, but the figure is tipped to rise further. The rise is also happening much faster than the Reserve Bank had been anticipating. Economists expect the central bank will keep interest rates on hold next month. Leonora Risse says Australians already feel like they are in a recession. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) "It shows that the Reserve Bank's efforts to slow down the economy are working," Queensland University of Technology associate professor in economics Leonora Risse said. National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Dr Risse said while Australia was not technically in a recession, for many Australians facing higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressures, it felt like they were already in one. "The Reserve Bank is trying to tap the brakes on the economy to avoid the economy falling into a recession," she said. "The problem is it can still very much feel like a recession when we see unemployment increase so quickly." Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said the latest jobs numbers showed the Australian economy "already has one foot in a recession" and that "could well mean we've seen the last interest rate hike" for a while. On Wednesday, retailer General Pants went into administration, placing 500 jobs in doubt . It follows the loss of about 1,500 roles at David Jones . From big retailers to banks, airlines and even tech companies, mass lay-offs are emerging. Corporate Australia is undergoing a restructure and investing in AI while some companies are sending jobs offshore. Experts speculate companies might be looking to ultimately replace those offshore jobs with AI. "That could be a financial strategy for some companies," Dr Risse said. What becomes of workers replaced by AI? Dr Risse said the country was now at a place where the unemployment rate could soon tip over the 5 per cent mark. Regulator warns of 'interruptions' as AI evolves The regulator that oversees Australia's banks, super funds and insurers will run "stress tests" to examine hypothetical doomsday scenarios linked to AI. "There's still a lot more shifting in the economy to come in terms of that structural change where people are moving out of jobs that are being affected by AI," she said. Mr Kearney is still looking for a job.

events.title: Australians urged to have back-up plan for when tech services go dark
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts After tech outages, experts say Australians must look for 'emergency exit' during failures A string of global outages have raised concerns about how prepared Australians are when technologies go dark. ( Getty Images: NUniverse ) A global outage kept users from accessing the organisation's email system Outlook, its workplace messaging app Teams, its AI assistant and more. It took more than 24 hours for services to fully recover, and in the meantime more than 7.4 million outage reports were logged worldwide. Outlook down as Microsoft outage hits Australians Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today. By then, another incident was already unfolding. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had grounded flights across the United States , blaming a communications issue affecting all air traffic control centres. It marked only the second time a national ground stop had been issued since 9/11, and thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed. The root cause is still under investigation. On Monday, local time, one of the largest banks in the US announced a software bug had sent parts of its system offline. At the same time, cyber criminals used third-party software Optimizely to plant malicious code on multiple websites, including the BBC, CNN and Zoom. Outages at tech giant Apple and US hotel chain Marriott International followed on Tuesday, local time. On Wednesday, the classified communications network of the US National Security Agency (NSA) confirmed it was also fighting a tech outage . Experts told the ABC the incidents, while unrelated and caused by different factors, highlight an unfortunate reality of the modern world. 'We have to prepare ourselves' for online outages Relying on digital services is not something the public can avoid anymore, according to Swinburne University computer science associate professor Ali Yavari. "Several years ago, it was a safe box that you could lock, or you had your data stored somewhere physically," he said. "But these days, because we are using cloud services … there is the possibility of exposure." The Microsoft outages affected businesses globally. ( Reuters: Bruna Casas ) Instead, he noted, everyday users had to be prepared with a backup plan for when services went dark. "I think for digital services it's a very similar thing … we have to understand that there is a possibility [of] disruptions, of cyber attacks. "We have to prepare ourselves, train ourselves, be careful about what we're sharing." Australia needs 'digital resilience' Shifting Australia's dependence away from US technology companies and towards resilience will require significant investments, experts warn. Queensland University of Technology post-doctoral research fellow Ashwin Nagappa likened the situation to being ready for a natural disaster. "We see public service announcements on ABC about bushfire preparedness, like keeping a radio at home in case of outages," he said. “We're aware of those situations, but in scenarios where Meta goes down, Google goes down, what is our plan? "[These] companies are building Jenga blocks [of systems] and then putting a small link in. Then that tiny link breaks and it collapses the whole Jenga tower." Microsoft blames 'latent defect' as investigations continue Microsoft's investigations have so far pointed to a "latent defect" for last week's outage, ruling out AI as the cause and finding its servers had become "overwhelmed and unresponsive". “There’s no sign of a hacker," said Walayat Hussain, an associate professor at the Australian Catholic University. "This looks like Microsoft's own systems tripping over themselves, and that is the real warning. At the NSA, officials blamed a software update, finding no evidence of a cyber attack. The only one so far attributed to a malicious force was the Optimizely incident, which affected visitors to the websites of 178 organisations. The more that people rely on digital services, the more they [need to] adjust when things go wrong, Dr Yavari said. The US NSA has been hit with a tech outage affecting its internal communication. "There will be a day [when] we get used to all these disruptions and find backup alternatives to use during the disruption," he said. "People will also become smarter in terms of cyber attacks. "We have to accept that we need to invest [in] things that can reduce the frequency of these sort of disruptions, and the cost of cyber attacks for users.
