events.title: Is having debt actually bad?
events.summary: Ask most people whether debt is bad , and the answer will come quickly. Ask a financial adviser the same question, however, and the response is more considered. “ Debt isn’t inherently bad,” says finance coach and chartered accountant Carol Glynn. “Having debt doesn’t mean you have failed financially. What matters is the purpose behind the debt and why you’re using it.” Steve Cronin, financial adviser and founder of Dead Simple Saving, frames his response in straightforward economic terms. “There is cheap debt like mortgages and car loans , then there is expensive debt like personal loans and credit card debt. Expensive debt is bad and can ruin your life. Cheap debt is fine and can help you get ahead in life, as long as you can afford the monthly payments.” A mortgage sits at the better end of the spectrum for both advisers. The interest rate is typically low, and the borrowing is attached to an asset that builds equity or generates income. For UAE residents, however, the mortgage question depends on how long you’ll stay . “Buying is worth it when you plan to spend at least seven to 10 years in the country, and you value stability,” says Mr Cronin. “If you prefer flexibility of location or country, then renting is much better.” The gap between good and damaging debt The gap between good debt and damaging debt often comes down to basic knowledge. Ms Glynn identifies a cluster of common failures among borrowers, including not understanding interest rates or the effect debt has on their monthly income. “They don’t check their debt ratio, which is how much of their income the debt absorbs. They don’t do scenario planning to check whether they could still afford the debt if their income dropped,” she adds. Mr Cronin says many borrowers do not even know what interest rate they are paying. Knowing your limits matters as much as knowing your rate. The UAE has a regulatory safeguard – a debt burden ratio that caps total loan repayments at 50 per cent of monthly income – but both advisers recommend more conservative personal thresholds. Mr Cronin becomes concerned once repayments exceed 40 per cent of income. “You could easily lose your job, face a pay cut or see your variable loan payments increase when interest rates go up,” he says. Ms Glynn’s rule for mortgage debt is 30 per cent, and she recommends holding a larger emergency fund for anyone carrying debt beyond that level. The UAE’s particular pressures Living in the UAE brings its own pressures. The country’s visible wealth can make certain kinds of spending feel expected. “Lots of people appear wealthy and successful in the UAE,” says Mr Cronin. “People are attracted to the glamorous lifestyle they see around them, and they go into debt to fund it. But it’s a trap, and it makes you vulnerable if anything happens to your income.” He also points to the supply side of the problem. “The banks are quite willing to give you loan top-ups, card limit increases and new cards, so the temptation is coming from both sides: extra spending and extra debt.” Ms Glynn, who works with clients across several markets, says the UAE has a lifestyle expectation she doesn’t often see elsewhere. Credit is significantly easier to obtain here than in other countries, with attractive perks – points, gym memberships, travel benefits – that draw people in before they fully understand the terms, she adds. “The issue is that not everyone understands how credit cards work, so they get into credit card debt without meaning to.” Navigating the products Credit cards, used correctly, draw measured praise from both advisers. Ms Glynn puts all her spending on hers to accumulate points, then clears the balance in full each month. “I never pay interest, because the rates are so high they would cancel out any benefit I get from points systems.” Mr Cronin agrees that credit cards are useful, offering purchase protection as well as points or cashback. But, he warns, “you must pay off your card in full each month, otherwise you’ll end up in a debt spiral”. Buy now, pay later services – prominent in the UAE through Tabby and Tamara – draw far more caution. “You are just kicking the can down the road,” says Mr Cronin. For Ms Glynn, they’re useful for covering a high, unexpected cost you cannot meet using cash. “Spreading that cost over a few months can help. They shouldn’t be used for everyday payments, because you lose clarity over your finances very quickly.” Personal loans, meanwhile, draw the harshest verdicts. “I don’t recommend personal loans at all,” says Mr Cronin. Ms Glynn has one exception: consolidation – moving multiple high-rate credit card balances into a single, lower-interest structured repayment. If you’re already worried For anyone concerned about existing debt, both advisers begin with the same instruction: clarity first. “Write down every debt,” advises Ms Glynn. “For each credit card or loan, note how much is owed, the interest rate and the minimum monthly payment. Then rank them from most to least expensive by interest, and from lowest to highest balance.” It is also important to be honest with yourself about why you ended up in debt, she adds. “Look at your financial habits and your money mindset. If you clear the debt without changing the behaviour behind it, you’re at high risk of building it up again and repeating the cycle.” Mr Cronin warns that debt problems build slowly, then all at once. “Don’t allow yourself to get anywhere close to the edge: make sure you are able to save some money each month and have an emergency fund so you can be resilient against whatever life throws at you.” The right size of emergency fund, which Ms Glynn calls a “cash cushion”, is personal, “but I would start with at least three months of living expenses”, she says. “Then decide if that would be enough to cover loss of income until you can find a new role. If not, then consider saving six months of living expenses. Keep it in a high-interest account so it is also growing in value while serving its purpose to protect you in the case of financial emergencies.”

events.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
events.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people". Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028. The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker. Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe. The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030. A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block. There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU. Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more Published 9 hours ago What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 10 hours ago Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 9 hours ago European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too." On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data. Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel". The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028. Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy? Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that". He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far." The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people. Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner". He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are. Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it. "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship." Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this. The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029. Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming". Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs". Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

events.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
events.summary: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips? The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue. Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024. But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision. That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers. However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue. Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space. Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts. That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale. events.title: ADGM aims to rank among top five global financial centres
events.summary: ADGM is aiming to join New York as one of the world's top financial centres, the head of its regulatory authority has said. ADGM ranked 13th on the Global Financial Centres Index, released in September. Financial centres are ranked by data from third parties including the World Bank, the OECD and the UN, as well as a questionnaire that attracts thousands of respondents. New York, London, Hong Kong, Singapore and Shanghai made up the top five, while Dubai International Financial Centre ranked ninth. “We want to be among the top five,” Rashed Al Blooshi, chief executive of the Regulatory Authority at ADGM, told The National on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in New York. “That means our services, our rules, our regulations, all of these things could be developed." ADGM currently holds roughly 14,000 total active licences after about 1,800 were added in the first half this year. Its assets under management grew 54 per cent year-over-year, while the workforce has climbed above 49,000. Mr Al Blooshi pointed to ADGM providing digital services and using artificial intelligence to speed up the licensing process, while also noting the need to attract high-net-worth people and asset management. “But we don't want them to come and just do the operation. We need them to get jobs, training, innovations, and in Abu Dhabi, and from Abu Dhabi to do investment even abroad,” Mr Al Blooshi said. Along with Dubai, ADGM operates under English Common Law, with independent courts and a regulatory framework supporting it. Mr Al Blooshi said operating under this framework makes it easier for multinational companies to understand the language and settle disputes. Mr Al Blooshi was part of a delegation this week that participated in the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum, which aims to advance partnerships with US companies and explore commercial opportunities. The first forum to take place in New York was held last year and resulted in agreements across digital infrastructure, financial services and other sectors. In his remarks on Thursday, Abu Dhabi Investment Office director Badr Al Olama said 26 financial institutions have announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM . More than half of those are US firms, he said. Cepa strategy Abu Dhabi's emergence as a major financial centre comes as the UAE continues to press forward with its Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa) initiative. The Emirates launched its Cepa strategy in 2001 as part of its diversification strategy to expand global market access and strengthen the country's position as a trade and logistics hub. The UAE has signed 38 Cepa agreements with trading partners, and aims to increase its non-oil foreign trade to $1.1 trillion by 2031. These agreements typically aim to reduce tariffs and other barriers to entry, facilitate investment and simplify customs procedures. The UAE signed its first Cepa with India in 2022, and most recently with Canada in October, although the latter has not yet gone into force. Mr Al Blooshi said the UAE has seen rising demand from other countries to enter into agreements that would boost bilateral trade. “It's becoming so effective to the economies," he said.

events.title: Bitcoin sell-off: Crypto is failing the 'digital gold' test again as it sinks with stocks
events.summary: Bitcoin’s recent sell-off has moved with risk assets again, weakening the case that it behaves as an independent market hedge. Experts point to rates, broad risk-off trading, ETF outflows and crypto-specific shocks as pressures on bitcoin. Institutional and corporate adoption has deepened, but it also gives investors more liquid ways to add or cut bitcoin exposure. Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency. Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors. The heavy midterm elections losses for the Republicans, the Binance hack, and a world on edge about the security of all things technology — FAA ground stop, the outage of the National Security Agency's highly classified internal communications system, several online banking outages — have not helped the mood when it comes to putting trust in the digital world. But the market itself may be the biggest factor. Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data. Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic. Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety. In the past month alone, bitcoin had dropped roughly $20,000, as of Friday morning, according to CNBC data. Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago." What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say. There have been many theories about how bitcoin would react based on different market and economic conditions. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida. When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said. Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield. Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show. How bitcoin is like gold, but also like the S&P 500 Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies. But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said. Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said. Did Democrats' midterms blue wave matter? Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective.

events.summary: The US tech sell-off rapidly accelerated on Friday as fears over the AI sector spreading across all major indexes, with newly public Anthropic plummeted more than 9 per cent. Worries that Wall Street’s biggest investment boom in decades is fizzling out drove the US equity benchmark to its longest slide since 2020, with the gauge down 3.5 per cent. The Nasdaq 100 lost 5.61 per cent, adding to its longest losing streak since 2020. Nvidia dropped 13.8 per cent as Reuters reported that US regulators are investigating its accounting practices. The past month has seen Nvidia lose more than 40 per cent of its value, after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Anthropic opened to huge fanfare on Thursday, reaching about $105 per share, but it has steadily declined since then. Other tech stocks were rocked, including Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet, all of which ended a brutal week in the red. “Smackdown!” said Steve Sosnick at Interactive Brokers. “The problem stems from investors’ rapidly changed perceptions about technology, particularly the pace and cost of the artificial-intelligence buildout.” Richard Saperstein at Treasury Partners said the stock market is going through an AI repricing, "reflecting an environment of slowing data centre buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth". The gloom is dragging other indexes down, too, with the S&P 500 losing 3.7 per cent on Friday while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.93 per cent. “We are in the midst of a garden-variety correction, with the market’s leadership moving around,” said Gaurav Mallik at Modera Wealth Management. “While we expect technology to recover and perform well, it may cede its leadership to other sectors like industrials and financials and more value-orientated areas of the market.” The sell-off has affected other assets as well. Gold dropped more than 4 per cent to $3,523, while Bitcoin was also down more than 4 per cent to roughly $58,880. The resurgence in volatility spurred demand for defensive shares and haven assets including Treasuries. The US dollar ended with a fourth consecutive weekly gain. Emerging markets were on the cusp of a bear market. Anthropic’s debut consumed the attention of investors, with stocks along the supply chain moving on even minor developments around the deal’s size or pricing. Now that the IPO is wrapped up, that exuberance is giving way to mounting doubts over the durability of the AI trade. Questions remain over whether the vast spending on the AI buildout can be sustained as regulation looks set to tighten and interest rates are likely to rise further. “In some investors’ eyes, the IPO was supposed to serve as a clearing event for stocks,” said Chris Senyek at Wolfe Research. “Instead, we see markets struggling for upside and continuing their downward trend.”

events.title: 'Life is hell on board': Dozens of crew members remain on Villa Vie's Odyssey 3 weeks after residents disembarked
events.summary: Villa Vie Residences' cruise ship, Odyssey, is at anchorage near Singapore. TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images The residents got off, but more than 60 crew members are still stuck aboard Villa Vie's Odyssey. Crew members say cabins lost AC, WiFi cuts out, and no one knows when they'll leave. "I just want to go home," one staffer told Business Insider. The residents of Villa Vie's Odyssey left more than three weeks ago, but dozens of crew members are still marooned on the cruise ship while it's anchored near Singapore . Two crew members told Business Insider they are struggling with difficult conditions aboard and a growing desperation to get home. "For us, it's becoming a real torture because all we want is to go home," one of them said. If you have worked on the Villa Vie Odyssey and have a story to share, get in touch with this reporter: jzitser@businessinsider.com . More than 60 crew members remain aboard On October 27, Villa Vie residents were given a few hours' notice to disembark in Cambodia after the company suspended operations of the never-ending cruise — which offered passengers the chance to live out the rest of their days at sea by buying cabins for between $119,999 and $439,999. The shutdown followed months of cash-flow difficulties that Villa Vie attributed to rising fuel prices, resulting in deteriorating services, shifting itineraries, and requests for residents to provide additional funds . While residents are now ashore trying to salvage their retirement plans , Villa Vie cofounder Mikael Petterson confirmed to Business Insider on Thursday that between 63 and 67 crew members remain aboard the Odyssey, which was placed under arrest pursuant to a court order. In a November 8 statement, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said that "the crew onboard are reported to be well, and arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors." This week, two crew members said life aboard had taken its toll. "While we have been at anchorage, the atmosphere has been quite difficult," said the first crew member. The second said, "Life is hell on board." 'The conditions aren't ideal' During the past 24 days, the crew members said some cabins lacked air conditioning as temperatures climbed above 90 degrees. Both complained of frequent internet outages, making it difficult to call their families at home. The second crew member said laundry services had been suspended and the crew bar had been closed. The crew members also said the uncertainty over when they will be able to disembark has been particularly challenging, "We feel like everybody forgot about us," the second crew member said. "The conditions aren't ideal," Petterson said Thursday, "but they're not torturous." A view of Singapore from the Odyssey, which is at anchorage. Business Insider Petterson said the Singapore sheriff must approve the Odyssey's move from anchorage to a berth before crew members can disembark because the vessel is under arrest. Singaporean authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. He said Columbia Cruise Services, the vessel's manager, is responsible for operating the ship. "It's Columbia's responsibility completely to operate the vessel and improve welfare and all that stuff," Petterson said. Petterson said NRP Maritime Asset Management, which now controls the ship as the administrator of Oceanus Capital's loan, is responsible for putting money toward improving conditions. Oceanus Capital's mortgage claims against Villa Vie led to the ship's arrest. Julia Siebert, Columbia Cruise Services' chief operating officer, declined to comment. Nicolai Heidenreich, managing partner of NRP Maritime Asset Management, told Business Insider he does not "dispute" the crew members' claims of internet and air conditioning outages and reduced services, but pushed back against their framing of the overall experience. "What you're telling me, what you're describing, is not correct," he said. Heidenreich added that crew members have now been paid for September and October, acknowledging that Villa Vie had previously fallen behind on paying out salaries, prompting some residents to organize fundraisers for the crew. The crew members said they hope to disembark by the end of the week, though they said their expected departure dates have repeatedly shifted. "I just want to go home," the second crew member said. "I want to forget about Columbia, Villa Vie, and everything." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry
events.summary: Prediction markets are facing new limits on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would bar platforms from offering contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, an individual’s death, war, or U.S. military operations—the first legislation targeting the burgeoning industry to clear either chamber of Congress. Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) introduced the bill, formally called the DEATH BETS Act, to prevent exchanges and clearinghouses overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from offering or processing those contracts. It would also ban contracts whose outcomes are reasonably expected to depend mainly on someone’s death, even if the wording does not mention death.  The bill passed the Senate by a voice vote and must still pass the House before heading to the president’s desk. “They are offered with no regard for national security and in far too many cases, even basic morality,” Schiff said on the Senate floor. “These markets are operating in a Wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails.” As platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown in prominence over the past two years, they have offered contracts on seemingly anything , drawing scrutiny over bets tied to war, violence, or human suffering. They have also raised concerns about insider trading, as users can trade without publicly revealing their identities, making it harder for outsiders to spot potential conflicts of interest. Several cases have drawn politicians’ attention to these issues. One involved a Polymarket trader who made more than $400,000 betting on Nicolás Maduro’s removal from power before U.S. forces captured the Venezuelan leader in January. Kalshi also drew scrutiny over a market on whether Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei would leave office , which sparked a dispute after his killing when Kalshi declined to pay traders who had bet he would leave office, citing a rule that excluded death as a qualifying outcome. In his speech, Schiff pointed to a Polymarket bet on whether NASA’s Artemis II mission would explode, raising concerns about wagers on astronauts’ lives. He also cited a bet on whether Russian forces would capture the Ukrainian city of Myrnohrad. The companies’ leaders have previously pushed back on these criticisms. “We don’t list markets directly tied to death,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour wrote on X in February. Speaking at a conference in March, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called conflict-related markets a “complicated question” but defended their value as a source of useful information. “Kalshi has never listed death markets,” a spokesperson for Kalshi told Fortune . Polymarket declined to comment. Other platforms, such as Novig, avoid these contracts altogether, limiting their offerings to sports markets and restricting trading to users 21 and older. Pressure builds in Washington The bill’s passage comes amid growing political scrutiny of prediction markets, particularly after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in this month’s midterm elections. Over the past week, several Democratic lawmakers have criticized the platforms on social media. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) pointed Wednesday to Kalshi’s decision to pause trading on contracts tied to President Donald Trump’s public remarks, which have drawn concerns about insider trading . “The CFTC needs to do more to stop insiders from cashing in,” she wrote on X. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) focused on younger users, calling Wednesday for an investigation and a ban on sports prediction markets. He criticized Kalshi for allowing 18-year-olds to bet on sports and said users under 21 had wagered $3.9 billion on the platform. “They call it a ‘prediction market.’ It’s gambling,” he wrote. Though Democrats have been the most vocal, the scrutiny has crossed party lines. Besides cosponsoring the bill that passed Thursday, Curtis joined Warren last month in questioning Kalshi and Polymarket about potentially improper election-related trading. The Utah Republican has also backed separate legislation to ban sports and casino-style prediction contracts, citing concerns about young users’ exposure to gambling. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also announced plans to introduce legislation that would bar prediction market platforms from offering sports contracts without state or tribal approval, according to Bloomberg Law . Update, Nov. 20, 2026: This article has been updated with a comment from Kalshi and Polymarket. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026
events.summary: The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. The demand was driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence. Costs rose 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. It also pushed timelines and risk for contractors. All that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. The gain this year was about three times the last ten-year average. The report looked at over 500 live or recently completed projects in 62 global markets. It also included a survey of 400 experts in the global data center industry. While there was some stabilization in cost inflation this year, it was not enough to offset the huge growth in not just demand but speed of construction and delivery. "More aggressive schedules tie to contractors in particular and subcontractors baking in more risk allowances in their pricing," said Paul Barry, North America data center lead for Turner & Townsend. "So whether that's acceleration allowances, whether that's more overtime and labor attraction allowances, even just higher fees for taking on the risk of delivering at a faster pace than what they would traditionally take on." All of those things, combined with the spike in demand and the strain on the supply chain, translate into higher costs, he added. Capital expenditure on global data centers is projected to rise from about $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion per year in 2050, according to a recent report from PwC. The U.S. is expected to capture almost half of all global investment in AI infrastructure, which includes both data centers and chips. Power is, of course, key to all data centers, and 56% of those surveyed by Turner & Townsend globally said it was a major obstacle to delivery. Just over half said utility connections typically take between one and two years, and almost a third reported timeframes of over two years. Costs for power vary regionally — from $15.01 per watt in Silicon Valley to $10.51 per watt in Dallas, based on a typical 60-megawatt design. As with every type of construction in the U.S., labor continues to be a significant headwind. Just over one quarter of respondents said their contractor capacity, that is, the ability to manage construction backlogs, was sufficient. Going forward, Barry said he expects costs to moderate somewhat, with cost increases in the 6% to 10% range in the next year. A lot of the major projects have already started or are starting now, so cost risk has been baked into those contracts. "If this demand continues, then there'll be more continued flow of project starts and so on, but I think we've hit a big surge in 2026, especially of new big major projects that have been procured," said Barry. events.title: The Pentagon has been reacting to weapons shortages instead of getting ahead of the problem, watchdog finds
events.summary: Without a broader plan that links production, requirements, and funding, the US risks ongoing shortages. US Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Emilio Murphy The Department of Defense is risking running low on munitions without better planning, a watchdog report said. Officials told the GAO that DoD is reacting to global events rather than focusing on total requirements. Major concerns surround US stockpiles and munitions management. The Pentagon's lack of an overarching plan for munitions production and requirements risks leaving it poorly positioned to adequately address munitions shortages, according to a new government watchdog report. The US war in Iran has raised major concerns about the state of weapons stockpiles, especially for critical munitions. While the Department of Defense can track munitions across the department, it lacks a broader plan and a centralized office for its long-term munitions goals and strategies. On Thursday, the Government Accountability Office , a Congressional watchdog agency, released a report on the need for planning and leadership to address persistent munitions shortages. The GAO said that the US war in Iran has spotlighted the importance of addressing munitions stockpiles and industrial base production issues. Conflicts in the Middle East, as well as US support for Ukraine, have taken a heavy toll on US munitions stocks. The problem, the GAO said, is that "DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements. According to DoD officials, in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements." The office cited the US Army's ramp-up in production of  155mm artillery shells as an example. The increase addressed shortages from US support for partner nations, Ukraine in particular, rather than the deeper need for better overall munitions management. "Without developing an overarching munitions plan that identifies long-term goals, strategies for achieving such goals, and metrics to gauge progress, DOD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement," the report said. Further, the Pentagon doesn't have a single office that's in charge of improving munitions stockpiles or planning. The services told the GAO that without dedicated leadership to address these issues, it could be challenging to pursue progress. And while DoD can track munitions data across the services, the report said that there is limited oversight and regularity for reviewing this information. The department-wide data is fueled by individual tools from each service. The GAO recommended developing an overarching plan to improve production-linked inventory levels, funding, and long-term goals; establishing a single point of authority for that plan; setting regular timelines; and developing a data management plan to track munitions. When asked about the GAO report, a DoD official told Business Insider the US is "fully equipped to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing, and has already conducted successful operations across multiple combatant commands while preserving a deep, ready stockpile to defend our people and interests." It declined to comment on external studies or reports. The Pentagon has been working with US defense firms to significantly increase Patriot interceptor and Tomahawk missile production, among other weapons. The US has burned through critical munitions like these combating Iran and its proxies in the Middle East. Replenishing key stockpiles, however, could be a substantial undertaking. In the meantime, some officials and analysts have raised concerns that US stockpiles of certain weapons may be dangerously low, threatening readiness for other conflicts, including a potential war with China . events.title: We took our 4- and 6-year-olds to Europe and hardly visited kid-focused attractions. It made the trip better for us all.
events.summary: Our family spent almost three weeks in Europe learning about local culture and history through a range of activities — most not kid-focused. Blythe Chadim On a family trip to Europe , my husband & I chose activities that appealed to us, not just our kids. We kept our kids engaged in more adult activities by finding ways to relate them to their interests. We set expectations ahead of each activity and left room for spontaneity and flexibility. In July, my husband and I took our then 4- and 6-year-olds to Europe for almost three weeks. We began in Poland visiting Warsaw and Krakow, then spent almost a week in Prague before ending our trip at a resort in the Austrian Alps . At each destination, we prioritized things we, as adults, would enjoy — and it made the trip better for everyone. Everything we did was kid-friendly, but our activities weren't necessarily kid-centric. Of course, we made time for park play, and we even visited a children's museum in Prague, but by choosing activities my husband and I wanted to experience, we gave our children a more culturally rich vacation, which is exactly what we wanted. We avoided sightseeing fatigue by keeping the activities varied We let our kids guide us through the Royal Castle to keep them engaged. Blythe Chadim I love learning about history, especially in places I've never visited, but even I don't want to spend every waking moment in a museum. Luckily, there are many ways to experience history and culture, and we kept that in mind as we chose activities for our family. In Warsaw, we visited the Royal Castle, which was severely damaged in World War II. My husband and I wanted to see this incredible story of resilience and reconstruction firsthand, and we knew our kids would enjoy the opulence and grandeur of a real-life castle. We chose a self-guided tour, and our kids enjoyed having their own earbuds and listening devices. We let our boys guide us through the castle, which kept them more engaged, and we left when they'd had enough. In Krakow, we tried one of Poland's most iconic foods in a family-friendly pierogi-making class. Our cooking-class guide shared her family's pierogi recipe, passed down through generations. My husband and I loved connecting to Polish culture in such a special way, and our kids loved the hands-on experience of kneading the dough and shaping their own dumplings. The best part was how excited they were to try the pierogi because they had helped make them. It's an experience we still talk about, and can even recreate at home once in a while. We made a few special stops at the Czartoryski Museum in Krakow. Blythe Chadim Though museums weren't our main focus, we toured two in Prague and one in Krakow. In each place, we chose a few exhibits we wanted to see and left the rest of our time open. At the Czartoryski Museum, we saw Leonardo da Vinci's "Lady with an Ermine," and it was a highlight of our trip. The museum was also small enough to walk through without our kids getting antsy. At the National Museum in Prague, we saw gems and minerals. Blythe Chadim At the National Museum in Prague, we focused on the gems exhibit and Czech history. The museum is quite large, so we broke it up into multiple days, including a stop at the children's museum. We also took ice-cream breaks when the kids needed to rest. We found fun ways to relate our cultural activities to our kids' interests Our kids were intrigued by the Wieliczka Salt Mine. Blythe Chadim Tell your kids you're taking them to visit a salt mine and you might get some eye rolls. But tell them you're going on a real-life Minecraft adventure, and their reaction becomes wonder and excitement. And for our tour of the Wieliczka Salt Mine near Krakow, we did just that. The 135-meter descent was a lot of stairs for young kids, but the excitement of bringing their favorite video game to life kept them motivated. The Wieliczka Salt Mine made the boys feel like they were in a video game. Blythe Chadim We explored excavated caves and intricate carvings, and the kids may have licked the walls a time or two, but with something different around every corner, our boys stayed engaged. Our children also love music, and now that our oldest takes guitar lessons, he's become more interested in how other instruments work. We used that interest to introduce our boys to classical music by taking them to a nighttime concert at Saints Peter & Paul Church in Krakow. We enjoyed live music together at Saints Peter & Paul Church. Blythe Chadim After a long day of exploring, we knew our kids would be tired, so we sat in the back so we could sneak out when we needed to. They especially enjoyed watching the violinists, and our youngest pretended to play along. When we took the kids to Europe, we did the things we wanted to do as adults, but we also kept our expectations in check and got creative. Blythe Chadim For us, traveling with kids means making time for children's activities and outdoor play, but it doesn't mean only doing those things. We found that by keeping our expectations grounded in reality and finding fun ways to include our kids in more adult activities, we enjoyed a more well-rounded experience. We've learned that kid-appropriate activities don't have to be solely kid-focused to be enjoyable for the whole family. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Anthropic slid to just 5 cents above its IPO price, a stunning reversal of its first day pop
events.summary: Anthropic’s stock has come within a hair of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made one day earlier during the AI company’s blockbuster Wall Street debut . Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.05 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading, before recovering some ground and climbing to roughly $87 in midday trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded. At its lowest point on Friday, Anthropic’s stock traded just a nickel above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion. The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks. Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day. Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless of how the stock trades in the coming days and weeks. events.title: Silicon Valley needs to listen to the AI backlash
events.summary: Ashley’s view Earlier this week at Semafor’s inaugural Silicon Valley & the World conference in Palo Alto, I interviewed Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat with some 2028 presidential buzz. At one point during our conversation, as he beamed in virtually from Washington, he described one particular data center project in New Mexico as being the size of “a thousand football fields.” A participant in the front row rolled their eyes and shook their head, clearly exasperated at the comment. As the interview continued, the audience laughed when Kelly joked about President Donald Trump threatening to jail him, stared blankly when he spoke about regulating AI, and perked up when he talked about how Washington is thinking about investigating the controversy surrounding ousted Nvidia leader Jensen Huang. Toward the end of the interview, Kelly made the 1,000 football field comment again, in the context of data center projects needing to be built thoughtfully — with guardrails and input from the local community. The same audience member that rolled their eyes raised their hands in disbelief. After the interview, I fact checked the claim that a data center project could be quite so large. According to a report in the investigative outlet Searchlight New Mexico, the project’s acreage is indeed equivalent to about 1,000 football fields. The exchange was a perfect encapsulation of the dynamic between Silicon Valley and the rest of the United States right now: Those building the AI-powered future are well aware that not everyone is bought in on their vision. That was abundantly clear after the midterm elections, in which more than 40 ballot measures seeking limits on data center growth passed across the country, and candidates who embraced pro-AI regulation messaging handily won in competitive districts. But the post-midterms soul-searching only goes so far, at least at the Rosewood Sand Hill, nestled among top venture capital firms dotting Menlo Park. From my permanent perch in Washington, I know that Silicon Valley knows they have a problem. But they’re squinting at it, red-teaming it and trying to invent their way out of it. It’s reminiscent of how Big Tech companies viewed the lawsuits, Capitol Hill investigations, and Justice Department antitrust cases that piled up as anti-tech sentiment grew in the last decade: Expensive, and a hindrance to all-out growth; but ultimately, the cost of doing business. Tech executives are looking to keep building and growing, even as the financing gets more precarious and the infrastructure as well as the regulations that control it get harder to navigate. For many in Silicon Valley, AI anxiety and disdain can be explained away as a marketing problem, an education problem, or a location problem. For these innovators, it is not, however, a sign to stop. This attitude from AI and tech companies is not new. But the raging anti-AI public sentiment, considerably more intense than the tech anxiety of past years, is. And governors and state lawmakers across the country are ready to pounce (some are already pouncing ). So while newly empowered Democrats on Capitol Hill may not ever manage to pass significant AI regulation in the new Congress, and companies will surely find ways to appease Washington, tech leaders should perhaps take complaints about the scale of AI growth, including data center projects matching the size of 1,000 football fields — more seriously. Room for Disagreement Tech executives may face a hostile environment in Congress and in most of the states, but they’ve still got a powerful ally in the White House. Trump this week warned that “robust” regulation of AI could “stifle” development. “We won’t allow that to happen, frankly,” he said at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

events.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
events.summary: The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times. In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports. And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move. The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers". Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow". Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK? This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout. Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East. It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers. This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry. However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced. No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports. Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape. In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market. But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports. The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040. Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation. The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes. The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale. Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people". Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year. A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal. This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments. The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations. Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions. The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off. There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents. The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere. Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals. The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market. The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

events.title: Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’
events.summary: Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds. Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm. "We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's " Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business. Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday. "We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here." The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic. In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF , Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX , representing more than 21% of the fund together. Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses. The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year. Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble. "Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

events.title: I've been to all 50 states. There's one unexpectedly cozy city that should be on everyone's winter bucket list.
events.summary: In my opinion, Charleston, South Carolina, is the best US city to visit in the winter. Emily Hart I've traveled to all 50 states and have found that some cities are even better in the winter months. In my opinion, Charleston, South Carolina, is the perfect winter-travel destination. From lower rates at some hotels to quieter beaches, I love visiting Charleston in the offseason. When thinking about a winter getaway , many travelers likely imagine either a snow-covered mountain town or a warm, tropical destination. After visiting all 50 states, though, I've found that my favorite destinations generally fall somewhere in between. For instance, Charleston, South Carolina , might not be the first place you think of when booking a winter getaway, but in my opinion, it's well worth the trip. The winter weather in Charleston is pretty mild. Emily Hart Unlike more traditional winter destinations like Aspen or Stowe, Charleston doesn't revolve around snow or skiing. It also doesn't have the heat of a tropical beach destination . However, the mild winter means I can enjoy plenty of time outside. With average highs in the 60s and lows around 40 degrees Fahrenheit from December through February, I feel like I get the best of both worlds — and it's part of the reason why I keep going back. I love being able to grab a coffee and stroll through the historic downtown and French Quarter in the morning, enjoy a patio lunch or happy hour in the afternoon, and even walk along a nearby beach in just a light jacket. The offseason means I can enjoy the city without the usual tourist crowds. Emily Hart Hospitality is a major part of Charleston's economy, with tourists visiting in large numbers year-round. But if, like me, you enjoy a more peaceful winter getaway, the offseason is where you'll find the fewest crowds. Especially after the holidays, I've found the city is quieter for a month or two before spring festivals and higher tourism begin again. Luckily, though, there's still plenty to do in the cooler months. The holiday season brings many street fairs and special events, and the popular Southeastern Wildlife Exposition and Lowcountry Oyster Festival — which are both on my Charleston bucket list — take place in February. Visiting in the winter can be more affordable, too. Emily Hart For me, one of the best parts of traveling in the winter offseason has been the chance to stay at some of the area's high-end, luxury hotels for a fraction of what they might cost during peak season. Some hotels even offer discounted rates and complimentary upgrades during the cooler months. During my last visit in December, I was able to combine lower rates with my American Express Platinum Card hotel credit to stay at The Dewberry — a luxury property right downtown — for less than half of what I'd pay during other seasons. The holiday season is especially cozy in historic downtown Charleston. DenisTangneyJr/Getty Images There's something magical about the holiday season in Charleston. My last visit was about a week before Christmas, and I loved spending my days walking around the extravagantly decorated homes on the Battery, wandering through the American Gardens Holiday Market, and strolling King Street to browse shops for holiday gifts. I especially love that I don't need an itinerary to enjoy Charleston — during any season. Some of my favorite moments have been simply wandering the historic streets, taking in the decorations, and stopping into shops wherever something caught my eye. The nearby beaches are typically quiet in the offseason. Emily Hart One of the things I love most about visiting Charleston in the winter is that the coast feels completely different from the busy summer months. Several beautiful beaches are within driving distance of downtown, and in the winter, I can often walk for long stretches without seeing many other people. Edisto Beach, Isle of Palms, Folly Beach, and Kiawah Island are a few of my favorites, each with its own personality. Although it might not be swimming weather, I love taking a long walk along the shoreline, watching the waves, and enjoying the kind of peace and quiet you rarely find at these beaches during peak season. The shorter days also make it easier to catch a sunrise or sunset along the coast before heading into town for dinner at one of Charleston's seafood restaurants. events.title: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
events.summary: Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit. Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell. Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares. Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock. Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources. “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July . events.title: A judge confirms student-loan borrowers can be forced off a key affordable repayment plan
events.summary: A judge ruled that the Department of Education can involuntarily transfer student-loan borrowers off the SAVE repayment plan. J. David Ake/Getty Images A judge will allow the Education Department's forced transfer of student-loan borrowers off the SAVE plan. Borrowers said that, despite reaching their deadline to leave the repayment plan, no action has been taken. The department originally gave borrowers 90 days to transition off SAVE after eliminating the plan. The Education Department is allowed to move student-loan borrowers off an affordable repayment plan, a new legal filing said. A federal judge this week denied a motion filed by the law firm Public Goods Practice to stop the forced transfer of borrowers off the SAVE repayment plan. The Trump administration eliminated SAVE — a Biden-era plan that allowed for cheaper payments and a shorter timeline to debt relief — and started sending notices to enrolled borrowers in July with a 90-day timeframe to transition off the plan. If they did not move within their timeframe, the Education Department said, they would be automatically placed on a standard plan with the most expensive payments. Judge Loren Alikhan wrote in her ruling that the plaintiffs did not sufficiently establish harm, thus permitting the department to involuntarily move borrowers off SAVE. The case, however, is still ongoing — the ruling did not decide on the merits of the lawsuit, including whether borrowers should receive the relief they might have qualified for under SAVE before it was eliminated. While the department emphasized a 90-day timeframe to leave the plan, the deadlines have shifted. After 90 days, borrowers received a "final notice" extending their timeframe by an additional 30 days. The notice told borrowers this was their last opportunity to switch plans before being placed in a standard plan. However, some borrowers who remained on SAVE past their final 30 days told Business Insider they have remained in forbearance, and no action has been taken on their accounts. Public Goods Practice filed a request earlier this month to provide details on the timeline for the transfer. The law firm said in its filing that, when it asked the Education Department's counsel about timing for the transfer, it said it didn't "'know when borrowers whose 30-day period has expired will be moved to new plans.'" The department has not commented on its plans to involuntarily move borrowers off SAVE. Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com . events.title: All the connections between Haymitch and Katniss in 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping'
events.summary: Haymitch Abernathy and Katniss Everdeen are connected. Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is out in theaters now. The story sheds new light on the relationship between Haymitch Abernathy and Katniss Everdeen. This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games" series. After months of anticipation, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is finally in theaters. Fans have been clamoring for its release since Suzanne Collins published the "Sunrise on the Reaping" novel, which follows Haymitch Abernathy's experience in the 50th Hunger Games, in March 2025. Haymitch — portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in "Sunrise on the Reaping" — has long been one of the most fascinating characters in the "Hunger Games" universe, as the reclusive drunk Katniss meets in book one transforms over the course of the trilogy into one of her fiercest allies and protectors. The pair understand each other so well they can almost read each other's minds throughout the books, and in "Sunrise on the Reaping," Collins revealed Katniss and Haymitch are even more connected than readers thought. This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games" series . Katniss' father tied her and Haymitch together before she was born. In the original series, Katniss is from District 12. Murray Close/Lionsgate Katniss' father dies in a mining explosion before the events of the original "Hunger Games" trilogy . However, in "Sunrise on the Reaping," Collins reveals that Katniss' father, Burdock Everdeen, was Haymitch's best friend throughout their childhoods, and their close relationship helped Haymitch be better prepared for the Hunger Games. Specifically, Burdock taught Haymitch to set snares, which helped him find food in the arena. Burdock taught Katniss to make snares as well, and he also showed her how to hunt with a bow and arrow, which became her weapon of choice in the arena. The knowledge he gave her about plants also helped her survive. Burdock gave both Katniss and Haymitch skills that ensured they survived the Hunger Games. The Covey family shaped both Haymitch and Katniss. Rachel Zegler as Lucy Gray Baird in a still for "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." Murray Close/Lionsgate In her first "Hunger Games" prequel , "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," Suzanne Collins introduced readers to the Covey , a group of traveling musicians forced to remain in District 12 after the first rebellion. In the novel , the found family consists of three cousins, Lucy Gray Baird, Maude Ivory Baird, and Barb Azure Baird; a set of brothers, Clerk Carmine and Billy Taupe; and a wandering soul named Tam Amber. Lucy Gray won the 10th Hunger Games, becoming the first tribute from District 12 to survive the arena. A young Coriolanus Snow mentored her during her Hunger Games, and they had an ill-fated love affair that led to her mysterious disappearance at the novel's end. Collins leaves "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" open-ended, as it's unclear if Snow killed her or if Lucy Gray fled to the woods. In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch says that Burdock has Covey cousins on his mother's side, making Katniss a descendant of the Covey. Likewise, Haymitch's girlfriend, Lenore Dove, is a member of the next generation of the Covey, tying both Katniss and Haymitch to the family. In fact, Haymitch wouldn't have even been in the Hunger Games if not for his love for Lenore Dove. Katniss and Haymitch had parallel reaping experiences. Lionsgate Fims In "The Hunger Games," Katniss volunteers as a tribute after her younger sister, Primrose Everdeen, is reaped. Katniss is widely known as the first volunteer for District 12 — making it all the more surprising that Haymitch was not actually reaped for his Hunger Games either. During the reaping for the 50th Hunger Games, Woodbine, one of the male tributes from District 12, fled after his name was called. Peacekeepers responded by shooting him, and when Lenore Dove tried to help Woodbine's mother protect his body, Haymitch threw himself in front of her to stop Peacekeepers from hitting her. His interference led the Peacekeepers to select Haymitch as Woodbine's replacement. Later, in "Catching Fire," Haymitch and Katniss became the last two people ever reaped for the Hunger Games. The tributes were reaped from the existing victors in the 75th annual Hunger Games, making Katniss the only option for female tributes and Haymitch and Peeta Mellark the options for male tributes in District 12. Haymitch's name is selected, but Peeta volunteers as tribute in his place. Haymitch tried to protect Katniss the same way he did Lenore Dove. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate For longtime "Hunger Games" fans , Haymitch's decision to jump in front of Lenore Dove on Reaping Day likely felt familiar. He makes a similar decision in "Catching Fire" when Katniss attempts to stop a Peacekeeper from whipping her friend Gale Hawthorne. Haymitch jumps in front of Katniss and scolds the officer for cutting Katniss' face ahead of her wedding to Peeta Mellark. The scene is eerily similar, but unlike his teen experience, Haymitch helps de-escalate the situation with the Peacekeeper during the interaction instead of making things more tense, protecting Katniss in a way he ultimately couldn't protect Lenore Dove. The mockingjay pin is significant to them both. A Mockingjay pin from "The Hunger Games." MediaNews Group/Bay Area News via Getty Images In the "Hunger Games" universe, mockingjays symbolize rebellion against the Capitol. They came to exist after jabberjays, mutts the Capitol designed to spy on rebels, mated with mockingbirds, creating a new species. Their existence highlights that the Capitol cannot control everything. Mockingjays are also meaningful to Katniss and Haymitch specifically. Katniss wears a gold mockingjay pin that originally belonged to Haymitch's competitor, Maysilee Donner, as her token from her district during the games. In "Sunrise on the Reaping," we learn that Tam Amber made the pin for Maysilee, who didn't like mockingjays until Haymitch taught her their symbolism. She says she will wear it if she survives the games, but she isn't given the opportunity. Years later, Katniss dons it, bringing down the Capitol with the pin on her chest. Katniss reminds Haymitch of his district partner from his Hunger Games. Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate One of Haymitch's fellow tributes from District 12 is Louella McCoy, a 13-year-old girl who wears her hair in two braids. Haymitch grew up close to Louella, who had a crush on Haymitch when she was 5 and told him he was her sweetheart. She got over her feelings quickly, but Haymitch called her "sweetheart" for the rest of their friendship, which was cut short when she died before the Hunger Games started.
