events.title: Don’t Bring Jensen Back
events.summary: Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar , the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd. Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . Under his leadership, billions of dollars ’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two ?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers. Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered. It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette? The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return. At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge. Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance.

events.title: White House replaces cyber director Sean Cairncross amid widespread tech outages
events.summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, and Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies is set to serve as acting director. The change follows a week of major U.S. technology outages affecting aviation, Microsoft services and government systems. The White House says it has no indication the recent outages were coordinated, state-sponsored or caused by a malign actor. White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies set to serve as acting director after a week of high-profile U.S. technology outages. The role, which advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates U.S. cyber policy across federal agencies, has been handed to Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, on an interim basis. A permanent national cyber director must first be nominated by the president and then confirmed by the Senate. Axios first reported Cairncross' exit, citing two White House officials who said President Donald Trump's chief of staff, Stephen Miller, pushed for his departure. The White House declined to comment. However, a source familiar with the White House's thinking told CNBC that the President fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position because he lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job. Davies has the credentials to excel in the position and has been Senate-confirmed, the person added. The Office of the National Cyber Director did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. It comes after a series of technology outages, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a worldwide Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency 's classified communications network. The White House has insisted that there are no indications of a coordinated cyberattack , state-sponsored activity or malign actor behind recent tech outages. Davies addressed her responsibilities in the new position and thanked Miller and Trump for their confidence late Thursday. "Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on," she wrote on X. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both congratulated Davies on her appointment. events.title: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
events.summary: Former GM CEO Dan Akerson says whoever replaces Mary Barra will have a difficult task because the next CEO will inherit rapid change in technology and the auto industry. Barra is the first female CEO of any major automaker, and the industry is facing ongoing challenges including artificial intelligence. Akerson's comments to CNBC come after The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside CEO candidates in addition to internal prospects. Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough." He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014. Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles. "It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change." Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson , CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable." His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession. Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise. "Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said. The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession. Stellantis , BMW , Toyota Motor , Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years. Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board. A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director. GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing. That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates." When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said. Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job. Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann , an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021. "Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job." Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946. Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker. "This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

events.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
events.summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force. Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason. Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all". But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers. The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed. Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities. Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said. Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it. If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks". Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients. But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests. Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party. There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers. Airbnb host Lisa Clewes said her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests Edinburgh-based holiday home owner Fiona Venter told the BBC that Airbnb's new rules were "nonsense" and would not accept bookings if guests refuse to take their rubbish away. Talking about a time when she was worried she might get a mice infestation after six bags of rubbish were left in her cottage, she said: "I would rather have my house still standing." But Fiona said increased cleaning costs due to the rule change would be unfair to those who do clean up after themselves: "Why should they pay extra for the guests that choose to abuse a cottage?" Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules Published 21 October No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests Published 1 November The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said. The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees. Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably. events.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
events.summary: A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web. The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices. According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed. The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk. Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution. Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.” From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts. Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish. Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket. “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.” “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg. The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter. It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email. Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online. The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes. Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors. “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted. Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web. Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes. “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Home Depot's AI bot helps shoppers avoid the dreaded second trip
events.summary: Home Depot says its Magic Apron AI assistant now fields millions of questions per month. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Home Depot was one of the first major retailers to deliver a customer-facing AI bot. The Magic Apron assistant now fields millions of questions per month, often about DIY projects. The retailer says the tech is leading to more complete carts and higher customer satisfaction. If there's one frustration many DIYers experience, it's the sudden realization that you brought home the wrong supplies for the job. It's a problem Home Depot is hoping to solve with AI . The home improvement giant originally built its early reputation in part on knowledgeable store associates, including plumbers, electricians, and other tradespeople who could help do-it-yourself customers. Now, with AI, the company is trying to put that project-based know-how right into consumers' hands. The company was one of the first major retailers to deliver a customer-facing AI bot, called Magic Apron. The platform was specifically trained on products and projects that Home Depot has loaded into the tool over the past two years, so it can serve as an advisor to shoppers. "What's important for our customers is the project and not the product," Rebecca Godecke, president of Home Depot's online division, said in an interview. "I think it's really easy to do single-item selling, but that's actually not what we think AI is best suited for." Godecke said she was recently with a shopper who had loaded her cart with a replacement toilet and other items for the project. They used Magic Apron to snap a photo of the cart's contents to make sure they had everything, and it delivered a helpful warning. "Magic Apron was able to identify that and say, 'You have an incompatible wax ring. You need to go back to this aisle and try again,'" Godecke said. A Home Depot store in Colma, California David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images "The last thing you want is you've taken off the old toilet, and you're about to put the new one on and you figure out that, 'Oh, I've got the wrong wax ring!'" she added. "That's a terrible conundrum to be in." Home Depot's journey with its AI assistant was an evolution to add more and more capabilities. When it first launched, Home Depot began by putting its know-how into a chatbot on its website. In March 2025, the assistant made a public introduction in the company's app and on millions of product pages. The app could answer product questions, summarize reviews, and give some how-to guidance. At a December 2025 investor meeting, a Home Depot executive said the app was beginning to move away from just answering questions and that the company was using the AI tool to build shopping carts for customers. The next month, the company expanded its partnership with Google to extend the app's AI capabilities. After testing in stores, the company rolled out in-store capability in August tailored to each of Home Depot's 2,000-plus locations, so that the assistant could guide shoppers to the inventory and layout of a particular store. It can also detect and communicate in multiple languages. As consumers have been using AI more in their own lives, shopping assistants are fast becoming a must-have for major retailers , including Walmart's Sparky, Amazon's Alexa, and Target's Ask Target. Walmart and Target both said this week that customer adoption of their AI agents is growing fast. A Home Depot store in San Jose, California David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Home improvement rival Lowe's has Mylow , which was developed in collaboration with OpenAI and serves functions similar to Magic Apron. Lowe's CEO Marvin Ellison said Wednesday that MyLow answers over a million questions per month and that users have a conversion rate three times that of non-users shopping online. Godecke said Magic Apron now fields millions of questions per month, and they're often about DIY projects that go well beyond simply finding a single item. Employees are also using Magic Apron to help shoppers complete projects that might extend beyond their specialties, she said. For example, a garden center associate may know a lot about plants, but feel less confident about exterior lighting. By solving for an entire project, she said the Magic Apron tool is leading to more complete shopping carts that get it right the first time. And that translates to fewer return trips to replace or return improper items. "What we're seeing is that as you use it once and you're familiar with it, you come back and use it more," Godecke said. events.title: Trump secretary's Christian messages to staff went "too far," judge rules
events.summary: A federal judge said Thursday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins' overtly Christian messages to department employees went "too far" and put enough pressure on staff to raise a First Amendment violation. The big picture: The Supreme Court has repeatedly weighed the boundaries of the Establishment Clause . While the judge said Rollins could express her religious beliefs with interested colleagues, she concluded the department-wide messages overstepped those boundaries by amounting to coercion. But a USDA spokesperson slammed the decision as "a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary" in a statement to Axios. Catch up quick: The complaint from a federal employees union and individual staffers alleged Rollins sent "increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including an Easter email where she celebrated "the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind." The USDA employees who sued, who came from varied religious — and nonreligious — backgrounds, reported that the messages made them feel pressured to share Rollins' beliefs. What's inside: District Judge Trina Thompson ordered Rollins to "recognize certain boundaries when disseminating messages which convey religious content." She determined the messages overstepped and suggested "acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure." "After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion," Thompson wrote. She said she was not trying to regulate Rollins' own religiosity; rather, she directed Rollins to follow her own department memorandum on religious expression rights, which states employees can't "use official authority to pressure subordinates." The other side: The administration argued that the employees lacked jurisdiction and that the secretary's messages fell "within this Nation's deeply rooted history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse, including on holidays." Members of the Trump administration frequently discuss their Christian faith, though the president himself has had a complicated relationship with Christians despite the evangelical MAGA base helping him reach the White House. The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What we're watching: A USDA spokesperson said the department "is evaluating all options including a prompt appeal." events.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
events.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how? Mercedes-Benz 's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it. In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high. Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure." The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant. German auto industry faces restructuring Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure. Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country. "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot." A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Berger agreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation." In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable. Unions dig in amid fight for survival Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek . The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached. Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic. Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation. "We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW. China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage. Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500. Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?' A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security." PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China. These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms. "The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany. With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit. Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi , which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year. "Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned. Production remains resilient despite decline Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well. Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA). IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability. events.title: As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive
events.summary: Anthropic options will list Monday, and they could be expensive. Traders estimate Anthropic implied volatility could land between 100 and 150. Traders are expecting heavy retail participation in Anthropic options trading. As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list. If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading. A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago. Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price. Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions. One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume." One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s." Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

events.title: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
events.summary: Anthropic underwriters exercised the “greenshoe” overallotment of shares, bringing the total amount raised to $93.5 billion. The AI company sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares at $83 per share in the record IPO. ANT stock closed 17% higher on the debut trading day. Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering , bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday. The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX , which held a record IPO in June. Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe." Anthropic defies the odds, holding record IPO despite ‘massively disruptive’ market Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices , Google , Microsoft , Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses. Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multitrillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout . CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI , now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise. The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone" in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic. "For us, it's like one stop on the journey," Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'" events.title: ‘Gloucestershire nouveau’: UK vineyard uncorks its 2026 answer to beaujolais
events.summary: Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years F orget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest. Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine. The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November . Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest. Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s. Customers can buy the wine directly from the vineyard’s shop or try it in its restaurant. In the 1980s, the harvest used to begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year, according to Three Choir’s winemaking director, Martin Fowke. This year’s prolonged summer of warm temperatures – and rain at the right time – meant the first grapes were picked on 20 August, a week earlier than the previous record set in 2025. The harvest ended on 9 October, by which time 200 tonnes of grapes had been collected across the vineyard’s 30 hectares (74 acres). The 2026 First Release is a run of 5,000 bottles of a dry, white wine containing solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes. “We now have an extra month to make the wine. We had riper raw material and longer in the winery,” said Fowke, calling 2026 a “record-breaking year”. He added that higher sugar levels and lower acidity allowed winemakers to make a product that was not possible in Britain 30 years ago. The early timing of the harvest surprised even the Three Choirs winemaker Jack Abbotts, who was on his summer break when picking started. “It’s usually a safe week for me, but this year it all snowballed,” he said. The changing climate has made it possible to grow grapes on a commercial scale in Britain, but it also brings challenges. “We found it hard this year,” said Fowke. “People kept saying: ‘This hot weather must be good for you’, but it was difficult because we knew the heat and lack of rain was challenging for farmers. We don’t need it to get any warmer, that’s for sure.” Vines have been planted as far north as Yorkshire and Scotland , as Britain’s wine industry expands. More than 1,100 vineyards are now registered in Britain. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning While Britain remains far down the list of global wine producers in terms of volume – behind countries including Uzbekistan and Tunisia – it is the fastest-growing wine region in the world , according to the property group Knight Frank. The area of planted vineyards in the country has quadrupled since the turn of the century, it reports. Some of the newer, smaller vineyards do not have their own winemaking facilities, relying on contract winemakers such as Three Choirs. The Gloucestershire vineyard also produces wine for about 40 others, including Llanerch, located west of Cardiff. English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, when the equivalent of 16.5m bottles, or 124,377 hectolitres, was produced, according to the industry body WineGB. The data for the 2026 harvest will not be available until early next year, although WineGB said in August it was “optimistic” about the size and quality after the hot growing season. If the UK climate continues to change and summers such as 2026’s become the norm, Three Choirs may consider growing new varieties. “We can evolve and change, but we would be planting cabernet sauvignon like they did in Bordeaux 50 years ago,” said Fowke, noting the shift from white to red grapes. “But that is not what we set out to do.” In the fog and damp of November in Gloucestershire, pruning of the vines ready for the 2027 growing season has already begun. “To have two good years in a row is not uncommon, to have three is unusual,” said Fowke.

events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has obtained a temporary restraining order, asset freeze, expedited discovery, and other relief against Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital, its co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s company Indianapolis-based Traders Point Capital, and Joseph Anderson to halt an ongoing Ponzi scheme. The SEC complaint alleges that Backward Hat, Williams, and Johnson fraudulently raised approximately $560 million from more than 2,000 investors and transferred more than $220 million to themselves to fund their luxurious lifestyles. According to the SEC’s complaint unsealed today, between about July 2022 and the present, Williams and Johnson utilized a web of entities to raise money from investors for alleged algorithmic high-frequency foreign exchange (FX) trading. Instead, the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi-like payments to previous investors and misappropriated investor funds to purchase exotic cars and expensive homes, to fund other unrelated businesses they owned, and to fund Johnson’s gambling habits. “The promise of a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money,” said Anne McKinley, Acting Associate Director for the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office. “We encourage the public to use the resources on Investor.gov to educate themselves on the traps and gimmicks bad actors use to lure them into fraudulent schemes.” As the complaint alleges, Williams and Johnson lured investors, including some of Williams’s investment advisory clients at a former employer, and used a network of promoters to sell limited partnership interests in a series of private funds to investors. All the while, Williams and Johnson promised that investor funds would be converted to crypto assets and then used to engage in FX arbitrage using a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm which they claimed always returned at least 6% per month. The complaint also alleges that Johnson expanded the scheme by raising money for another series of private funds he created under the names AI Capital and Traders Point Capital, which allegedly offered a similar investment opportunity as Backward Hat Capital. Also charged in the scheme is Joseph Anderson, who allegedly created fake financial reports for distribution to investors, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report, from a so-called third-party independent audit firm. The reports falsely stated that the purported returns generated by the Backward Hat funds had been confirmed and verified through a review of bank and brokerage records. In reality, Anderson and his company allegedly did not perform financial audit work, were not independent, and had significant financial interests in the scheme, and the reports contradicted bank records. The SEC’s complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, charges Backward Hat Capital, Traders Point Capital, Williams, Johnson, and Anderson with violations of the antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 and of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Williams and Traders Point Capital are also charged with violations of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against the defendants. The complaint also names an individual and several entities associated with the defendants as relief defendants and seeks from them disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest. In parallel actions, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York filed charges against Williams and Johnson and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) filed charges against Williams, Johnson, and several Backward Hat Capital entities. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the CFTC, the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Southern District of New York and the Southern District of Indiana, the FBI, the Indiana Securities Division, and the Utah Division of Securities. events.title: Senegal's president enacts budget by decree after rejection
events.summary: Senegal’s president enacted this year’s revised budget by decree on Thursday after it was rejected by parliament. Bassirou Diomaye Faye took the step a day after lawmakers voted down the first part of next year’s spending plan, widening a rift with the president that threatens to delay a new IMF loan. The proposed $12.3 billion budget for 2027 trims spending as the government tries to meet the lender’s conditions. Ousmane Sonko, the parliament speaker and a former ally of the president, opposes the government’s plans to cut expenditure and restructure foreign debt. Faye could again use his powers to enact next year’s budget by decree once parliament’s deadline expires in December, though some analysts expect him to dissolve the chamber first and call a parliamentary election for early next year. Final approval of the $2.2 billion IMF deal, agreed in principle in September, would help Senegal regain access to international debt markets, where some of its bonds traded below half their face value on Thursday. The new program would replace one that was frozen after billions of dollars in unreported government debt surfaced in 2024. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park
events.summary: Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset . Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory. Wendy Jones, 68, a grandmother from Hereford, was sitting in her mobility scooter for bingo with about 100 others when the ceiling collapsed. She was among six guests to be treated in hospital after the incident and died six months later. A postmortem examination revealed a clear link between the injuries she suffered and her subsequent death. Britannia Jinky Jersey, the parent company of Pontins, pleaded guilty at Bristol crown court to failing to discharge its duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. On Friday the company was fined £1m for the offence. Stephen Bennison, 60, an unqualified contractor who had been employed by Britannia Jinky Jersey to install soundproofing in the ceiling, was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months. An investigation by Avon and Somerset police, Somerset council and the Health and Safety Executive found that the ventilation ducting had originally been poorly installed decades earlier, before the site became a Pontins holiday park. But the immediate cause of the collapse was linked to soundproofing work carried out in 2015 when it was under Pontins’ control. During that work, Bennison stacked heavy sound-insulation slabs on top of the ventilation ducting, the investigation found. It concluded that the insulation in the ceiling appeared to have been leftover material which could not be returned to the supplier – and stacking it on the ducting served no practical purpose. The court heard that neither Britannia Jinky Jersey Ltd nor Bennison properly assessed whether the ducting could safely bear the significant additional weight. Rachael Taylor, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “A family holiday ended in tragedy because basic safety responsibilities were not met. “Wendy Jones had every right to expect she was entering a safe environment. Instead, failures by Britannia Jinky Jersey Limited and Stephen Bennison resulted in the collapse of ventilation ducting and the death of a grandmother who was there to play bingo.” Taylor said Jones’s death was avoidable. She added: “Those responsible for the safety of the public must ensure work is carried out competently and safely. Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Mrs Jones, and anyone else affected by this tragic incident.”

events.title: These US fishers see offshore wind as a ‘godsend’. Trump wants to shut it down
events.summary: Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream O n a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island. “God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy. Souza and his three-man crew were fishers by trade, but this trip was different. Instead of fishing, they were working for Sea Services North America, a co-op funded through contracts with offshore wind developers. It was welcome work for these fishers who weather a legally restricted scalloping season. Sea Services retrained the fishers to work in offshore wind and gave them a second stream of income. But this work put them at odds with other fishers who viewed offshore wind as an existential threat to their industry. Commercial fishers have sued wind companies, arguing that the projects could displace them from their traditional fishing zones and wreak havoc on marine ecosystems (US fishers are allowed to fish in wind-lease zones , except for 500-metre exclusion zones around construction sites, and construction can have positive and negative effects on marine life). Yet, now, in New England, a cooperative of about 200 fishers is challenging the idea that offshore wind and the fishing industry are natural opponents. Sea Services North America trains and equips fishers to support offshore wind construction, an opportunity that provides them with a second stream of income. Sea Services pays each fishing boat $4,500 a day plus fuel. Souza, who was initially skeptical of offshore wind, says the opportunity has been a “godsend”. That godsend, however, may soon come to an end. Since returning to office last year, Donald Trump has systematically attacked offshore wind projects, saying his goal is to not allow any “windmills” to be built. In January 2025, the president issued an executive order halting construction of five offshore wind projects on the east coast. Sea Services North America was founded in 2020 by another once skeptical fisher. Gary Yerman, 76, had been fishing for more than four decades when he began hearing about proposed commercial-scale offshore wind projects. He and other fishers feared the windfarms could harm their industry. He didn’t want windfarms in his fishing zone, but he believed they were too big to fail. “They’re gonna win,” he thought, deciding to cast his lot with the projects. In 2019 he and Gordon Videll, a friend and local lawyer, visited Northern Ireland, where they met with fishers who were working with developers building offshore windfarms and other structures. “We saw how it was benefiting the fishermen there,” Yerman said. Videll noticed that the local fishers drove nice cars. “This provided a real annual income, which, if you’re raising a family, it means everything,” he said. They returned to the US eager to find a way to bring similar benefits to their fellow fishers – which meant earning the trust of a skeptical industry. “There was a lot of fellas that were very angry because we joined in on building these windfarms,” said Videll, Sea Services’ CEO. “Nobody trusted it.” They convinced just one fisher to give it a shot, and over time, more joined. The pandemic, which struck just as Sea Services was getting off the ground, may have helped Yerman and Videll’s recruitment efforts. As restaurants closed , demand for seafood fell, meaning fishers in New Bedford and nearby fishing towns were looking for extra work. “People had to make decisions they might not have made otherwise,” Videll said. They found a relatively eager labor pool in local scallopers, who work on boats that are legally restricted from fishing more than 36 days a year to prevent overfishing, leaving the owners of these highly specialized boats looking for extra sources of income during the off-season, said Capt Jack Morris, who owns a fleet of scallop boats including the Pamela Ann, and joined Sea Services in 2021. “It’s a huge benefit Sea Services has brought,” Morris said. “With the [scallop] fishing season being so short, they are able to continue buying groceries, paying insurance, taking care of the house.” Stacy Alexander-Nevells, a business owner who works with Sea Services, runs a 19-boat commercial fishing operation with her father. Their boats mostly harvested scallops, but revenues were inconsistent and federal restrictions were always changing. “Working with Sea Services was another income stream,” she said. “We had to diversify. Now the boats aren’t just sitting at the dock, and the guys aren’t unemployed.

events.title: I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
events.summary: In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity. I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them. In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be. The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.” Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it. I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.) I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second. A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory. Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters. My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real. But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view. This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake. Signaling a Video’s Provenance When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do? The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording. Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID , embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin. Apple recently took these ideas a step further . On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed. These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be. Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.” Real-Time Verification This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls. In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again. All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop. This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes. Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by fra

events.title: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
events.summary: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier. From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace. If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward. The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed. You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording. The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages. Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk. Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table. The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month. If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year). Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier. The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma. Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes. Starting at $479 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas. Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries. If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you. Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday ), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls. The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls. Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday. Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits. The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window. events.title: UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned
events.summary: Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year's U.N. climate summit reaches its final day ANTALYA, Turkey -- This year's U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators still debating how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects. Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31 , after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft. Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding. Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, said they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday. Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year's disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding . If phasing out fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country's Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed. “The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.” In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. “There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!” One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035. But the final draft doesn't spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push. “At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa. The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change. Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time. Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31 , are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text's draft. Trump pardons late baseball great Pete Rose after historic China trip Russian attacks on Kyiv kill 3, cripple bridges and cut power Inside the brutal murder of Tom and Angela Strussion “We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey's Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said. “Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere," said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.” Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don't emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change. They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need. The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft's previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually. Many of the world's most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year's talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter.
