events.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
events.summary: A recent 'SNL' sketch called 'Sister' lampoons gender roles in caring for aging parents. NBC A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free? The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families. According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women. As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts. While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch immediately went viral. Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities. Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements . This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025. For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends. Medicaid can help, but access is limited Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer. Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023 . The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew. However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance. Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services . Who provides care in the meantime? As the sketch suggests, daughters are more likely to care for their aging parents. Visual Vic/Moment via Getty Images There’s a shortage of paid caregivers Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle. The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born . The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned. Caregiving often has financial consequences When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care. Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out. Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks. Families often have to shoulder responsibility Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs . In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers . Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage . In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance , an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place. When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter. Jane Tavares receives funding from the RRF Foundation for Aging. events.title: Paid sick leave laws are no guarantee for Philly’s immigrant restaurant workers
events.summary: Philadelphia workers who work for a private company with more than 10 employees may be entitled to paid sick leave. andresr/E+ Collection via Getty Images What do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day . There is no federal right to paid sick leave . However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide , requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees. In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck. For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy. I study restaurant work , an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born . Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala. I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez . Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015 . During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act , a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees. A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees. What I found , though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers. ‘$300 for a simple flu’ Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “ reasonable documentation ” – but only after an absence of more than two days. Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance. If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them. Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.” What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said. Gaps arise when restaurants have different policies for front-of-house workers, who interact with customers, than back-of-house workers, who staff the kitchen. Willie B. Thomas/DigitalVision Collection via Getty Images Different policies for back-of-house workers In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America. The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid. In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white. I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers. “The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.” In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born. Fear of retaliation Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about. Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves. “The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’” Healthy workers, healthy public My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California . Gaps in access based on immigration status are an equity issue. But beyond that, research suggests that everyone wins if it’s easier for workers to get paid sick leave. events.summary: Data by Topic by Place by Economic Account Tools Interactive Data Application Programming Interface (API) Global Value Chain Analyzer Income Distribution Analysis Tool (IDAT) Country Facts BEARFACTS Industry Facts GDP & Personal Income Mapping RIMS II eFile News Economy at a Glance News Releases Release Schedule The BEA Wire | BEA's Official Blog Survey of Current Business Archive For Journalists Research Offices of Research Meet the Researchers Papers Special Sworn Researcher Program Research Using Company-Level Data Fellowship Program Resources Learning Center Methodologies Multimedia Article Collections For Congressional Users For Developers For Students About Who We Are BEA Leadership Innovation at BEA Advisory Committees Budget and Performance Policies and Information Working at BEA Help Contact Us Ask an Expert For Survey Respondents Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) Glossary Guidelines for Citing BEA Worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises increased 0.9 percent to 44.2 million workers in 2024 (preliminary) from 43.8 million workers in 2023 (revised), according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on the operations and finances of U.S. parent companies and their majority-owned foreign affiliates. Employment in the United States by U.S. parents increased 0.1 percent to 29.9 million workers in 2024. U.S. parents accounted for 67.6 percent of worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs), down from 68.1 percent in 2023. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates of U.S. MNEs increased 2.7 percent to 14.3 million workers and accounted for 32.4 percent of employment by U.S. MNEs worldwide. U.S. parents accounted for 21.7 percent of total private industry employment in the United States in 2024, down from 21.9 percent in 2023. Employment by U.S. parents was largest in manufacturing, in “other industries,” led by transportation and warehousing, and in retail trade. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates was largest in India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom. Worldwide current-dollar value added of U.S. MNEs increased 8.0 percent to $7.4 trillion in 2024. Value added by U.S. parents , a measure of U.S. parents’ direct contribution to U.S. gross domestic product, increased 8.5 percent to $5.7 trillion. U.S parents accounted for 21.8 percent of total U.S. private-industry value added, up from 21.2 percent in 2023. Foreign affiliate value added increased 6.5 percent to $1.8 trillion. Value added by foreign affiliates was largest in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada. Worldwide expenditures for property, plant, and equipment of U.S. MNEs increased 7.1 percent to $1.2 trillion. Expenditures by U.S. parents accounted for $968.7 billion, representing 36.5 percent of all U.S. private-business capital expenditures. Expenditures by foreign affiliates accounted for $216.2 billion. Worldwide research and development (R&D) expenditures of U.S. MNEs increased 10.1 percent to $622.7 billion. U.S. parents accounted for expenditures of $536.5 billion, representing 69.6 percent of business R&D performed in the United States. Foreign affiliates accounted for expenditures of $86.2 billion. Additional statistics on the activities of U.S. parent companies and their foreign affiliates , including sales, balance sheet and income statement items, compensation of employees, trade in goods, and more are available on BEA’s website. More industry detail for U.S. parents and more industry and country detail for foreign affiliates are also available on the website. Statistics for 2023 were revised to incorporate newly available and revised source data. Preliminary statistics for 2023 were released in August 2025. events.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
events.summary: The stock was last trading at US$88.87, about 9% below where it closed following its smooth debut on Nov 19. Anthropic’s post-listing slide deepened the gloom over the AI sector on Nov 20 , underscoring how even one of the most eagerly anticipated listings in history has struggled to revive investor enthusiasm. Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain momentum after a turbulent stretch. But the stock was last trading at US$88.87, about 9% below where it closed following its smooth debut on Nov 19 , giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about US$1.6 trillion (S$2 trillion) and a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding. The stock could find support later in the year. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30% of Anthropic’s shares by year-end. Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained. “We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results,” said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation “assumes years of rapid growth”. The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Nov 19 , while futures pointed to further declines on Nov 20 . Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia and Meta Platforms fell more than 2% each in premarket trading, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped more than 1%. Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Sandisk down 7% each and Intel losing more than 5%. The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which would be another major test of investors’ appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public in 2027 . Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record. While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing. “There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co. Retail investors traded about US$772 million of Anthropic shares on Nov 19 , the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012. The stock’s sharp swings have left investors weighing whether to bet on a rebound or brace for further losses. Options trading, due to begin next week, could add to the volatility. “It’s not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment,” said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg. Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment. Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, Bloomberg News reported on Nov 20 . REUTERS

events.summary: The court of the Abu Dhabi Global Market issued a $6.5 billion worldwide freeze on stolen Binance assets, the cryptocurrency firm said, as it tries to recover the funds taken last month in the largest-ever crypto hack. ADGM, which granted Binance three licenses last year, regulates the company’s global platform. Law firm Gibson Dunn described the decision as a “mega-injunction” and “one of … the largest publicly known freezing orders ever made.” It applies to 18 companies , including Trump family- and Abu Dhabi-backed World Liberty Financial, Reuters reported. The FBI said North Korea was behind the huge theft — which Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told Semafor resulted from the company’s own failings — but Pyongyang has denied involvement. — Damian Zane

events.title: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear
events.summary: Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.” Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, as well as by humiliating people. According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them. Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications. events.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
events.summary: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement . “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added. The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen). The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position. The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government. The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors. Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: AI-fuelled cyberattacks drive claims surge at Japan insurers
events.summary: Attackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods as AI advances, and unauthorised access has led to a string of personal data leaks in Japan. Japan insurers report a sharp rise in cyberinsurance claims as AI-driven attacks and data leaks increase. Tokio Marine saw three times usual October notifications, and Sompo saw 2½ times more claims. The higher claims may lift payouts, but insurers say losses are still manageable. Tokio Marine expects some full-year impact, while Sompo says customer requests for more cover have tripled. The market is still small for smaller firms, with only 8.8% of Japanese SMEs insured. Insurers are adding prevention tools and tighter terms, as Sompo plans a new monitoring service from December. Japan’s biggest property insurers are reporting a sharp jump in cyberinsurance claims as artificial intelligence-driven attacks grow more sophisticated and hacking incidents surge nationwide. Tokio Marine Holdings received three times as many cyberinsurance claim notifications in October as usual, according to the company. Sompo Holdings said claims in October were running at 2½ times higher than the average over the one-year period ending Sept 30, 2026. Both insurers disclosed the figures at earnings briefings on N ov 19 . Attackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods as AI advances, and unauthorised access has led to a string of personal data leaks in Japan . The increase in claims raises the risk of costly payouts even as rising numbers of incidents fuel demand for protection. Payouts on cyberpolicies could rise, but the surge has yet to translate into a significant earnings hit. Yoshinari Endo, a managing executive officer at Tokio Marine, said his company expects some impact on full-year results, though it is managing the profit risk and expects losses to stay within the assumptions of its initial annual plan. Junsuke Koike, an executive vice-president at Sompo, said inquiries about raising coverage amounts or adding coverage items had tripled from normal levels. Japan’s experience mirrors a broader rise in cyberclaims globally. US insurers reported more than 56,000 cyberclaims in 2025, up 20% from a year earlier, while large companies are facing increasingly costly incidents. Cyberpolicies typically cover damages owed for data breaches, recovery costs and profits lost from disruptions, making insurance a growing part of corporate risk management. Cyberinsurance penetration in Japan remains low for smaller companies. A 2025 survey by the General Insurance Association of Japan found that only 8.8% of small- and medium-sized business owners said they had cyberinsurance as a defence against attacks. Yasuko Fukuda, a senior executive officer at MS&AD Insurance Group Holdings, said at an earnings briefing on Nov 19 that there is “significant room for the market to expand”. The insurers are trying to limit losses by helping customers prevent attacks. Starting in December, Sompo will offer a new service with Trend Micro and others that monitors for vulnerabilities on the internet. Insurers are being selective about underwriting. Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten coverage terms depending on a customer’s risk profile, Endo said. The company expects its cyberinsurance business to remain profitable in the fiscal year through March 2027. Standard total payout limits in Japan and overseas run from about 100 million yen (S$812,000) to several hundred million yen per contract. BLOOMBERG

events.title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars. In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it. Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever. AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?” Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.” It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.” There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.” To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand . Want to join the conversation? events.title: How Anthropic co-founders and investors are expected to make billions through blockbuster IPO
events.summary: Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) is delivering a windfall to its co-founders, early investors and employees, as the AI giant’s stock soared on its Nasdaq debut on Thursday. The San Francisco company raised $81.3 billion in the blockbuster IPO, eclipsing the previous record-setting debut of Elon Musk's SpaceX in June. It offered 980 million shares as part of the deal, valuing the company at $1.5 trillion at the time of listing, with the price set at $83 per share. However, the share price surged to $111.50, 34 per cent above its price at the opening of trade, briefly giving it a fully diluted valuation of about $2 trillion. Dario Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive and co-founder, is projected to amass more than $20 billion through his shareholding. Other co-founders, including Tom Brown, Sam ⁠McCandlish, Christopher Olah, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan and Daniela Amodei, are also expected to earn $20 billion each through their equity stakes. “All seven co-founders each hold roughly 1.4 per cent of the company, according to Anthropic's IPO filing. At the IPO price of $83, each stake was worth approximately $20 billion,” Noureldeen Al Hammoury, head of market insights and community engagement at Equiti, told The National . As the share prices jumped following its debut on Nasdaq, the fortunes of its co-founders, employees and investors also surged. By the first-day intraday peak of $115.10, each founder's stake reached about $33 billion, pushing the combined founders' wealth to an estimated $231 billion, Mr Al Hammoury said. By the close of trading at $97.17 on Thursday, the combined figure settled at about $166 billion, or $24 billion for each investor. “The group first became billionaires less than two years ago, and the IPO has now vaulted all seven into the top 300 of the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, wealthier than well-known finance figures such as Bill Ackman and Stan Druckenmiller,” Mr Al Hammoury said. Employees gain Anthropic's IPO is also helping thousands of its employees become multimillionaires through its stock holdings. Private-share marketplace Hill.com estimates that about 5,100 of Anthropic’s roughly 5,300 employees, or 96 per cent, held company stock worth more than $1 million when the AI company began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. “The IPO is expected to mint thousands of millionaires among Anthropic's employee base, with most staff holding equity that has now converted into real liquidity,” Mr Al Hammoury said. “The wealth effect is already visible in real estate markets. Homes in San Francisco are drawing offers millions over asking, with AI workers using their newly liquid stakes to make all-cash bids in New York and Miami as well.” Wall Street banks, including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, BNY Mellon, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo, had been competing to manage the wealth expected to flow to Anthropic employees post-IPO, he added. Anthropic was co-founded in 2021, when it consisted mainly of defectors from OpenAI who were concerned about its approach to AI regulations and safety. The company’s Claude AI tool and other models gained in popularity, particularly in corporate and government spheres, making Anthropic one of the top AI firms. Ashton Kutcher and Damac investments Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, who invested in the company through Sound Ventures, is also expected to earn billions. The company initially invested $35 million in Anthropic and proceeded to pour in another $400 million. It currently has a stake worth nearly $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. UAE-based Damac Properties made early investments and is raking in billions, according to its founder and chairman Hussain Sajwani. “What I have made in 30 years [since starting his business], I made in Anthropic in less than two years,” Mr Sajwani said at the Bloomberg Invest event in Dubai last week. “Between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, we're making [a] few billion dollars a month,” he added. There are also other companies that have made investments in Anthropic, as listed by Bloomberg, that stand to gain from the IPO. These include Iconiq, a wealth management firm turned Silicon Valley private markets investor, Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Coatue Management and global investment company General Catalyst. The UAE technology investment company MGX is also one of the investors, having participated in Anthropic's $65 billion series H funding round in May, and its $30 billion series G funding round in February. Former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt, who was one of Anthropic’s first investors, is also expected to benefit from the deal. “The IPO is notable not just for its scale but for what it represents – Anthropic is the first frontier AI lab to go public, having built its brand around AI safety and “ethical” AI development,” Mr Al Hammoury said. “The company reported $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue ahead of the listing and achieved profitability on an adjusted basis in that quarter.”

events.title: An entrepreneur fights for workers’ protections after his mom was fired after being assaulted at her Saks Fifth Avenue job
events.summary: Jeff Vinokur is using his newly minted wealth from the sale of his edtech company to hold the retail store accountable L ate in the afternoon of 28 June, Jeff Vinokur received a call from his mother that sent him running. “I was assaulted,” Vinokur, a popular science educator known as the “ Dancing Scientist ”, recalled his mother saying. Vinokur’s mother, Laza Susuni, was working in the women’s ready-to-wear section at Manhattan’s Saks Fifth Avenue that day when a client attacked her in the dressing room. A court document reviewed by the Guardian corroborates that a woman was arrested at that location on assault and harassment charges. Vinokur, 36, who was in New York City visiting Susuni, bounded out of bed, threw on clothes and rushed to the famed department store – not even taking a moment to brush his teeth. Susuni, who said she was kicked in the stomach, was evaluated at a hospital. While Susuni, 62, was discharged from the hospital later that day without permanent physical injuries, she reeled from panic. “I could not sleep at all,” said Susuni, who came to the US from Russia as a teen. “I was just so afraid that … she would just come back [to] hurt me, to punish me, and just send somebody to stab me because they put her in handcuffs in front of her own children.” Susuni said she asked Saks for five days off to recover from her anxiety. She claims that the company instead terminated her. Vinokur sprang into action, contacting lawyers because he believed that surely such a firing would be illegal. When an attorney said there wasn’t anything he could do, Vinokur thought: “This guy is an idiot, this cannot be, let’s go talk to other lawyers.” They spoke with about 10 attorneys. “They all say the same thing: that there is no law that protects [against] this,” Vinokur said. Now Vinokur is taking it upon himself to push for change in New York law to provide broader legal protections for workers against firing if they have been the victims of violent crime on or off the job. While an employer almost certainly would not tell an employee they were fired for being a crime victim, a workplace might effectively do so by taking issue with things like time off or medical requests, or make spurious claims about lapsed job performance in the wake of the crime. Alice Jump, a partner at the Reavis Page Jump law firm, said “it doesn’t seem rational” for an employer to behave in such a way, but imagines they might use “taking a lot of time off, or being distressed or emotionally or physically compromised”, as an excuse to terminate a crime victim. While there are some laws on the books in New York state and city that protect workers from firing in relation to being crime victims, there are limitations. New York state human rights law bars employers from discriminating against, or firing, people because they are victims of domestic violence. New York state law also prohibits employers from penalizing or firing crime victims for taking time off to appear in court or meet with prosecutors, so long as they give notice of the absence. New York City law makes it illegal for an employee to be fired because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, said Jump. “So if it’s a non-sexual assault, then you’re not specifically covered,” Jump said. “The law doesn’t extend to all crime victims.” For Jump, it seems that amending legal protections to shield employees who suffer other assaults or violent physical attacks wouldn’t be difficult. “Any kind of assault or violent physical act – you shouldn’t be fired because you’re a subject of that.” There is no federal law providing termination protections for crime victims, Jump also said. As part of Vinokur’s campaign for change, he launched a website, Saksfiles.com , outlining not only his mother’s situation but several other alleged instances at Saks stores where former employees have claimed they were fired in relation to being purportedly victimized. Vinokur, who holds a PhD in biochemistry from UCLA, is also using the media savvy that propelled him from quirky science educator to edtech founder – and vast resources following the sale of his company – to launch an ongoing, in-person protest against Saks. From 12 November, Vinokur is paying anywhere from more than one to several dozen people to stand outside Saks every day toting signs with text such as “MY MOM IS THE 7th VICTIM. BEATEN AT SAKS. THEN FIRED. I WANT ANSWERS.” Vinokur said that he will pay them to hold signs outside Saks every single day from 1 to 7pm throughout the holiday shopping season – and potentially indefinitely. I was majority shareholder,” he said. “I don’t have a boat. I don’t fly private.

events.title: Ebola vaccine trials launch amid security concerns
events.summary: The News Large-scale trials of three vaccines against the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola strain in the epicenter of DR Congo’s outbreak could yield a breakthrough early next year if security challenges can be overcome, the head of a global vaccine body told Semafor. The Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no proven vaccine, has killed more than 5,500 people since May’s declaration of an outbreak — now the second-largest ever recorded. Most of the cases, amounting to more than 11,000, have been concentrated in the conflict-hit east of the country. The Tumaini trial — a study to test vaccine candidates — will see jabs tested on at least 1,000 people to check their safety and efficacy. A trial of Ervebo, a vaccine developed by Merck that has been approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, began on Oct. 23. The two other vaccines, which were designed to target the Bundibugyo strain and will join the trial in the next few days, are a jab developed by Oxford University scientists and another by Moderna that harnesses technology used to create vaccines for COVID-19. “In a best case, we could look towards early next year for a result,” said Richard Hatchett, CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations. He added that even if data suggested a vaccination was effective and safe, Congolese and global health regulators would still take time to conduct a review before issuing a formal decision about authorizing it for emergency use. “There is the potential, if the regulators approve, for expanded access to the vaccine while that review is going on,” he said. Emanuele Capobianco, director of global health security at GAVI, a global vaccine alliance, in a separate interview, said if trials were successful, vaccines could potentially be deployed in the first half of 2027. The Ervebo trial kicked off in Ituri, the worst-affected province, but the CEPI chief said the testing area could be widened to include other provinces, including the eastern region of North Kivu. Conflict and misinformation The Congolese army has for decades fought various rebel groups including M23, which DR Congo’s government has accused neighboring Rwanda of supporting — claims denied by Kigali. The conflict has hampered efforts to bring the outbreak under control, with thousands of people forced to flee their homes. Health workers and surveillance teams have also come under attack in communities that distrust outsiders. Both Hatchett and Capobianco warned that insecurity in the east of the country was a major obstacle to trialing vaccines. “There’s lots of conflict, there’s lots of misinformation,” said Hatchett. “The biggest variable is how quickly can we enrol the necessary number of subjects, and that is a dynamic process,” he said. Similarly, Capobianco — who called eastern DR Congo a “complex environment in which to operate” — said the involvement of healthcare workers, religious leaders, and community authorities would be crucial in moving forward with trials. The View from Geneva “While the response has slowed transmission in the initial epicentres, 400 to 500 new cases continue to be reported each week,” the World Health Organization said in an update this week. It said delays in paying frontline health workers and responders also created tension and slowed the response to the outbreak. Notable The director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention warned that the outbreak is still not under control , six months after being declared. US pharmaceutical company Gilead signed royalty-free licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers for potential future access to an antiviral being trialled as a treatment for people exposed to the Bundibugyo strain.

events.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
events.summary: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency. The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather. “Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s Be Ready campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, the chief economist at the ONS. Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month on month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April. Oliver Vernon-Harcourt, the head of retail at Deloitte, said: “Consumers responded to the government’s Be Ready campaign by stocking up on long-life grocery items, which reflects a broader attitude from shoppers to prioritise essentials.” But Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics , said the jump in household “prepping” could mean slower food sales growth in the coming months. “The cupboards only need to be stocked once for this, hopefully,” he told clients. “It seems unlikely that households can continue to spend at this rate with a further energy-induced rise in inflation around the corner.” Separate data last week showed that British shoppers had been stocking up on essentials such as bottled water, tinned goods and hand sanitiser in preparation for possible emergencies. The ONS also reported that textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost in October. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January. The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month on month in October. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges. However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose. “October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, the European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal. “Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season. “Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

events.title: Fresh off a record $3 billion CMU pledge, Ken Griffin sends Pittsburgh 3 dinosaurs and $5 million
events.summary: Nearly two months after his record-breaking $3 billion pledge to Carnegie Mellon University, billionaire Ken Griffin is sending Pittsburgh three dinosaurs. The founder and CEO of Citadel is lending three rare long-necked dinosaur fossils to the Carnegie Museum of Natural History for 10 years, alongside a $5 million donation to support paleontological research and education, the museum announced Wednesday. The deal adds to the tens of millions of dollars Griffin has already poured into dinosaur collecting, research, and exhibitions. It also keeps a rare find in scientists’ hands at a time when record auction prices are pushing more fossils into private collections, a trend many paleontologists warn could put specimens out of research’s reach. The fossils, nicknamed Daisy, Lucky, and Lucy, belong to three plant-eating sauropods, one adult and two juveniles, discovered together in roughly 150-million-year-old rock in Wyoming and excavated between 2023 and 2025. Pittsburgh public radio station WESA reports that all three are Diplodocus carnegii , the same species as Dippy, the museum’s most famous dinosaur, which was named for founder Andrew Carnegie . Griffin purchased the fossils last year through Sotheby’s for an undisclosed amount, according to the Financial Times . Finding an adult and two young animals together gives researchers a rare chance to study how these dinosaurs grew and potentially interacted, according to a statement from Griffin Catalyst , Griffin’s philanthropic initiative. Scientists will also examine fossilized skin that the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reports may be the largest sauropod skin sample found to date. The $5 million will also give visitors a closer look at how paleontologists work. It will fund a new fossil-preparation laboratory open to public view, where visitors can watch scientists free fossils from rock and preserve them, a painstaking process that can take years and usually happens behind closed doors. The specimens are expected to arrive as soon as December, museum director Carey Miller told WESA. Preparation will begin in the museum’s existing lab before moving to the new facility once it is completed. Miller called the chance to prepare the fossils in public view and display them later “something that is unusual and really exciting.” WESA also reports the donation will fund two additional fossil preparers and educational programming, as well as expand the museum’s annual DinoFest event. “Daisy, Lucky, and Lucy offer an extraordinary window into our planet’s history,” Griffin said in a statement . “I hope these experiences spark curiosity and inspire the next generation of scientists.” Griffin’s multimillion-dollar passion for dinosaurs Griffin is part of a growing set of billionaires treating dinosaur fossils as a luxury asset , as Fortune previously reported. In July 2024, he paid $44.6 million at Sotheby’s for a remarkably complete stegosaurus skeleton nicknamed Apex, then a world-record price for a dinosaur fossil. That record fell this July, when a T. rex nicknamed Gus sold for $50.1 million to an unnamed bidder. Griffin loaned Apex to New York’s American Museum of Natural History , where it is on display. Alongside the four-year loan, he provided undisclosed funding for educational and research initiatives, including a new three-year Griffin Postdoctoral Fellowship for Paleontology. His other dinosaur projects include a $16.5 million gift to Chicago’s Field Museum in 2017 to revamp its dinosaur exhibitions, and funding of an undisclosed amount for an excavation and research project in South Africa aimed at better understanding the end of the dinosaur age. His scientific philanthropy extends beyond paleontology. In 2019, he gave $125 million to Chicago’s Museum of Science and Industry, which has since been renamed in his honor. A major donor to higher education The 58-year-old has an estimated net worth of $56.3 billion as of Thursday, according to Forbes , making him the world’s 33rd-richest person. He began investing from his Harvard dorm room in 1987 and founded Citadel in 1990, a year after graduating. He cofounded market-making giant Citadel Securities in 2002. Griffin Catalyst says his total giving exceeds $5.7 billion, and education has been a major focus. In 2023, he gave his alma mater, Harvard University, $300 million , and its Graduate School of Arts and Sciences now bears his name. His biggest commitment yet came on Sept. 30, when he pledged $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University . Of that, $2 billion will build a new campus in Miami, where Griffin moved Citadel’s headquarters in 2022. The remaining $1 billion will support the university’s Pittsburgh campus, including $500 million for its computer science school , now the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first-100-days agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt
events.summary: While it’s the responsibility of the U.S. Department of the Treasury to finance the interest on the $40 trillion national debt, it is members of both parties in Congress who have added to Uncle Sam’s borrowing. With the Democrats winning a wave of seats in the midterm elections, everyone from Wall Street analysts to CEOs of America’s largest companies are wondering what a more divided government will mean. Budget watchdogs are doing the same, and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) has put a number on how much the Democrats’ plan for their first 100 days will cost. The Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with slim majorities in both chambers, and they have been clear about what they want to achieve in their first three months with more power. Hakeem Jeffries, nominated by Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House, wrote in November that they aim to “reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs, and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran.” Some factors come with obvious budget implications: De-escalating the war in the Middle East would save money, while ending Trump tariffs would axe a revenue stream that generated $287 billion in customs duties, taxes, and fees in 2025 per the Richmond Fed—up 192% on the prior year. The CRFB estimates that, in total, the “first 100 days” policies would cost $4.1 trillion through 2037. Without offsets (spending cuts or revenue increases used to balance new policies), $4.9 trillion would be added to the debt burden over the next decade, including interest costs. But the factor analysts—and budget hawks— really care about is the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio . This describes the level of borrowing a nation has relative to its economic growth, and therefore its ability to service that borrowing. At the moment, it stands at around 121% , per the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Economists suggest that if this balance were to tip further, then U.S. lenders may begin demanding higher premiums to offset the risk associated with the borrowing —sparking a bond crisis. The House Democrats’ policies would increase the debt-to-GDP ratio to 135% by 2037 without offsets, versus 125% of GDP under an adjusted Congressional Budget Office baseline, the CRFB added. The budget watchdog does offer some alternatives for how revenue to offset these proposals could be generated, though the reforms are unlikely to be popular with voters. “Repealing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s (OBBBA) tax cuts for high earners would generate about $2 trillion of savings—enough to offset an agenda scaled back by half,” the budget watchdog wrote. “Repealing all of the tax cuts and spending increases in OBBBA—including its low-income and middle-class tax cuts—would generate about $7 trillion. That would be enough to pay for the First 100 Days agenda 1.7 times over.” Price breakdown The CRFB broke down each aspect of the proposals. Starting first with the policies that could save money, the CRFB pointed to Iran. It noted that while ending the conflict would not immediately reduce deficits, it would likely avoid increases in military and defense spending. Continuing the war in Iran, the committee writes, costs approximately $30 billion a year and could be avoided. Regarding policy costs for 2027–37, removing Trump’s tariffs leaves the largest budget hole. This represents $1.8 trillion in total, from repealing Section 301 tariffs (costing $955 billion alone) and Section 232 tariffs ($780 billion) to undoing Section 338 tariffs on certain Canadian goods ($35 billion). Reversing the OBBBA health provisions would cost $1.6 trillion by 2037, the committee adds, including $600 billion to cancel provider tax and state-directed payment limits, as well as $485 billion to remove Medicaid work requirements. Reversing SNAP provisions would cost $250 billion over the next 10 years. Increasing the deficit would also mean larger interest payments on the debt, the CRFB added—some $840 billion over the next 10 years. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Anthropic is public, now comes the hard part
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios With its IPO done and dusted, Anthropic's shareholders will be watching its progress toward becoming a business that doesn't need constant capital infusions from investors and vendors. Why it matters: Anthropic — along with OpenAI — is at the heart of the industry that's dominated the equity and debt markets for the last four years. Much of the AI infrastructure boom is ultimately aimed at supplying computing power to these two companies. Yes, but: The bill for that data center investment will start to come due over the next few years. And Anthropic and OpenAI are going to have to pay for quite a bit of it. How it works: Anthropic has covered much of its computing costs thus far by selling parts of itself off to compute vendors like Amazon and Alphabet, and by raising more cash from other investors. But eventually the company's core business will have to generate enough money to cover those costs on its own. Case in point: Anthropic's filings say it is on the hook for roughly $900 billion in spending commitments — mostly for data centers and computing power — with about half of that due before the end of 2030. After the IPO, Anthropic is expected to have roughly $200 billion in cash and short-term investments in the bank, which should buy it some time. But its sales will have to be a lot higher to just cover computing obligations, let alone the profits ANT's new shareholders are expecting. By the numbers: As the chart above shows, Anthropic posted a loss of roughly $23 billion on revenue of nearly $17 billion in the third quarter. It's true that much of that loss stems from a non-cash accounting charge of almost $22 billion. But even the more favorable metric of operating income — which strips out the paper losses and gains that can obscure the company's core earnings power — still shows an operating loss of more than half a billion dollars in the third quarter. The bottom line: Anthropic still has a long way to go before it is going to be standing on its own feet, financially speaking.

events.title: An urban test for South Africa’s unity government
events.summary: The News South Africa’s African National Congress is negotiating with smaller populist parties for control of three cities that anchor the country’s economy. The proposed deal, following local elections this month, could leave the Democratic Alliance in opposition in all three, even though it finished first in each. The two parties govern together nationally, but now the prospect of a fight across Gauteng province — which is home to Johannesburg, the financial hub of Africa’s biggest economy — is adding to investor anxiety about how long that partnership can last. On Thursday, Helen Zille, a former DA leader and Western Cape premier who ran as the party’s mayoral candidate, conceded defeat in her bid to become mayor. Zille’s concession came as a frantic bargaining window entered its final week. South Africans voted on Nov. 4, and councils have until Nov. 27 to hold their first meetings, following the publication of elected councillors in the Government Gazette. Nationwide, 140 of 213 councils emerged without a party holding a majority, roughly twice as many as in 2021. Herman Mashaba, whose ActionSA party finished third in Johannesburg, told Semafor the proposed deal would return him to the mayor’s office, which he held from 2016 to 2019. He said ActionSA would also share power with the ANC, Economic Freedom Fighters and uMkhonto weSizwe Party in two other Gauteng cities, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. For the ANC, the deal would mean returning to power in Gauteng’s cities with the help of its own radical-left populist breakaways. The EFF was founded by Julius Malema after his expulsion from the ANC in 2012, while uMkhonto weSizwe was founded by former president Jacob Zuma, whose campaign helped cost the ANC its national majority in 2024. Mashaba, who left the DA, completes a coalition of defectors. Voters who deserted the ANC in the metros would find it back in government, supported by parties that campaigned against it. “All parties, large and small.” The ANC’s national leadership gave its negotiators a broad mandate last week to talk to “all political parties, large and small.” Within a day, Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula was in talks with the EFF. A source familiar with the leadership’s discussions said the ANC remained open to a deal with the DA, despite calls from the ANC Youth League to end the national partnership. For investors who had hoped the ANC and market-friendly DA would extend their national partnership to Gauteng, the proposed deal would be a setback. It would give the EFF and uMkhonto weSizwe influence over two major cities, adding uncertainty for businesses planning around municipal rates and infrastructure spending. The bigger concern is whether the dispute will undermine confidence in the Government of National Unity. Sam’s view The GNU was a marriage of necessity. After the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in May 2024, it assembled a 10-party coalition with 287 of parliament’s 400 seats. The DA brought its votes and standing with investors while the ANC kept the presidency and most of the cabinet. The parties have since clashed over the 2025 budget, VAT, land expropriation, national health insurance and schools policy, but neither has walked out. A collapse would reopen the question of who governs Africa’s most industrialized economy and threaten reforms investors are counting on to revive growth. Ronak Gopaldas, a director at Signal Risk, told Semafor the national coalition’s stability “is itself being used as a bargaining chip in the municipal negotiations.” His firm expects the coalition to hold, partly because of the market backlash a breakup could trigger. He sees practical reasons for the ANC and DA to keep governing together, even as recurring disputes limit what they can deliver. President Cyril Ramaphosa’s position, potentially, compounds the risk. His term as ANC leader ends next year, although he remains president until 2029. A source familiar with the party’s discussions said its national executive took collective responsibility for the election defeat, shielding Ramaphosa from being singled out. But the argument over the coalition he built will carry into the succession contest, when every compromise with the DA could become ammunition against him within his own party. If the ANC helps put Mashaba in the mayor’s office, the DA could spend the run-up to 2029 fighting the ANC across South Africa’s economic heartland while governing alongside it nationally. Both parties may have enough reason to stay in the cabinet. Agreeing on what to do there could get harder with every fight outside it. Room for Disagreement Hill-Lewis said this week the DA was not yet considering pulling out of the GNU. But its ministers could find themselves defending a national government while their councillors fight ANC-backed administrations across Gauteng. That contradiction could make it harder for DA ministers to compromise with the ANC on budgets and economic reforms. Notable How South Africa’s ANC and partners worked out a coalition deal to sideline poll-topping DA in Johannesburg.

events.title: South Africa’s AGOA exit jeopardizes US chicken deal
events.summary: The News South Africa is “considering its options” over a decade-old concession to US chicken producers after Washington decided to take away the benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program, a government spokesman told Semafor. Kamill Allie’s comments come as relations between the two countries deteriorate following the US decision this month to strip the country of duty-free access to its markets, and opens an early test of the extent to which Pretoria is prepared to unwind compromises made with Washington. A decade ago, the country agreed to allow a quota of American poultry to enter Africa’s biggest economy without anti-dumping duties as part of a deal to retain its benefits under AGOA . This act, which gave eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market, has been the cornerstone of US-Africa trade since 2000. But South African poultry producers said the concession had run its course, with Izaak Breitenbach, head of industry lobby group South African Poultry Association telling Semafor that it should disappear now that the country is no longer benefiting from AGOA. A South African customs notice published on Nov. 6, days after Washington announced the country’s AGOA exclusion, did link the annual US chicken quota to the preferential trade agreement.But the concession’s suspension requires written confirmation from Trade Minister Parks Tau. ‘Nothing in return’ Breitenbach said the industry has repeatedly asked Tau to withdraw the rebate, including after Washington imposed additional tariffs on South African exports. Pretoria, nevertheless, preserved the concession. “We got nothing in return,” Breitenbach said, while acknowledging that the industry was not party to the government negotiations with Washington. The chicken deal dates back to South Africa’s last big fight to remain in AGOA, agreeing in 2015 to allow 65,000 tonnes of US poultry to escape anti-dumping duties each year in a politically contentious compromise that helped preserve the country’s place in the program. The quota has since risen to about 74,000 tonnes. Its fate lands amid a broader deterioration in relations between South Africa and the US, which has imposed visa restrictions on South African officials over Pretoria’s race and land policies, falsely accused it of persecuting white South Africans, and ejected it from AGOA in a decision Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III called “ predictable and preventable ”. Notable The leaders of the US and South Africa have not spoken in the 18 months since an Oval Office meeting that Cyril Ramaphosa now calls an “ambush,” a silence that has coincided with the steepest decline in relations between the two countries since apartheid ended.

events.title: Indonesia revokes Riau forestry permits of APRIL Group unit over alleged peatland fires, violations
events.summary: Recurring peatland fires are among the reasons that have been cited for the enforcement action. Indonesia revoked RAPP’s forestry permits covering 338,536ha in Riau after alleged peatland fires, illegal plantations and damage to protected areas. The task force said the land returns to state control and all activity has stopped, but APRIL Group still faces restoration duties and possible legal action. The crackdown targets major forestry players amid haze concerns, and officials also flagged risks to Tesso Nilo National Park and Sumatran elephants. JAKARTA – Indonesia has revoked forestry permits covering 338,536ha held by Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP), a subsidiary of Asia Pacific Resources International Limited (APRIL) Group. The move, which affects an area about 4.5 times the size of Singapore, was taken over alleged environmental violations, including recurring peatland fires, illegal plantations and damage to protected areas, the government’s forest enforcement task force said on Nov 20. The enforcement push comes amid heightened scrutiny of companies linked to forest fires and transboundary haze; the latest move marks a significant crackdown on major corporate players in the forestry sector. The permits were revoked under a Forestry Ministerial Decree dated Nov 19, with the entire concession area in Riau province returning to state control, said the Forest Area Enforcement Task Force, known as Satgas PKH, in a statement on Nov 20 . “All activities within the revoked concession areas have been halted, while the government has taken back control of the land,” it added. “The revocation does not absolve the company of its environmental restoration obligations or potential legal liabilities.” The task force cited recurring peatland fires, oil palm plantations spanning 18,362.74ha, unauthorised mining activities covering 541.46ha, and damage to protected areas spanning 211.54ha as grounds for the revocation. It also raised concerns over the protection of areas surrounding Tesso Nilo National Park, which provides habitat for endangered Sumatran elephants. APRIL Group said it learnt about the government’s decision through media reports. It added that it was awaiting formal notification and further clarification from authorities. “We respect the authority of the government and will continue to communicate constructively with the relevant authorities,” the company said in a statement. It added that it would respond through the appropriate channels once it received formal notification. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Anthropic’s listing draws massive interest from S’pore retail investors, but valuation fears remain
events.summary: Anthropic’s initial public offering, the second blockbuster of 2026, was six to seven times oversubscribed and raised US$81.3 billion, beating SpaceX’s raising of US$75 billion in June. Singapore retail investors rushed into Anthropic’s IPO, making it the most-traded stock on debut. The offer was six to seven times oversubscribed and raised US$81.3 billion. The stock jumped 34.3% at the open, but closed up only 17%, showing sharp volatility. Analysts warned that high AI valuations, heavy losses and rising costs may test future gains. GIC’s large stake gave some investors confidence, but experts said it is not a direct endorsement of the current price. The next day, Asian markets fell as AI and chip stocks sold off on valuation fears. SINGAPORE – Forget the doom and gloom of an impending AI bubble bursting and the uncertainty of a post-Jensen Huang world. When it came to Anthropic’s record-breaking debut on Wall Street, Singapore investors were ravenous and had no intention of missing out. Online brokerages told The Straits Times that interest had swelled well ahead of the Nov 19 listing, and Anthropic was the most-traded stock on its debut day, with trading activity exceeding Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO), the second blockbuster of 2026, was six to seven times oversubscribed and raised US$81.3 billion (S$104.8 billion) , beating SpaceX’s raising of US$75 billion in June . Anthropic opened on Nasdaq at US$111.50 – 34.3% higher than its IPO price of US$83. Its market value briefly exceeded US$2 trillion in intraday trading before closing the day at US$97.17, with a market capitalisation of US$1.8 trillion. Some observers may say it was perhaps not the best time for the developer of the AI model Claude to launch its IPO. Sentiment about AI weakened as investors grew increasingly cautious about massive capital expenditures, which has sent tech stocks tumbling since October . Its Wall Street debut also came days after Jensen Huang, CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia, resigned , casting a pall of uncertainty over the future of AI and the semiconductor industry. Anthropic itself had also laid out over 90 pages of risk factors to its operations in its prospectus, the most frightening of which was the catastrophic risks its AI tech posed to humanity. But all the fears and controversy did not deter retail investors hungry for a slice of the AI pie, and Anthropic passed a seemingly challenging test of investor appetite with flying colours. Anthropic’s stock churned out more retail trading activity on its public debut than any other stock on its listing day going back to 2012, according to data from US-based financial research firm Vanda Research. Investors traded US$772 million worth of Anthropic shares, exceeding the US$669 million recorded during SpaceX’s first trading session in June. In Singapore, investor appetite was just as voracious. “Anthropic was the clear focus of US trading on Syfe,” said the platform’s managing director and group head of investment and advisory Ritesh Ganeriwal. Pre-orders on the platform were double those for SpaceX, and nearly half of Syfe customers who traded US stocks that day traded Anthropic’s. Anthropic made up about one in four US stock trades on Syfe, making it the platform’s most-traded US stock. It drew more than twice as many trades as Nvidia, the second most-traded stock. Syfe added that 83% of Anthropic trades were market orders, compared with about 65% for US trades normally. According to Moomoo, Anthropic single-handedly captured around 48% of total trade count and 45% of total trading value across the platform’s trading basket of the AI company and Magnificent Seven stocks that comprise the largest US tech companies . Retail investors were more inclined to buy than sell the stock, suggesting they were accumulating shares rather than flipping them the same day, a Moomoo analyst said. Buy activity on the company’s stock outpaced sell activity by nearly four to one in trade count. On Longbridge Securities’ platform, Anthropic shares recorded a trading value around 4.5 times the average for the Magnificent Seven stocks . A better or more uncertain outlook? Analysts say Anthropic’s debut was largely a success, but questions remain over whether it can sustain its first-day momentum . Even though it closed 17% above its IPO price, it was still significantly below its opening price of US$111.50, demonstrating the volatility that investors can face during a strong debut. “Investors wanted Anthropic, but they would not pay any price for it,” said Syfe’s Ganeriwal. “Price trajectory will be closely watched as a signal of institutional conviction in AI at current valuations. The broader AI sector’s decline yesterday may reflect scepticism around the durability of the AI trade, though a single data point does not constitute a trend,” said the Moomoo analyst.
