events.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
events.summary: Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures. Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said. The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks. Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying . The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes. Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended. Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser. The latest official sales figures , external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling. "Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said. "Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again." The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September. As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October. The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers. Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further". Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises. Published 23 October Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October. Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn. Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago. These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate. Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel. events.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
events.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned. Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets. The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members. Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs? This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million). The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful." " Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said. At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year. How else is Lufthansa planning to save money? The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets. Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter. The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing. In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization. In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook. events.title: The US national cyber director is stepping down
events.summary: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown. Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director. We’ve reached out to the White House for comment. events.title: Why is gold price going down?
events.summary: Gold is heading for its worst weekly decline in eight months as interest-rate fears, forced liquidation and bearish bets combine to intensify bullion’s sell-off, with investors increasingly betting on further declines. Analysts warn prices could fall further before finding a floor. Spot gold dropped 2.7 per cent to $3,525.25 an ounce on Friday, after touching a 14-month low, and was down about 9.2 per cent for the week. Gold prices hit a record $5,515 an ounce in January. A stronger US dollar and mounting expectations of another Federal Reserve interest-rate increase eroded demand for the metal. “Gold is facing a perfect storm of macro headwinds and forced liquidation,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone. A hawkish Federal Reserve has revived the dollar and pushed Treasury yields higher, creating a challenging environment for gold, which pays no interest and becomes less attractive when returns on other assets rise. However, the sell-off is being amplified as investors rush to raise cash, selling assets – including gold – to meet margin calls amid a broad decline in global equities, especially technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade . Buying into IPO boom? So, are investors liquidating gold assets to buy into the initial public offering IPO boom? The surge in demand for high-profile AI listings, including Anthropic , could offer another competing destination for investor capital as gold loses momentum, according to analysts. However, there is little evidence yet of a direct rotation from gold into IPOs. “The aggressive sell-off across global equities, notably the crowded AI trade, has forced investors to reduce leverage, meet margin calls and raise cash,” Mr Weston said. “Gold has become a source of liquidity rather than a destination for safety.” Gold’s Friday slide reflects bearish forces that are now reinforcing one another, said Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “A hawkish Federal Reserve has revived the dollar, pressuring gold,” he said. "At the same time, the sell-off in AI-linked equities has prompted investors to raise cash across asset classes instead of driving them into havens." The Fed’s message that inflation remains too high has prompted markets to price in an almost certain rate increase in December, with the possibility of further tightening in January and March, Mr Weston added. Investors bet on further declines The bigger concern is that selling pressure could have further to run. Trend-following funds have already increased their short positions in gold, while exchange-traded fund investors have yet to capitulate, leaving the possibility of more selling ahead, Mr Valecha said. Despite the aggressive decline since the onset of the Iran war , gold has struggled to find a durable bottom. Options markets are also signalling a shift in sentiment. Investors typically pay a premium for call options on gold as insurance against macroeconomic and geopolitical shocks. That premium is now shrinking relative to puts, which protect investors against price declines. But a sharp correction does not necessarily mean gold’s longer-term investment thesis has collapsed, but it marks a significant cyclical repricing after investors became heavily positioned for further gains. “The options market tells the story best,” Mr Valecha said. "Investors usually pay more for gold calls than for puts because they buy them as insurance against macro and geopolitical shocks. That premium is shrinking. Why isn’t gold acting as safe haven? Gold’s traditional role as a safe haven has not been lost, but it is being overshadowed by the need for investors to raise cash during a period of market stress. “Gold’s safe-haven characteristics haven’t disappeared, but they don’t operate in isolation,” Mr Weston said. "In periods of acute market stress, investors often sell what they can rather than what they want to." Gold is being sold alongside equities and other risk assets, while the dollar is attracting defensive demand and higher Treasury yields are making bullion less attractive relative to interest-bearing investments. “For buyers to return with conviction, I’d want to see three developments: a stabilisation in US real yields, a sustained pullback in the dollar and evidence that forced selling has largely run its course,” Mr Weston said. “Until then, geopolitical uncertainty alone may not be enough to restore gold's safe-haven appeal.” How low could gold prices go? With gold trading at about $3,525 an ounce, the immediate focus is whether buyers can defend the psychologically important $3,500 level. A sustained break below that could expose the $3,400 to $3,300 region, where longer-term investors and physical buyers may begin showing greater interest, Mr Weston said. Investors should wait for selling pressure to ease, volatility to moderate and, ideally, a reversal in the dollar and US real yields before concluding that gold has established a sustainable low, he added. The shift suggests traders are increasingly positioning for further downside rather than simply unwinding bullish bets, Mr Valecha said. Gold may, therefore, continue to fall more than it recovers, with any near-term rebound potentially proving temporary rather than marking a reversal in the trend. Mr Valecha also sees stronger support potentially emerging closer to $3,500 an ounce, despite the risk that prices could fall further in the near term. On the upside, bullion would need to reclaim $3,600 before moving towards $3,700. The former support zone of $3,800 to $3,850 could now act as resistance, Mr Weston said. Gold's price action suggests it could remain under pressure in the coming days, with next week's US economic data likely to prove important. For investors and jewellery buyers in the UAE, analysts advise adopting patience and a staggered approach to buying rather than committing all their money at a single price. Gold’s immediate downside focus is around $3,500 an ounce, following the break below the previous support level, said Frank Walbaum, market analyst at Naga.com. “A sustained move below this psychological level could expose the metal to further losses towards the $3,200 level,” he said.

events.title: Lufthansa to eliminate 1,000 jobs at struggling flagship airline
events.summary: Lufthansa will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees. Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its main airline in Munich and Frankfurt to help turn around the loss-making unit. It will also cut short- and medium-haul capacity and replace some Airbus A320 planes with smaller A220s. The airline faces high fuel costs, strikes and a €180 million operating loss, while talks with unions are still unresolved. Deutsche Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its namesake airline to turn around the unprofitable mainline unit, as high fuel costs put more pressure on Europe’s largest aviation group. The company will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees seen by Bloomberg. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its fleet of Airbus A320 aircraft, switching to the smaller A220 type, it said. The planned reductions are the second culling in little over a year and reveal the extent of the struggles to revive the fortunes of the airline’s flagship product. The airline group announced in September 2025 that it intended to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030. Lufthansa is undergoing its biggest efficiency drive in years as high jet-fuel prices and an underperforming mainline airline weigh on results. Lufthansa Airlines posted an operating loss of €180 million (S$254.8 million) in the first nine months. “After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future,” management wrote in the letter. “In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and our already very high cost base have made the situation more acute.” Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, said earlier in 2026 that “significantly greater efforts” may be needed to improve the airline’s flagging performance after losing ground to rivals in what he called self-inflicted damage. The measures revealed on Nov 20 come as Lufthansa tries to resolve a dispute with labour unions, though no agreement has been reached so far. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Oil prices on track to post third weekly decline despite Middle East tension
events.summary: Oil prices are on track to post a third weekly decline as investors weigh the risk of continued Middle East tension against a rise in crude supply. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil, was trading 1.34 per cent lower at $90.75 a barrel at 1.16pm UAE time on Friday. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading down 1.2 per cent at $81.36 a barrel. Brent is set to end the week more than 3 per cent lower, while WTI is on course to post a loss of more than 6 per cent. Tension in the region persists. Yemen’s Houthi rebels attacked a Public Investment Fund tower in Riyadh’s financial centre on Thursday and ships continue to face Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for one third of the world’s crude and liquefied natural gas supplies. This week, a vessel belonging to Adnoc Logistics and Services was attacked while passing through the strait. Eleven seafarers were injured and one is missing. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump appeared to push a decision whether to renew major strikes against Iran into next year. He gave three separate interviews as he returned to Washington from a historic trip to China, where he held talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin. “We’ll see what happens after January 1,” Mr Trump told Fox News in an interview broadcast on Thursday. In an interview with Axios and Israel’s News 12, he said he was "rushing to make any decisions on Iran". He made similar comments to Reuters. Rising supply from the Middle East is also affecting prices. The International Energy Agency said oil markets had returned to surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as Gulf exports recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly market report last week. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, rose to 18.4 million bpd in October but were still 26 per cent below prewar levels. The US Energy Information Administration said in a report that commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, rose by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week to November 13. That points to more supply in the market.

events.title: As attention spans move on from Iran and oil, the world is forever changed, and the conflict is escalating again
events.summary: The November news cycle has fixated on elections, Nvidia , and Anthropic, but the Iran war has quietly escalated this week, and there is no “credible pathway” for the world to return to its previous norm, the International Energy Agency warned in its annual World Energy Outlook released Thursday. Even as gasoline and diesel prices have fallen from record highs in recent weeks, the Middle East will never be the same, and the rest of the world is still racing to develop more of its own energy sources—both renewables and fossil fuels—as global supplies remain tight and food security is threatened in much of the world, especially Asia, the report stated. All this is transpiring as global energy demand spikes both from the AI boom and the rise of the middle class in developing countries. “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol. The nearly nine-month Iran war and the prolonged shuttering of the vital Strait of Hormuz represent the greatest energy supply shock in modern history—far more than the Iranian Revolution or the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s—and its reverberations will be felt in ways that remain unclear, the report said. After all, the war is ongoing, and Iran this week struck U.S. facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the U.S. countered by striking Iran’s Qeshm Island. “Attention is elsewhere now. I don’t know if it’s complacency or a lack of anxiety, but [the war] is still a pretty big deal,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm. “What I worry is if the Iranians feel they have to make people anxious again. Do they view it in their strategic interest to create more anxiety?” Pickering noted to Fortune . “I think we’ll have this uneasy conflict going on with Iran for a bunch of 2027.” Between alternative pipelines and routes, and U.S. escorts through Hormuz, Middle Eastern oil exports are approaching 90% of their prewar levels despite the ongoing military strikes, said Pavel Molchanov, Raymond James energy analyst. “This indicates that the oil market has become acclimated to periodic flare-ups, just as long as there is no return to all-out war,” he added. “That said, the lack of a U.S.-Iran deal still translates into a hefty risk premium.” Because of seasonal demand dips, rising Middle Eastern exports, and President Donald Trump’s emphasis on de-escalating the war since the midterm congressional elections, global oil prices have fallen below the $100 per barrel threshold, even though the global benchmark remains high at more than $90. After all, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is dangerously depleted at a 44-year low, and the world has cumulatively lost 2.8 billion barrels of oil over nearly nine months, the IEA report stated. A world forever changed The Iran war has triggered record-high fuel spikes in the U.S. But keep in mind that the U.S. leads the world in oil output, currently producing an all-time high of more than 14 million barrels daily. The rest of the world is left even more at the mercy of the war, and the price spikes and physical shortages are amplified, especially in Asia and Africa. More than 4 billion people—roughly half the global population—depended on the Middle East for over 30% of its oil supplies. And about 80% of Middle Eastern oil exports were destined for Asia before the war. Even as Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Iraq move to build pipelines to divert oil supplies through alternate routes, those projects will take years, and long-term Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would maintain uncertainty going forward. “That’s not a particularly comforting outlook to the consumers of Middle East crude,” Pickering said. “The finish matters, and I don’t think we have visibility on what the finish looks like.” The Americas are leading the increase in oil production—the U.S., Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Guyana, and now Venezuela—as well as a slate of African nations. And more countries are investing in renewable energy and electrification for electric vehicles. Birol and the IEA forecast that renewables—solar, wind, and batteries—are picking up momentum throughout the world even as the globe falls short of its climate change goals. Nuclear power also is gaining steam. EV sales are projected to rise in most of the world next year—less so in the U.S.—in part because of cheaper, subsidized Chinese EVs being exported worldwide. Global oil demand is now expected to peak by 2030 and slowly decline from there, the IEA said. Natural gas demand will grow through the mid-2030s and plateau. The IEA outlook noted that August was the hottest month ever on record worldwide and a strong El Niño could add to weather-related strains heading into 2027. “High energy prices and shortfalls in fertilizer supply are creating hazards for food security,” the report stated. “Emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) and air pollutants from fuel combustion remain dangerously high. Energy geopolitics are fracturing, and trade restrictions are on the rise. Trust is in short supply. Each vulnerability deepens the others.” That is why—more than ever—the world requires “credible road maps to phase out fossil fuels, backed by the public finance needed to ensure a fast and fair transition,” said David Tong, global industry lead at Oil Change International. “Fossil fuels are driving chaos and high energy bills, and the energy choices we make now will shape all our futures,” Tong added. “After yet another fossil fuel crisis, governments cannot afford to keep people and economies hooked on volatile oil and gas markets.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Deals and buys Intel Foundry signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P semiconductor manufacturing process, according to Intel executives. The customer has not been identified, and Intel has not disclosed a production timetable. Siemens plans to acquire Breker Verification Systems , a developer of AI-driven test suite synthesis and system-level verification technologies. The acquisition is expected to close in December. Microsoft selected Intel Foundry ‘s EMIB advanced packaging technology for custom silicon used in Azure’s infrastructure. The multiyear agreement also expands cooperation on Xeon processors, memory, and security technologies. Infineon and Megmeet are teaming up on 800V DC power architectures for AI data centers, using Infineon’s gen-2 CoolSiC MOSFETs in three-phase power shelves. GlobalFoundries and Boston Dynamics expanded their robotics collaboration to deploy autonomous Spot inspection robots across fabs in the U.S., Germany, and Singapore. GF also plans to begin evaluating Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots for semiconductor manufacturing tasks in early 2027. AMD completed acquisitions of AI inference chip developer Taalas and AI model research company World Labs . Funding The European Commission said more than 20 semiconductor projects have been approved under the EU Chips Act, representing over €33B in public and private investment . General Flash raised $128M to scale production of critical metals used in semiconductor and other industries. Atom Computing finalized an up to $100M CHIPS Act R&D award for neutral-atom quantum computers. Science Corporation raised $400M for its retinal implant chip that aims to restore form vision for certain types of macular degeneration. Chip trade and export controls The U.S. Department of Commerce introduced new restrictions addressing remote access to advanced U.S. AI computing through overseas data centers, along with new semiconductor licensing requirements affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The U.S. received license requests covering 3.4 million advanced Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China and approved more than 879,000 , according to U.S. government data. It is unclear how many were actually shipped. TSMC and Samsung reportedly suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following new U.S. export restrictions, pending licensing approvals, per the Financial Times. TSMC is also reportedly halting affected Chinese customer orders at 16nm and below without U.S. approval and generally limiting those customers to 28nm and 40nm processes, provided those chips do not use HBM or advanced packaging. The U.S. government released new details of an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed over suspected semiconductor export-control violations. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list in June 2025, but its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix , later received more than $800M in Nvidia AI technology , mostly through third-party manufacturers, per the NYT. Nvidia says it blocked new orders and obtained government authorization for certain repair parts shipments. An investigation is underway. The Trump administration is moving toward restrictions on Chinese optical transceiver imports , despite opposition from major U.S. cloud companies, reported Reuters. Manufacturing capacity Nvidia expanded its manufacturing agreements with Amkor , Samsung Electro-Mechanics , SPIL , TSMC , and others. The commitments cover additional substrate manufacturing, advanced packaging, and wafer capacity. As part of the expansion, ASE subsidiary SPIL signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Nvidia to triple its advanced semiconductor packaging capacity in Taiwan by mid-2029, including new production lines for wafer bumping, assembly, and testing. ASE Technology inaugurated the first phase and began construction of the second phase of its Lujhu advanced packaging facility in Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Lam Research broke ground on a technology center in Zhunan , Taiwan , as part of its five-year, $3B global R&D expansion. GlobalFoundries broke ground on a new 300mm semiconductor fab in Malta, New York , under a U.S.-Japan investment initiative providing up to $21B for two fabs. The first 300mm fab is expected to begin production in 2029. ADEKA and Entegris agreed to collaborate on advanced semiconductor materials production in Japan. Silicon Box advanced its proposed semiconductor packaging and test facility in Novara, Italy , into the basic design stage. The project is intended to establish additional European advanced packaging capacity for chiplet-based semiconductor devices. SC26 The annual supercomputing conference kicked off this week in Chicago. Nvidia announced a Rubin HPC GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores on a single GPU, along with sparse data acceleration capabilities. It also announced a 192-CPU Vera rack-scale platform for HPC with more than 200TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth. Penguin Solutions unveiled a photonics-based HBM-class memory appliance that uses Marvell technology to enable CPUs and GPUs to share memory across servers. Lambda is deploying Nvidia’s CPO switches to connect GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs. Nvidia claims up to 5× better power efficiency and 15× higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. AMD announced that its Lux supercomputer at ORNL , powered by EPYC CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPUs, is now open to scientific users. Fig. 1: Chicago’s SC26 event this week. Source: Liz Allan/Semiconductor Engineering Reports and analysis NAND flash contract prices are expected to decline in 2027 as Chinese cloud providers cut enterprise SSD orders amid GPU shortages and high inventories, reports TrendForce . Global NAND capital spending is projected to rise ~27% to ~US$30B. CSIS examined the risks of using Chinese memory chips , including CXMT DRAM, citing security and supply-chain concerns. The report recommends restricting their use in sensitive government systems and expanding independent chip testing. China still trails in leading-edge semiconductor fabrication, HBM, and chip manufacturing equipment , but it’s trying to work around those gaps through DUV multi-patterning, advanced packaging, 3D stacking, and photonics, said the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission in its annual report to Congress. Standards JEDEC previewed the DDR6 specification . While still subject to change, the current plan includes higher data rates and a wider bus, a pseudo-channel architecture, optimizations for die stacking and high-capacity modules, and data-center-focused low-power modes. JEDEC also started a System Level Reliability Testing subcommittee to develop qualification methodologies, reliability practices, and evaluation approaches for emerging system applications. events.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
events.summary: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 T he name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. “It was something quite different. Most people reacted really well to it,” said Steve Anderson, 57. “The only negative reaction I heard was to the ginger shot, which some found too strong … but that’s a preference thing. The pods themselves were very palatable.” Global packaging waste is on course to hit a projected 434.5m tonnes in 2025, rising to 525m tonnes by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 3.9%, according to research from Smithers . Plastic is at the heart of this: between 2000 and 2019, the volume of plastic waste doubled, with packaging responsible for about 40% of it. Yet plastic is among the least recycled materials, with a worldwide recycling rate of just 27.9% in 2024. The UK’s overall plastic packaging recycling reached 52.5% in 2023, up from 51.4% in 2022. Edible packaging could be part of the answer to this problem, with the market size valued at $1.04bn (£790m) in 2024 and poised to grow to $1.84bn by 2033, driven by consumers’ environmental concerns. But market research says challenges exist. One report said this was “due to the sensitivity of edible packaging to fluctuating environmental conditions, necessitating special handling during shipping and storage ”. It also said customers were reluctant to use edible utensils and the challenges hindered “widespread adoption”. However, beyond the science of packaging, a wider debate remains about our consumption habits. Environmental campaigners argue that the ultimate solution to the plastic waste crisis is not finding better ways to wrap single-use items, but moving away from a throwaway culture altogether. Even for those who do want to create better packaging, money remains a hurdle. Prof James Elliott at the University of Cambridge, who is working on plastic packaging alternatives, said manufacturers were not keen to pay more for biodegradable alternatives. “They are very cost driven,” he said, adding that the non-biodegradable plastic market was $265bn “so the $1bn proportion being edible is small”. Andrew Wallis, packaging lead at Innocent Drinks, said 78% of consumers would consider buying ginger shots encased in seaweed, according to a survey. He said it could also be used in Innocent’s kids’ range, which currently uses paper straws in plastic packaging. “Could that wrap be exchanged for a seaweed wrapper?” he said. Notpla created similar pods for the London Marathon. Other examples of innovation in this area include Xampla, which created a stock cube wrapped in edible film, and Cupffee, which made the world’s first edible cup. At Notpla’s headquarters, in east London, seaweed is used to encase small amounts of olive oil as well as for sandwich packaging and to replace plastic film in cardboard packaging. The team has also made spoons out of seaweed, which are used in ice-cream parlours including Ice Cream Union in London. Rodrigo García González, co-founder of Notpla, said seaweed was a good sustainable solution because it grew rapidly. “Some seaweed can grow up to 60cm a day,” he said. “It’s one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth, much faster than bamboo, and it doesn’t compete with anything on land.” He also said it biodegraded more quickly than a leaf. At Notpla, a machine pushes out ginger shots into seaweed casing, like sausages on a factory conveyor belt. The company is still working out how a product such as this could work in a supermarket: it lasts only three days, but in an unopened bottle could be kept for weeks. Elliott said one of the big problems with edible packaging was about scale: “About 30-40% of all plastics used worldwide are used in packaging … the scale is phenomenal. We use 2m tonnes of plastic in the UK per year.” He said it would be hard to “harvest that much seaweed without making huge changes”. But González said seaweed “already operates at a scale most people don’t realise”. He added: “Around 40m tonnes are harvested every year, almost all of it farmed, and it’s already in everyday products from toothpaste to ice-cream. It’s also one of the fastest-growing organisms on the planet.” Elliott has been working on developing a non-edible packaging made from cellulose. “It’s designed to be composted. Cellulose is abundant in every plant, so we take waste plant material and turn it into films.” The planet's most important stories.

events.title: A rare EU-UK summit as Andy Burnham seeks to mend Brexit damage
events.summary: A decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences and possibly pave a way to get back together BRUSSELS -- A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union , top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together . Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners. Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week. Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining. Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.” The two sides are expected to sign a trade deal for food and drink, an agreement on emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain’s economy. American surfer Kurt Van Dyke's girlfriend among 2 arrested in his Costa Rica death A long-buried ancient library in Rome opens to the public after restoration Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC The war in Ukraine , and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration. “Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.” Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions. events.title: Get rich quick, or lose it all: The shared fun and frustration of Monopoly's capitalist world
events.summary: Monopoly, with its colorful money and metal tokens, is a game night staple that has entertained and frustrated players for decades NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Buy Marvin Gardens. Draw a Get Out of Jail Free card. Put a hotel on Boardwalk or Baltic Avenue. And when you pass Go, collect $200. It’s easy to name the game being played . With its iconic colorful paper money and metal playing tokens , Monopoly has entertained and frustrated countless players as they vie to win it all or go “bankrupt” trying. Even with its reputation for long and cutthroat gameplay, the property-trading, rags-to-riches board game has become entrenched in the American experience and part of a global lexicon. It’s both a game-night staple and a cultural symbol that draws parallels to — and to some extent lampoons — the highs and lows of capitalism and the American dream. Parker Brothers launched its Monopoly in 1935 while America was still in the throes of the Great Depression. In “Monopoly: The World’s Most Famous Game and How It Got That Way,” Philip Orbanes, a former Parker Brothers executive, explains that the board game quickly became “a common language, a shared reservoir of enjoyment and experience that players from the four corners of the Earth could share with equanimity.” He gives Parker Brothers a lot of the credit for that. The American game maker didn’t invent Monopoly, though it bought the rights to Charles Darrow’s version and to its predecessor, Landlord’s Game by Elizabeth Magie . Monopoly evolved over time through various adaptations of Magie’s game. But according to Orbanes, Parker Brothers standardized Monopoly, including rewriting the rules. He explains that this “meant that consumers in every part of the country played Monopoly the same way,” personal house rules aside. A British game maker helped ensure that standardization carried over to international versions as well. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The game's standard rules continue to give players a shared starting point. But whether you know all the official rules or not, breaking them — or coming up with new ones — is also a Monopoly tradition. The instructions for several Monopoly editions advise against using personal house rules in order “to keep your game short and sweet.” But Hasbro, which owns Monopoly, recognizes that fan-created rules are part of gameplay for many. Some house rules have even inspired official Monopoly variations. In a news release about the game's 90th anniversary, Hasbro executive Brian Baker explained: “It’s a cultural phenomenon that has transcended generations and resonates deeply with players across the globe. ... We’re celebrating the elements our players have loved for nearly a century.” Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. events.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
events.summary: Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score. Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision. "When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says. It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud. "Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says. "Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says. Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story. "As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance. Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data. "A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa. "But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says. Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history. But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to? In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms. But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness. "Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement. Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk." If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion". But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns. "Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains. Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford. "We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past". While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation. She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past. "Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination." Upstart says it is tackling that issue. "We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement. Evangeline Atkinson (left) and Laura Mills co-founders of Noggin HQ Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score. "I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls. "When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies." That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

events.title: US chip equipment maker KLA opens expanded site in Singapore, with plans for further growth
events.summary: Semiconductor equipment maker KLA’s expanded site in Ang Mo Kio gives the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space. KLA opened its expanded Building 22B site in Ang Mo Kio, adding about 210,000 sq ft and making Singapore a major global production hub for the chip equipment maker. The firm plans a third expansion phase, pending land and approvals, and expects the site to support about 1,000 new jobs in R&D, supply chain and manufacturing engineering. Singapore leaders said KLA strengthens the country’s semiconductor ecosystem, supports local suppliers, and fits with $800 million in RIE 2030 research plans for the chip industry. SINGAPORE – US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened an expanded plant in Singapore and announced it has plans for a third phase of expansion, making the Republic one of its major production hubs globally. The expanded site, Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, was announced in October 2024 and is now fully operational – giving the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space. KLA, which makes machines and tools such as surface profilers, testers and semiconductor assembly solutions for chipmakers, established its presence in Singapore in 1996 and began manufacturing here in 2006. Theo Kneepkens, KLA Singapore country president and senior vice-president of global operations, said the company has also outlined plans for a further expansion phase here, subject to finalisation of land arrangements and relevant approvals. “I was actually hoping that this would already be a ground-breaking of our next phase. But we’re still defining a few details of our next phase of expansion before we can officially announce that,” he said. “But it’s clear that our next phase of growth will be bigger than the current expanded site .” Kneepkens said KLA’s plans for an additional phase reflect its conviction that Singapore – with its exceptional talent, supportive governance and strategic position – will remain indispensable in how the world manufactures critical semiconductor equipment powering AI and advanced computing. In the longer term, Building 22B and the planned phase are expected to support about 1,000 new jobs across research and development, supply chain and manufacturing engineering. KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins said: “We’ve added hundreds of new roles, with over 2,200 employees working across multiple shifts, and 90% of KLA Singapore employees are locals, including both Singaporean citizens and permanent residents.” He noted that KLA’s long-term investment in Singapore has been driven by the local talent, highly collaborative partners and access to suppliers and customers. “We are experiencing unprecedented growth across the industry, and our customers show no signs of slowing. If anything, the demand environment is only accelerating,” he said. KLA’s expansion comes on the heels of several investment commitments announced in the past few years by companies that fabricate semiconductors or are part of the manufacturing value chain, such as processors of silicon substrate materials and companies that test, assemble and package chips. Chip firms that have made fresh investments include GlobalFoundries, Micron, Siltronic, Soitec, UMC, Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP Semiconductors. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said at KLA’s opening ceremony that Singapore has built a strong ecosystem for semiconductor equipment manufacturing, and the Republic now accounts for around one-fifth of global production. “Singapore must keep building the specialised capabilities that companies need to compete. “By working with partners like KLA, we can support their growth while creating good opportunities for our people and enterprises,” he said. Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that as chips become more powerful and specialised, manufacturing them requires greater precision. Hence, equipment made by companies like KLA, which can measure process variations and detect defects early, is increasingly important. “KLA is a key part of Singapore’s strength in this field. Its process-control tools help chipmakers bring advanced technologies into reliable, high-volume production,” he added. He said Singapore is also investing in the research capabilities needed to seize new opportunities in the chip industry, committing $800 million under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to the RIE Flagship in Semiconductors. He lauded a three-year collaboration between KLA and A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics, saying such partnerships will help turn research into practical manufacturing solutions, so Singapore can continue to meet the semiconductor industry’s changing needs. Local suppliers are evolving alongside the multinational companies they support, Gan added.

events.title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
events.summary: UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent Treasury watchdog, said the latest figures were “broadly in line” with its October forecast for a £1.1bn fall in total borrowing for the 2026-27 financial year. However, it warned there were “several risks” amid the sharp rise in energy costs, and public spending on cost of living support measures. Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly. “However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.” The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October – £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997. Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs. Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s. Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran. “This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added. Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend. In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs. After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year. Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP. Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year. Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year. Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”

events.title: Singapore-based DayOne to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns: Sources
events.summary: DayOne was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.45 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter. DayOne Data Centers has paused its planned US IPO, which could have raised up to US$5 billion, because investors are worried about high AI and data centre valuations. The Singapore-based firm may still list in 2027 if market sentiment improves. It has not made a final decision and declined to comment. The delay follows wider sector pressure, with other data centre IPOs also stalled. US rules on advanced chips in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia add more risk. SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering (IPO) on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom. The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.5 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously. But the company started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks. Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing. Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment. Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets. The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008. Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement, and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company. Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector. In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever IPOs, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027. DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba Group. The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators that they will need a licence to purchase American tech hardware. DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

events.title: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
events.summary: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided- missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.” In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.” Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.” As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves. Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components. When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone. Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in. “A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says. To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch. In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US. Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.” Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.” When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said. The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.

events.title: A third of David Jones staff told employment ends days after Christmas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones staff issued with redundancy notices More than 1,600 David Jones staff will lose their jobs after Christmas. ( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) Nearly 1,700 David Jones employees have been served their redundancy notices today. Staff were told December 30 will be their last day, as the union seeks to find them alternative employment. Those made redundant are expected to receive their entitlements, but for customers delivery options such as click and collect are unavailable. A total of 1,689 David Jones employees were served their redundancy notices on Friday. Staff were informed their employment will officially terminate on December 30. The union, the SDA, says it will be working overtime to help members find alternative employment. "We will leave no stone unturned in our efforts to find alternative employment for our members, and are grateful that already a number of companies have come forward seeking the skills and experience our DJs members have to offer," NSW secretary Bernie Smith said. The SDA says it is communicating directly with members and has established a dedicated help desk to ensure what David Jones is offering redundant employees is in line with their financial and legal entitlements. The iconic retailer went into voluntary administration earlier this month. New South Wales (7): Macquarie Centre, Macarthur Square, Parramatta, Wollongong Central, Hornsby, Green Hills and Warringah Mall Victoria (3): Malvern Central, Highpoint and Glen Waverley Western Australia (3): Hay Street Mall, Garden City and Carousel Queensland (2): Robina Town Centre and Sunshine Plaza South Australia (2): West Lakes and Marion Australian Capital Territory (1): Woden Receiver David McGrath and Joseph Hansell of FTI Consulting confirmed it would close 19 of the retailer's 38 stores across Australia and New Zealand on November 11. In a letter to suppliers, David Jones said: "We expect the affected stores to continue trading through the peak seasonal period, with closure dates anticipated to occur later in the year." Friday's news confirms staff will be asked to leave a day before New Year's Eve. "There is never a good time for a company to go under, but it is even more stressful for our affected members as it occurs in the very shadow of Christmas, normally a happy and relaxed moment in an otherwise busy year," Mr Smith said. Retail analyst Gary Mortimer described the news as "deeply disappointing". "While employees should receive their entitlements, that provides little comfort to workers and families now facing an uncertain future just weeks before Christmas," Professor Mortimer said. Earlier this week ABS data showed a broader surge in Australia's unemployment rate, and that was before the David Jones redundancies. David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. "With Australia's unemployment rate now sitting at 4.9 per cent, the loss of around 1,500 positions will place even more pressure on the labour market and add to the number of Australians seeking work," Professor Mortimer said. "My thoughts are with the affected employees, many of whom have dedicated years of service to the business and are now confronting a difficult holiday period." There has been a surge in online orders since the receivership was announced and the David Jones website warns that "deliveries may take longer than usual". Common delivery options such as express, same-day, Saturday delivery, and click and collect are unavailable. The ABC has confirmed David Jones is up to date with superannuation payments to its 6,000 employees, in line with new pay-day laws that came into effect in July. events.title: Social poker with £5 stake is booming, says dealer
events.summary: Phillip Steer says the cost-of-living crisis might have increased the appeal of the game, he says "you can have a night out for a fiver" A man who organises social poker sessions in pubs and clubs said the game's growing popularity could be down to the cost-of-living crisis. Phillip Steer, from March, Cambridgeshire, has run poker nights in Fenland for 14 years and said he has seen a 35% rise in the number of players in the area since 2022, with now about "100 players across 15 clubs and pubs". Steer added that as people can only place a maximum £5 stake, the game was often "cheaper" than other pastimes. Player Violet Cunningham said: "I have been playing poker for about 10 years; it's nice to get out of the house... it's fun and exciting." Tom Brady, the director of Live Pub Poker League (LPPL), said he had also seen an increase in the number of players joining for social tournaments in pubs and venues post-Covid, with the past 12 months being particularly busy. Steer said that poker can reduce social isolation and also improve players' numeracy On a chilly November evening about 15 people congregated in a pub in March, where they are given the use of a warm side room to set up their poker tables, cards and chips. Steer said all sorts of people get involved in the game, adding: "We have men, women, retired and working people." He said most people treat the game as a bit of fun and he did not worry that players would get into debt by taking part, due to the low-value stake. "You buy 12,000 chips at the start of the night for £5 and once those have gone it is game over," he added. Donald Rofe, 81, is dubbed "Stetson" because of his hat and says he does not mind if he wins or loses but just loves "getting out and meeting people" Donald Rofe is a widower and lives alone in March, he said his family live in Wisbech and Cambridge. "[Poker] gets me out of the house, although I have recently had my cataracts done, so I have some issues with reading the cards properly," he said. Rofe admitted that he mistook a diamond for a heart, which cost him a victory. "I put in all my chips because I thought I had a flush but I didn't, but it was still fun", he added. The cost of play is another bonus for Rofe, who added he normally has one soft drink that will "last me all night". Violet Cunningham plays poker under the name of "Ultraviolet" Violet Cunningham is a full-time carer and said she liked to relax by playing poker. "I have been playing poker for about 10 years, it's nice to get out of the house - it makes your brain tick, it's fun and exciting, but can be frustrating," she said. Cunningham said she and her family grew up playing card games on holiday and she has always enjoyed playing them. "I think women are harder to read than the men, play a bit tighter, unless they have it [a good hand] they probably won't bet on it," she added. The Gambling Commission , external said that pub poker was classed as "exempt gaming" and can be carried out without a gambling licence or permit. Players cannot place a stake more than £5 and combined stakes for the premises hosting the game cannot exceed £100 per day. Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. events.title: Survey reveals 'major increase' in cost of living
events.summary: Island Global Research said the survey was completed by more than 3,000 people across Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man There has been "a major increase" in the overall cost of living in the past 12 months in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man, a survey has found. Island Global Research, a market research and consultancy company, found more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man said they had noticed a cost increase , external . The survey, which was completed by over 1,000 people in each island, saw 57% of respondents describe themselves as "less than comfortable" with about one in 10 going without essentials like food and heating. The survey also found 65% said they now spent less on non essentials and 53% said they are shopping around more because of the price rises. In Jersey, 10% of respondents reported they could not afford the increased costs and often have to go with out essentials, while in Guernsey it was 11%. The survey also showed that two thirds of people in Jersey said they had found it difficult to meet living costs in the last 12 months, an increase of 17 percentage points compared to 2024 . Guernsey also saw an increase with 58% reporting they found it difficult to meet living costs. The survey also found about one in four received support to help finance their everyday living expenses in the last six months. On the Isle of Man, 36% said they cut back on groceries and 30% received support to help finance everyday living expenses over a six-month period.
