events.title: You tell AI everything. But who else is listening?
events.summary: The meteoric fall of Nvidia's Jensen Huang , following controversy over his personal relationships and US national security, has raised questions about judgement, trust and the people leading the world's most powerful technology companies. But it also prompts a broader question. How much do we really know about the people behind the technologies we increasingly trust with our information? And how private is that information we’re sending in confidence kept? I know I’m not alone in treating artificial intelligence as my personal doctor, giving it detailed information about my health in exchange for bespoke medical advice without needing a co-pay. It’s also my instant therapist, answering personal questions about how I should engage with problematic people in my life. Basically information I probably wouldn’t want anyone to know. We use ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, and Anthropic's Claude to research, analyse documents, draft correspondence, and solve problems. In addition, people may share sensitive personal information, professional dilemmas and confidential business material. Sometimes, all we do is ask a question. And that is revealing in itself. But what actually happens to that information once we press enter? Who can see it, and where does it go? The answer may surprise people who assume their conversations with AI are entirely private. How much is out there When we enter information into a cloud-based AI platform , it travels to computing infrastructure operated by the provider or its partners. There it is processed, and depending on the service and privacy settings, it may be stored, checked by automated systems, reviewed by authorised humans or used to improve AI models. These companies are surprisingly candid about this in their posts. OpenAI says that authorised employees and contracted service providers may access consumer conversations for safety investigations, technical support, legal matters and model improvement, where permitted. Google's Gemini documentation goes further. It confirms that trained human reviewers, including external service providers, may examine information processed from connected applications. This can include excerpts and summaries of emails and documents, and sometimes the complete contents of a short email or file. Google advises users not to connect applications containing confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see. And if this is said publicly, imagine what else is happening behind closed doors that should give us pause. It's not a free-for-all, as these companies have access restrictions and operate under national and international laws. But the key message is clear: just because your entered information is not public, it doesn’t mean it's private. You might assume that, because you are using a personal AI account, it's a closed-loop conversation. But that depends on how you access it. Using office Wi-Fi alone does not ordinarily allow your employer to read encrypted AI conversations, although it may reveal which services you visit. A company laptop equipped with monitoring software, however, could expose more. Microsoft's own security tools, for example, can inspect information typed or pasted into AI prompts. The situation is different again when you use an employer-managed AI account. OpenAI confirms that authorised administrators may, depending on permissions and configuration, access or export employees' prompts, files and conversation histories. Anthropic similarly confirms that designated owners of Claude for Work accounts can request exports containing employee conversations. In other words, what feels like a private conversation may be accessible to your employer, depending on the account, device and security systems you use. Rest assured, encryption generally prevents employers from reading AI prompts over office Wi-Fi, according to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a US-based digital rights organisation. This is true unless additional monitoring tools are in place. Nevertheless, the combination of workplace monitoring, managed accounts and third-party AI platforms creates a complicated privacy landscape that few employees fully understand. There is another side to this. What happens when executives handling sensitive information use personal AI accounts to analyse confidential acquisitions, strategic plans or financial projections? Research from Cyberhaven's 2026 AI Adoption and Risk Report found that 39.7 per cent of observed data movements into AI tools involved sensitive corporate information. Meanwhile, IBM's 2025 breach research found that one in five organisations studied had experienced breaches linked to unauthorised AI use. The risks are no longer theoretical. The recent $6.34 billion Binance hack highlights this danger. In its November investigation, the cryptocurrency exchange revealed that attackers had exploited compromised employee devices and an internal AI tool as part of the breach. Our privacy rights? Beyond corporate security lies a more fundamental question for everyday people: What rights do we have over the information we voluntarily give these systems? The UAE's Personal Data Protection Law, under Articles 13 and 15, and Europe's General Data Protection Regulation, under Articles 15 to 17, give individuals rights to access information about their personal data, correct inaccuracies and, under certain conditions, request its deletion. But these rights are not absolute. Having the legal right to request deletion does not necessarily mean every trace of an AI conversation can be erased from all systems. Google states that certain conversations reviewed by humans may remain stored for up to three years, even after the user deletes their activity. Switching off Gemini's activity history still allows temporary retention for operational and safety purposes. We can choose privacy settings, but those choices do not always amount to complete control. For the UAE, where AI is central to economic ambition and business transformation, this deserves particular attention. Companies need clear policies for AI use, while individuals need to understand the implications of using personal and corporate accounts. The issue is not whether we should abandon AI. Its benefits are enormous, world-changing even. The question is whether we can trust these technologies and the organisations behind them to keep our private information actually private, on our own terms. History clearly shows that regulation often lags behind technological innovation, leaving society exposed to risks that take years to address. We saw this with the internet and social media platforms designed to exploit reward mechanisms, particularly among young people. More than two decades later, countries such as Australia and the UAE are now introducing tougher age restrictions to protect children. Are we repeating the same mistake with AI, allowing its rapid adoption to outpace safeguards? Must we wait another two decades to act? We

events.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
events.summary: Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee Jones "This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives. But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity. The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition. A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block. The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people. About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat. The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence. The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview House Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined. While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support . Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment. We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation. Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity. Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved". The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added. Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth" Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives. Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies. Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices. Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently. Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common. The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan. But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act. He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat. "Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building.

events.title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
events.summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses. And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation. The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one. “For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel. It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too. Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic. But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few. “For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.” In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute. “Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum. “You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.” At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it. “I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.” And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?” If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment. Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade. Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.

( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) SA Health has revealed that a former staff member inappropriately accessed 503 patient records. A formal investigation was launched after SA Health was notified of a privacy breach in late June. SA Health says all impacted patients have been notified in writing by the YNLHN. SA Health has revealed that a former staff member inappropriately accessed 503 patient records since September 2024. It says the Yorke and Northern Local Health Network (YNLHN) staff member was immediately put on leave when the investigation began and no longer works for SA Health. In a statement, SA Health said the incident had been reported to the relevant authorities, and the staff member will have "a note on their permanent record". SA Health says all affected patients have been notified in writing by the YNLHN. "SA Health has policies and processes in place to ensure staff only access information that is necessary and appropriate for their role," the statement read. "This includes requiring staff to verify they are authorised to access the information when they log into the electronic medical record system." SA Health says it's considering additional measures to prevent further breaches, including strengthening audits for potential inappropriate access to patient information. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) The statement noted additional measures were being explored to prevent further breaches, and that any staff member accessing information without a legitimate work-related reason may be subject to disciplinary processes, including possible employment termination. YNLHN chief executive Zoe Bishop said the Network sincerely apologises for any harm and distress caused. "Any unauthorised access of information is taken very seriously, and after a careful and comprehensive investigation process, the staff member is no longer employed by SA Health," Dr Bishop wrote in a statement. "We acted as soon as we were made aware of these potential breaches. "I want to reassure the community that this behaviour falls well below the standards we expect, and people should continue to have trust in our health services and our hardworking staff." Robyn Lindsay is the Department for Health and Wellbeing's chief executive. ( Supplied ) Department for Health and Wellbeing chief executive Robyn Lindsay said the "vast majority" of SA Health staff access patient information appropriately. "Where we find that a patient's information has been inappropriately accessed, we have a responsibility to inform the patients of the breach and take appropriate action during and after the investigation," she wrote. "While breaches such as this are rare, we must continue to remain vigilant to ensure we maintain the highest possible standards of integrity when it relates to patient information." In a separate incident in July, SA Health apologised to the family of Tony Modra amid revelations staff may have inappropriately accessed his patient records. Multiple staff members were being investigated at the time for alleged privacy breaches. In December 2024, 18 SA Health staff members resigned or were sanctioned for unauthorised access to the records of Charlie Stevens , the late son of Grant Stevens. SA Health reports quarterly on staff members who have been reprimanded or terminated from their employment for inappropriately accessing patient records. events.title: Anthropic shares close 17% above IPO price after volatile Nasdaq debut
events.summary: Anthropic shares closed 17 per cent above their offer price on their first day of trading , as an early rally in the world's largest initial public offering faded amid broader caution over artificial intelligence stocks. The company behind the Claude chatbot opened on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $111.50, 34 per cent above its $83 IPO price, briefly giving it a fully diluted valuation of about $2 trillion. The stock then pared back its gains to close at $97.17. That values the company at about $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis, or about $1.27 trillion on the shares now outstanding. Anthropic, led by chief executive Dario Amodei, raised $81.3 billion by selling 980 million shares, and a further $26 billion through a private placement, bringing the total to $107.3 billion. The deal overtook SpaceX's $86 billion listing in June as the largest on record. The closing price is well above PitchBook's estimate of $79 a share, or $1.42 trillion fully diluted. Harrison Rolfes, a senior research analyst at PitchBook, said orders for the IPO reached about six times the number of shares available. "The first year will test the price," he said. PitchBook expects 2027 to be the weakest year in its forecast, with locked-up shares released in stages around Anthropic's first earnings reports. Before trading began, Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, said the listing was being watched as a "verdict on the wider AI trade", after valuation worries, rising infrastructure costs and Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia affected the sector. The debut did not lift the wider market. Major US indexes fell on Thursday and Asian chip stocks dropped on Friday.

events.title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
events.summary: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower... WASHINGTON -- The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices. The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year. The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure , saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate. A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels. “Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said. Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.” The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators. “I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved.

events.title: General Pants owner warned of trouble long before collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts General Pants owner Alquemie Group warned of trouble long before collapse General Pants Co went into voluntary administration this week. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) Documents seen by the ABC show General Pants's owner Alquemie Group was told by auditors there was doubt about its operation. Financial reports show the company has lost $57 million in the 2024 and 2025 financial years. General Pants Co has been placed in the control of voluntary administrators. The owner of General Pants Co had been warned multiple times about the retailer's ability to keep operating long before the company collapsed into administration. Documents seen by the ABC show Alquemie Group, which acquired General Pants Co in 2022, was told by auditors BDO its ongoing reliance on cash injections from shareholders, combined with challenging retail conditions, cast doubt on its ability to continue operating. General Pants, which started as a jeans retailer in 1972, is the last remaining retailer of the group which once had six brands to its name, and was handed to administrators Alvarez & Marsal late on Wednesday evening. Alquemie Group reported losses after tax shot up from $2 million in 2023 to $29.6 million in 2024 and $27.2 million in 2025. General Pants was the last brand owned by Alquemie Group. ( ABC NEWS: Michael Barnett ) During that time there was a management change, with the former chief executive of the now collapsed Mosaic Brands, Scott Evans, joining the group in May 2024 "with a clear mandate to restructure the business and return it to profitability", according to its financial report. Following Mr Evans's appointment, the group sold loss-making companies SurfStitch and Ginger & Smart and shut the doors of National Geographic, which had cost it $4.4 million the year prior. Alquemie also underwrote the value of the General Pants brand by $13.2 million, leaving its worth at $38.2 million, a far cry from the $60 million it paid to acquire the company. General Pants Co in voluntary administration There are now 500 jobs in question as the administrators plan to continue trading through the busy Black Friday sales period. It received a $14 million cash injection from private equity firms and key shareholders in 2024 and a second one of $8 million in 2025. Even with the injection, the company continued to breach conditions with its main bank lender CBA, managing to carry the loans forward to avoid defaulting. But during that process, its loans ballooned from $4.6 million in 2023 to $43.8 million in 2025. Lego stores could not stem the bleeding Alquemie sold its Lego Store business earlier this year. ( AAP: Dean Lewins ) The group touted the excellent performance of its licensed Lego Stores yet sold the business for a reported $65 million to Kennedy Consolidated in May this year. Company staff numbers were also slashed from 1,246 to 929. In 2024 logistics firm Mainfreight issued the company a winding-up order, saying it was owed $125,000, and supplier UCC did the same in 2025, saying it was owed almost $70,000. Financial auditors raised concerns multiple times about Alquemie's ability to continue operating. "Ongoing challenging conditions within the retail industry, compounded by the broader economic impacts of the cost of living crisis, have contributed to the Group producing a loss before tax of $31,955,000 for the financial year, resulting in a continued breach of covenants related to the Group's loan facility with CBA," BDO audit director Josh Bresolin wrote in the financial report. It went on to say that outside factors affecting the business "were exacerbated by internal operational issues". This included decisions within General Pants that led to subsequent operating losses "which, under new leadership, have subsequently been rectified". It further pointed out that its debts, economic climate and customer sentiment indicated that "a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the Group's ability to continue as a going concern". An Alquemie Group spokesperson said the retail trading environment and the growing dominance of offshore online-only retailers had seen General Pants progressively reduce its physical store footprint. "To address this, Alquemie Group actively focused on a range of options for General Pants including a sale process or significant capital injection to help it better compete against large scale competitors," they said. They said a voluntary administration process would explore restructuring scenarios which could allow General Pants the opportunity to be restructured into smaller-scale, more focused and, ultimately, viable business.

events.title: Senate passes Trump-backed permitting bill
events.summary: The Senate passed a sweeping, bipartisan bill Thursday night that's designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects. Why it matters: The eyes of the entire energy industry are on this bill. If it becomes law, it could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers. Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles and creating a more predictable process for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the plan, which has White House support, would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. Driving the news: The vote was 62-33. The bill would still have to pass the House before the end of the year, and any differences would have to be worked out by both chambers before President Trump could sign it into law. Catch up quick: It would make significant changes to federal permitting, including: New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. Language that would make it more difficult to revoke permits once they're issued, a priority for renewables groups and Democrats upset with Trump administration barriers. State of play: There are also provisions to ensure that data centers pay for needed grid upgrades, and expand federal authority over the siting and approval of certain interstate transmission projects. Friction point: Many environmental advocates argue that the bill would dangerously erode safeguards in the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. Multiple tribal groups still oppose it despite changes aimed at easing concerns about consultation on historic preservation. Energy and business groups, ranging from renewables developers to manufacturers to the oil and gas industry, are lobbying for the measure. The AFL-CIO and many individual unions back it, too. What's next: The measure now heads to the House. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Bloomberg last week that he expects to have the votes to pass the plan. Some Democrats have called for hitting the brakes, with some arguing they can write a better package when they control Congress next year. Yet multiple backers within the wider Democratic coalition argue there isn't political space for an altered bill that President Trump would sign.

events.title: ‘IPO and beyond’: GIC to stay invested in Anthropic following Nasdaq debut
events.summary: Anthropic made the largest stock market debut on record on Nov 19, raising about US$81.3 billion (S$105 billion) through its IPO. GIC says it will stay invested in Anthropic “through the IPO and beyond”, and has become one of the AI firm’s largest backers after three funding rounds in under a year. Anthropic made a record Nasdaq debut, raising about US$81.3 billion and opening above its IPO price, even as the wider tech market fell on AI valuation worries. GIC has put in more than US$4.5 billion, with support beyond cash, including AI infrastructure, global contacts and expansion help. Anthropic’s rise has created huge gains for investors. SINGAPORE – GIC intends to remain invested in artificial intelligence company Anthropic beyond its blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), as the Singapore sovereign wealth fund looks to deepen its partnership with the Claude chatbot maker. Chris Emanuel, managing director and head of GIC’s Technology Investment Group, said in a LinkedIn post on Nov 20 that the fund was one of Anthropic’s largest investors, having participated in three funding rounds in less than a year. “An IPO is an important milestone, but it’s just one moment in a company’s journey,” he said. “We invest across multiple rounds, through the IPO and beyond. That’s life-cycle investing in practice.” His comments came after Anthropic made the largest stock market debut on record on Nov 19 , raising about US$81.3 billion (S$105 billion) through its IPO, which valued the company at around US$1.5 trillion at the offer price. The American company priced its shares at US$83 apiece, above its initial range of US$70 to US$78, after increasing the size of its offering to 980 million shares amid strong investor demand. Anthropic’s shares opened at US$111.50 on the Nasdaq, briefly lifting its valuation above US$2 trillion, before paring gains to close at US$97.17, up 17.1 % from the IPO price. Its strong debut contrasted with a broader Wall Street sell-off, as the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell about 2.3% on Nov 19 amid concerns over elevated AI valuations and spending. Emanuel said GIC’s partnership with Anthropic extended beyond capital investment, with the fund drawing on its global network and investment platform to support the company’s expansion. “Three rounds, three moves forward, in under a year. Today, GIC is one of Anthropic’s largest investors, and our partnership has grown well beyond the cheque,” he wrote. The sovereign wealth fund has invested more than US$4.5 billion in Anthropic across its last three funding rounds, with its stake valued at about US$15 billion at the IPO price, Bloomberg reported. The investments included Anthropic’s US$30 billion Series G funding round in February, which GIC co-led with US investment company Coatue. The round valued the AI company at US$380 billion. Beyond financing, GIC has supported Anthropic’s AI infrastructure requirements through Theseus, connected its management with senior business leaders across the fund’s global network and assisted its international expansion, Emanuel said. The fund has also invested in Ode, which helps enterprises deploy Anthropic’s technology. Anthropic repeatedly stood out in conversations with customers, while its technical capabilities, mission and emphasis on developing AI responsibly strengthened the fund’s confidence in the company, he added. “We build conviction, back it with scale over time, and bring the broader capabilities of GIC to the founders and companies we believe in,” said Emanuel. Multibillion-dollar gains for investors Anthropic’s listing has generated substantial paper gains for its early and late-stage backers, reflecting the rapid increase in the company’s valuation. According to the Financial Times, Spark Capital, which invested in Anthropic when the company was valued at about US$4 billion in 2023, stood to hold roughly US$11 billion worth of shares at a US$1.4 trillion valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested around US$3.2 billion, was estimated to hold a stake worth more than US$25 billion. Menlo Ventures’ investment of about US$1 billion was expected to be worth around US$21 billion. Strategic investors Amazon and Google’s parent Alphabet collectively held close to 30% of Anthropic following the listing. Anthropic’s rapid rise has been underpinned by strong demand for its AI models and enterprise services, although the company faces substantial computing and infrastructure costs as it expands. Its annualised revenue reached about US$81 billion last month, up from roughly US$1 billion at the start of 2025, according to Reuters. The company’s valuation has also climbed sharply, from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in its latest private-funding round in May 2026. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Alibaba defrauded shareholders by concealing ties to suspected spy in Nvidia scandal, lawsuit says
events.summary: Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business, the proposed class action says. Alibaba was sued by shareholders in New York for allegedly hiding ties to Megaspeed and a suspected spy, which they say inflated its share price and hid export control risks. The suit says Alibaba shares fell 14% in four days after media reports linked the company to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, and warned of tighter US rules on Chinese AI access. Alibaba denied no comment, while chief executive Eddie Wu said it still aims for $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin by 2030, despite US curbs. NEW YORK – Alibaba was sued on Nov 19 in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation last week. According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business. The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14% over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer. They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of advanced processors. Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant. Nvidia faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors. Wu said on Nov 19 that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion (S$129 billion) in external cloud revenue and a 20% earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company’s products and services in 2027 . The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia . In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the US Department of Defense linked to China’s military. events.title: Oil prices gain as Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise supply concerns
events.summary: A screengrab image from a social media video showing a tanker on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Oman, on Nov 17. Oil prices rose slightly after Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh and tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz raised supply fears. Brent and WTI are still set for weekly falls, as traders expect a surplus, though OPEC+ cut hopes and Middle East risks support prices. The wider conflict is disrupting global energy trade, while attacks in Russia and Putin’s warning add more pressure to oil markets. TOKYO – Oil prices edged higher on Nov 20, though set for a weekly decline, as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures rose 59 US cents, or 0.6%, to US$92.57 a barrel by 0720 GMT (3.20pm Singapore time) . US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures for December climbed 42 US cents, or 0.5%, to US$83.63 a barrel , while the more-active January contract gained 60 US cents, or 0.7%, to US$83.04 . Both benchmarks settled little changed on Nov 19, but Brent is set for a 3.5% decline for the week while the December WTI contract is set for a 6% weekly drop, as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. Brent and WTI are set to fall for the third week in a row. “Concerns over Middle Eastern crude oil supplies have resurfaced due to attacks on Riyadh by the Houthis, prompting buying,” said Satoru Yoshida, a commodity analyst at Rakuten Securities. “Expectations that coordinated production cuts will continue at the OPEC+ meeting later this month are also providing support,” he said. The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-aligned movement. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and “exploded” and “are burning”, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps Navy in a statement carried by state media on Nov 19. Iran’s intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the waterway, “running at roughly one incident per day in November”, still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to the global oil and gas trade, and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Nov 19. However, some analysts were still expecting softness in the broader equity markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Nov 20 – heading for their worst week since 2020. “Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices,” said Saxo analysts in a note. In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Nov 18. Separately on Nov 19, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow would hit back hard after Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week and said he was dropping any idea of a moratorium on attacking energy sectors and shipping. events.title: Stocks slide as AI sell-off deepens; Asia has worst week since 2020
events.summary: Investors have retreated from one of the hottest corners of the market in 2026 as mounting doubts over the AI trade pressure technology stocks. Global stocks fell as the AI sell-off deepened. Anthropic’s IPO did not restore trust, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 2%. Asia had its worst week since 2020. MSCI Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped 8% this week, while Japan’s Nikkei fell 5%. Investors moved into safe assets. US Treasuries and German bonds rallied, the VIX rose, and the US dollar stayed near a 20-month high. LONDON/HONG KONG/SINGAPORE – Stock markets stumbled around the world on Nov 20 after Anthropic’s initial public offering failed to restore investors’ faith in the AI sector, with US futures dropping and Asian shares heading for their worst week since 2020. Government bonds rallied as investors sought safe-haven assets. The debut did little to revive excitement over the broader AI theme, however, as investors continued to question whether the huge amounts of spending would deliver returns . “The Anthropic IPO gave us some brief respite from the cloud of negativity,” said Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar. “That pause is well and truly over unfortunately.” Futures for the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 fell 2% after the index dropped the same amount on Nov 19. The Nasdaq is now down around 15% since hitting a record high in early October. S&P 500 futures were in the red after the index fell for a sixth straight session on Nov 19. A seven-day run of declines would be the worst streak since the pandemic. The STOXX 600 gauge of European stocks fell almost 2%, while MSCI’s world index of stocks fell for a seventh straight session, its longest losing streak since 2023. The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan tumbled and has sunk 8% this week, its worst performance since the Covid-19 pandemic in March 2020. Nvidia’s blowout earnings earlier in the week a nd Anthropic’s IPO have both failed to restore confidence, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at bank and investment firm Saxo. “The market is no longer looking for proof of AI demand alone,” she said. “It wants evidence that the extraordinary spending across the ecosystem can generate sustainable returns.” The VIX index of expected volatility on Wall Street stocks jumped and traded at its highest since March on Nov 20. Adding to the unease, a report on AMD from a media outlet associated with short-selling fund Hunterbrook Capital raised concerns that the chipmaker’s ties to Chinese entities, some linked to blacklisted firms, could draw greater US regulatory scrutiny to the sector. “No one headline drove the roll, though some pointed to an AMD short report which tapered overall sentiment,” said Goldman Sachs analysts in a trading note. All of that has piled further pressure on the AI trade, already battered in recent weeks by Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia and growing anti-data-centre sentiment exemplified by the Democrats’ sweep of the US midterm elections. Japan’s Nikkei tumbled 5%. Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, their biggest weekly decline since 1990. Despite the sharp drop in stocks, however, equity markets remain up for the year after a blistering rally in the first half on AI optimism. Treasuries rally as investors take cover US Treasuries rallied as stocks took a beating, sending investors towards assets deemed safe havens. The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes fell for a fifth straight session, to below 5%, while German 10-year bond yields fell 10 basis points (bps), the most since April. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the US dollar held steady at around its highest level in 20 months, also garnering support from growing expectations of a more hawkish Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures imply that a quarter-point rate hike in December is essentially locked in. Oil prices were steady, with Brent crude futures trading at US$90 a barrel and on track for a third week of declines. REUTERS

events.title: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
events.summary: On his way back from China Thursday aboard Air Force One, President Trump called in to a meeting his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were holding in Berlin with a group of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. "Putin wants to end the war, he wants the deal done, he is getting tired of this," Trump said, according to people in the room. Why it matters: Instead of turning his historic trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin into a modern-day Yalta Conference, as some European and Ukrainian officials feared , Trump tried to use it to propel his push for peace in Europe. Driving the news: Trump met Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen. Their meeting wasn't originally on the schedule, but Trump wanted to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine directly with the Russian president, a U.S. official said. "Who is he? He's my friend," Trump said when he entered the meeting room where Putin was waiting. Later in the day, Witkoff and Kushner told European leaders in Berlin that Trump pressed Putin to move on the peace talks, telling the Russian leader that now is the time to get a deal, according to a European official. Trump also asked Xi for his help in ending the war during their bilateral meeting. "He sent a very strong message to both of them [Putin and Xi] on the desire for peace, and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said at a press conference on Thursday. Behind the scenes: As Trump wrapped up his meetings in China and headed back to Washington, his envoys started their talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Zelensky and other European leaders. Kushner and Witkoff tried to reassure the group that Trump doesn't intend to cut a deal with Putin over their heads. "President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He's not looking to impose anything unilaterally," Kushner said. Shortly after, when Trump called in to brief the European leaders, he urged them to engage directly with Putin. "Friedrich, you can make a call to Putin and this will make a deal," Trump said, referring to the German host. Trump added, "Xi respects Zelensky. Putin is ready to do the deal. Zelensky can do a great deal." What they're saying: A European official said the talks in Berlin were substantive, unlike the summit in Shenzhen, which was mostly symbolic. "We think we have good coordination between the U.S. and Europe," the European official said. State of play: One of the key U.S. objectives at the moment is to get Europe directly involved in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. At the same time, U.S. officials also want Europe to engage in talks with Russia on a new European-Russian security agreement . Putin said publicly for the first time Thursday that he is open to allowing the Europeans to participate in peace talks with Ukraine. "We understand that it is pointless to discuss security issues, including those in Europe, without them," he said at a press conference after meeting with Trump. Putin added that Russia needs to understand what the Europeans are prepared to bring to the negotiations. Putin also signaled willingness to present an updated proposal for a security agreement with Europe. "Life changes, so it makes no sense to return to geopolitical realities of the 1990s," he said. What to watch: After the leaders' meeting in Berlin, Kushner and Witkoff huddled for another few hours with Zelensky and national security advisers from Germany, the UK, France, Italy and Poland, as well as senior officials from the EU and NATO. The group coordinated ahead of the next round of talks with the Russians, possibly next week. The European official said the group was skeptical Russia will actually allow Europe to participate in peace talks. The bottom line: U.S. officials said their goal is to get the Europeans and Russians to start talking to each other. "We also will go back and relay to the Russians that we see strength and unity and commitment [in Europe], but we also see a real desire for peace," Kushner said. "And I think that we're doing a lot of work to organize on how to give it the best shot to get there."

events.title: Apple working on AI agent for device control, apps, browsing and coding
events.summary: Apple outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. Apple is developing an autonomous AI agent for device control, app use, web browsing and coding. Job listings say it will work privately and handle multistep tasks. The company is moving into a fast-growing market already led by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google. Apple’s App Store already shows strong demand for AI agents. Apple is also adding stricter warnings in macOS 27.3 for third-party computer-use tools. It wants stronger privacy and safety, while pushing Siri towards deeper app integration. Apple is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta Platforms and others. The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one listing, Apple said it is seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post. The move follows the breakout success of Meta’s Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel arrangements and prepare news briefings. There has also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software. Anthropic recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc’s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk’s Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user’s behalf – in addition to offering standard AI agent features. Apple’s App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No. 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Nov 19. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude were also in the top five. OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor. Bloomberg News reported earlier in November that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company’s plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as end- 2027 , but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the job listing reads. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” The listing says the company has a team building the “foundation for that future” and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to “make it real”. John Ternus, the tech giant’s new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI – with an agent being key to that effort. “People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same,” the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks” across apps, browsers, command lines, code and application programming interfaces, and they can “coordinate specialised subagents along the way”. The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of “general-purpose computer-use agents”, the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Nov 19. Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system’s design. “Agents that can run code, use credentials and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency.” Sandboxing is a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet. As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the upcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, it has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs. With the change in 27.3 , ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition.

events.title: Japan’s core inflation accelerates in October, cementing rate hike expectations
events.summary: Japan’s core consumer price index rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3% gain. It followed a 2.1% rise in September. Japan’s core inflation rose to 2.2% in October, above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for a second month, strengthening expectations of a near-term rate hike. The BOJ will review the data at its Dec 18 meeting, and many market players expect rates to rise to 1.5% from 1.25%. Capital Economics said firms are still passing on higher raw material costs, and it now expects the BOJ to lift rates to 2.5% by mid-next year. TOKYO – Japan’s annual core inflation accelerated in October and exceeded the central bank’s 2% target for the second straight month, a sign of broadening price pressures that cements the case for a near-term interest rate increase. The data will be among factors the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will scrutinise at its next two-day policy meeting ending on Dec 18, when many market players expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.5% from the current 1.25%. The core consumer price index (CPI), which strips away the effect of volatile fresh food, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, data showed on Nov 20, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3% gain. It followed a 2.1% rise in September. An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier after increasing 2.4% in September. Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, expects inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, to accelerate sharply over the coming months as firms continue to pass on rising raw material costs. “The upshot is that we now expect the Bank of Japan to lift rates to 2.5% by the middle of next year,” he wrote in a research note. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September after delivering a hike in June – a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept rates steady in October, declaring victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target. REUTERS

events.title: Future of $600m Maryvale mill waste incinerator in doubt
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Latrobe Valley waste to energy incinerator in doubt as grant quietly scrapped Opal Australia planned to generate energy from waste at its Maryvale paper mill. ( ABC News: Kerrin Thomas ) A $48m federal grant for an energy incinerator in the Latrobe Valley has been terminated, putting the project in doubt. The incinerator was to be fuelled in part by waste from a new transfer station in Melbourne, but that project has been rejected. A waste management expert doubts the incinerator project will go ahead. A federal government grant for a Victorian-first waste to energy (WTE) project in the Latrobe Valley has been quietly terminated, raising questions about its future. The $48 million grant was given to Opal Australia in 2022 to develop the $600 million incinerator at the Maryvale Paper Mill. It planned to burn residential and commercial waste, creating jobs and reducing the mill's use of gas. The Victorian Labor government later approved the project, the first WTE incinerator allowed under its circular economy laws. But the project hit a snare when a permit for the construction of a new transfer station in Melbourne's east was rejected by the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) in 2025. That station was proposed in part to receive waste from several councils to then be transferred to Maryvale for incineration. Many Hampton Park residents opposed the new waste transfer station that was needed for the Latrobe Valley incinerator. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) A Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) ruling from April upheld the EPA's rejection of the Hampton Park proposal and noted a "significant volume" of complaints from residents about potential odour. Deakin University senior lecturer in sustainability, Trevor Thornton, specialises in waste management and said getting a consistent supply of waste, or feed stock, for the Maryvale incinerator was crucial. "The refusal to grant a permit for the transfer station where their feed stock was going to come from was the main catalyst for this waste to energy facility not being viable," he said. The federal Department of Industry confirmed the grant had wound up just a few months later. "The department and Maryvale mutually agreed to terminate the agreement in July 2026," a spokesperson said. "All unspent funds have been fully repaid to the Commonwealth." The ABC asked how much of the money was returned and received this response: "The department will not comment further on the terms of the termination, including financial arrangements or other information that is confidential or commercially sensitive." Waste from Melbourne's east was to be used to generate energy for the Maryvale paper mill. ( ABC News: Rick Rifici ) The consortium behind the incinerator project includes Opal Australia, waste management multinational Veolia, and WTE incinerator specialist Masdar Tribe. Veolia was also behind the failed application for the Hampton Park transfer station. A spokesperson for the consortium declined to answer questions or comment on the future of the project. Dr Thornton suggested the grant termination may have been linked to missed milestones on securing consistent supply of waste. Trevor Thornton says without a transfer station, the incinerator project will not be viable. ( Supplied: Trevor Thornton ) "I would imagine the consortium putting it together would have done a lot of work to try to find solutions to the existing problems with it becoming operational," he said. "I think it would be very much a last resort if they've decided not to go ahead." The Latrobe City Council approved construction of the incinerator and has a waste offtake agreement with the consortium. "The proposal has an active planning permit and council understands they are continuing with planning for the project," a spokesperson said. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) Rio Tinto will contribute $370 million to address environmental and social impacts caused by the Panguna mining project in Bougainville. An impact assessment has determined mine waste and decaying infrastructure continue to affect thousands of people decades after its closure. Locals say clean water and transport infrastructure are immediate priorities. Nearly 40 years after mining giant Rio Tinto was forced to abandon its Panguna mine in Bougainville, the company says it will provide $370 million to address the site's toxic legacy. Local opposition to the gold and copper mine forced its closure in 1989, sparking a decade-long civil war known locally as the Bougainville Crisis. An estimated 10,000 to 15,000 people were killed in the war that ensued until a peace agreement was reached in 2001. Rio Tinto said it would voluntarily contribute the money over the "coming years" to a new fund set up to address the mine's environmental and social impacts. The company's chief safety and technical officer, Mark Davies, described it as an important milestone. "Rio Tinto's contribution towards addressing findings of the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment (PMLIA) is intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation," he said. Rio Tinto abandoned operations at the Panguna mine in 1989. ( ABC ) The PMLIA was initiated following a human rights complaint brought by Australian non-profit The Human Rights Law Centre on behalf of about 150 Bougainvilleans in 2020. The assessment found that mine waste and decaying infrastructure continued to affect thousands of people in the area, violating their human rights. Landmark report uncovers human rights abuses A large-scale study of social and environmental impacts from Rio Tinto's abandoned Panguna mine in Bougainville finds a plethora of actual and potential human rights violations, including risks to life. It also revealed violations of Indigenous people's rights to water, education and culture. Lead complainant Theonila Roka Matbob, a traditional landowner from Makosi just downstream from the mine, said she was overwhelmed by Rio Tinto's announcement. "Obviously no amount of money will restore our environment to where it was but at least we can be able to invest into education for our children to find their own solutions later on." Theonila Roka Matbob says it has been a long fight for justice. ( Supplied ) Human Rights Law Centre legal director Keren Adams said Rio Tinto's commitment was a significant and historic moment. "This is an environmental disaster that has been unremedied for decades," she said. "The Bougainville government and communities have both spent many years campaigning for justice and for Rio Tinto to return and take responsibility for dealing with the huge problems that have been left by the disaster." Despite the mine ceasing operations in 1989, some families continue to live in the area. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) Rio Tinto was the majority owner of Panguna until 2016, when it gave its stake to the Bougainville and PNG governments. At its peak, it was one of the largest and most profitable gold and copper mines in the world, responsible for almost half of Papua New Guinea's exports. It was forced to close abruptly in 1989 when conflict broke out. However, the Bougainville government has recently indicated plans to reopen it after inking a deal with Indian mining company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (LMEL). To this day, locals are making use of old machinery at Panguna mine in Bougainville. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) Clean water, transport and education Following Rio Tinto's announcement, work will now begin on developing the new fund's structure, governance and activities, with input from affected communities and the Bougainville government. The company said the fund and its activities would remain separate from the Bougainville government's current effort to redevelop and reopen the mine with Indian firm LMEL. Ms Matbob said clean water and transport infrastructure were immediate priorities. BCL discharged mine waste into local river systems when it was in operation, the Human Rights Law Centre alleges. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) "What we are looking at is getting the basics right in accessibility to clean drinking water for our communities and also to ensure that bridges are built to give proper access to our communities, our families and our children," she said.

events.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
events.summary: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things. The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.” “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.” TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response. Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit. Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers. The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
