events.title: The future of medicine: Could AI help predict and prevent disease?
events.summary: Can AI help build a healthier future? By Doug Burger , Technical Fellow and Corporate Vice President, Microsoft Research Ava Amini , Principal Research Manager Eric Horvitz , Chief Scientific Officer Dr. Eric Topol , Executive Vice President, Scripps Research Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first? Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential. This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come. DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse. Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come. In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI. Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend. Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab) , the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab) . So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician. Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo , a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer. So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here. It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable. And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI. I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava. I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare. Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists. In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcare. And after a couple of years of intensive work, I and just fabulous colleagues at Microsoft worked intensively on taking healthcare challenges when it comes to applications of AI and benchmarking—medical diagnostic challenges, for example—and moved it into what I would call the realm of medical cognition, where instead of looking at a whole case that’s given to an AI system and looking at the accuracies that are reported on its ability to diagnose, for example, a form of differential diagnosis, we instead put the AI system in the, in the shoes of a clinician. You get an initial set of symptoms, you get chief complaint, some history, a little window on what’s going on when a patient comes in in an ambulatory setting, and then it’s up to the clinician to ask the right questions and to then think about tests, balancing the information value with the cost of the tests. This is the sequential diagnosis challenge.

events.title: Scoop: Trump names Kirsten Davies as new national cyber director
events.summary: The White House named Kirsten A. Davies to be its new national cyber director Thursday as President Trump overhauls his AI team, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Davies, who currently serves as the Pentagon's chief information officer , has more experience in the field than the outgoing director , Sean Cairncross . Cairncross' departure was described as amicable by two sources. But two White House officials said President Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, sought the change and pushed out Cairncross because, one said, he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." The search for Cairncross's replacement was begun two weeks ago, a third source said. Zoom out: The Office of the National Cyber Director coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. The position requires Senate confirmation. Davies previously was cleared by the Senate as the Defense Department's chief information officer. "Kirsten has the credentials to excel in this position and has already been Senate-confirmed," an administration official said. At the Pentagon, Davies has been the top adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance," according to her bio. Before serving in the Trump administration, Davies worked for Unilever and "led global cyber resilience for one of the world's largest consumer goods enterprises," her bio says. Davies' career also has included technology and cyber roles at Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard and Siemens. She founded the Institute for Cyber, a nonprofit organization dedicated to citizen safety and security in the digital universe. State of play: The administration's AI team has taken shape on the fly , but Cairncross was involved in key decisions. He held technical meetings with Anthropic leaders over the summer after Commerce Department export controls effectively scrubbed the company's models from the internet. Cairncross brought experience in Republican politics and national security, having worked with the intelligence community and dealt with cyber threats at the Republican National Committee. During Trump's first term, Cairncross represented the White House chief of staff on National Security Council committees before leading the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. Cairncross' head of policy and senior adviser Thomas Lind left in June and joined OpenAI in October, further depleting the Trump administration of technical expertise. The big picture: The latest turnover in cyber personnel comes as the country grapples with critical infrastructure outages and increasingly powerful AI poised to empower cyber defenders and hackers alike. Democrats have criticized the administration's response to outages and warned that U.S. cyber defenses are falling behind AI-fueled threats. What we're watching: Trump is also filling other key cyber positions. His pick for the top job at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps defend federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, Palantir executive Michael LoSapio, faced a combative confirmation hearing Thursday. What they're saying: In a written statement, Cairncross said, "it has been the honor of a lifetime to serve President Donald J. Trump. I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence." This story has been updated with details on Davies' appointment and background.

events.title: Wall Street tumbles to its longest losing streak since 2024 as the Dow drops 1,100 points
events.summary: The U.S. stock market tumbled again as AI stocks kept falling on worries their boom may be over NEW YORK -- The U.S. stock market tumbled again as beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence kept falling Thursday on worries their breathtaking boom may be over. The losses came even though a leading AI lab, Anthropic, found a strong welcome for the debut of its own stock on Wall Street. The S & P 500 dropped 2% for a sixth straight loss . That’s its longest losing streak in two and a half years, and the index at the heart of many 401(k) accounts is now down 8.2% from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101 points, or 2.2%, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3%. The losses were widespread, and more than 90% of the stocks that make up the S & P 500 index fell. Leading them downward was Williams-Sonoma, which dropped 15.2% after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was a bit weaker than Wall Street expected. It also stuck with its forecast for how much revenue it will make throughout 2026, and the midpoint of that range was below what analysts were expecting. Walmart sank 1% even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations. For a while Thursday morning, gains for several AI-related stocks seemed to be enough to more than make up for such losses. The S & P 500 jumped as much as 1.3% after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold shares of its stock at $83 apiece in its initial public offering . That’s more than the $70 to $78 it earlier thought it would get, and its price quickly surged above $115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. Anthropic later pared its gain and finished the day at $97.17, still up 17.1%. Even before its stock began trading, the strong demand for Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remained among investors in the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost following sharp recent drops for AI-related stocks on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology. But AI stocks quickly returned to their jittery ways in what Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, called “a very turbulent, white-knuckle period.” Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared because of the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8% and then swung to a loss of 2.1%. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, went from a 10.5% leap in the morning to a drop of 6.1%. Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 3.3% amid the lengthening list of worries dogging the entire industry. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech At first it was criticism that AI stocks had broadly gone into a bubble after shooting so high, along with doubts that AI could produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments in data centers worth it. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI. Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He was one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth. Other companies, meanwhile, offered more encouraging signals about AI. Palo Alto Networks climbed 6.4% after the AI cybersecurity company topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also agreed to buy Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, to help customers adopt AI securely. The all-stock deal is valued at $4.5 billion. Everpure, a company that helps businesses manage and store their data, said its revenue jumped last quarter by more than analysts expected in part because of AI-related offerings. Everpure’s stock rose 4.7%. All told, the S & P 500 fell 147.80 points to 7,175.83. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 to 49,097.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 550.69 to 23,879.20. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased as the drops for stock prices sent investors toward investments seen as safer. When prices for Treasury bonds go up, their yields go down, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.04% from 5.07% Wednesday. Also weighing on yields were a couple reports on the U.S. economy that came in weaker than economists expected. One said slightly more U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, though the number remains low compared with history.

events.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
events.summary: Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported . When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality. Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands. It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience. Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm. events.title: Firmus talks down 'modest' data centre in bid to avoid major project status
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus argues proposed AI data centre not major project amid only 'modest' economic benefits Works at Firmus Technologies' Wesley Vale site. ( Supplied: Erin Woodcock ) Firmus Technologies says one of its AI data centres should not be assessed as a major project. The company argues that unlike previously declared major projects, the data centre has only "modest" economic benefits and about 20 ongoing jobs. The State Planning Office is assessing the major project proposal made by the Latrobe Council. Firmus Technologies is fighting a local council push for one of its proposed AI data centres to be declared a major project. Latrobe Council in Tasmania's north-west has sought to defer a decision on Firmus's proposed Wesley Vale AI data centre to the state government. It has said the council's 1993 planning scheme is dated and councillors would not be able to consider all the relevant issues, such as energy, water and environmental impacts of a large AI data centre. A letter from Firmus's lawyers to Planning Minister Kerry Vincent, who is assessing the request for a major project declaration, has now been made public. "We respectfully ask that the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure not be declared a major project," the letter reads. It states that the project would have only "modest" economic benefits and ongoing job opportunities: Although the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is expected to generate some economic activity, these benefits are relatively modest and largely confined to employment opportunities, with approximately 70 jobs anticipated during the construction phase and around 20 permanent full-time positions once operational. Beyond these direct employment outcomes, the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is not expected to materially alter the economic structure of the region, establish a significant new industry cluster, or drive broader regional economic transformation. The submission states the development cost of its facility would be $31.25 million. It compared this to major projects such as Chambroad's Kangaroo Bay Hotel proposal near Hobart , which it said would support 443 ongoing jobs and generate $42.7 million in additional annual visitor expenditure. Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) "The economic benefits of the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure are considerably more limited in scale and are largely confined to construction activity and a relatively modest number of ongoing jobs," the letter reads. The process of declaring and assessing a major project in Tasmania can take years, while the council approval process is usually much quicker. A sign near Firmus' proposed AI data centre site at Wesley Vale. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Firmus told inquiry of $46b economic benefit from three projects Last week, at a Tasmanian parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres, Firmus co-CEO Tim Rosenfield was asked about the benefits to Tasmania of its three projects. Tim Rosenfield appeared at a Tasmanian inquiry into data centres in Hobart. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) "This is a large-scale investment we're making," he told the inquiry. "We have actually, at the request of the government some months ago, commissioned a third-party study which is close to being finalised. "It puts total state gross product contributions of up to $46 billion to the Tasmanian state economy through 2035. "We're operating these supercomputers, and that requires skills, it requires on-site presence, it requires learning pathways. "The preliminary modelled outcome shows about 8,900 ongoing FTEs [full-time equivalent jobs] through 2035 created." Firmus is building an AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards and has approval for another at Long Reach in northern Tasmania. The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston, showing its research and development lab. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Firmus 'deeply disappointed' by council's referral In addition to saying the economic impact of the project would not be "significant" to the region, the letter from Firmus's lawyers also said the impact on the area's environment and social fabric would be limited. It also said the project would not deliver advanced regional development objectives or significant public infrastructure to the region. events.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
events.summary: It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life. Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days. The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues. Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more. While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly. Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related. The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch. The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said. This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said. Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X . AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with. In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up. When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.” Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said. Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.” Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues. And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said. “There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.

events.title: Uber tests rides for kids as young as 10, with extra pay for drivers
events.summary: Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids , launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin. The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids. The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off. Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber. Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early. Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids web page. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete. The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum. Uber opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens , although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. events.title: China bars Bloomberg reporter from trilateral meeting after she shouted question at earlier event
events.summary: Chinese officials have blocked a Bloomberg TV journalist from a key event for shouting out a question to President Donald Trump NEW YORK -- It's a scenario seen every day: A reporter shouts a question out to a leader at an event. The leader either answers or ignores it. In China, though, Bloomberg TV journalist Annmarie Hordern was blocked from a key event by Chinese officials Thursday, apparently as retribution for having shouted a question in a way that the government considered rude. Hordern was barred from Thursday's trilateral meeting among President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, after having called out a question during an Trump meeting with Xi. She had asked Trump if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. A White House official said the Chinese insisted the reporter not be allowed in despite the White House having pushed for admission. The official insisted on speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity around the issue. The White House did not immediately respond to a query about what steps it took to advocate for the reporter. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents' Association, said on X that it was “commendable that the WH is advocating for press access.” A pool report from the incident said the Chinese “have passed along a message that yelling questions is considered extremely rude and we will be pulled from the room if we do so.” China’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press, and an email to Bloomberg seeking comment was not immediately returned. The incident, which reflected the way China typically seeks to tightly control news events, recalled a previous one in 2022, in which a White House pool reporter said she was knocked off balance after being yanked by her backpack when she tried to shout a question to President Joe Biden. The question was about human rights ahead of a meeting between Biden and Xi in Bali, Indonesia. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The reporter lost balance without falling and was pushed toward the door, a pool report said at the time. Two White House staff members intervened and said the producer should be left alone. China's approach to journalists, particularly foreign media, has long been chilly and uneven. In recent decades, international reporters have been expelled both for their coverage and for perceived misbehavior during news events. Resident correspondents are occasionally detained and questioned — and in some cases in past years, compelled to sign “self-criticism” reports — for showing up where the government doesn't want them to be. Chinese journalists who stray from the party line can face even more stringent measures, including censorship, dismissal and at times even imprisonment. Associated Press reporter Michelle L. events.title: Trump administration auctions deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa in first sale of its kind
events.summary: The Trump administration has auctioned deep-sea mining leases for millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa The Trump administration on Thursday auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa , giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters. The two 20-year leases are the first of their kind in the U.S., following President Donald Trump’s directive last year to leverage deep-ocean minerals to counter growing competition for resources from China. The leases are already the source of several legal challenges. The two lease areas each sold for the minimum bid amount of $3 million to deep-sea mining startup Wetstone U.S. Ventures, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. While there were two bidders at the auction, only Wetstone placed bids. Wetstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. The leases grant the company the ability to begin initial surveys of the seafloor to explore for minerals and prepare their testing or mining plans. It has the exclusive right to mine those areas commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. The auction moved forward despite passionate opposition from locals in the territory and three lawsuits seeking to halt the sales. The auction was held at the Ventura County Fire Department Headquarters in Southern California, where a few dozen protesters gathered outside. “We had hoped it would never come to this,” Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, an American Samoa resident who has fought the auction for more than a year, said in a statement Thursday. Globally, deep-sea mining is still at an experimental stage. A handful of other countries have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals, but no company has started commercial operations. The U.S. has never issued a lease for deep-sea minerals beyond a short-lived mining effort in California waters more than 60 years ago. The federal interest in seafloor minerals stems from an April 2025 executive order, when the president directed his administration to search for and responsibly develop critical minerals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. The Marine Minerals Administration is considering further auctions of the seabed near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters. It’s unclear if the leases will withstand legal challenge. On Monday, a court ordered the National Marine Fisheries Service to more thoroughly assess the impacts the mining activities could have on endangered species, saying the agency's “cramped, expedited, informal” review violated the Endangered Species Act. The Marine Minerals Administration said in a statement that it had addressed the court's opinion by starting to consult with the fisheries service on another environmental assessment. But it did not cancel or delay the auction. David Henkin, deputy managing attorney at the environmental law group Earthjustice, said the ruling made Thursday's auction unlawful. In order to issue the notice of sale, the government needed to comply with the Endangered Species Act, he said. events.title: Christie’s halts Frida Kahlo painting from auction at Mexico’s request
events.summary: Christie’s has withdrawn a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York after Mexican authorities requested more information about its provenance MEXICO CITY -- Christie’s withdrew a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York this week after Mexican authorities requested additional information about its provenance, the auction house confirmed Thursday. The painting, “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz,” or “Congress of the Peoples for Peace,” had been scheduled for auction on Tuesday. It depicts a white dove on a tree bearing fruit alongside a smiling sun, the moon, and two slices of watermelon. Mexican authorities asked Christie’s to hold the sale until the painting's provenance could be clarified, citing a declaration that recognizes Frida Kahlo’s work as an artistic monument of Mexico . “In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research,” a Christie’s spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. “We look forward to selling this work at a later date." The same painting was auctioned in 2020 by Sotheby’s without any objections. Kahlo’s works in Mexico are considered artistic monuments and are protected under the country's federal law on monuments and archaeological, artistic, and historical sites. Mexican authorities said they were working with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museums Trust, administered by the Bank of Mexico. The painting left Mexico more than three decades before the 1984 decree declaring Kahlo’s work an artistic monument. The decree prohibits the permanent export of her works that were in Mexico when it was published. Kahlo, whose health was seriously deteriorating, sent the painting to the congress through her husband, the painter Diego Rivera. She died in Mexico City two years after creating it. The trip to Vienna was recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s last wife, and has also been mentioned by historians such as Raquel Tibol. Last year, Kahlo’s 1940 self-portrait “El sueño (La cama)," or The Dream (The Bed), sold for $54.7 million , setting an auction record for a work by a female artist. events.title: Suspects charged in brazen train heist ring that netted $22 million in cargo from major retailers
events.summary: Authorities have charged more than a dozen people for allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation LOS ANGELES -- More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers. A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country. Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world's largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon. The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit. “The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise. events.title: Exclusive: Sen. Ernst rebukes lack of "transparency" from Pentagon on Iran
events.summary: Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) said "a lot of people would be able to guess" if she regrets voting to confirm the embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, during Axios' Future of Defense Summit Thursday. Why it matters: The retiring Iowa senator, who served in the military for more than two decades, has been notably skeptical of Hegseth and hasn't always been in lockstep with the Trump administration. Catch up quick: Despite her hesitancy over his nomination, Ernst ultimately voted to confirm Hegseth . However, she's continued to question him throughout his tenure. She recently asked whether the embattled Pentagon leader has been "truthful" about the status of the Iran war, which she said Iowans rejected in the midterms. "If there is deception coming from our Pentagon and being transmitted to the president, I would want to know that," Ernst told reporters earlier this month. Driving the news: "There is very little transparency right now with what is being discussed between the White House and the Department of War," Ernst said of the Pentagon's communication about the war in Iran in a conversation with Axios' defense and space reporter Thomas Novelly. "As Congress, we would expect that we would be read into some of those conversations, and unfortunately, we have not been read into those conversations," she added. That's made it "difficult to know" the state of the war and its impact on munitions levels , she said. Friction point: House Republicans blocked an impeachment effort against Hegseth earlier this month, but the reprieve may be short-lived with a Democratic majority taking control in January. "I think we would be having a very different conversation today, if the House Democrats had actually showed up for that vote," Ernst told Axios, a nod to the 11 members who missed it, some citing traffic delays. "So, now they will face it again come January, likely, and that will be up to the House Democrats to decide how they handle that," she continued. "And then, certainly, if they decide to move forward with impeachment, then Senate Democrats will also have the majority." State of play: Ernst sits on the Senate Committee on Armed Services, where she chairs the Emerging Threats and Capabilities subcommittee. "In the past 12 years, while I have been in the Senate, the Armed Services Committee has been one of the most bipartisan committees in the Senate, and it's necessary for the safety and security of our country," she said, adding that the National Defense Authorization Act "has been a very, very bipartisan product." But Ernst predicted that given the "not even hidden animosity" between Democrats and Hegseth, "it will be very difficult" for new Senate Armed Services Committee leadership to obtain information. events.title: The Jensen Huang Blast Radius Has Hit His Favorite Restaurants
events.summary: Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang . In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went. But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero. Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World , a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China. “It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.” At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?” Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023. Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island. “When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.” At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up. “I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.” Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth. Owner Tu Chang-chun said he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop. In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars. The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments. But not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business. The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors. Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.” Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.

events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 17, 2026: Nvidia posts strong quarterly earnings, says it does not plan to reinstate Huang Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. events.title: Call for ACCC to take up 'strong case' for burn victim hurt by Temu product
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Calls for consumer watchdog to help family harmed by recalled Temu product Daniella Jacobs-Herd sustained burns to 13 per cent of her body when a spark ignited a hoodie purchased via Temu. ( Supplied: Hannah Jacobs-Herd ) Daniella Jacobs-Herd was injured in 2024 when a hoodie purchased via Temu caught fire. Her family had tried to pursue legal action against the seller, but has run out of options. Consumer experts say the ACCC should take up the case. More than two years after she was badly burnt while wearing a hoodie purchased via Temu, Daniella Jacobs-Herd is still traumatised by flame and smoke. Burnt toast and birthday candles send the 10-year-old Hervey Bay girl into fits of rage. "Half the day is spent trying to calm her down and explain that it's okay and safe," Daniella's mother, Hannah, said. Hannah Jacobs-Herd says her daughter Daniella is triggered by burnt toast and birthday candles. ( ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor ) On a winter's night in 2024, Daniella had been standing near a backyard fire pit at her mother's birthday party when sparks ignited her jumper. She suffered severe burns to 13 per cent of her body. Temu recalled the unicorn-themed hoodie for failing to meet mandatory safety standards, and Ms Jacobs-Herd sought compensation through a local Queensland legal firm. But the online shopping platform said it was merely an intermediary and liability for product safety rested with its suppliers. The Chinese supplier, Sunshine Towels, has not responded to the lawyer's repeated attempts to contact it since the July 2024 incident. Temu recalled the hoodie for failing to meet mandatory safety standards more than four months after the incident. ( Supplied: ACCC ) Last month, law firm Shine Lawyers told Ms Jacobs-Herd it was closing the case and advised her to engage an international lawyer. Ms Jacobs-Herd lives on a disability support pension and said the legal fees were out of her reach. "$15,000 for a 20-minute consult — I don't have that sort of money lying around," she said. 'Nothing more important than safety' In 2010, when Australian consumer law was last updated, online shopping made up 6 per cent of total Australian retail sales. That surged to 24 per cent by 2025, led by online marketplaces selling products made by overseas suppliers. Australian consumer law requires suppliers of goods to comply with mandatory safety standards. Temu has become Australia's most-used retail marketplace app. ( Supplied: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission ) In a complaint to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) in June, consumer advocate Choice said that left a regulatory gap for online marketplaces claiming to be intermediaries between the supplier and consumer. The ACCC acknowledged the need for reform in its response to Choice, noting that a July meeting of consumer affairs ministers had prioritised introducing a general safety provision — laws making the entire supply chain liable for selling unsafe products in Australia. However, those ministers recently decided a general safety provision would not be part of a consultation process currently underway for Australian consumer law reform. Allan Fels says a general safety provision should be introduced as soon as possible. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) Allan Fels was the ACCC chair when a general safety provision was last considered in a 2019 review of Australian consumer law. He said the Jacobs-Herd family's experience showed the provision should have been introduced at that time. "Given the dangers of products like this, it was probably best if they had enacted the law in 2019," he said. "But certainly now, in the light of experience, the law should be enacted as soon as possible." The assistant minister responsible for Australian consumer law, Andrew Leigh, said the government's current focus was on improving processes for recalling unsafe products, and a general safety provision would be a reform option for 2027. He said there were protections already enshrined in law that meant the Jacobs-Herd family should not be forced to pay for their own international lawyer. Australian consumer law empowers the ACCC to make compensation claims on behalf of consumers harmed by unsafe products.

events.title: Retailers shake up Thanksgiving meal deals amid rising food costs
events.summary: Major grocery retailers are switching up their Thanksgiving dinner deals this year, with a few lowering prices, others swapping out items and some shifting toward more flexible meal options. The big picture: Lower advertised prices from some retailers could offer relief to Americans already stretching their holiday budgets , but shifting menus mean shoppers may not be getting the same bang for their buck. State of play: Higher fuel costs, poor growing conditions and other inflationary pressures have pushed up food prices ahead of the holiday. The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for ten has increased 6% since 2025, totaling an estimated $58.63. The increase is largely driven by price hikes for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries, the federation said. Driving the news: Walmart is advertising a lower price for its Thanksgiving meal than in 2025, while offering 18% more individual items. The retailer said this year's meal , which serves ten people for $35, is its "lowest priced one-click basket" ever, down from $39.93 last year. The complete meal comes with a turkey, multiple sides and pumpkin pie to finish. It adds ingredients for sweet potato casserole and corn muffins, but drops macaroni and cheese and baby carrots from last year's spread. Fried onions were the only item to switch from name-brand to store-brand in 2026. The other side: Aldi is also promoting a Thanksgiving meal $1 cheaper than in 2025, though several dishes have changed . Instead of a 14-pound turkey, the 2026 dinner will have a 16-pound bird. It includes several sides, but not fan favorites such as mashed potatoes and gravy, macaroni and cheese or green bean casserole. Zoom out: Costco's gourmet Thanksgiving dinner is more elaborate than its cook-at-home grocery counterparts, with a similar menu and the same advertised promotional price as last year. Both 2025 and 2026 dinners cost $199.99, serve eight people and include a five-pound turkey breast. The prepared meal includes the same traditional sides and desserts, with the addition of candied yams. This year's dinner is marketed as 30 pounds, compared with 28 pounds in some descriptions of last year's offerings. The intrigue: Kroger is shifting away from the fixed-price "Freshgiving" Thanksgiving meal bundle it offered in previous years. Instead, it is promoting individual holiday discounts and prepared foods in various portion sizes. Kroger's chief marketing officer said the approach is intended to make holiday meals more convenient and accommodate gatherings of different sizes. In 2025, Kroger advertised a Thanksgiving meal for 10 for under $4.75 a person, providing a 14- to 16-pound frozen turkey and traditional sides. The bottom line: Your food preferences, guest count and budget will help determine if a Thanksgiving meal deal is the right choice for you. Go deeper: Wholesale food prices are on the rise

events.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
events.summary: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work. An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model , developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation. Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services. Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA.

events.title: UAE highlights $1tn in US investments during Abu Dhabi Investment Forum
events.summary: The UAE on Thursday promoted its more than $1 trillion of investments in the US and its broader framework, as businesses and investors gathered in New York for the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum to expand business ties between the two countries. The Abu Dhabi Investment Forum, organised by the Abu Dhabi Investment Office , was part of broader engagements in New York this week to advance partnerships with US investors and explore commercial opportunities. “What brings us together is more than just investments. It is the strength of the relationship between the United States and the United Arab Emirates, a connection that has been built over many decades through institutions, shared objectives and, more importantly, people,” said Badr Al Olama, the director of Adio. Mr Al Olama said more than half of the 26 financial institutions that have announced plans to establish a presence in the Abu Dhabi Global Market are US companies. Health care and AI were seen as the two major sectors at Thursday's forum, which also touched on advanced manufacturing, travel and food innovation. Abu Dhabi investment firm MGX in July linked up with BlackRock on a $40 billion digital infrastructure investment. MGX also plans to invest up to 80 per cent of its total portfolio in US projects. The company said at the time that it had raised $49 billion from investors across North America, Asia, Europe and the Gulf for its AI Fund. And this month, Adnoc and AI firm G42 signed a multiyear partnership with OpenAI that would increase the company's presence in the Emirates. “We see the next chapter of Abu Dhabi-US investment extending beyond the companies we already know,” Mr Al Olama said. Among the delegates at the forum in Manhattan were representatives from a Brooklyn-based biotech venture company looking to find co-investors to launch in Abu Dhabi. Another delegate from the Colorado-Abu Dhabi Trade and Investment Council was also hoping to deepen ties between the US state and the emirate. Bilateral trade between the US and UAE totalled an estimated $55.4 billion in 2025, a 16 per cent increase from 2024, according to data from the Office of the US Trade Representative. US goods exported to the UAE totalled $31.4 billion, while it imported $7.7 billion in goods. US services trade with the UAE totalled about $16.3 billion last year. The UAE's Ministry of Investment reported in July that the Emirates had attracted $48.3 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, in a 6 per cent annual increase. Total FDI stock rose to $318.9 billion at the end of last year. The UAE aims to attract $65 billion in annual FDI and raise total FDI stock to $600 billion by 2031. No planned FDI into the UAE have been cancelled this year despite the uncertain outlook caused by the Iran war, The National previously reported. The Emirates also continues to back its $1.4 trillion investment and economic framework with the US. In a March letter to the US-UAE Business Council, Yousef Al Otaiba, UAE ambassador to the US and Minister of State, said the Emirates remains “open for business”. “The past year has reminded us that what defines us is not the challenges we face, but how we respond to them with confidence, clarity of purpose and a continued commitment to progress,” said Amna Almheiri, consul general of the UAE in New York. Despite the regional conflict, Abu Dhabi has continued to attract global capital. The Abu Dhabi Global Market said assets under management grew 54 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026 as Bain Capital, Blue Owl Capital and other major US funds have expanded into the financial centre. More than 1,500 US companies are operating in the Emirates, it said. The inaugural Abu Dhabi Investment Form in New York was held last year, when agreements were signed across digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, financial services and new energy.

events.title: For these Australians, the recession has already arrived
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians describe life in a recession-like squeeze Many households feel as though they are in a recession, even though Australia is not technically in one. ( ABC News: Kylie Silvester ) The ripple effects from years of rising living costs continue to make life challenging for Australians. Hundreds of you have shared your experiences with the ABC. Small businesses fear losing customers and staff. Home owners worry about paying bills and putting food on the table. While Australia has so far avoided a technical recession, many of the warning signs associated with one are becoming harder to ignore. The unemployment rate has climbed to 4.9 per cent , its highest level of the post-pandemic period, and a Roy Morgan poll shows consumer confidence is at its lowest in seven months. Artificial Intelligence, offshoring, restructuring and slowing economic activity are why Bunnings, Canva, NAB, ING and Qantas are just some of the major businesses that have cut thousands of jobs in recent months. At the same time, living costs continue to rise faster than many household budgets can absorb. But whether that amounts to a recession depends on how you define one. Technical recession versus lived reality A recession is usually described as a period when the economy stops growing and starts going backwards. The most commonly used measure, known as a "technical recession", is two consecutive quarters of negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP), which is the value of all goods and services produced across the country. When recessions happen, businesses tend to earn less, consumers cut back their spending and unemployment often rises as companies reduce staff or delay hiring them. By that definition, Australia is not in a recession. In fact, the economy is still growing, albeit slowly. GDP rose 0.4 per cent in the June quarter and was up 2.1 per cent over the year. Oxford Economics director of global macro research, Ben May, said some of the conditions that had historically preceded recessions were visible today in economies around the world. "These features are visible in elevated energy prices, rising bond yields, and the AI boom," Mr May said. "Still, compared with the 1970s and 1980s, economies are better positioned to weather shocks. "It would take a further escalation in these or a sharp reversal of the AI boom to push the world economy into recession; a possible but not inevitable outcome." So, Australia is not in an official recession, but there are other measures in the economists' tool box. For instance, years of rising prices, higher mortgage repayments and wages that have struggled to keep pace with household costs have created what economists often describe as a "per capita recession" or a decline in living standards despite continued economic growth. But even here, there's a disparity between how Australians feel about the economy and what the numbers say. Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics, said Australia had not yet entered a per capita recession, with official data showing real GDP per person fell slightly in the March quarter before edging higher in the June quarter. "However, that's far from a stellar outcome," Mr Surya said. "With the economy set to slow markedly, we wouldn't rule out the possibility that Australia enters a per capita recession over the next few quarters." That disconnect has become a growing part of the national conversation. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock recently acknowledged that conditions were "going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer" following the central bank's decision to raise the cash rate to 4.85 per cent. So while the economy may still be growing "on paper", around kitchen tables and business counters, many Australians tell a different story. Albury resident Nicole Thurgate is feeling the economic pain at home. "I feel like I'm in a recession and it definitely feels like we're going backwards," Ms Thurgate said. The 57-year-old said it was around the time of the third interest rate rise of 2026 that the combined pressure of rising mortgage repayments and living costs became impossible to ignore. Since then, she has cut back on almost every discretionary expense she can think of. Her car is off the road because she cannot afford repairs, she has sold personal belongings including her mother's jewellery and a perfume collection, and has stopped buying takeaway food and red meat altogether. "It's not just giving up luxuries here," she said. "[It's] basic things, right down to the kind of tea bag I'm buying. It's become every cent.

"I will work with you in the spirit of equality, seeking common ground despite differences, and mutually beneficial cooperation to take forward the China-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership." Chinese President Xi Jinping says there has been a "full turnaround" in relations. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Mr Albanese said the Australia-China relationship "delivers prosperity for both of our countries" but promised "frank" conversations. "And the relationship that we are building is positive, is calm, is not defined by our differences, but one where we can have clear and frank exchanges for our mutual interest," he said. It's the fifth meeting between the pair since Mr Albanese came to office in 2022. At that time relations had plunged to their lowest point in decades, with Beijing imposing trade restrictions on Australian exports and high-level talks between the two countries effectively frozen. Mr Albanese is due to travel to Beijing tonight for formal talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang and the Australia-China CEO roundtable where businesses are expected to push for greater trade certainty. Chinese President Xi Jinping has met with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in China. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Albanese says government 'worked hard' to stabilise relationship Speaking after his meeting with Mr Xi, Mr Albanese said his government had "worked hard to stabilise the relationship" with China "for the interests of our relationship with our major trading partner". Mr Albanese said he discussed a full range of issues with Mr Xi. "It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," he said. Mr Albanese says the Australia-China relationship "delivers prosperity" for both countries. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Asked whether China's longer term ambitions meant differences between the countries would endure, Mr Albanese said the two countries were able to discuss those issues "constructively and very directly". "That's something that we do in meetings," he said. "We have different political systems, different histories, but that doesn't mean that you can't have constructive dialogue, and that's what Australia seeks." Mr Albanese said it was "positive" that Mr Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump had met yesterday. "It is always better to have dialogue than to have conflict," he said. On confronting Mr Putin over Ukraine during his APEC speech, Mr Albanese said he had made it "very clear" Russia needed to stop the war. "Well, he certainly heard it, as did others in the room," Mr Albanese said. "I have a responsibility to put Australia's position clearly and directly, and that is what I did." China talks follow Australia's deals on defence, AI The high-level talks come after Australia signed a series of agreements that Beijing is unlikely to welcome. Just days before arriving in China, Mr Albanese oversaw the signing of a new defence cooperation agreement with the Philippines aimed at strengthening military ties, maritime surveillance and information sharing. He reiterated Australia's support for Manila, which has repeatedly clashed with Beijing over disputed territorial claims in the South China Sea. Mr Albanese also joined Mr Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for a Quad summit in the Philippines, where the four leaders announced plans for a new joint exercise in the region next year. Anthony Albanese was placed near host Xi Jinping for the Economic Leaders Meeting.
