events.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
events.summary: Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job. Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension , CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there. Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan County Title Extension regional specialist Member grade Senior member Alma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products. Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business. She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside. “We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in. Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and the U.N.’s International Telecommunication Union , and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC) , and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP). She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture . An early love of design and problem-solving Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors. As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs. That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings. “I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says. She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career. She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University , in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education. She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016. That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry , in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020. From outreach to extension work After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College , in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator. She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water. She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain , helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park. In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County ’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns. She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds. Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System , a nationwide network run by land-grant universities , schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states. The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture , managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties. The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program , which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship. Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person. She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says. “We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says. events.title: Trump to Axios: I'm "not rushing into a decision" on Iran
events.summary: President Trump said in a brief phone interview Thursday that he won't make a determination on his next step in the Iran war until the new year. "I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," Trump told Axios from Air Force One, on his way back to the U.S. from China. Why it matters: The president's comments come as he faces heavy pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to unleash a decisive bombing campaign soon. Yes, but: Trump could change his mind at any moment. And he wouldn't telegraph plans for an imminent attack even if that's what he was intending to do. A day before the war began in February, Trump said he hadn't made a decision, when in fact he had already ordered strikes. Between the lines: Trump's stated timing could mean he's giving more time for the naval blockade and the economic pressure campaign to play out, as many of his advisers and leaders of Gulf countries are urging. But it could also indicate that if Iran doesn't make concessions by the end of the year, Trump wants to leave himself enough time for military action before the new Democratic-controlled Congress settles in. Driving the news: While stating last week that a major new round of strikes on Iran was " quite unlikely ," Trump is still considering a joint attack with Israel, Axios reported on Wednesday. The president's deliberations are likely to pick up when he returns from Asia. Any U.S. operation would involve Israel and could include strikes on suspected Iranian nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain. Bridges and power plants could also be targeted, as well as Iranian military and civilian leaders. Behind the scenes: The White House has asked the Pentagon and intelligence experts for their assessments of how Iran would respond to each of the strike scenarios the U.S. military has prepared, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. The White House has asked whether any of the options would avoid triggering a devastating Iranian retaliation against Gulf countries' oil and gas facilities. The intrigue: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad, Roman Gofman, visited Washington and Miami last week for talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe and White House envoy Steve Witkoff. Gofman, one of Netanyahu's closest confidants, was sent by the Israeli prime minister to press for resuming the war against Iran, an Israeli source said. The Mossad director relayed Israel's concerns about Iranian activities related to chemical weapons development, U.S. and Israeli sources said. Israel claims it has intelligence showing that Iran has stepped up its research and development of chemical weapons as well as conducted tests. Trump was briefed about this new intelligence, a U.S. official said.

events.title: Average US 30-year mortgage rate rises to 7.28% this week, ending a four-week slide
events.summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate rose this week for the first time since early October, reflecting a ramp-up in U.S. government bond yields amid signs that inflation is heating up The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate rose this week for the first time since early October, reflecting a ramp-up in U.S. government bond yields amid signs that inflation is heating up. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. rose to 7.28% from 7.11% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.26%. The average rate eased in the four weeks heading into this week and hadn't increased since Oct. 8, when it hit 7.40%, its highest level in nearly three years. Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power at a time when affordability challenges continue to sideline many aspiring homeowners. Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also rose this week. That average rate climbed to 6.66% from 6.45% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.54%. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. That yield had been mostly trending lower since early October, after climbing to its highest level since 2002, but it has been rising again following new data showing hotter inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield was at 5.05% at midday on the bond market Thursday. The signs pointing to accelerating inflation have raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The central bank kept rates unchanged late last month , after raising them in September. While the Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately influence rates on home loans. Newborn dies after suspected female genital mutilation in Senegal; relatives arrested American surfer Kurt Van Dyke's girlfriend among 2 arrested in his Costa Rica death Number of people seeking unemployment aid ticks higher yet still low historically “The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves,” said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com. “That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market.” Mortgage rates have been marching higher overall since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began , pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher . In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. Going by the latest average rate, a home shopper financing a $400,000 home loan is now paying roughly $343 more a month than when the rate was just below 6%. Elevated home loan borrowing costs have weighed on home sales this year, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged. And the latest monthly tally of home purchase transactions that have yet to be finalized points to potentially more sluggish home sales in coming months. Pending U.S. home sales fell 4.7% last month from September and sank 16.7% from October last year, the National Association of Realtors said Wednesday. There’s usually a month or two lag between a contract signing and when the sale is finalized, which makes pending home sales a near-term bellwether for the housing market. events.title: Trump backs Elon Musk in latest MAGA breakup
events.summary: President Trump still considers Elon Musk an ally despite the world's richest man saying he's "not MAGA," the president told NBC News on Thursday. Why it matters: Musk's latest break from Trump's political movement comes after he spent millions backing Republicans in the midterms, only to see Democrats win control of Congress and many state governments. Trump and Musk have weathered public feuds before, repeatedly reconciling despite disagreements. Driving the news: "He's a friend of mine," Trump told NBC News of Musk. "There are lots of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don't do very well," Trump said. "Elon's got very good intentions," he said. "I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me." Catch up quick: Musk said at the The New York Times' DealBook Summit Wednesday that he considers himself politically moderate. "I'm not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that," Musk told the New York Times. Musk said he felt "pretty foolish" about spending millions in the midterms. "If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money," he said. Yes, but: Musk reportedly accompanied Trump to China this week, underscoring how their personal relationship has endured despite their political differences. Between the lines: Musk may reject the MAGA label, but he has spent years championing its culture wars, bankrolling Republicans and turning X, the social media platform he bought for $44 billion, into a megaphone for far-right voices. He has attacked diversity initiatives, amplified anti-immigration rhetoric and promoted an antisemitic conspiracy theory for which he later apologized . He has also railed against what he calls the "woke mind virus" and backed far-right political movements abroad. Flashback: Musk has clashed with Trump over government spending, tariffs, climate policy and the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein . In October 2024, Musk joked at a Trump rally , "I'm not just MAGA, I'm dark MAGA." Despite their disagreements, Musk has repeatedly reentered Trump's orbit. What we're watching: Sen. Yassamin Ansari ( D-Ariz.) suggested the tech mogul could still face Congressional probes once Democrats take office next year regardless of whether he breaks with MAGA.

CFDs are high-risk derivatives, and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has previously found that approximately 80% of customers lose money when investing in them.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said:'With more than two million Instagram followers, Chalmers exploited his online influence to illegally promote investments to a vast audience. Agbodza made significant profits from an unlawful investment scheme. These cases send a clear message: we will take decisive action against those that break the law and put consumers at risk.'Separately, earlier this year the FCA issued cautions to 2 individuals for posting illegal financial promotions on social media. The cautions will appear on their criminal records.The FCA is also calling on social media platforms to do more to stop illegal financial promotions at source. Google, Bing (Microsoft), Meta, X and TikTok have agreed to restrict paid-for financial services advertising to FCA-authorised firms, helping to reduce scam adverts significantly. But illegal promotions remain prevalent. events.title: Anthropic makes record market debut
events.summary: Anthropic shares soared in the company’s record-breaking debut Thursday, climbing as high as $111.53 per share, well above its initial pricing at $83. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion from selling 980 million shares, with a $26 billion private placement bringing the total haul to $107.3 billion. Initially, the tech giant had been aiming to sell 825 million shares at a target range of $70 to $78. The offering comes amid a broader tech selloff as investors reconsider the AI trade after a Democratic midterms sweep and Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia CEO. Anthropic received orders for about six times the number of shares on offer, Bloomberg reported, nearly double the demand SpaceX reportedly drew ahead of its IPO earlier this year. Anthropic is largely seen as a bellwether for the AI boom, marking the first frontier AI lab to go public. OpenAI is reportedly targeting a 2027 IPO; CEO Sam Altman said earlier this week at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including market volatility. Despite the headwinds, Altman isn’t concerned about a shortage of dollars to go around, even if his chief competitor is first up to bat in the public market. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply,” he said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Meta rethinks climate goal as AI emissions soar 45%
events.summary: Meta's greenhouse gas emissions surged 45% last year amid its AI infrastructure boom, prompting the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2030. Why it matters : Other tech giants have reported rising emissions as they race to build data centers, but Meta is going a step further by explicitly reconsidering its climate deadline. Driving the news : The just-released sustainability report of the tech giant, one of North America's largest data centers operators , shows just how much growth in the AI industry is outpacing any efficiency gains. Meta executives said they were "re-evaluating" the 2030 goal, first announced in 2020 when the company was still known as Facebook and before the generative AI boom. They didn't specify what changes they're considering or when they'll make a decision. By the numbers : Meta's electricity use jumped 35%, comparable to other tech giants. But Meta's emissions increase of 45% is far higher than its peers, Google (18%), Amazon (16%) and Microsoft (25%). What they're saying: "When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned," wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability. "The reality has been far more complex." Zoom out : The race among tech giants to dominate AI is pushing their climate goals into the backseat, even as they continue investing heavily in clean energy. State of play : Meta says it has contracted more than 30 gigawatts of clean energy, including nuclear, solar and geothermal, though less than half that capacity is generating electricity so far. The intrigue : Meta's report says it may turn to natural gas plants to power data centers when utilities can't deliver electricity fast enough — even though such projects are already underway. It's also seeking to offset some of the methane emissions associated with its natural gas use by paying for cleaner gas production elsewhere. Reality check : Meta's 45% emissions increase doesn't yet reflect the full impact of some of its biggest planned natural gas projects, suggesting its footprint could grow considerably more. In Louisiana, utility Entergy is pursuing seven new gas-fired generating units totaling more than 5,200 megawatts to serve Meta's data centers. Separately, Ohio regulators approved a 200-megawatt gas plant built specifically to power Meta's data centers, while research firm Cleanview identifies a 521-megawatt gas project under construction for Meta in Utah. Friction point : Meta's report was also revealing about water, a more immediate concern for many communities near data centers. The company's direct water consumption fell 4%, but consumption in highly water-stressed regions rose 24%. The estimated water consumption associated with generating its electricity — an often-overlooked environmental impact — rose 37% before accounting for its clean-energy purchases. How it works : Natural gas plants typically use substantial amounts of water for cooling, meaning Meta's growing reliance on gas could increase its indirect water footprint even as its data centers become more water-efficient. Yes, but : Meta is the only tech giant to disclose the water consumption associated with electricity, earning it high marks for transparency from Alex de Vries-Gao, a researcher at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who has studied AI's environmental footprint. What we're watching : Meta's reconsideration of its climate deadline raises the question of whether other tech giants will eventually follow suit as the AI boom continues to strain their environmental commitments.

events.title: Myanmar becomes first state found responsible for genocide by UN court
events.summary: Myanmar became the first state the International Court of Justice has held responsible for committing genocide in a landmark ruling Thursday. Why it matters: The decision could have far-reaching implications for other genocide cases, including South Africa's case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. State of play: The court ruled 9–6 that Myanmar's violent 2017 military crackdown was intended to destroy the country's persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority. The onslaught killed thousands and forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In 2021, Myanmar's military coup also sparked a civil war that killed over 100,000 people and displaced 5.2 million, according to the Council on Foreign Relation's Global Conflict Tracker. Myanmar has repeatedly denied allegations of mass rape, murder and arson. Yes, but: The legally binding ruling does not guarantee that the roughly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh will be able to safely return home. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, provide reparations to the Rohingya and allow refugees to return. Still, the ICJ has no direct way to enforce its ruling. What they're saying: "This judgment must now translate into real action," UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk said in a statement . "The Court has made clear Myanmar's responsibilities. It sends a strong message to all States around the world that those responsible for genocide will be held to account." Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government welcomed the ruling, saying it would "carefully consider the Court's findings and any orders issued" and remained committed to holding perpetrators accountable and preventing further atrocities. Flashback: In 2022, the Biden administration formally declared that Myanmar's military committed genocide against the country's Rohingya minority and crimes against humanity. The ICJ in 2020 ordered Myanmar to protect Rohingya from genocide while the case was pending. Go deeper: UN court rejects Myanmar's objections to Rohingya genocide case

events.title: FDA's long-term vacancy
events.summary: The News The leadership vacuum at the FDA won’t be filled anytime soon. The White House’s last-minute decision to pull the nomination of Heidi Overton leaves the chances of Congress acting during the lame duck around zero, with the Senate health committee’s chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., predicting the job will “fall to the Senate Democrats.” The White House has a slim chance of finding a nominee who supports President Donald Trump’s health agenda and who could win support from the new Senate majority. Former FDA officials told me they expect a string of acting commissioners to fill in for the next two years. One potential temporary leader is Sara Brenner, who held the acting title in early 2025 before departing the agency earlier this year to work as a senior counselor for public health at HHS. Another name being floated is Karim Mikhail, the FDA’s top regulator of vaccines and biologics. The leadership void arrives as Congress takes up industry user fees, a critical source of about half of FDA’s funding. They require approval every five years. Lawmakers could attach agency reforms to the package. FDA leaders have urged Congress to empower regulators with new authorities to mandate drug recalls and compel drugmakers to share data on their supply chains. Without a permanent agency leader, it’s unclear who would champion these changes. And there are critics of the funding structure itself on both sides of the aisle. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who will lead the Senate’s health committee next year, told reporters he shares concerns with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that the user-fee programs pose an “incredible conflict of interest.” “If we’re going to regulate a very, very significant industry, it might be a good idea not to have the industry paying for their regulation,” Sanders told reporters on Wednesday. If the user-fee programs are not renewed, Congress would have to come up with more than $3.5 billion in taxpayer money to cover the gap. And the agency won’t have a permanent leader to make the argument for it. Notable My colleagues and I reported this week that Republicans were looking at Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., as a potential Overton replacement. Marshall declined to comment on Wednesday on whether he was still under consideration.

events.title: The U.S. Paid Insurers Billions to Cover Civilians Harmed in War. Even the Government Says the System Is Ripe for Fraud.
events.summary: It was supposed to be a safety net for the workers who helped the United States fight its wars — a federal program that provided healthcare and financial support to the employees of government contractors injured or killed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Instead, a handful of America’s insurance companies have become its biggest beneficiaries. While reaping billions in government payments, they have delayed care for legitimate injuries and received reimbursements for fraudulent claims, a ProPublica investigation found. Over the past decade, American taxpayers have paid nearly $5 billion to insurers through the obscure program, which the government itself has described as “ripe for potential fraud or, at the very least, gamesmanship for profit,” according to an internal memo ProPublica obtained. Nobody knows the true amount of misspent money. The official who oversaw the program under the Biden administration estimated that between $100 to $150 million is being wasted annually. The money has poured from a forgotten system for forgotten people who suffered forgotten injuries and deaths in America’s wars. It would be difficult to find another federal program with more incentives for graft and fewer controls to prevent it, the investigation found.  The Labor Department has proven incapable of policing the program. No standards exist to determine whether an insurer has asked for excessive or unreasonable payments. The department’s computer system is so dysfunctional it can’t issue fines. Until recently, federal examiners relied on decades-old CD-ROM technology to process thousands of reimbursement requests. An effort to hire experts to investigate insurance industry books failed. The agency also created the opportunity for abuse, the ProPublica investigation found. After lobbying by industry executives, officials loosened the rules for documenting PTSD cases in 2018. The change spurred a wave of questionable claims by workers and suspect payments to insurers, according to industry insiders. Reimbursements to insurance companies more than tripled after the decision, reaching nearly $1 billion through September 2026. Former Labor officials admit that the agency does not possess the expertise or employees to oversee the money flowing to insurers. “You can’t look under the covers. You just had to pay,” one former senior manager at the agency said. At issue is a workers’ compensation program for civilians deployed to war zones. In recent conflicts, the U.S. has supplemented its armed forces with hundreds of thousands of workers from across the world to provide security, maintain weapons systems and supply troops with food, housing and transportation. Without them, military officials say, it would be all but impossible for America to go to war. To protect their workforce, contractors purchase private insurance that the government pays for as part of the bid. When an employee is injured, the insurers cover the cost of medical treatments and lost wages. If a worker dies, they pay benefits to survivors. But there is a significant exception. If the injury or death is a result of hostilities — as opposed to an ordinary workplace accident like slipping on a wet floor — the U.S. government reimburses the insurance company for the claim. It also adds a handling fee.  Some insurance companies have used this exception to exploit the system in several ways, ProPublica’s investigation found. In many instances, they have settled dubious claims quickly, with little or no investigation, assured that they will receive reimbursement from the government, according to the Labor Department’s internal memo. It’s a churn strategy — cycle cases fast, get paid fast. Then there’s the opposite tack. Insurers will fight workers in courts for years, racking up expenses as they do so. If they decide to settle the claim, they are able to turn to the Labor Department and report that the injury they sought to deny is in fact authentic. They can then seek reimbursement from the government by asserting that the employee suffered an injury related to hostilities, according to department records. Put bluntly: Insurers change their stories and get paid when they do it. ProPublica uncovered additional abuses during its investigation, which is based on interviews with scores of current and former federal employees, insurance industry insiders, attorneys for workers and insurers, and civilian employees, along with internal memos, corporate documents and tens of thousands of pages of records obtained through court filings and the Freedom of Information Act. Do You Have Information on the Defense Base Act or the War Hazards Compensation Act? We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please get in touch. T. Christian Miller I am interested in hearing from insiders and whistleblowers — people who know how their organizations work and what is going wrong. I welcome documents and data that deliver concrete evidence. Contact Me In at least one case, the federal government reimbursed an insurance company for so-called medical expenses that had nothing to do with treating a wounded worker. The insurer received more than $24,000 for “medical” fees that included the cost of hand-delivering records to the insurer’s hired doctor and deposing one of its paid experts. The miscategorization — approved by the Labor Department — allowed the insurer to also collect handling fees on those expenses, adding another $25,000 that it was not entitled to receive, according to department regulations. Since 2014, four large insurance companies have benefited the most from the system. American International Group, or AIG, has received more than $1 billion, CNA Financial Corp. more than $740 million, Starr insurance more than $730 million and Allied World more than $350 million, according to a ProPublica analysis based on Labor Department records. None of the companies has been accused of wrongdoing. These are hidden costs of the United States’ wars on terror. They are reported here for the first time. “Lacks Safeguards” The Labor Department has been on notice about failures in the Defense Base Act program for years. It was the focus of a 2009 ProPublica investigation that prompted congressional hearings. The Pentagon and other agencies documented profiteering by the insurance industry. A senior official at the time acknowledged “systemic problems.”   The agency worked with Congress and the White House on initiatives to fix the system. The central idea: have the federal government — rather than insurance companies — pay for benefits for injured workers, just as it did for its own employees. In the industry, this is called self-insurance, and it is generally cheaper than using private insurers. Legislation introduced by Democrats in 2013 died in committee. events.title: Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences.
events.summary: Corpus Christi’s Western Well Field Brenda Bazán for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Late in 2024, Corpus Christi, Texas, was desperate for water after years of drought. So city officials hatched a plan to tap millions of gallons of water a day from an aquifer that serves dozens of counties across the Texas Gulf Coast. The city would drill wells — lots of them.  Corpus Christi’s drilling frenzy alarmed rural residents, who worried it threatened their access to water. They mobilized to create a groundwater conservation district that would regulate drilling and, they hoped, limit how much water the city could pump.  Then Corpus Christi officials came up with a peculiar idea. Fearing the residents’ effort could hamper the city’s ambitious plans to tap significant amounts of groundwater, officials asked a local entity to serve as its well regulator.  The advantages: City Council members appoint that entity’s board of directors, and its staff is made up entirely of city employees. Since that decision last fall, the entity — called the Corpus Christi Aquifer Storage and Recovery Conservation District — has greenlit every city request to drill more wells. In doing so, The Texas Tribune and KRIS 6 found, it fast-tracked its permitting process for the city and overlooked steps that would have slowed down the process for approving the permits — safeguards its own rules require to protect other well users.  A city-commissioned study released this summer found that the drilling plan could cause land around the wells to sink and water levels in other nearby wells to drop significantly. But by then, the district had already approved permits allowing the city to pump up to about 40 million gallons a day from 20 wells, although the city draws less than a third of that daily on average. The city defended the approvals. It said the district’s rules let the board decide when it has enough information to sign off on a permit and that before it does so, the city gives estimates of how pumping could affect water levels.  But water experts warn that the amount the city is allowed to pump in such a small area is exorbitant. “It’s absolutely unfathomable,” said Drew Molly, the former chief operating officer of Corpus Christi’s water department.   Molly, who is now chief water officer at Houston’s water department, said the district’s “lightning speed” approval of the city’s permits will cause ripple effects locally and across the state. A water well for pumping groundwater from underground aquifers Brenda Bazán for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune In Texas, fights over limited groundwater supplies will likely intensify as the population booms. Groundwater comes from aquifers and makes up more than half of the state’s water supply .  Aquifers stretch underground across counties and, sometimes, across states. The aquifer Corpus Christi draws from serves dozens of communities along the Gulf of Mexico, including some in Louisiana. Overpumping from aquifers is a key concern in Texas because they need rain and time to refill. As droughts get longer, the state’s water plan shows larger drops in groundwater’s availability compared with other sources. Groundwater pumping must be approached with caution, experts say. In worst-case scenarios, excessive pumping “can wipe an aquifer out,” said Jarrod Reynolds, a groundwater resource engineer. “It can be a stopgap, it can be a supplement, but it’s something that’s got to be managed,” Reynolds said. Corpus Christi’s rapid expansion of groundwater wells offers a critical, if not extreme, example of the challenges presented by a patchwork system for regulating the water that cities, businesses and citizens can extract from the ground. The coastal city of more than 300,000 residents nearly reached a crisis point earlier this year after persistent drought and years of inaction. It was months away from being unable to meet water demand and faced harsh restrictions to conserve supplies.  Drilling for groundwater became an important fix. So when the possibility of tougher regulation loomed in the wake of the rural residents’ efforts, city officials turned to Corpus Christi’s storage and recovery district, an entity created two decades earlier with the power to approve well permits.  The storage and recovery district is one of nearly 100 such groundwater districts in the state, but it’s the only one with City Council-appointed leaders. Most groundwater districts are led by leaders who are either elected or appointed by county officials — an important distinction since counties are not water suppliers, so there is less concern about any conflict of interest.  Corpus Christi leaders insisted in a written statement that the close ties the city shares with its well regulator will not hamstring efforts to protect the aquifer.  “There is no conflict of interest. City employees involved with the District have no personal or financial interest in permitting decisions,” said Ashley Marion, strategic business manager for the city water department, in the written statement. She added that, “The City and District share an interest in protecting and sustainably managing regional groundwater.” Marion also said the city tracks water levels and physical conditions at the wells and adjusts pumping rates based on daily data and long-term modeling. But the arrangement has drawn concern from water experts across the state, an outgoing state lawmaker and at least one of the storage and recovery district’s own board members.  “That’s the fox guarding the henhouse,” said Robert Mace, executive director at Texas State University’s Meadows Center for Water and the Environment, which focuses on water and environmental management policy.  “It tells me that the district is looking out for Corpus Christi’s interests and not necessarily the interests of other landowners that might be affected.” Choke Canyon Reservoir, west of Three Rivers, is one of three reservoirs Corpus Christi relies on for its water supply. Despite warnings that it needed to diversify its water sources, the city has repeatedly waffled on whether to invest in long-term solutions. events.title: Trump wants Supreme Court to let EPA cancel billions in Biden-era climate grants
events.summary: The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever and one that could affect Republican President Donald Trump's push to defund the priorities of prior administrations. The justices have not said whether they will take the case. If they do, it could resolve a fight over grants that the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded in 2025. Democratic President Joe Biden's administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels. Trump has targeted other grants, such as those considered to be supporting diversity, equity and inclusion. A favorable outcome at the high court could help his administration defeat other grant lawsuits, according to the government's filing this month . At issue is the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund , commonly referred to as a “green bank." Climate United Fund and other nonprofits were picked to operate the program authorized by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act . If the justices decline to take the case, the groups could regain access to their money because a federal appeals court already ruled in their favor. The EPA canceled the nonprofits' grants soon after the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025, with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin accusing the groups of mismanagement and potential fraud . The nonprofits' lawsuit argues that the EPA broke the law and violated the Constitution. It demands access to their grant money so they can run the program. The administration says it is immune from legal and constitutional claims and contends the groups filed their case in the wrong court. If the justices eventually side with the EPA, it could "have far-reaching implications for the government’s ability to reshape grant programs and to terminate grants that do not advance a particular administration’s policy priorities,” said Romany Webb, deputy director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University who has supported Climate United’s arguments. The EPA says the $16 billion at stake is the largest grant cancellation case ever and is another reason it warrants Supreme Court review. The courts have so far tried to thwart the administration's priorities, the EPA wrote in its petition to the Supreme Court. The EPA and Climate United declined to comment. In August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants. The release of any money was paused to give the Supreme Court a chance to weigh in. The justices ruled for the administration recently in decisions over canceled National Institutes of Health grants and teacher training grants . The administration has built its arguments around the Tucker Act, which gives the Court of Federal Claims exclusive authority over contract disputes. The claims court can award money, but not direct the government to take certain actions in the way federal courts can. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The nonprofits argued the way the EPA canceled the grants did not upend a contract with the federal government, but was done illegally and undercut spending on entire programs Congress had required, a constitutional violation. The government argues the matter is a contract dispute. The administration’s broad use of contract cancellations to enact policies is a novel approach, according to Bob Wagman, president of the Court of Federal Claims Bar Association and a partner at the firm White & Case. “I would hate to think that the only programs that could be supported have a four-year life,” he said, mentioning cancer research as an example of a grant program that would need longer than a single administration to pay off. “It is just not good for the country.” Zeldin last year told Fox News that he suspected the green bank “was a clear-cut case of waste and abuse.” U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said that when the government was asked for evidence of fraud, the EPA did not provide it and shifted its position to more general concerns about the level of oversight over the program. Chutkan said the government cannot terminate the contracts in violation of the law and that the groups should have access to some of their frozen money, which is held in an account at Citibank. The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups. Passage of the Inflation Reduction Act created the green bank.

events.summary: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test. Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot. The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share. The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI , as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months. The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion. This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion. Anthropic raises $81 billion in record-breaking IPO First of the AI giants to go public Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT -maker OpenAI, has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027. Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers. That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst. Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public? events.title: Anthropic IPO is largest in history, overtaking SpaceX
events.summary: Anthropic's debut on Nasdaq on Thursday marked a significant moment for the company and a major achievement for the artificial intelligence sector. Shares in Anthropic were priced at $83 each, placing value for the company at about $1.5 trillion. The company had about 980 million shares as trading began. Its stock price jumped to about $100 in the afternoon, and at the closing bell it was priced at $97, having gained 17 per cent on the day. An additional private sector investment of $26 billion in Anthropic means that in total the company sold $107 billion in shares, breaking SpaceX’s IPO where that company raised $86 billion. Anthropic’s chief executive and co-founder Dario Amodei struck an optimistic yet cautious tone during a speech just before markets opened. "Our customers, the world's most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we've built to stimulate economic growth," he said, before pivoting and acknowledging growing concerns about the potential for AI to create labour disruptions and lead to a spike in cybersecurity problems, among other worries. "We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable and we are building anyway, but because we think they are avoidable, avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI,” he said. Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, reflected on Anthropic's blockbuster debut. "At $83 per share, Anthropic is coming to market above its initial pricing range, but still below our $92 fair value estimate,” he said, while also pointing out that companies such as Anthropic are by no means bulletproof. “Investors should not mistake a discount to fair value for an absence of risk,” Mr Khan added. “Anthropic will need to sustain rapid growth while managing the enormous cost of developing and running its models, and there is still considerable uncertainty around how the competitive landscape and economics of generative AI will evolve.” Varun Datta, an AI-centric venture capitalist and founder of Truth Ventures, said that although there's definitely enthusiasm amid Anthropic's IPO, the company's lofty valuation leaves little room for disappointment. "Personally I'll be looking closely at customer retention and how much enterprise clients are spending year on year," he said. "This will give a clearer picture of the business behind the IPO." Mr Datta said it's also important not to overlook that Anthropic's IPO might create ripples throughout the entire AI sector for many companies. "From a VC point of view Anthropic's IPO could have a knock-on effect on how private AI companies are valued, such as smaller AI companies building applications on top of models like Claude," he explained. Some analysts had believed its competitor, OpenAI, would beat it in going public because it was among the first to launch one of the first consumer AI products, ChatGPT, in 2022. Anthropic was co-founded in 2021, when it consisted mainly of defectors from OpenAI who were concerned about their former company's approach to AI regulations and safety. The company’s Claude AI tool and various other models gained in popularity, particularly in the corporate and government spheres. Its ascent, however, has not been without controversy, especially as recent polling indicates increasing public concerns about the rise of AI. Some researchers, elected officials and technology analysts have accused Anthropic of reneging on promises about regulation and safety guardrails. On Wednesday, about 80 high-profile technology researchers, executives and academics called Anthropic reckless. They expressed concerns about AI's increasing ability to build new versions of itself in what has been called the “misanthropic statement”. Turing Award laureate Judea Pearl, Future of Life Institute co-founder Max Tegmark and Centre for Humane Technology president Tristan Harris are among those to sign the document. OpenAI is widely expected to stage its IPO next year. Anthropic has not yet responded to The National's requests for comment on this article.

events.title: Kenya picks US consortium for critical minerals project as residents seek answers
events.summary: Kenya’s government has selected a consortium of U.S. companies to develop niobium and rare earths deposits on its coast NAIROBI, Kenya -- Kenya’s government said Thursday that it had selected a consortium of U.S. companies as the preferred bidder to develop niobium and rare earths deposits on its coast , while residents said they were still waiting for information on the project. The mining ministry said it had issued a notice of its intention to award the Mrima Hill project in Kwale County to the Frontier Minerals Consortium, which comprises Frontier Minerals LLC, Bunker Hill Mining Corp., ReElement Technologies and American Resources Corp. The ministry stressed that the notice is not a license. It said the consortium must now “go to the ground,” engage communities and obtain “all requisite consents” before applying for a prospecting license. Residents and farmers have told The Associated Press that they fear losing their land. Elders from the local Digo community worry about damage to a sacred forest where they say their ancestors are buried. “Until now, we have received no information from the government on the content of the project,” said Justus Mwero, chairman of the Mrima Farm Owners Community-Based Organization. “It will be hard for us to express our consent or opinion to the company with no information.” Countries including the U.S. are racing to secure the rare earth minerals used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines and defense technologies, seeking alternatives to China’s dominance. The ministry said it had “deliberately” chosen investors before starting formal consent processes. Mining Minister Hassan Joho told the AP on Nov. 2 the community was consulted before seeking bids. The government should not distance themselves from their responsibilities and leave it to the investor,” said Fakii Omar of the Kwale Mining Alliance. The Mrima Hill Sacred Grove was designated a national monument in 1992. “The notice does not mention if the protected status of the forest has been revoked," Omar added. "Can the proposed mine coexist with the protected status under current laws?” A previous attempt to mine the site ended in arbitration. In 2013, Kenya’s environment regulator rejected an environmental assessment for a license held by Cortec Mining Kenya, citing the site’s protected status, according to Extractives Daily. An arbitration tribunal of the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes later ruled that the license should not have been issued without environmental approval, and Kenya won the case. The Centre for Litigation Trust, a Kenyan civil society group, has asked the High Court in Kwale County to suspend a proposed Kenya-U.S. agreement on Mrima Hill’s minerals until residents are consulted. events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged eight Colorado-based entities, likely operated by individuals located overseas, for defrauding U.S. investors out of more than $37 million. The defendants allegedly lured investors to believe they were working with a real investment adviser and crypto asset trading platform, when in fact the adviser and platform were entirely fake, simply fronts to steal investor money. “The SEC continues to seek out and expose fraudulent investment scams that prey on U.S. investors,” said Laura D’Allaird, Chief of the SEC Enforcement Division’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit. “We encourage the public to continue reporting these schemes by using our online portal .” According to the SEC complaint, the defendants lured investors through advertisements on social media that directed investors to group and private chats controlled by individuals perpetrating the fraud, likely from overseas. The individuals in the chats, claiming to be associated with an alleged investment adviser, first gave advice to trade stocks on U.S. markets before luring their victims to send as much money as possible to a supposed crypto asset trading platform, leading victims to believe they were buying real crypto assets on the platform. The defendants used a variety of tactics to feign legitimacy, including by making fake SEC certificates, making filings with the SEC, FINRA, or FinCEN, and directing skeptical investors to those certificates and filings. The scheme operated in four adviser-platform pairs from August 2024 through May 2026, with the perpetrators abandoning one pair for the next after operating for a few months. The complaint, filed in the United States District Court for the District of Colorado, charges Advisor WeChat Capital, Tech Brokerage Asset Alliance Ltd., HB Wealth Advisors, IdeaCrypto Exchange LLC, Convergent Wealth Advisors Inc., RealSimple Crypto Exchange Inc., Associated Wealth Advisors Ltd., and Essential Crypto Exchange with violating Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b‑5 thereunder. The complaint additionally charges Advisor WeChat Capital, HB Wealth Advisors, Convergent Wealth Advisors Inc., and Associated Wealth Advisors Ltd. with violating Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Convergent Wealth Advisors Inc. and Essential Crypto Exchange with violating Section 207 of the Advisers Act. The complaint seeks permanent injunctions, conduct‑based injunctions, disgorgement of ill‑gotten gains, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. The SEC’s Office of Investor Education and Assistance has issued investor alerts warning investors that fraudsters may use popular group chats or claim to be officially registered with the SEC to lure investors into scams. The SEC encourages investors to use Investor.gov to check the background of anyone offering or selling them an investment. Separately, a Form D filed by Tech Brokerage Asset Alliance Ltd. and Forms ADV filed by Convergent Wealth Advisors Inc. and Essential Crypto Exchange have been removed from the Commission website. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, and the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, among other authorities and regulators. events.title: Why the Senate energy permitting bill might become law
events.summary: If the sweeping Senate permitting bill becomes law, it will reflect a rare convergence of political and market forces strong enough to trump the Beltway aversion to big, bipartisan deals. Why it matters: The bill could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers. Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the plan would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. The latest: A vote on final passage of the White House-backed bill could occur Thursday after the Senate plows through some more amendments. The big picture: Many industries — pipelines, transmission, housing, you name it — call permitting a long bureaucratic and judicial maze that stymies projects. Yes, but: That, on its own, isn't nearly enough to get this far. Here are other reasons the bill has a path to becoming law after years of failed efforts to upend permitting. 🗳️ The cost-of-living election. The midterms were soaked in affordability politics at a time of rising energy bills. While critics can call the projected savings modest, cost is politically front and center. The Rhodium Group estimates that big provisions it analyzed would cut average residential power prices by 3%-4% in 2035. Third Way, a group that favors the bill, supported the research firm's work. 📈 Rising electricity demand. U.S. power thirst has been rising in the last few years after staying largely flat for decades, driven partly by AI and wider electrification of the economy. 🦋 A maturing clean energy industry. As sectors like renewables and storage become more mainstream, " more developers and companies are seeing the real-world challenges" of doing projects, clean energy lobbyist Jeff Navin notes via email. That puts them in agreement with utilities and oil and gas companies. "They all run into problems getting the permits needed to build energy infrastructure," said Navin, an Obama-era Energy Department aide and former Democratic Capitol Hill staff member. Easier permitting is needed for transmission to carry the industries' power, as well as for building new generation itself. 😣 A mercurial White House was focused. The White House's National Energy Dominance Council was engaged with the bill. Co-author Shelly Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) credited then-chief of staff Susie Wiles as a helpful player at the Sept. 30 bill rollout. Axios' Alex Isenstadt reported that new chief of staff Stephen Miller also wants a permitting bill. Trump officials have also allowed some onshore wind projects bottled up by Pentagon reviews to proceed. 🔀 Shifting Democratic coalitions. Multiple analyses show the bill bringing somewhat lower power sector emissions compared to a world without it. But when climate had more political juice a few years ago, a bill backed by oil industry groups probably would not have had this much Democratic buy-in. Democratic co-authors and other supporters in the Dem coalition say easing the clean energy buildout is key to more climate progress in the future. More moderate center-left voices and think tanks have new cachet, while environmental groups opposing the bill haven't made enough inroads despite longstanding ties to Democrats. The intrigue: Data centers have been and remain a wildcard. There's a big political and public backlash, and opponents of the bill have seized on it, charging that the bill would help Big Tech by making the buildout easier. But bill authors and backers are emphasizing language designed to ensure that data centers pay for grid upgrades and have higher transmission service costs. What we're watching: The House. If it can pass the bill before the end of the year, there's a good chance the bill will get signed into law. If not, it's just another failed effort. events.title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
events.summary: Nvidia's board is now coming under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions , it’s even more difficult. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks . Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. CHIP SOMODEVILLA/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. events.title: ICJ finds Myanmar guilty of 'genocidal intent' against Rohingya
events.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar was guilty of “genocidal intent” over the killing of 10,000 Rohingya nearly a decade ago, a decision with huge consequences for ongoing conflicts today. Naypyidaw insists its crackdown on the mainly Muslim Rohingya, which forced upwards of 700,000 to flee to neighboring Bangladesh, was a fair response to attacks by a militia group. But the ICJ found Myanmar troops “killed thousands of Rohingya ⁠civilians, perpetrated widespread acts ⁠of sexual violence as well as acts of ⁠extreme violence against children.” Beyond the case itself, the ruling has major ramifications for other suits pending at the ICJ: South Africa has brought a similar case against Israel over its war in Gaza. — Prashant Rao

events.title: In reversal, IMF forecasts growth for UAE
events.summary: After predicting contraction just a month ago, the IMF has reversed course and now says it expects the UAE economy to grow 0.2% this year. The emirates have slowly started to regain momentum thanks to rebounding trade, aviation, tourism, and oil sales — although the fund pins much of its prediction for rapid growth next year on non-oil activity. In October, the IMF said the Middle East and North Africa would be the only region in the world to shrink in 2026. It predicted Gulf economies would contract almost as much as during the COVID-19 shock. The UAE did better than most of its neighbors because it could pipe crude around the Strait of Hormuz to Fujairah, while enjoying “substantial public-sector and external buffers,” according to Said Bakhache, the fund’s mission chief. Even so, its non-oil private sector fell to a five-year low in June as flights ground to a halt and visitors all but disappeared. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Walmart raises its outlook for the year for the 3rd time after a solid quarter
events.summary: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices NEW YORK -- Walmart reported solid third quarter sales gains as the retailer continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum that are seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices . The company topped Wall Street’s profit and sales projections, and it raised its annual guidance for the third time this year, but the outlook released Thursday was more conservative than industry analysts had expected. Comparable sales, which include digital channels and stores, rose 2.9%. That is better than last quarter's 2.6% increase, when Walmart reported its weakest comparable sales growth in six years. But it's still a slowdown from the 4.5% growth registered during the same period last year. Still, slowing comparable sales, particularly in Walmart stores, also reflect a strategic shift toward e-commerce, Walmart+ memberships and advertising. Global e-commerce sales rose 17%, while U.S. e-commerce sales increased 23% during the latest quarter, the company said. Walmart said that more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders are being fulfilled from stores, including its third party marketplace orders. Stores enabled faster delivery speeds on a wide range of assortments, the retailer said. “We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” Walmart's CEO John Furner said in prepared remarks. “The strength of our omnichannel model gives us room to do even more.” Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers use its website or visit its stores every week, according to Walmart. Analysts look to the massive retailer for clues about what to expect from the industry as a whole during the critical holiday shopping season. Consumers in the U.S. have remained resilient in the face of painful inflation , but they have also grown more selective about what they buy. Many rely on retailers like Walmart as a one-stop shop for low-priced household goods, groceries and pharmaceuticals. The latest U.S. retail sales data revealed that shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as Americans pulled back on a variety of purchases, from cars, clothing and furniture and even their own hobbies. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to Commerce Department data released this week. Walmart is also trying to increase subscriptions to its shipping programs. During the third quarter, Walmart launched a combined Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus annual membership bundle for $120 per year. The package saves shoppers nearly $100 compared to buying both plans separately, it said. Walmart, based in Bentonville, Arkansas, has begun to capture a larger share of wealthier consumers. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart have been coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000, the retailer has said. Walmart’s quarterly net income was $4.94 billion, or 62 cents per share, in the three-month period ended Oct. 31. Adjusted per-share results were 65 cents, higher than the 64 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet. In the year-ago quarter, the company earned $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share. Sales rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion in the latest quarter. Analysts were predicting $187.38 billion, according to FactSet. The company said that comparable sales were driven by groceries and general merchandise categories like furniture and toys. But the figure was once again hit by federal legislation that requires pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said. For the full year, Walmart now projects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.84 to $2.89, up from the prior guidance of $2.80 to $2.87. Sales should be up anywhere from 4.9% to 5.2%, up from the prior forecast of 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $748.12 billion to $750.25 billion, according to FactSet. Analysts expected $2.89 per share and sales of $752.68 billion for the year, according to FactSet. events.title: The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks. They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.
