Although total dry natural gas production during the 2026 refill season was 3% higher than the same period in 2025, according to S&P Global Energy, most of the increased production during this period was used to meet rising demand from liquefied natural gas export terminals . Mild spring temperatures during the first several weeks of the refill season mitigated seasonal residential and commercial natural gas demand, allowing the surplus to the five-year average to grow, peaking at 198 Bcf (7%) for the week ending August 7, before declining for the next 10 consecutive weeks, as warmer-than-normal temperatures during the summer months increased power generation demand for natural gas. events.title: Why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding
events.summary: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry PARIS -- Russia is responding forcefully to confirmation from France that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine to provide training and maintenance help with some of the weaponry it has supplied for the war . Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said: “This is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,' but direct participation in the war.” France says the soldiers and weapons specialists are noncombatants. “Since we are not at war with Russia, these, in fact, are not combat units,” French Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said. Speaking on Wednesday to French broadcaster RMC, Rufo said French personnel are “a very long way from the front line. They come to carry out occasional missions.” She didn't specify their numbers, but said that they are “a few soldiers, specialists, including armaments engineers, who work — or can come to work — on an occasional basis to maintain complex equipment, such as Mirage aircraft or Caesar howitzers, and provide targeted training on certain equipment.” France first delivered Mirage 2000-5 fighters last year to Ukraine and trained pilots and mechanics for them. The French Defense Ministry says the aircraft have helped fend off missile and drone attacks. It also says that with donations from allies and purchases, Ukraine's force of high-precision French-made Caesar howitzers has grown to become the largest in the world. France has also supplied precision bombs, cruise missiles, air defense systems, light tanks and other equipment. Rufo told French lawmakers on Tuesday that France is “accelerating” its support in light of Russia's air campaign against Ukrainian targets. She spoke of a “complete absence of any intention to engage in combat” and described as “absurd” Lavrov's accusation that France is directly participating in the war. JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Only a “very limited" number of French personnel are engaged in “the extremely limited” missions, Rufo said. Her comments came after French media, including broadcaster RFI and Le Monde newspaper, reported that small contingents of French military officers stay in Ukraine for short rotations as part of the so-called Operation Volia, since at least this summer. French military personnel have been operating in Ukraine for more than six months and France isn't alone in providing such support, Lavrov said Tuesday at a news conference in Manila, Philippines, where he was attending a summit of Southeast Asian nations. “We have conveyed our concern through the available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,’ but direct participation in the war,” he said, without naming the countries. “This is just like the assistance with target designation, the provision of satellite data and much else,” he said. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that Moscow will regard any foreign troops in Ukraine as legitimate targets and it will be up to the Russian military to determine a response. The United Kingdom has soldiers in Ukraine, but officials haven't disclosed how many or what their role is. The U.K. Defense Ministry confirmed two deaths of British soldiers in Ukraine in the past year, in both cases in accidents. Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, dozens of countries have trained more than 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers, at locations outside the country — in France , the U.K. , the United States, Poland, Germany and elsewhere — including on Patriot missile batteries, F-16 combat jets and other equipment. They have also trained recruits, officers, medics and other specialists for combat. Jill Lawless in London, Sylvie Corbet and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report. events.title: Rwanda in deportation deal with European countries
events.summary: Five European countries aim to start deporting failed asylum seekers to Rwanda, which has long been criticized for its human rights record, by next year. Many EU nations are tightening immigration rules in response to far-right electoral pressure. The removals are seen as a means to “confront the massive challenges of illegal migration ,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. Austria, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands are also involved. Rights group Amnesty International described the deal with Rwanda as “ disgraceful ,” highlighting the country’s “track record” of silencing political opponents and critics, allegations Kigali has consistently denied. Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said “we need to go beyond the existing cliche ,” adding that refugee rights were respected in the country. A previous UK-Rwanda deportation plan — which differed as it targeted anyone who had come without permission, rather than those who had failed the asylum process — was abandoned in 2024 after a change in government. — Damian Zane

events.title: U.S. drivers are just absorbing high gasoline prices
events.summary: Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive. Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost. This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab. The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year. State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data. There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic. That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year. The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits. He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving. Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less. How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied. EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals. There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year. The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes. "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run," he writes.

events.title: Adnoc sees sulphur output doubling as Hormuz disruption sends prices to record highs
events.summary: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's sour gas unit expects its sulphur output to double or even triple over the next decade, betting that a by-product it once paid to get rid of has become a core business after the Iran war pushed prices to record highs . “Sulphur will be the future gold,” Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive of Adnoc Sour Gas, said at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai on Wednesday. He said Adnoc produces about 7 million tonnes a year, and that could rise to between 14 million and 20 million tonnes as the company increases gas output. Most of the gain would come between 2030 and 2035, he added, and the final figure depends on which projects are sanctioned. Sulphur will be the future gold Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive, Adnoc Sour Gas The plan shows how the closure of the Strait of Hormuz turned an overlooked commodity into a strategic one. The Gulf accounts for about 47 per cent of global seaborne sulphur exports , according to S&P Global, and the disruption pushed free-on-board benchmarks above $1,000 a tonne and delivered prices to about $1,200 to $1,300 by July. Sulphur is a key input for phosphate fertiliser and for the sulphuric acid used to process nickel and copper. When Adnoc started developing its Shah field 10 to 15 years ago, sulphur traded at minus $8 a tonne because producers had to pay buyers to take it away, Mr Al Jaberi said. “Nobody was thinking about applications at that time,” he said. During the crisis, it hit record prices. “That's the journey of sulphur.” Prices climbed from an average of about $500 a tonne before the conflict to $1,100 to $1,200 in late June, according to CRU. Adnoc set its own July official selling price for the Indian subcontinent at a record $1,000 a tonne free on board Ruwais, $180 to $200 above the previous high set in 2008, according to Argus. Prices have eased since then as buyers pulled back. Adnoc cut its October price by $70 to $890 a tonne, and spot Middle East prices fell to $740 to $790 a tonne by mid-October, according to Kpler data. Adnoc ships its sulphur mainly to China and Morocco for fertiliser. Mr Al Jaberi said the company is working with the Adnoc Research Centre and Khalifa University on new uses, including solid-state batteries, new types of fertiliser, cosmetics, cement and soil improvement. The extra sulphur will come from a push into harder-to-produce gas. Mr Al Jaberi said Adnoc's upstream unit produces about 12.5 billion cubic feet a day and aims for about 17.7 billion in the coming years, which means developing marginal and sour fields. Shah gasfield, which was suspended after a drone attack caused a fire in March, now produces 1.45 billion cubic feet a day, and Adnoc plans to raise that to 1.85 billion or possibly 2 billion. Earlier this month, Adnoc took a final investment decision on the Ruwais Diyab unconventional gas development, its first large-scale unconventional gas project. Mr Al Jaberi said a single sour gas well once cost as much as $50 million. AI-driven reservoir modelling, drones and robots have since cut costs and inspection times. Demand is also coming from data centres. “Out of 5 megawatts, 1 megawatt at least will go for AI,” he said. Iman Nasseri, senior vice president of Middle East and Asia at FGE NexantECA, told the panel that the region's LNG exports will double to 200 million tonnes within a decade. He warned it would be “naive” to treat every announced data centre as new gas demand.

events.title: Your favorite Thanksgiving dishes won’t cost substantially more this year – here’s why
events.summary: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on Unsplash Inflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute . That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022 , the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began . I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report , published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time . As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data . Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive . Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5% , and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data . But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak , which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more . Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data . Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers . Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35 , Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people . Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. Elizabeth Canales receives funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

events.title: Jeffries nears historic speakership as power shifts in Congress
events.summary: Hakeem Jeffries could soon become America's first Black House speaker, even as Black lawmakers confront rising threats to their power in D.C. Why it matters: Proposed committee term limits and another round of redistricting could weaken Black lawmakers' influence they spent decades building. By the numbers: The number of Black lawmakers in the 120th Congress will be stable from the 119th, based on results so far. The House will likely seat 59 Black voting members, down from 61, according to the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies . All four Black House Republicans are departing, while Black Democrats have gained two seats. Black membership in the U.S. Senate will rise from five to a record seven, including Sens.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi and Juliana Stratton of Illinois . Zoom in: Democrats are in the middle of a sometimes messy generational power transfer, with younger lawmakers challenging more senior members for committee chairmanships. Those chairmanships have long helped Congressional Black Caucus members exercise power beyond their numbers. "For CBC members, the power is seniority," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) told Politico in 2014. "I've been around a while. ... Some wisdom, at least, is important to what we're going through right now," Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, 81, (D-N.J.) told Axios in 2025. Sticking point: Democrats are considering a four-term limit for committee leaders , starting after the 2028 elections, that could eventually force three veteran Black Democrats to step aside as committee leaders. Bennie Thompson, 78, of Mississippi, leads Democrats on Homeland Security. Bobby Scott, 79, of Virginia, leads Democrats on Education and Workforce. He faces a challenge from Connecticut Rep. Jahana Hayes, 53. Maxine Waters, 88, of California, leads Democrats on Financial Services. She faces a challenge from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54. Zoom out: A Democratic wave helped Black incumbents survive redistricting this year, but that level of support may not be repeated in future elections. The Supreme Court's April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais narrowed protections against maps that watered down the Voting Rights Act, potentially exposing more Black-held districts to redistricting. Texas' new maps pushed veteran Democrat Al Green into a primary against another Black incumbent. Green lost. His heavily redrawn former district elected Latina Democrat Leticia Gutierrez. Black Democrats Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina won in redrawn districts. Louisiana's 6th District heads to a December runoff. Between the lines: Hispanic Democrats are also gaining influence, with their numbers in Congress reaching new highs. California Rep. Pete Aguilar, a Hispanic Democrat, appears headed for majority whip, a top party leadership job. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus expects 55 members, including senators and Puerto Rico's nonvoting resident commissioner — its largest membership since its 1976 founding. Yes, but: Hispanic gains don't necessarily come at Black lawmakers' expense. Hispanic Democrats on Financial Services have backed Waters , showing how the two groups can work together as their members seek more influence. Younger lawmakers say term limits could open doors for the next generation of Black and Hispanic leaders.

events.title: Bahrain's war-hit Sitra refinery weeks away from full capacity, Bapco Energies CEO says
events.summary: Bahrain's Sitra refinery, hit six times by Iranian strikes since the regional war began in late February, is still weeks away from returning to full capacity, the chief executive of energy company Bapco Energies said on Wednesday. The 415,000 barrels-per-day plant is now running at more than 80 per cent of capacity and will hit 100 per cent by the end of the year, Mark Thomas said on a panel at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai. The refinery is “near returning to its design capacity”, Mr Thomas said. “If you give us a few more weeks, hopefully we'll get to that point.” The final step is restarting conversion units such as the hydrocrackers, which come last in the sequence after the crude and distillation units. The recovery is a turnaround for Bahrain's only refinery, which was in the last stage of commissioning, with 27 of 32 units running, when the attacks began. It was targeted daily for about six months. “There was a moment in time that I actually felt we could be offline for one, two years,” Mr Thomas said. With the Strait of Hormuz still largely closed to normal traffic, the war has also upended where Bapco sells its fuel. Before the war, the refinery exported about 85 per cent of its output through Hormuz. Now about 80 per cent is used within the Gulf, because damage to refineries across the region has left neighbours short of fuel. Bapco is selling jet fuel to Qatar and the UAE, diesel to Iraq and fuel to Saudi Arabia. Calling the shift temporary, Mr Thomas said export pressure will build again as rival plants are repaired. Naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas, which have no buyers in the Gulf, still have to be transported through the strait. Moving LPG has been “extremely” difficult because it needs specialised carriers. Charter rates are four times the norm and insuring one vessel for the roughly eight-hour transit costs $17 million, Mr Thomas said. “On a cargo of 300,000 barrels of diesel, it's outrageous.” Bahrain's nuclear future Bapco is also preparing to bring small modular nuclear reactors to the kingdom. The company would like to be “principally an investor, potentially an operator”, Mr Thomas said on the sidelines of the conference. A civil nuclear deal with the US, known as a 123 agreement, is “in final stages”, he said, but he declined to say when it might be signed. Mr Thomas described a 10-year development period. “We won't have anything on the ground till 2035,” he said. Asked about a target of two gigawatts by then, he said Bapco is “incubating the whole concept” for now. Bahrain, which has the Gulf's smallest hydrocarbon reserves, is looking for new sources of power as its main gas reservoir, in production for 42 years, is in decline. Bahrain and the US signed a preliminary agreement in July 2025 that opened the way to talks on a 123 agreement, which US law requires before American nuclear material or equipment can be transferred. Market volatility has helped Bapco's trading arm, which “far exceeded our expectations” this year, Mr Thomas said. It was set up to market the refinery's barrels but has quickly moved into trading third-party cargo. This year Bapco also imported crude by ship for the first time, in addition to its supply through the AB-4 pipeline from Saudi Arabia. Mr Thomas declined to name the source. LNG setback Bahrain's plans to import liquefied natural gas have been set back by the war. Demand collapsed after Aluminium Bahrain, Gulf Petrochemical Industries Company and an iron producer were hit. Bapco bought eight LNG cargoes in 2025, five of them from the US. Mr Thomas said 2027 will be “a transition year” and expects demand to return to prewar plans by 2028 or 2029. At home, Bapco is mapping offshore seismic with US company EOG Resources and expects the prospects to be gas-rich. Results will take about another year and a half, Mr Thomas said.

events.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver. How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us? —Amit Katwala Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure. Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power . —Casey Crownhart MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century. As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid . events.title: SpaceX $40 billion chip financing to stay off balance sheet
events.summary: The colossal $40 billion financing that Apollo is lining up for SpaceX could hit markets as early as this week, but it won’t be hitting their balance sheet, according to people familiar with the matter. The financing will go into an SPV, or special-purpose vehicle, allowing SpaceX to keep it off its own balance sheet and instead rent GPUs from its subsidiary. Apollo will be lending close to $20 billion of the deal upfront and then syndicating it or selling it to other investors later. Other companies, including Meta, have utilized this kind of financial workaround to keep debt off their bottom lines. It also allows the companies to keep their ratings elevated. Portions of the seven-part deal could be sold to investors as early as this week. The arrangement includes an array of pricing — the bulk of which, $35.5 billion, will price at 8.3% and 7.75%, Semafor reported earlier . Other, riskier parts of the deal will price even higher, at a blended rate that could exceed 9%, but will account for less than $3 billion of the overall financing. Pricing for debt related to data centers and artificial intelligence has gotten more expensive for borrowers as investors get choosier about where they put their money and fret over the growing debt loads at companies in the AI buildout. Apollo declined to comment. SpaceX didn’t respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Inside Google’s push to make AI the new Auto-Tune
events.summary: Google is trying to prove that AI won’t replace artists. The tech giant has rolled out a suite of generative AI music features over the past year, including Flow Music — a tool it acquired in February when it bought the startup ProducerAI — which allows users to create songs from a single prompt, in the same style as AI music giants like Suno and Udio. But the company’s pitch to artists is that its technology can also act like a tool in their creative process, not unlike Auto-Tune or MIDI. To prove it, Google launched Flow Music Sessions earlier this year, an artist residency program for those curious about integrating the technology into their creative processes. Residents work in Spaces, a Flow Music feature carried over from ProducerAI that allows artists to vibe code their own tools and plugins. The fusion of art with artificial intelligence makes some artists queasy, and it has since ChatGPT launched in 2022. But, Google has long found ways into the creator economy from different angles. It grew YouTube, today a juggernaut video-sharing site rivaling cable, largely by giving platforms to independent creators. Now, it’s betting that artists wary of AI can be won over in the same way: on their own terms. For artists in Google’s Flow Music residency, that distinction is important. “I draw creative fuel and energy and joy from making things myself,” Avanti Singh, a sound designer and resident at Flow Music, told Semafor. “I’m not particularly interested in prompting an entire song to be created because the most fun part for me is writing lyrics and singing and collaborating.” Instead, artists in the program vibe code to bolster the creative process, cutting down on the most tedious production steps. Mike Costanzo, a producer in the residency, built a “perfect kick” plugin in Spaces that he says cuts down the time it takes to find an apt kick drum for a song. He picks a genre, taps a musical key to tune the drum, and the plugin handles the rest. Google has come under fire for its AI music generation. A group of independent musicians and songwriters filed a lawsuit against Google in March, alleging the tech giant trained its music model Lyria 3 on copyrighted recordings from YouTube without permission or compensation. Google Flow now runs on newer versions of that model. Google has moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that music uploaded to YouTube is already broadly licensed for AI training in accepting the platform’s terms of service.

events.title: A flawed test for African banks
events.summary: Fitch’s downgrade of the Africa Export-Import Bank in June 2025 sparked a furious debate about the assessments of multilateral development banks by global rating agencies. Then in February, Moody’s proposed changes to its methodology for assessing these types of banks. The revisions, applied since July, introduced a potential two-notch downgrade if a bank does not have large, highly rated, and non-borrowing shareholders. This could make it difficult for African-owned development banks to secure higher ratings without bringing in non-African shareholders, effectively forcing these lenders to surrender part of their ownership and control. Credit ratings are intended to provide an independent assessment of an institution’s capacity and willingness to repay its obligations. In the case of assessments of multilateral banks, rating methodologies have a bias towards non-African shareholders. In effect suggesting that African governments, irrespective of their demonstrated financial commitments, cannot provide sufficient capital to the institutions they have established. The nationality of shareholders may be relevant to risk analysis, but it should not become a substitute for examining fundamentals. If the institution has strong risk management and governance structures, adequate capitalization, quality assets, and high liquidity, where the shareholders come from should be less important. Foreign investment and diversity of shareholding are valuable, but they should be a strategic choice for the institutions themselves rather than a condition implicitly imposed by the architecture of credit assessment. A more fundamental issue is the difference between paid-in capital that shareholders have actually contributed and callable capital that they have promised to provide if there is a need. Afreximbank is a good example. Shareholders’ funds stand at approximately $9 billion, while its net income increased by 30% in the first half of 2026. The commitment of African shareholders is also significant. According to the bank’s leadership, African governments contributed approximately $2.6 billion in additional paid-in capital by the end of 2025. A further $526 million had been paid or committed in cash contributions in 2026. In addition, shareholders have committed substantial callable capital. This is another important layer of protection for creditors. But Moody’s new methodology still places more value on callable capital from foreign highly rated shareholders than substantial paid-in capital from African shareholders. A more balanced assessment should recognize capital contributions and other tangible financial commitments regardless of the creditworthiness of shareholders. Today’s rating methodologies characterize geographical concentration and an exclusive focus on the African business environment as indicators of high risk. This creates a further structural disadvantage for African-owned multilateral development banks whose mandates require them to serve African economies. To secure higher credit ratings, these institutions need to reduce lending to the very economies they were established to support. This will diminish their role and purpose. Rating agencies should not be expected to overlook weaknesses in African governance, capital adequacy, liquidity or risk management. Independence and analytical integrity remain essential to the credibility of the ratings industry. To maintain this, three changes are necessary. First, ratings should be accurate and consistent in their assessments. African institutions should not be penalized simply because their shareholders are African and operate in Africa. Nationality should not be a proxy for financial capacity and willingness to pay. Second, African governments must continue to support their institutions with capital and affirm their legal commitments established through their agreements and treaties: This pushes rating agencies to assess multilateral banks based on their legal and operational merits. Lastly, African countries must strengthen cooperation among their multilateral financial institutions, deepen domestic capital markets, and support the development of independent African credit rating capacity. Greater competition and analytical diversity will improve the quality of credit assessments, provided all agencies maintain rigorous standards. Africa cannot build its own strong multilateral financial institutions if the price of recognition is surrendering the ownership and control to foreign shareholders.

events.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak is spiralling , with the disease spreading at a record pace despite a surge in funding. Rampant misinformation, widespread violence, and a lack of medical equipment have aided the spread of the Bundibugyo strain, which is now Africa’s biggest-ever Ebola outbreak by geographic reach. A lack of treatments or vaccines has also meant that the current outbreak is more fatal than ever: Around 50% of those who are infected die, the highest-ever mortality rate for Ebola. Although authorities are seeking more funding, more than $700 million remains unaccounted for by the DRC, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, while frontline workers have gone unpaid for months. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ.
events.summary: Michelle Urra for ProPublica In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration. After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.” It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor. Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found. Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show. That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data . But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools. “The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.” To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys. More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show. ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.” Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed Note: This analysis of federal pay codes does not include experience ranges for supervisors. We also exclude some special assistant U.S. attorneys for whom we cannot infer experience or supervisory status. Pratheek Rebala/ProPublica The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors. Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported , the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience. While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan. “The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.” Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said. “It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.” While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.” As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment. Shifting Personnel, Shifting Caseloads The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades. Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows. As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat. Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. events.title: America's measles return leaves infants vulnerable
events.summary: The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease. Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat. Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected . That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times . (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.) Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized. State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease. Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC . Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children. But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months. The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months. Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life. What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X. "The community protection we took for granted is gone, and U.S. moms now must live in fear that their babies will be harmed by a completely preventable disease, while they do [everyday] tasks." Some experts are raising the prospect of an official three-dose schedule for the MMR vaccine, in which all infants get the earlier dose in addition to the two already recommended. Details: Infants can receive a dose as early as 6 months if they live in or are visiting places with a high risk of exposure or are traveling internationally. "For those under 6 months of age, the best thing we can do is awareness and improve that cocoon and immunity the best that we can," said Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics. Parents should "make sure whoever you are around or whoever is around your baby is up to date on all of their vaccines," she added. Zoom in: New research has also documented how measles infections acquired during pregnancy are becoming more common and can have dire consequences. Between January 2025 and the end of September this year, 112 cases of measles during pregnancy — almost entirely among unvaccinated women — and 13 cases of congenital measles (meaning a case in a newborn contracted from its mother) were reported to the CDC, according to research published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine . Nearly a quarter of the pregnant women were hospitalized for reasons other than labor, and adverse outcomes for babies delivered within 14 days of their mothers developing a measles rash included preterm delivery and admission to intensive care. Congenital measles can also result in severe neurologic complications, the report notes. The bottom line: "We will likely be dealing with measles this year, next year, and the year after," Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, wrote on Substack . "And, until immunization rates increase, we will continue to see more suffering, more hospitalizations, and more deaths from this entirely preventable infection."

events.title: Democrats offer Republicans an ‘open door’ on Medicaid cuts
events.summary: The News One of the incoming Democratic Congress’ top priorities next year is reversing the GOP’s Medicaid cuts. The new majority might even get Republican votes to do it. Democrats are already deep in internal discussions about whether to court support across the aisle for delaying the steep Medicaid reductions passed as part of last year’s GOP megabill — which will result in large coverage losses. While they’re ready to pursue a party-line spending bill if Senate Republicans mount a filibuster, Democrats also sense an openness in President Donald Trump’s party to roll back the cuts. “There’s disquiet on the Republican side about implementing these at all,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. He described an “open door” for bipartisan discussions about changing the Medicaid cuts, which the Trump-backed bill phased in through 2028. The prospect of a bipartisan vote to change the cuts grew more real after the Trump administration announced last week that it would give states an extra six months to enforce the megabill’s Medicaid work requirements. Democrats viewed that as a sign that even Republican-led states are having difficulty complying with the new rules, which require verification of Medicaid beneficiaries’ continued qualifications for the low-income healthcare program. How Democrats approach reversal of the Medicaid cuts will be a crucial early test of whether the party can deliver on a cost-of-living agenda that delivered large blue majorities in both chambers in the midterm elections. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said he has recommended to Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and other top Democrats that the party start off with targeted bills addressing the work requirements and the megabill’s cut to the provider tax, a mechanism states use to finance their Medicaid programs. Booker said he’s had private conversations with Republicans already about the Medicaid changes. “My strategy, advice I’m giving to leadership and others is, the more finite bills we pass, the clearer it makes the issue for the American public. When you pack in these big bills, it makes it easier to give a pass to Republicans,” Booker told Semafor. He also said he’s open to broader negotiations with Republicans: “We’ve got to negotiate with them to get to 60.” Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., who will chair the Finance Committee, said Democrats want to pull out the Medicaid changes “from the roots.” He wants Democrats to use the six-month pause in enforcement of the work requirements to “make sure the country sees what’s going on.” But he declined to commit to a finite approach or a broader package: “I’ve been meeting with my colleagues on and off the committee. I don’t want to front run them.” Battleground-seat Democrats are signaling a particular willingness to negotiate with Republicans over the work requirements, even as the whole party pushes to roll back as many of the Medicaid changes as possible. Even though their sizable House majority would allow Democrats to pass their preferred Medicaid bill, they’ll still have to contend with the Senate filibuster. “I’ve always been willing to compromise on the work stuff,” said Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who just narrowly won his race. “There’s already been a history of work requirements in our state and a lot of these different programs over the years. So I don’t think we get caught in the weeds on that just yet.” But Democratic leaders are doubtful a deal is possible. “We’re going to move forcefully and expeditiously to reverse all of the damage that was in the ‘one big, ugly bill.’ If the Republicans are willing to come to the table, we’ll have that discussion. That hasn’t been the case to date,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters. He’s pledged a multi-pronged health care agenda next year, including an expansion of Medicare eligibility, saying on Tuesday that “a return to the status quo is not acceptable.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told Semafor that Democrats won’t get his vote to reverse the work requirements. But he also said he would work with them to protect Medicaid benefits and blunt the pending changes to the provider tax. “When it comes to benefits, when it comes to the provider tax … I not only want to reverse that; I think we ought to provide a new dedicated stream of funding to rural hospital emergency rooms to see that no more of them close,” Hawley said. “We’ve got whole counties now in Missouri, they don’t have hospitals within 50, 60, 70 miles.” Room for Disagreement The majority of Republicans are, at this point, not in favor of delaying or scrapping the work requirements. The crop of swayable GOP votes for most of what Democrats want to do is not large, unless there’s a broader deal or Trump gets involved. “It’s not a Medicaid cut. Medicaid was never designed to say that an able-bodied adult with no kids and no disability should be able to get free healthcare,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who will chair the chamber’s GOP campaign arm next year. Burgess, David, and Nicholas’ View The Trump administration’s decision to give states six months of flexibility to enforce the Medicaid work requirements may be an early sign that further delays could be on the horizon. In fact, the GOP megabill allows the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to grant extensions of up to two years to states that are encountering difficulties implementing and enforcing work requirements — as long as they are making a good-faith effort. Yet even if Democrats are simply going through the motions by talking about courting GOP votes for Medicaid changes, that exercise may be worth the trouble for their purple-district members. A lot of newly elected Democrats, even some progressives, say they’ll start off the 120th Congress willing to work with Trump and across the aisle. Few in Washington see compromise as likely, but it’s not impossible. A Trump veto of party-line legislation to claw back Medicaid cuts could set up a politically disastrous scenario for the GOP if millions of Americans on Medicaid suddenly find themselves without coverage in the middle of the 2028 presidential campaign. Notable Advocacy group Keep Your Care led a group of 400 organizations this week asking Republican and Democratic leaders to include a two-year delay of the Medicaid work requirements in lame duck legislation . Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard Neal, D-Mass., and Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, D-N.J., are asking the Trump administration for details on the decision to disenroll 750,000 Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollees earlier this year.

events.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
events.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.  Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.  OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.  Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes. But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn’t a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.” Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.  But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.” In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies . For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. events.title: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
events.summary: A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock , breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders. Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime. Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed. Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks. The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. In a separate report Friday, Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks. Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex. Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector. CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month. Reality check: Cyberattacks are still scary, and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks. A litany of popular services — including Microsoft , Apple , Chase , United , Workday , the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week. An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI . Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now. What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios. "The open-weight models are getting close to frontier-level capabilities," and when combined with tools like Artex and Cairn, they are "really hitting organizations hard," he added. Incident response firms worldwide are stretched to capacity, with some turning away cases because they lack resources, John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google's threat intelligence group, told Axios. How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves. A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network. AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points. The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision. Between the lines: Hackers are also stealing the computing resources needed to sustain their AI-powered attacks. Amazon's findings show how attackers can steal access to AI models and use that access to find more credentials, expanding their operations without paying for the computing power. The intrigue: These frameworks aren't necessarily good at hiding their activity, but that might not matter. Hultquist said autonomous attacks generate substantial suspicious activity, potentially making them easier to detect. But financially motivated hackers may only need to steal valuable information before defenders stop them. He also warned that state-backed hackers could use these capabilities to disrupt critical systems before defenders can intervene. What we're watching: Security teams may need to fundamentally change their defenses to keep pace with automated attacks.

events.title: Alaska Native strongholds push Peltola into Senate history
events.summary: Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead. Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence. The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory. By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count . Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes. In Bristol Bay/Aleutians , for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes. In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound , she led by roughly 2,300 votes. In North Slope/Northwest Arctic , she led by approximately 900 votes. Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead. Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled. Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures. About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census . State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation , where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate. Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages. Organizers saw gains in some rural communities, though definitive statewide turnout comparisons remain pending. Zoom in: In Kwethluk, the Yup'ik village where Peltola grew up, she outpolled Sullivan 136–9. In Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island , she led 157–5. In Tlingit communities Angoon and Kake , she led 109–22 and 140–30, respectively. The Navy apologized in 2024 for destroying Angoon in 1882 and bombarding and burning Kake in 1869 . Flashback: In 1915, Alaska's territorial lawmakers required Native citizenship applicants to abandon tribal ties and customs. In 1925, after Congress extended citizenship to Native Americans, Alaska imposed an English literacy requirement that disenfranchised many Native voters. During World War II, the U.S. removed 881 Unangax̂ people from nine villages to Southeast Alaska camps plagued by disease and poor shelter. The intrigue: In April 1969, Sen. Ted Kennedy traveled 3,600 miles over three days through Native communities, following a poverty tour his slain brother Robert had planned. TIME documented villages with 60% unemployment and homes without plumbing, comparing the trip to Robert's visits to Appalachia and the Mississippi Delta. Partisan accusations over publicity overshadowed the poverty Kennedy sought to expose. Yes, but: Alaska Native voters today don't vote as a bloc. The Alaska Federation of Natives endorsed no one in the Senate race. And district returns can't establish how individual Native voters voted — or prove a statewide turnout surge. Between the lines: In communities covered by the EPA's Alaska Native Villages data, 1,129 homes lacked drinking water, wastewater service or both in 2025, down from 6,892 in 2005, per an EPA report . Native leaders continue pressing Washington on subsistence rights, infrastructure, education and self-determination.

events.title: What to expect from Jeffries’ big day
events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning, setting the stage for a floor vote by the full chamber in January. Despite some criticism from the left, no formal opposition has emerged to Jeffries’ bid to become the first Black speaker in US history, and he’s assuaged key constituencies. Democrats will hold a recorded internal vote — it’s the same procedure used when the House flipped in 2018, but it’s also a way for the leader to force his opponents to go public. The vote will “give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned,” Jeffries said. Democrats will elect a full slate of leaders: the speaker, majority leader, whip, caucus chair, vice chair, and assistant speaker. The only contested race is for vice chair, between Reps. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., and Lauren Underwood, D-Ill.; all other current Democratic leaders are set to jump to their equivalent spots in the majority. The caucus will elect the rest of its leadership circle on Thursday, including the co-chairs of the caucus messaging arm known as the DPCC. That race is between Reps. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., and Sarah McBride, D-Del. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: White House pulls Overton's FDA nomination
events.summary: Capitol Hill is grappling with the prospect of the Food and Drug Administration operating without a Senate-confirmed leader indefinitely, after the White House pulled the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the agency Tuesday night. It’d been unclear whether the embattled White House official could get the necessary votes to be confirmed by the Senate’s health committee from lawmakers skeptical of her positions on vaccines, the abortion pill, and flavored vapes. But Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., asserted after the nomination was dropped that he believed the White House “abandoned a viable confirmation path.” “Pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” Cassidy said. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.” Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, is being weighed as a potential replacement, but there are questions swirling about whether anyone could be confirmed on a compressed timeline before Democrats take power. Chris Meekins, a Raymond James healthcare analyst who worked at HHS during Trump’s first term, predicted the FDA will not have a permanent leader anytime soon, a development that “inevitably creates uncertainty.” “Had the White House heeded warnings by many before and after her nomination, they could have avoided this unfortunate outcome,” Meekins said. — David Lim

events.title: Can AI Agents Really Shift Chip Design Left?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agent orchestration at various stages of design, verification, and validation will require new methodologies and coordination across tools. Engineering expertise remains essential, and proprietary data is still siloed. Cost and complexity could limit adoption, giving larger companies an advantage. Experts at the Table : AI agents are moving into more parts of the chip design flow, but connecting them across different tools and processes remains a challenge. Questions also remain about how to capture decades of engineering expertise, protect proprietary design data, and keep costs manageable. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: If AI agents are modifying code, and you keep updating AI models and agents, how much can you really shift left? Darbari : This is going to be a new methodology direction the industry will be taking, much like UVM, where you combine these different flows together. How do you combine all the agents together? I don’t get a sense that anybody really knows today how this combination is going to work. From what I have seen in different presentations, they’re still looking at how these things unfold. A lot of agentic AI companies lack the field experience of having seen these problems firsthand, so what they’re building is not what the consumer wants. In many cases, the big consumers are building their own stuff because they know what they want. They have the field experience. They have data from many years. So, where will the big EDA vendors go to streamline this, and how will that shape the end use? I don’t know. Laviv : One of the challenges with emulation is that when running in co-simulation mode, the simulation slows down. Maybe, instead of having UVM or other languages that slow it down, AI will get its own language and get SystemVerilog RTL synthesizable code that you can put in the machine. Then you’ll need less of the software, and you can run faster in emulation. I’m not sure yet if the methodology would change quickly, but UVM might not stay forever. Darbari : That’s what Nvidia’s head of GPU said at DVCon U.S., isn’t it? The formal is replacing simulation, or is going to replace simulation. I’m less interested in how each of these individual technologies works with each other, but I’m very interested in whether all of this adoption will lead to a coherent story. Schirrmeister : You have lifecycle, manufacturing, digital implementation, functional verification, and you have specification engineering. Making sense of it is the light bulb — making sure it works, getting it to layout, getting it into the actual physical silicon and 3D, and then observing it during the lifecycle. Each of these flows has many sub-components. Functional verification to emulation is like one of the five. There is virtual prototyping, formal, simulation, emulation, and prototyping. Everybody gets their own agent. So you have an agent doing something localized. Now you start getting an agent that orchestrates these things together as a functional thing, and then you get an agent that connects to the front end. This is an onion of agents, with more and more layers on top. EDA vendors are all saying we have Level 5 stuff, and there’s truth to that within the scope of the operating domain. Berg : This is very much about hierarchy. Darbari : But who’s going to pay for all this? Do the small companies have the budget to tokenize their banks and run all of this? Schirrmeister : Do you mean the guys building the product, or the guys building the tools? Darbari : The ones running the product. These are the consumers. They would need to pay for the tokens. I have a feeling that only the big companies will be able to afford this. They’ve been running it full-on, saying they haven’t written any code. All of this is agents. But it would get very interesting if the cost of doing all of this could be significantly reduced. Schirrmeister : What’s exciting about this is that all the smaller designs that used to be difficult because you had to go through all of this will benefit. If you want to be an Nvidia competitor, you still cannot do this out of your garage. That still has to be a big company. Berg : You’ve got levels of agents at this point, and a Level 5 orchestrating the whole thing. The industry is going to work on building each of these and then iterating and improving them. That’s the only way in which you’re going to get agents to learn and replace large groups of engineers doing the grunt work that’s necessary here. SE: But that hierarchy needs to start with whatever shifts left to include in each one of these different blocks, right? You need to at least define, in general, what you’re going to be doing. Berg : You’re going to have information being fed back to ensure that when they go to the specification of the functional, there are constraints placed here. That way, you can improve the probability of manufacturability. Schirrmeister : Can I have an agent model and predict that path? Berg : Yes, you can. Schirrmeister : But you want to check, right? You need to make sure early on what the multi-physics effects of what you’re doing will be. Berg : Yes, and without that, it will be dead on arrival in manufacturing. Schirrmeister : So now the question becomes, ‘How much can you really abstract?’ Laviv : AI is doing a great job on, say, 80% of the challenges. But then you have experience from individuals who have been in the industry for 30 years with unique skills that AI doesn’t have. We had a discussion where we talked about 250 different skills for power, emulation, format, and verification. AI doesn’t have those skills today. The industry needs to figure out how to gather those skills in order to really get to a flow where an agent can talk to an agent and has all the decades of experience that is hidden in Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel. Berg : It took 50 years, but in 2024, the Nobel Prize in chemistry was given in part to a software called AlphaFold , which predicted with uncanny certainty how proteins fold. Proteins are much more complicated than the crystalline structures that we deal with on a daily basis. But it took 50 years to get there. That said, it’s a proof of concept. Whether or not you believe it can be done in semiconductors, it’s going to happen.
